Uniform Title: Kamikāgama Pūrvabhāga Description: Transcribed from an edition in Grantha script published in Madras in 1909. Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: September 17, 2008 Year of Publication: 1909 City of Publication: Madras
Country of Publication: India || Śrīḥ ||
Salutations to the illustrious Umā and Maheśvara.
I bow to Mahāgaṇapati, the son of the enemy of Madana,
whose body is embraced by the arms of the beautiful woman seated upon his left thigh—
the elder brother of the Lord of the Vallyas, who grants the desires of those who take refuge in him.
Whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods, headed by the Lord of Speech (Brahmā).
Table of Contents for the First Part of the Kāmikāgama

The introduction to the Tantra, the extraction of mantras, ritual bathing, worship, the components of worship, the procedure for food offerings, and the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 1/1 ||
The fire-ritual, the rule for the proper time, the examination of the occasion, the inspection of the ground, the offering for entry, and the characteristics of villages and so forth. (1.2)

Furthermore, the installation of the gnomon, the sequence of measuring instruments, the various methods for laying out the site, and the characteristics of the threads, vital points, and so forth. (1.3)

Next is the bali offering to the deities of the site (vāstudeva), followed by the characteristics of villages and so forth, the measurement of width and length, the determination of auspiciousness based on the lunar mansion (āya) and other factors, and the diagram of the lunar mansions (nakṣatracakra). 1/4.
The rules for the *daṇḍaka* and other elements serve as the standard for the dimensions of the streets, gates, and so forth;
they also prescribe the location for the village deities and the number of twice-born men [to be settled]. (1.5)

The specific details of the layout, including the positions for Brahmā and the deities, the locations for those who subsist on the ritual limbs, and the characteristics of the foundation-consecration (garbhanyāsa). || 1/6 ||
Then follows the ritual for the site of the child, according to the different layouts of villages and so forth;
thereafter, the pacification of the building site (vāstu-śānti) and the construction of the hall. 1/7.
The Nandyāvarta, the Dviśālā, the one known as Sarvatobhadra,
the Vardhamāna, the Svastika, and thereafter the Rūcakākhya.
The four-winged, the five-winged, the elephant-stable, and the garland-pattern; the one called the plough, the root-pattern, and finally the garland-lotus. (1.9)

The classification of the nagara and other styles, the method for attaining the ground, the primary brick-work, the pedestal (upapīṭha), and the measurement and characteristics of the bases (pādas). || 1/10 ||
The rule for the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara), the ornamentation of temples (prāsāda),
and the characteristics of the neck, the pinnacle (śikhara), and the finial (sthūpikā).
Subsequently, there is the installation of the *nāla* and other elements, characterized by the single ground and so forth;
then the laying of the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*), and the offering of the sprout-marked emblem (*liṅga*) upon the pedestal. (1.12)
The installation of the Śiva-liṅga, the characteristics of images, the consecration of the trident, and thereafter that which is known as the installation of the deity. 1/13.
The consecration of images, the supreme installation of celestial chariots,
the characteristics of pavilions, and the characteristics of enclosures.
The installation of the attendants, as well as the worship of the attendants;
at the end, the installation of the bull, and finally the supreme installation of the gateway (gopura).
In the *Pūrvakāmika*, there are seventy-four chapters enumerated.
The Table of Contents for the Latter Section of the Kāmikāgama.
The worship of the western gate and the worship of the southern gate,
as well as the veneration of all [the deities] characterized by the great ablution. (2.1)
First is the procedure for the daily festival, followed by the procedure for the great festival;
first is the rite of lustration (nīrājana), and then the worship of Phalgunī. (2/2)
The consecration with ghee, mounting the swing, worship with honey, the performance of the row of lamps, and the worship of the ghee-blanket. (2.3)
Śivarātri, then the worship with fragrances, the veneration of *damanaka*, the spring sacrifice, the cold-water jar, the worship with fruits, and the sacred thread (*pavitraka*). (2.4)
The worship with fresh offerings, the initiation known as the *samaya*, the ritual for the *sthālīpāka* oblation, the chapter on dreams, and the funeral rites for liberation. (2.5)

The initiation of the preceptor, the determination of the lineage and the ancestral sages (gotra and pravara), the hundredfold initiation (śatābhiṣeka), the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), and thereafter the ritual for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña). || 2/6 ||
Then follows the Śaiva-śrāddha, after which comes the universal expiation (sarva-prāyaścitta),
followed by the regular and occasional expiations and the atonement for festivals.
There shall be the pacification of portents and the performance of the subsequent rites;
then follows the sprinkling of the pedestal and its installation. (2.8)
The installation of Bāṇa’s Kāmyaliṅga, both according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis and that of human beings;
the characteristics of the temple, and the characteristics of the temple determined by the nature of the Liṅga. (2.9)
The installation of the manifest liṅga for the ascetics of all regions, the installation of the subsidiary liṅgas, and then the establishment of the local deities. (2.10)
There was also the installation of the Goddess, of Vighneśvara in his dancing form, and of Somāskanda—the enemy of Tripura—who bears the crescent moon upon his crest. (2.11)
Likewise, there is the installation of the Liṅgodbhava [form], as well as that of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Bhikṣāṭana, Kaṅkālamūrti, and Pāśupata. (2.12)
The installation of the trident, Śarabheśa, Caṇḍeśa, and others, as well as the ritual for the weapons of the devotees of Śiva and the procedure for the lion-throne. (2.13)

The characteristics of chariots and their components, the rites for ensuring happiness, the destruction of diseases, protection for kings, and likewise the ritual procedure for the worship of Durgā. (2.14)
The Śāntinīrājana, the Puṣyābhiṣeka, the Grahayajña, the binding of the Pratisara, and the procedure for the Tulābhāra; 2.15.
The gift of Hiraṇyagarbha, the gift of a mountain of sesame seeds, the gift of gold and land, and the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree. (2.16)
The gift of Gaṇeśa, the bestowing of a golden cow and Lakṣmī, a thousand sesame-cow gifts, and a thousand gifts of cows (or the gift of a golden horse). // 2.17 //
The gift of a maiden, the gift of a golden bull, the gift of an elephant, the eight Lokapālas, and likewise the "Gift of All"—these are the most excellent of all gifts. (2.18)
Thus have the ninety-six chapters of the *Kāmikottara* been declared.
|| Śrīḥ ||
The Kāmikāgama.
The First Part:
The Chapter on the Introduction to the Tantra.
On the southern peak of Kailāsa, which is endowed with various wonders and is exceedingly vast, covered by the shade arising from a fully grown banyan tree— 3:1.
Upon a seat adorned with jewels and covered with a tiger skin,
[he was attended] by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and others.
While Mahādeva Śrīkaṇṭha, the leader of the universe, was being served, Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Agastya, Gautama, and likewise Nārada [were present]. (3.3)
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanātana, and Sanandana;
Bhṛgu, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, and other great sages (maharṣis). || 3.4 ||
Desirous of supreme knowledge and directed toward the power of Śiva, they bowed at his feet and spoke to the Lord, the consort of Umā. (3.5)
The Sages said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, liberator from the bonds of Paśu, you who effect creation, maintenance, concealment, dissolution, and grace! (3.6)
The direct instigator of the manifestation of the great illusion beginning with space, whose nature is characterized by self-awareness and the abundance of innate bliss. (3.7)
Endowed with the supreme Śakti whose nature is the consciousness of others, you are free from direction, space, and time, and are the cause of joy for the world. (3.8)
"O Lord of Gods, we have been appointed by you to the worship of Śiva;
for that purpose, [we seek] the scripture originating from the mouth of Śiva, which is the very essence. (3.9)
"O Lord of Gods, you should speak out of compassion for your devotees.
Thus questioned by the sages, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull— || 3.10 ||
He whose crest is the shimmering crescent moon spoke with a profound voice:
"Well asked indeed by you; listen, O you of firm vows! (3.11)
This supreme scripture, extracted from the great tantra known as the Kāmika, has descended upon Mount Meru through the Avatārakas beginning with Praṇava. (3/12)
"Endowed with ritual action and conduct, and supreme, possessed of yoga and knowledge"—having been addressed thus, the sages prostrated themselves upon the ground like a staff. (3.13)
Having given them his command, Śiva spoke this unsurpassed Tantra:
"In the beginning, knowledge was twofold, according to the distinction of those qualified [to receive it]. (3.14)

The supreme Śivajñāna is traditionally defined as that knowledge which reveals the distinction between the higher and the lower, which shows the nature of the Lord (pati) and the individual soul (paśu), and which illuminates Śiva. (3.15)

The knowledge derived from the Vedas and other sources reveals the nature of the fettered soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa), just as the eye perceives things differently by day and by night for a human and a bat. (3.16)
Likewise, knowledge is of diverse characteristics; thus it is both supreme and non-supreme, worldly and Vedic, as well as purely spiritual. (3.17)
This Tantra, known as Mantra, is the Atimārga and is manifold;
it consists of the forms of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, and Puruṣeśāna. (3.18)
Each of these has five faces, and by them the worldly [teachings] and so forth were spoken;
thus the division of the streams is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five varieties. (3.19)
The entire corpus of speech that expresses reality is included within these very [categories];
likewise, that which is called Mantra and Tantra, issued from the mouth of Sadāśiva, is contained within them alone. (3.20)
The Siddhānta, Gāruḍa, Vāma, Bhūtatantra, and Bhairava correspond respectively to the faces directed upwards, eastward, toward Kubera (the north), and southward. (3.21)
From the Īśāna face situated above comes the knowledge known as Kāmika and so forth,
which exists in ten and eighteen divisions through the incarnations of Śiva and Rudra.
By the command of Śiva, it was taught in sequence through sixty-six [parts], according to the divisions of the ages (yugas), by means of the forms beginning with Sadyojāta. (3.23)
Manifested in four divisions according to the number of its forms, the Gāruḍa likewise emerged from the eastern face in that same numerical fashion. (3.24)
The Sāvitrī-mantra and others were taught by the founders for the sake of spiritual accomplishment;
through the divisions such as the Nayas and Sūtras, the Vāma [tradition] emerged from the Vāma. (3.25)
By the command of Śiva, the twenty-four-fold [Tantra] has descended;
and from that very moment, the Bhūtatantra, numbering twenty, beginning with the Kaula, has likewise descended. (3.26)
The Bhairava Tantra emerged in two forms from the right face;
it was proclaimed on earth in many ways by Asitāṅga and the others. (3.27)
If each individual division of the tantras were described, there would result an excessive expansion of the text;
therefore, the introduction of the Siddhānta tantras is now being declared. (3.28)
Because it extends vast benefits based on reality and mantra, and because it provides protection, it is called "tantra. (3.29)
The *Kāmika* belongs to that which is called *Praṇava*, with a number of verses equal to a *parārdha*;
from *Praṇava* the *Trikala* was obtained, and from *Trikala* then *Hara*.
O best of Brahmins, there are three further subdivisions: Vaktrāraṃ, Bhairavottaraṃ, and Nārasiṃha; these are declared to be the triad of the Kāmika.
The ash produced by yoga from that which is called Sudhā is said to be obtained in the number of one hundred thousand;
from that Sudhā-ash, the All-pervading Lord was subsequently attained in due order.
Vīṇā, Śikhottara, Tāra, Santa, and Santati—these five, along with Ātmayoga, are the divisions of the Yoga-tantra. (3.33)
It is said that from Sudīptasaṃjña, Cintya was obtained through hundreds of thousands [of efforts];
from Dīpta, Gopati was obtained, and from him, Ambikā was obtained. (3.34)
The well-considered, the fortunate, the left, the destroyer of evil, that which arises from another, and the immortal—these six types of the *Cintyatantra* have been proclaimed. (3.35)
The cause of that which is called the "Cause" (Kāraṇa) was proclaimed by Koṭigrantha; from Kāraṇa, Śarva-Rudra [received it], and from Śarva, Prajāpati obtained it. (3.36)
The purifying *kāraṇa* is *dorga*, as well as *māhendra* and *bhīma*; thereafter, the slaying *kāraṇa* is *dveṣṭa*; thus, the *kāraṇa* is sevenfold. (3/37)
Ajita [received it] from the one named Suśiva, who possessed a collection of a million verses;
Śiva received it from Suśiva, and from that Śiva, Acyuta [received it]. (3.38)
The *Prabhūta*, the *Parodbhūta*, the *Pārvatī*, and the *Padmasaṃhitā*—this Tantra is proclaimed in this [work] as having four divisions. (3.39)
The blazing [form] of Īśa, renowned for its extent of one hundred thousand verses, was attained;
from that, the form of Īśāna was reached, and thereafter the Fire-god was obtained.
Immeasurable, beyond the reach of sound, incalculable, and of infinite splendor; it is bliss, born of the source of sweetness, wondrous, and likewise indestructible. (3.41)
The *Dīpta* is said to be of nine kinds; now understand the *Sūkṣmatantra*.
The *Sūkṣma* is proclaimed as belonging to the *Sūkṣma*, and its knots are equal in number to the lotuses (ten). (3.42)
From Sūkṣma, Vaiśravaṇa was obtained; from him, Prabhañjana was obtained.
That Sūkṣma is of a single division and is thus designated as "Sūkṣma. (3.43)
A thousand [years] of Kālasaṃjña were indeed declared by the count of conch shells;
from Kāla, Bhīma was obtained, and from Bhīma, Dharma arose in that same manner. (3.44)
The past is auspicious, pure, and immeasurable, yet it possesses birth;
it is awakened, wise, the hand, an ornament, and well-enlightened. (3.45)
These ten are proclaimed as the number of the Thousand Tantras;
Aṃśumān is said to belong to the Ambu cycle, which consists of five hundred thousand [verses]. (3.46)
From Agra and Ambusaṃjña, Ravi was obtained from Agra;
as well as Vidyā, Purāṇa, Tantra, Vāsava, and Nīlalohita. (3.47)
The Prakaraṇa, the Bhūtatantra, and the Ātmālaṅkāra, as well as the Kāśyapa, Gautama, Aindra, Brāhma, and Vāsiṣṭha [Tantras]. (3.48)
That which is known by the name Aiśāna is declared to be the twelfth part;
the great scripture Suprabheda is proclaimed as belonging to the Lord of the Ten. (3.49)
The Moon is obtained from Gaṇeśvara as the lord of the tenth house from the lord of the Daśā;
this difference is said to be three crores in number, and no further distinction exists here. (3/50)
Within this very [system], the Tantra is seen to extend from ritual action up to knowledge;
it is proclaimed as the Śivabheda, and likewise the Rudrabheda is spoken of. (3.51)
The supreme tantra, the Vijaya, belonging to Rudra who is known as Anādi, was then received by the Supreme Lord in a volume numbering thirty million verses. (3.52)
Vijaya, Udbhava, Saumya, Aghora, Mṛtyunāśana, Kubera, Amāghora, and Vimala—this is the Vijayāṣṭaka. (3.53)
The Niḥśvāsa is said to belong to Daśārṇa, numbering ten crores;
from Daśārṇa, it was obtained by Śailajā, divided into eight branches. (3.54)
The superior exhalation, the subsequent exhalation, the emergence of the mouth of the exhalation, the path of the exhalation, and likewise that which effects the exhalation. (3.55)
The one known as Ghorā, the one called Yamā, and likewise the Guhyā—these eight are proclaimed as the self-manifested forms of Nidhanā, consisting of half of three crores. (3.56)
From the Lord of the End (Nidhaneśa), the Lotus-born (Brahmā) heard the threefold tradition: the Svāyambhuva, the Padma, and the Prajāpatimata. (3.57)
From those thirty thousand granthas of the Āgneya [portion] of the Vyoman [Tantra], the single Āgneya Tantra was extracted; from that, the Fire-god (Hutāśana) obtained it. (3.58)
Then Tejas attained the heroic [state] consisting of a hundred thousand (niyuta) granthas;
thereafter Prajāpati attained the thirteenfold division. (3.59)
Prastāra, Phullamalla (or Phullamala), Prabodha, Bodhabodhaka, Amoha, Mohasamaya, Hākaṭa, and Śākaṭādhika. (3/60)
Hala, Vilekhana, Bhadra, and Vīra—these thirteen are for the Vīra [class];
and Raurava belongs to Brāhmaṇeśa, numbering eight Arbudas. (3.61)
Then Nandikeśa arrived, and the sixfold division is prescribed:
Kālaghna, Kalātīta, Raurava, and Rauravottara. (3.62)
The Mahākālamata, the Aindra, and the Raurava are considered to be of six kinds;
the Makuṭa, however, belongs to the one called Śiva and consists of one hundred thousand [verses]. (3.63)
Then Mahādeva arrived, and the division becomes twofold;
the Makuṭottara and the Makuṭa are prescribed according to these two types. (3.64)
From that [source], Vīrabhadra obtained the pure [Tantra] consisting of three hundred thousand verses, which encompasses all things; its divisions number sixteen. (3.65)
Ananta, Bhoga, Ākrānta, Vṛṣapiṅga, Vṛṣodara, Vṛṣādbhuta, Sudanta, Raudra, and likewise Bhadravighna. (3/66)
The sixteenth [chapter] indeed is the *Arevatam*, which transcends [all], is adorned with the *Aṭṭahāsa* [laughter], is honored, the *Dhāraṇa-tantra*, and is stainless. (3.67)
The *Candrajñāna* of Ananta consists of thirty million verses;
from that, Bṛhaspati received it, and herein there are fourteen divisions. (3.68)
Sthira, Sthāṇu, Mahānta, Vāruṇa, Nandikeśvara, Ekapāda, Purāṇa, Śaṅkara, and Nīlarudraka. (3/69)
The Śivabhadra, the Kalpabheda, the Śrīmukha, the Śivaśāsana, the one proclaimed as the Śivaśekhara, and likewise the Mata of the Goddess. (3.70)
The tantra of Candrajñāna shall consist of fourteen types;
the face and form of the Tranquil One [is described] by a number of one hundred thousand. (3.71)
Then Dadhīci attained fifteen divisions:
the four-faced, the impurity, the union, the paralysis, and the reflection. (3.72)
Ātmālaṅkāra, Vāyavya, Tauṭika, Tuṭinīraka, Kalātyaya, Tulāyoga, Kuṭṭima, and Paṭṭaśekhara. (3.73)
The Great Vidyā, the Great Solar Orb, consists of exactly fifteen [syllables];
it is proclaimed as the "Proclaimed" (prodgīta) of the Wielder of the Trident, numbering three hundred thousand [recitations]. (3.74)
Then the one called Kavaca was obtained, consisting of sixteen divisions:
the Kavaca, the Vārāha, and the Piṅgalāmata. (3.75)
Pāśabandha, Daṇḍadhara, Aṅkuśa, and Dhanurdhara; as well as Śivajñāna, Vijñāna, and Śrīkālajñāna. (3.76)
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, the piercing of snake fangs, song, the art of Bharata, instrumental music, and vocal chanting— these indeed constitute the sixteen [arts]. (3.77)
The Lalita of the Lord of Ālaya is said to consist of eight thousand [verses].
From Ālaya, Lalita (Bhairava? attained the Lalita and the Lalitottara.
And that division, the Kaumāra, is proclaimed to be threefold; this Tantra was perfected from the *bindu* in a number of fifty million times ten million verses. (3.79)
The supreme Caṇḍeśvara attained the [tantra] called Siddha, which is known by the name Bindu; then there is another, Sārottara, as well as Auśanottara. (3.80)
The division of the Śālā, the Śaśīkhaṇḍa, and the fourfold Siddha-tantra;
this lineage of one devoted to Śiva consists of six thousand [verses] in number. (3.81)
Consequently, non-concord was attained, and there arose a sevenfold division:
Liṅgādhyakṣa, Surādhyakṣa, Śaṅkara, and Amaleśvara. (3.82)
The *Asaṃkhya*, *Anila*, *Dvandva*, *Santāna*, and *Saptadhārita*—these were spoken by Śarva to Somadeva with a total count of exactly two hundred thousand verses. (3.83)
Nṛsiṃha obtained it from Soma; the division shall be fivefold.
Likewise, there is the Śivadharmottara and that which was proclaimed by Vāyu. (3.84)
Next, the *Divya* is proclaimed, then the *Aiśāna*, and the *Śarvodgīta* is prescribed;
the supreme *Pārameśvara* is fully expounded by the venerable Goddess. (3.85)
That [scripture], consisting of twelve hundred thousand verses, was spread in seven ways,
having been received in due order by Uśanas, the Sage, and the Illustrious Goddess.
Mataṅga, Yakṣiṇīpadma, and Pārameśvara, as well as Puṣkara, Suprayoga, and Haṃsa, which is indeed common to all. (3.87)
The *kiraṇa* [tantra] exists within the divine manifestation (*devavibhava*) in a number of five crores;
from that, the *saṃvartaka* was obtained, and its divisions are nine in number. (3.88)
The Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Nīla, Rūkṣa, Bhānuka, Dhenuka, Prabuddha, Buddha, and Kālaka—thus the ray becomes ninefold. (3.89)
The Vātula of Śiva is said to consist of one hundred thousand verses;
from that, the Mahākāla was obtained, which indeed has twelve divisions.
The Vātula, the Uttara, the Kālajñāna, and the Prarohita—all these are of the nature of Dharma, supreme, eternal, pure, and the Great Mouth. (3.91)
In the Vātula, twelve [tantras] are recorded as being both the universe and the universal self;
these are proclaimed to be the root divisions of the twenty-eight tantras. (3.92)
The pair of feet is Kāmika, and the two ankles are Yogaja;
the toes are said to be Cintya, and the shanks are Kāraṇa. (3.93)
The region of the knees should be Ajita, the region of the thighs Dīpta; the secret organ (guhya) should be Sūkṣma, and the region of the hips Sahasra. || 3/94 ||
The back surface should be Aṃśumān, while the navel region is Suprabheda;
the area of the belly should be Vijaya, and the heart is Niḥśvāsa. (3.95)
The two breasts are Svāyaṃbhuva, the eye is Anala, the region of the throat is Vīra, and the ear is Raurava. (3.96)
The *makuṭa* is the *mākuṭa-tantra*, as are the limbs and minor members;
the *vimala* is said to be the arms, while the *candrajñāna* is the chest. (3.97)
The Bimba-tantra is the beautiful face, while Rasanā is the song that has been sung forth;
Lalita is the cheek, and Siddha is indeed the forehead. (3/98)
One should know that the *kuṇḍala* is the lineage (*santāna*), the *upavītaka* was spoken by Śarva, the *hāra* by the Supreme Lord (*pārameśa*), and the *kiraṇa* is the jewel-ornament. (3.99)

In the *Śivadharma*, wearing the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) is declared to be the "wind-garment" (*vātula-vasana*); and likewise, in the application of the *Śivadharma* ointment, it is the "kalpa" [of liberation] when combined with it. (3.100)
The image is presented according to the established doctrine both in flowers and in garlands, by means of the body consisting of the tantra and composed of the form of mantra. (3.101)
Through the subdivisions of these, the Tantra consisting of Śiva and Rudra, which is embodied and designated as Sādākhya, exists in twenty-eight forms. (3.102)
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, it shines and may manifest in one way or many ways;
for even if there be but a single speaker, it appears manifold due to the diversity of the listeners. (3.103)
One should perform all rites from the plowing of the ground up to the consecration using the root mantra alone;
if it is performed with a secondary mantra, the performer and the patron shall perish. (3.104)

(Verse 3.105) Sacrifice alone has been described in detail through its various subdivisions; however, it is best when the rites beginning with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are performed according to the root [tantras], namely the twenty-eight.

Whatever [rite] has been commenced according to a particular tantra—from the initial plowing up to the final worship—all that must be performed by means of that very tantra; one should not perform it according to another tantra. (3.106)
If something has not been specifically mentioned in another tantra, one may have it performed; for things may be stated, prohibited, and then restated again. (3.107)
The words of Śiva are manifold, both dependent and independent;
endowed with four quarters, they alone are the means for achieving the goals of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (3.108)
Having heard these very things from the best of sages and others, the gods have also related them in brief out of compassion for all. (3.109)
The study of these [texts] must be performed by Śiva-brahmins according to the lineage of their gurus; it must not be performed by other men, nor should they cause them to be studied. (3.110)

Brahmins and others of the three higher castes who are devoid of initiation, those born of the Śūdra caste, those born in the direct order (anuloma) from women of their own or lower castes, as well as artisans, craftsmen, and the like— 3/111.
If they recite the scriptures of Śiva, there will be the destruction of both the king and the kingdom before long due to that sin; therefore, the king should prohibit it. (3.112)
One should perform the initial rites, such as the plowing of the ground, according to the Śivasiddhāntatantra;
one should not do so according to another scripture, for if one were to do so, it would result in a confusion of tantras (tantrasaṃkara).
Through the fault of mixing tantras, the king and the kingdom perish;
[this includes] the Gāruḍa, the Bhūta-tantra, the Bhairava, and the Vāma-tantra. (3/114)
The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Lākula, the Kula-śāstra, the Pāśupata Tantra, and other Purāṇas and Dharmaśāstras. (3.115)
The Itihāsa with its six auxiliary limbs, that which is known as Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma, as well as Atharvaṇa, and likewise the doctrines of the Buddhists and the Ārhats. (3.116)
Following that sequence, the Śiva-knowledge beginning with the *Kāmika*—which is other than the scripture of Akṣapāda (the Nyāya) and the *Ūrdhvasrotas*—is always the head of the Blessed One. (3.117)
The other limbs of Maheśa, such as the heart, throat, and so forth, have indeed been described here by Śambhu as constituting the "prior position" (pūrvapakṣa). (3.118)
In the definitive determination of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted according to ultimate reality, the Śaiva Siddhānta is proclaimed as having surpassed all of that. (3.119)

And by Śiva-brahmins devoted to the Siddhānta scriptures, having installed the Liṅga according to the sequence of their respective texts, that Liṅga serves the purpose of both [the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions]. (3.120)
For the prosperity of the king, the village, and the sacrificer, a devotee of Śiva (śaiva) shall be the presiding authority over all matters, both in his own domain and elsewhere. (3.121)
All those excellent twice-born householders who are Śaivas perform [their rites] according to the Yāmala, the Mātṛtantra, the Kāpāla, and the Pāñcarātra. (3.122)

In the Buddhist and Arhat systems, as well as in the Lākula and Vaidika traditions, and even in other paths, according to their respective scriptures and their own specific doctrines, [the truth is established]. (3.123)
The Śaivas perform initiation and so forth, as well as the installation of that Liṅga and other rites;
for here, the Śaiva [tradition] is primary, both by virtue of its preeminence and because of the greatness of its mouth (face). (3.124)
In the Śiva-darśana, there is authority for everyone, but not for others [in other systems].
Therefore, for the sake of others and for one’s own sake, there should be the installation and likewise the worship [of the Liṅga]. (3.125)
A Śiva-brahmin should perform [rites] for others solely for his own benefit;
however, he may also act for the sake of others, provided it does not cause any detriment to the king. (3.126)
And there will be the destruction of that kingdom before long; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the Introduction to the Tantra, in the Kriyāpāda of the great tantra named Kāmika.
Now begins the chapter on the introduction to the mantras.
Now, I shall briefly describe the extraction of the mantras in their proper sequence.
Without a mantra, there is no ritual action, from the initial plowing [of the site] up to the final worship. (4.1)
"Manana" means omniscience; "trāṇa" means the favoring of those in saṃsāra.
Because it possesses the nature of both reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), it is designated as "mantra. (4.2)
Mantra should be understood as being of two forms, distinguished as the signified and the signifier.
That which has the form of speech is declared to be the signifier, while that which consists of meaning is remembered as the signified. (4.3)
In some cases, identity between the signified and the signifier is indeed accepted;
sound is declared to be the mantra, and that sound arises from the Supreme. (4.4)
From the Nāda, the Bindu is produced; from the Bindu, the first vowel arises.
From that, two vowels [emerge], and from those, there are two by two; their divisions are thirteen. (4.5)
The sixteen vowels are known as the living souls (jīva), while the consonants beginning with 'ka' are considered to be like the body;
in number they are thirty-four, and these alone constitute the consonants (vyañjana).

Pervaded on all sides by those very [energies] through the differentiation of the limiting adjuncts of the vital breath (prāṇa), it is by those very same [energies] that the scripture—distinguished as supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā)—is composed. (4.7)
The ninth section, called Nāda, is divided into fifty phonemes, numbering four, five, five,
four, four, and one.
O Brahmins, the determination of the parts by means of the phonemes is likewise ninefold; that resonance (nāda) is described by synonymous names of Śiva. (4.9)
It is recited as being threefold—gross, subtle, and supreme; its nature consists of sound, cognition, and experience, and it resides in the hearts of all living beings. (4.10)
The Mātṛkā should be known by practitioners who perceive the reality as being established through the fiftyfold division of Rudras and the fiftyfold division of Śaktis. (4.11)
"O Brahmins, Vyāsa will explain that later through descriptions of the paths and classes of beings.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, the living beings in this world have their strength diminished and their lifespans are short. (4.12)

"O Treasure of Compassion, for those who are joined with greed, delusion, great pride, passion, hatred, and so forth— being incapable [of the higher path]— the true essence of mantra should be taught in various ways, according to their respective capacities. (4.13)
Īśvara said:
In whatever manner may a means to happiness arise for human beings, in that very manner I shall explain it in brief. (4.14)
(The Cintāmaṇi mantra:
The fifth [syllable] preceded by *jīva* (the letter *ja*), followed by the wind [letter *ya*], joined with cause and effect. 4.15.
This mantra, which expresses Śiva, is renowned as the Cintāmaṇi. || 4/16 ||
The twenty-fifth [letter] of the fourth [varga], the fifth of the twenty-fifth [varga],

the pair that is the fifth from the eighth [varga] conjoined with the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), and the pair that is the fifth from the sixth [varga] conjoined with the fire seed-syllable (*raṃ*). (4.16)
The differentiation [of the seed-syllables] residing in the second seed-syllable, preceded by the elements, is according to their sequence. (4.17)
The heart, head, crest, armor, and weapons—these are for the eminent sages; or else [the mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta are used, or indeed both may be placed in those locations. (4.18)
Or even a complete mantra may be the designator of Śiva;
for instance, when the five-syllabled mantra "Haṃsa Śivāya" (or, according to another reading, "Hauṃ Sa") occurs. (4.19)
Then, the arrangement of the faces and limbs should be performed according to the distinction of their respective colors;
or else, the characteristics of the mantra are stated in another manner. (4.20)
From the conjunction with the seed-syllable of the Sun (Ra), [one should place the mantras] on the feet, heart, secret place, and head;
and [from the seed-syllable of the Moon (Sa)], the heart, crest, mouth, armor, the upward-rooted [weapon], the eyes, and the weapon.
The practitioner of mantra should gradually extract the [mantras] of creation and the weapon, together with their flames;
or else, seated upon the fire-throne, by means of the syllables, the ether, the moon, and the sun.
Through the union with the limbs of the seed-syllable of space (haṃ), this mantra—consisting of earth, water, fire, and so forth—is indeed the root; its assignment of limbs is as before. (4.23)

Furthermore, the cause of the union between the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* is said to be the white-syllable (*sitārṇaka*), which resides within the seed-syllable of the fire-seed (*khabījānala*). (4.24)
One should extract the *sasṛṣṭi* [syllable], which is short, or else that which is joined with the word "Śiva."
The first is the seed-syllable *tāra*, the next is the seed-syllable of space (*kha*), and for oneself as well, it is not [the same]. 25.
One should raise the lamp as before; this is declared to be the root mantra.
Therein, the arrangement of the Brahma-mantras and the limbs [of the deity] occurs in both direct and reverse order.
The Mantra of Kālāntaka: Now, I shall here describe the characteristics of the mantra of the Self of Time (Kālātman).
Having drawn a lotus with its stalk, one should place the letters beginning with 'A' on the eastern petal and the others [in sequence]. (4.27)
Having first placed [the seed-syllable] in the eastern petal and so forth, one should place the modification of that in the south;
thus, by proceeding clockwise according to the sequence of the petals, occurs the extraction of the mantra through its placement.
The venerable *sthiti* (the state of persistence) is situated in *visarga*, and the letter *ma* is [expressed] through the form of *mū*.
O Lord of the Universe, whatever particles (*nipāta*) there may be begin with vowels; they do not begin with non-vowels. (4.29)
Ma, va, bha, ka, ra, ti, ja, kṣi, jña, rva, sta, na, followed by ta, ma, ne, tā, tā—this is the perfected *dīpaka* which, when explained, provides assistance. (4.30)

Furthermore, there is no *na*, *a*, *ni*, *pa*, *ñca*, *pra*, *yo*, *cā*, *tha*, *syā*, *cci*, *tu*, *śca*, *na*, *sa*, *sthataḥ*; nor are there *dhyā*, *śi*, *yaś*, *ca*, *ya*, *kā*, *ra*, *ca*, *va*, *kā*, *ro*, *yaś*, or *ca* following that. (4.31)

Neither by various afflictions nor by the flow of the undivided [elements], nor by those who possess knowledge, nor by the two-fold darkness—is that [reality] obstructed from its manifestation. || 4.32 ||
Ya, ra, ma, and ka; the first vowel (a) and likewise nā, na, mā; the two excellent ones (va and ra) preceded by d; tu; and likewise na and da at the end. (4.33)
Then Yamādi, Vasubhena, Sameda, Pranadhu, Tathā, Nirgarhāsi, Prasāprāśca, Svakuśāmī, and Plaka likewise departed. (4.34)
Vyoma, the vowels and so forth, the two *y* sounds, *ru*, *caumaḥ* with the visarga, *va*, *sva*, and likewise *dīṃśca*; thus it is for the three, and likewise for *dhūthamata*. (4.35)
Furthermore, *marva*, *bhūta*, *āśca*, *paptau*, *na*, *kāra*, *ante*, *nanau*, as well as *śāgīndra*, *igu*, *yora*, *vyama*, and *varāṭikā*. (4/36)
The *dhūna* (shaking) is the emission (*visarga*), while *oja* is the earth; likewise, *tathā* is *na*.
The letter *m* with emission is space (*vyoman*), and both *na* and *bhava* are likewise [without emission]. (4.37)
Likewise, *bhya-bhyām-gā-pa*, as well as *piṅga-te-dhū-dhū-niścayo-śatā*;
and at the end of *taś-ca-darśikā-roṃte-mayaṣkā-syāś-cave-tathā*. (4.38)
The agent, the lunar days and their rites, the letter *ja*, and the visarga; the letter *ma*, the lamp, and the one who has crossed over passion—*sū-rū-pū-pag-va-sū-pava*. (4.39)
The vowels beginning with *rū* (ṛ), as well as *ya*, *na*, *ra*, *sa*, *ga*, and *kṛ-ca-ya*—these are the vowels and so forth. Then, *bhūḥ*, *āmo-dhi-śa-khā-dy-arpitam*, and *kṣathā*. (4.40)
Pānāyohā, likewise Svaradyodya; Hyātā, Svarādya, and Bījādya, which is the letter Ja with the visarga. (4.41)
The letter *a* is the lamp, the eye, existence, and likewise splendor;
it is the direction, the incense-lamp, and likewise the abode of the rays. (4.42)
And likewise Jayā’s [son] was Ugra, Rūpa, Jyotsna, Bhasman, as well as Yaḥ, Danta, Bhānuratā, Pīṭha, Kṣma, and also Eva. (4.43)
The *sayavīyā* and the two *rau*s, the *taga* and the twenty *jyotā*s;
those beginning with *svara*, along with the *savisarga*, the *upaśiva*s, and likewise the *mucava*s. (4.44)
The first of the vowels (A), together with the letter Sa, and Ma with the Visarga;
likewise, Dṛ with the first of the vowels (A) and Ma; and also the illuminator Śā-dṛ-mū. (4.45)

The vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*; the two nasals (*ṅ* and *ṇ*); the two semivowels (*y* and *v*); the two sibilants (*ś* and *s*); the letter *r*; the letter *l*; and the letter *kṣa* together with the visarga—these constitute the twenty [consonants]. (4.46)
The vowels and so forth, likewise *ru*, the letter *ka* joined with *visarga*, *deśa*, *ṣadbhāmura*, *kāra*, and those ending in *sārcisāgaśā*. (4.47)
One should place the letter *ma* along with the visarga at the end, proceeding in a clockwise direction;
then, having worshipped the wheel with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should reveal it.
A disciple who is a devotee of Śiva, a wise Śiva-brahmin, should likewise receive this supreme mantra only after having obtained the permission of his guru. (4.49)
Otherwise, if one were to recite [the mantra] elsewhere after having accepted it for another purpose, it would cause misfortune;
[it governs] everything from Śiva down to the earth, and the elements and their states in due order. (4.50)
Knowing that [the deity] is established within this mantra, one is liberated from the bondage of the fetters.
Beginning from the first day of Caitra until the final day of Phālguna. (4.51)
One should worship each syllable daily, beginning with the *praṇava*, on the eight petals of the navel-lotus; these eight syllables are preceded by the "lamp" (*dīpaka*). (4.52)
Having formed these into a *saṃpuṭa*, one should recite [the mantra], meditate, and perform sacrifice;
or one may perform the sacrifice in a single day within this wheel situated on the left.
The Rudra-mantra-cakra: Now, therefore, the characteristics of the cakra of the Rudra-mantra are described.
The group of limbs [consisting of] the goddesses and the kanyās belongs to the categories of the elements of space (vyomatattva). 4/54.
In these [groups], the placement (*nyāsa*) and extraction (*uddhāra*) are established in sequence from the upper row:
*dīpaka*, *vyāpya*, *dīkṣā*, *vā*, and likewise *nā*. (4.55)
The two pairs of *yakāras*, as well as *rūpa*, *piṃścala*, and *ila*; the two *sat*s, *āyata*, and that which begins with a vowel—these are for the purpose of pervading the desired [state]. (4.56)
One should write "na," "pāru," "te," "ja," "kā," "la," "śca," "tu," "śca," "ṇe," "ca," "natī," "tathā," "dyā," "kā," "la," "ta," "dha," "nā," and "syā" in the first row. (4/57)
Mavyārūpa, Vyāyau, Hāpāpaghna, Śeśava, Tvamānāla, Bhāśi, and likewise Bhuvaṃ dadhacita. (4.58)
*Rū*, *rūpa*, *te*, as well as *rū* and *lāva-bhoga*; likewise, *pra* and *sa* at the end of the second [line]—these are to be led as the illuminators of the universe (*viśvadīpaka*). (4.59)
Hāsā and Viṣāka, Pathaśrī and Varāśayā, Dagusā as well as Ṇeru, and likewise Vivilāma. (4/60)
O Śiva, *pāpikāraḥ*, *tathā*, *niśca*, and *dvayaṃ* are joined with *retha*; likewise, *trepa*, *pū*, *stra*, and *stu* are always [joined] with *nātre* in the third case. (4.61)
Likewise, *riyanena*, *ca dayau ca*, *panādītaṃścale*, as well as those preceded by the letter *r* (*rephapūrvopeta*), *yau*, *yavayāpyama*, and likewise *tathaiva*. (4.62)
Likewise, one should write *dyodhān*, *tathāneṇe*, *ṇeyanese*, and *tathāpare*, as well as *nantaśca* and *adbhyavyāpī*, within two rows of Vedic lines.
Saṃpramāṇa, likewise vāca, adaśāṣṭva, and likewise tathaiva; ṣṭāli-traya-gakāra, and ādadaśceyayau likewise. (4/64)
The *jāpa*s, as well as the *visarga*, the letter *ṇa*, the letter *e*, the *mūpaṣṭa*s, and the *caru*s;
furthermore, the *tapa*s, the *vyokāra*s, and those born from *aneva*—these are [the phonemes]. (4.65)
One should place *tāraṃ*, *kaṃ*, and the fifth [vowel] in the fifth row in successive order;
likewise, for the sake of sacrifice, one should place *yāśiyāne* with its various forms, as well as *yū* and *vī*.
Āśivā and Talau, Śaś and Ralātrāba, Virūyayau, Tuḥsaviḥ, Sargo, Maṃvāvyodakā, Rūḍhī, and Vibhoyā. (4.67)
Hara, the lotus-born Brahmā, and the lotus-seated Viṣṇu are said to be external; likewise are the two Dācaras, Liñca, and Vinā.
Yava, Avya, Udaka, Barūddhi, Svapiha, Uccāgara, and Upādacamū are also mentioned. (4.68)
Mava, Sādhe, Yarutama, Nādiyamecakā,
Ayodyodi, Kalahalanya, Māyāma, Mī, and likewise Canara— these are the seven [classes]. 4/69.
One should write *kā*, *śa*, *bā*, *hu*, *ta*, and *tha* within the row of flavors (*rasapaṅkti*);
on the outside, *sa*, *śa*, *rū*, *rū*, *sa*, *mā*, *dya*, *ya*, and *śca*, as well as *ṇe*. (4.70)
And those who are *nepi*, *tathā*, *tathāśa*, *bhīru*, and *dvijātika*;
likewise, *brāhmya*, *kadāścaru*, *vinayeta*, and *sāya*. (4.71)
Yaru, tato, yetha, mecaka, ayodyoni, kava, hali as the seventh, vātrayāta, dīṃ, vaśaśirū, dvidāditika.
And those who were at the joints, on the rows, in the waters, on the earth, in the sky, as well as those who had departed, along with the seed and so forth—what indeed [remained]? 4.73.
Śavabha, Tatha, Thya, and those others of his; likewise the Tisisarūlitas, the Jīnas, the Śāstis, and the Vavacās. (4/74)

The syllable *ma*, the letter *ka*, the letter *śa*, the letter *ra*, the letter *ṇa*, the letter *tra*, the letter *vi*, the letter *ṣṭa*, the letter *ṇā*, the letter *gu*, the letter *hyā*, the letter *p*, the letter *rva*, and likewise the letter *śa* ending in *ra*. (4.75)
Likewise, having written them in sequence, the practitioner should know the *kāmaka* [mantra]: the letter *va* preceded by *ra*, followed by *pākināṣṭa*. (4.76)

The letters preceded by *na*—namely *drī*, *pā*, *ś*, and *śa*—as well as *na* [itself], and the letters *kha* and *ru*, one should place in the eleventh row. (4.79)
If there is *śi*, *cā*, *na*, *śa*, and *ṛ* at the beginning of a vowel, followed by *ya*, *na*, *di*, *śa*, as well as *jya*, *vi*, *ṇe*, and *ṇe*. (4.80)

*Naśca*, *śabdaśca*, *bābhadrā*, *yokārānte*, *arkapaṅktyuktike*; *naṭyanāt*, likewise *kyannāme*, and *viśca viśaṣmaṇe*. (4.82)

One should write the *pikāra*, the *dīpaka*, the *tha*, the *viṣūśāna* and so forth, as well as the *ṇa*, the *añca*, the *sarga*, and the *sakāra* in the thirteenth [section]. (4.84)

Dāta, caṃhya, acirā, nābhaya, yāṃ, hrīṃ, rāṣṇa, ṣāḥ, tathā, ṣāṃ, ca, sa, pa, sau, saṃ, repādi, evau, and the letter va, which is the illuminator at the end. (4.86)
The Yakas, Gandharvas, Pṛṣadhras, Śāntas, Carāyanas, Ṇeyās, Śidhas, Aśvāras, Tadyās, and Viniṇīyus—[these are the classes]. (4.87)
In the divisions following Sthūṣānta, there are four; in the row of lunar days (tithi-paṅktika), Līna, Ga, Śiva, Va, Rāya, Yā, Yayā, and Gā likewise [occur]. 4.88.

The letter preceding *na*, the one beginning with *svara* (vowel), and that which comes from *rūpa*; the *visarga* of *ma*; *na*, *nā*, and *vidya*; *hrīṃ* preceded by *svā*; and *la* in the worship of *bhā*. (4.89)
One should place the syllables *ra*, *śi*, *ra*, *śi*, *baṃ*, *pū*, *rvo*, *maḥ*, and *ca* in the first row; then *so*, *sa*, and *śe* in the second;
then *dhā*, *pa*, *va*, and *ntā* for the bridegroom; and *dvi*, *dvi*, *to*, *yā*, *sa*, *re*, *po*, *ha*, *rū*, and *caḥ* for the bride. (4.90)
Bhañca, viyaṃca, vaidyāta, svarādya, para, rūsūcyapāḥ; again, bhapaurikā, lolā, nana, and yābhā. (4/91)
In the seventeenth [syllable], one should write the letter *ma* joined with the *anusvāra*, followed by *ta*, *ya*, *ya*, the earth (*bha*), *ka*, and *ni* preceded by *ka*. (4.92)
The letter *śa* preceded by *ra*, the letter *dha* preceded by *na*, the letter *rū*, as well as *rūpikāṇe*, *sani*, *śadatā*, and *vit*. (4.93)
The *dhū* and *dhau* [pratyāhāras] consist of *ta*, *ru*, and *sa* with the visarga; they are considered to have *kha* as their companion.

One should write the opposing sides ending with the *visarga*, the letter *ma*, *pya*, *na*, *ca*, *saḥ*, *sarvaśiva*, and *tega*, along with *ha* and *jña*, in the eight directions.

The letter *ya*, *cakṣiḥ*, *satadīpaṃ*, *raḥ*, *kāca*, as well as *javaḥ*, *lasat*, *dhakāraḥ*, and *viḥ*—these are in the nineteenth [chapter]. (4.97)
Mavighna, abhyāva, vīru, ṇereyan, dhāśiya, tathā, nadyobha, dhṛtija, and suyaṃraṇya—these are the twenty. (4.98)
The *rākāya* [ending], likewise the *tathāne* [ending], the *puśca* and *taśca* [endings], those ending in *navantāmo*, as well as *vaśca*, and the *tāraka* [ending] with the *visarga*. (4.99)
Then, *sarva* with its own flame (*svārci*), joined with the letter *sa*, the vowel *u*, and the *bindu*;
*namaḥ* with the final *visarga*; and the letter *va* joined with *ma* and *repha*. (4.100)
Baśca, vaśca, pasasphuśca, cakāśca—these are in the twenty-first [section];
likewise māca, vaśca, te, pi, ṇeñca, vāca, preceded by ṣa. (4.101)
The letter *sa* is the destroyer of the *bhaṅgurāma* [mantra]; the letter *na* does not arise from the wind; the letter *ka* is the bull among men; and the letter *ta* is the eye. (4.102)
One should arrange the *jākāra* and the *tantra* preceded by *ā*, as well as those preceded by *na*, *jña*, *carva*, and *rabhauta*, within twenty-two rows. (4.103)
The arms, the knees, the earth, the beloved, the sky, the fearless one, as well as the leaf;
likewise, the *pā*, the *ja*, the *ca*, the *visarga*s, the *dīpana*, and that which begins with a vowel. (4.104)

The syllables *ve*, *rā*, *ja*, *vā*, *bha*, *ga*, *va*, *vo*, *da*, *kṣa*, *dā*, *ne*, *ca*, *ka*, *mau*, *ca*, *śi*, *ma*, *śca*, *yā*, *ca*, *ta*, *thā*, *va*, *śca*, *sa*, *śca*, *du*, *śca*, *ta*, *thā*, *ca*, *pau*. (4.105)
One should write *pṛścaya*, *makāra*, and [the others] in the twenty-third [cell];
likewise, *secaya*, *lā*, *pu*, *to*, and *varūcaṇe*. (4.106)
So, Tha, Va, Dya, Ka, Ra, Hu, Śa, Śca, Pra, Ja, Cha, Tha, Yu, Śi, and the various forms of Pa, as well as Ma with the visarga. (4.107)
One should place five, nine, and nine [syllables] for the protection of the cooked offerings;
likewise, one should insert those belonging to the state of enjoyment into the twenty-fourth [position].
The one with two eyes, the one with a deformed form, the one who crosses over, and likewise the man;
those who cook, the one with a multitude of offspring, and the one who releases the abandonment of the lotus-stalk. 4/109.
The letters *va*, *śca*, *pot*, *vava*, *āś*, *ca*, *varāru*, and likewise *rā*;
those with an *anusvāra* (*sānusvara*), and that which is joined (*saṃyukta*) before a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) at its end. (4.110)
One should draw twenty-five [syllables] in a row with colors in their proper sequence;
[the first is] Nārūpin, and Viṇeśa is at the end, together with the letter 'Sa' and the creative power (Sarga). || 4/111 ||
The letter *ra* with the first vowel (*a*) likewise brings a hundred faults;
so too do Punarvasu and Ārdrā—this is the command regarding the groups of ten.
One should place *bhara*, *kā*, *dī*, *pa*, *vā*, *ge*, and *cati* in the twenty-sixth;
likewise, *pañca*, *ṇe*, *ca*, *vi*, and *bhā*, as well as *moca*—this is indeed my body. (4.113)
The *rūśca*, the *sapta*, the *pañca*, the *bhagavant*, the *vaśā*, and the *pau*;
the *savau*, the *masavisarga*, and the *pamavāś* are the *śiścataḥ*. (4.114)
The syllables *ta*, *ma*, *la*, *ka*, *śa*, *ca*, *ya*, *ta*, *ya*, *ta*, and *ya* constitute this *kāra* in the *bhadrajāti*. (4.115)
In the twenty-seventh [chapter], there are indeed the words *ma*, *śa*, *ya*, *pra*, *śca*, as well as *dyā*, *yā*, *ye*, *vo*, and *ta*, denoting dogs. (4.116)
The syllable *oṃ*, the *roṣadhi*, the *visarga* (*maḥ*), the deity, the *ṣacara*, the *pīyu*, the *sthī*, the *catāra*, as well as that, the *necara*, the *sara*, and the *ya*. (4.117)
The letter *ā*, *makarī*, and likewise *taṃkāra* preceded by *sa*;
*na*, *caka*, the *visarga*, together with *dhī*, *bahiḥ*, *cahina*, and *sathā*. (4.118)
One should place Na and Ku in sequence within the twenty-eighth [position];
then Ku, Ya, and the letter Ya, which is the first of the vowels and moves through the Ra-syllable. (4.119)

The syllable *va*, the syllable *ga*, the syllable *va*, the syllable *ma*, the syllable *ta*, the syllable *ś*, the syllable *ca*, the syllable *ś*, the syllable *oṃ*, the syllable *kāra*, the syllable *bhū*, the syllable *ta*, the syllable *e*, the syllable *va*, the syllable *ā* with the bindu (*m*), the syllable *ye*, the syllable *na*, the syllable *me*, and the syllable *pra*. (4.120)
Ja, Va, and likewise Bha; Bhā, Ka, Ta, and Bha;
Oṃkāra and Vi-ma-kāra; and likewise Ka, Ta, Pa, and Ma. (4.121)
One should place the letter *dra* and likewise those twenty-nine others; *pi*, *na*, *ci*, *ṣi*, *ta*, *gu*, *pa*, *śca*, and *na*. (4.122)
The letter *ha* with the visarga, the two letters *da* and *pa*, and likewise the letter *buṃ*, the letter *sṛ*, and the letter *ī* with the bindu constitute the illuminator (*pradīpaka*). (4.123)
The letter *ma* with the *sa* and the *visarga*, followed by the letter *śi*;
the letter *bha*, the letter *sa*, the letter *li*, and the letter *va* preceded by the letter *ra*. (4.124)
Ka, ca, ha, and ca; the letter u, ya, ca, gu, and ca; va, tau, and hiṃ; yena, ca, and yanva; likewise, the letter da at the end, and ya, ya, and au. (4.125)
One should place the letter *na* and the letter *va* in the thirtieth row; likewise, the letter *ta* with the *visarga*, and the letter *la* with the *acama* (anusvāra) and the *visarga*. (4.126)
Hyā, agni, and pradīpa; likewise, the letter ma followed by na; na, śi, and pa; and the letter ma preceded by sa. (4.127)

The modification (vikāra), the letter preceded by *ka* (kha), the letter *ya* with the bindu (*ṃ*), the letter *ma* with the visarga (*ḥ*), and likewise the first vowel (*a*) in the sun (the second syllable). 4/128.
The two nasals (ṇa), the letter va, the letter ka together with the vowel u, the syllable huṃ, and likewise the letter ma preceded by the letter na. (4.129)
The letter *ta*, the letter *vi*, likewise the letter *ga*, and the letter *ti* do not precede [the others];
*la*, *to*, *ma* with a *visarga*, and the letter *li* joined with a *bindu*. (4.130)
One should write the letter *sva* joined with the letter *ra* as the thirty-first;
likewise, *na*, *śi*, *ti*, the letter *ya*, the vowel *u*, and the letter *ja*. (4.131)
Var, ga, va, bha, ja, śa, as well as sva, rā, dyo, kha, ñ, and catu;
ṣya, ca, ja, and the letter mṛ; vaha, nā, svā, and ma. (4.132)
He made something else with the letter *ma* following it, and he placed that behind the letter *pa*. (4.133)

The letter *na* with two dots (*ṇa*) and with the *visarga*, as well as the letter *ma* not preceded by another [consonant], the letters *ka* and *ra*, and likewise *kā* and *li* joined with the *anusvāra*. (4.134)
One should place the letters *ma*, *bha*, and *na* joined with the visarga (*visarga-yukta*), as well as the portions of the letter *ya* and *ra*, in the thirty-two squares of the grid.
Kha, cha, ga, and the letter *s* at the beginning of a word; the *dhū* sound, the *c* sound, the *visarga*;
likewise *ni*, *śa*, *si*, *na*, *pu*, *ru*, and *gau*. (4.136)
And likewise the Tārās, the Mohāśisūris, the Tathāsvas, the Śibhas, the Prāyas, and the Gāruḍas. (4.137)
One should write *yanaya* and *tathāva* in the thirty-third [square]; then *takāra*, *vāgava*, *sta*, *nahuṃṣaṭsvā*, and *sa*. (4.138)
The letter *ta*, conjoined with the *bindu* and flowing through the *ū* and *ca* eyes, together with *śi*, *ra*, and the *bindu*, preceded by *ja*, is the maker of knowledge (*jñakāraka*). (4.139)
Sūca, maśca, pradīpa, tatau, viprabhā, dāhāte, lilana, ūnanā, and calī—these are indeed the Viprabhas. 4/140.
One should write the letter *te* at the end of the fifth row in the thirty-fifth [square];
likewise, there are six [letters]: *bha*, *va* with a visarga, *ni*, and *ta*. (4.141)
The letter *va* preceded by *na*, as well as *da* joined with *ra*; likewise *ga*, *te*, *ja*, *ve*, *ce*, *na*, *gā*, *ma*, and *śa* preceded by *ta*. (4/142)
Sva, pa, ka, ya, kṣa, ma, śa, dra, ga, and ya; likewise, ma preceded by ta, and ma followed by va—these are the syllables of the deities to be given. || 4/143 ||
The *sa* with the *visarga*, the letter *ma*, and the letter *pa* joined with the vowel *e*;
likewise, the letter *ma* with the *visarga*, and *mo* and *cagā*. (4.144)
One should write the thirty-six rows joined with the essence (sāra), beginning with *mṛ* and *vā*, followed by *naḥ*, *sa*, *ra*, *saṃ*, *yu*, *ktaḥ*, *ṣaṭ*, *triṃśat*, *paṅkti*, *ke*, *li*, *khe*t;
and likewise *oṃ*, *kā*, *ro*, *dhaḥ*, *ca*, *bhaḥ*, *āḥ*, *ca*, *eva*, *ṣaṭ*, *ca*, *suḥ*, *ca*, *tathā*, *ca*, *sā*. (4/145)
Salutation likewise to the lamp joined with the deficient anusvāra;
and [the syllables] ya, va, ha, and ma, preceded by ta. (4.146)
Va, ca, te, ca, vaprau, ca, pra, and likewise vā; vā, ca, pradī, ca, lā, and ma, with the visarga. (4/147)
The letter *ya*, the letter *bha*, and the letter *dau* joined with the *li* [vowel] and the *bindu*;
likewise, the two *śi*s, as well as the letter *ma* accompanied by the *visarga*. (4.148)
One should write [the letters] upon the thirty-seven squares of the *jña*-karma-vāsa-vāna;
having thus arranged them in the wheel, one should extract the mantra from the wheel. (4.149)
The peak-syllable (kūṭārṇa) consists of the sun (repha), fire (ra), and the vowel of the limbs (u); this is the root-mantra of that [deity].
It ends with the individual soul (jīva), is joined with the individual soul, and is endowed with the bindu and the creation (sṛṣṭi). || 4/150 ||
Because Brahmā’s limbs are conceptualized according to the primary color of these [syllables], one should likewise take the name of other deities as their color, together with the bindu. (4.151)
One who knows the mantra should extract the mantra ending in the dative case using each respective name;
one should apply this same method for yakṣas, rākṣasas, grahas, and so forth. (4.152)
The Mātṛkā-mantra:
In this world, the Mātṛkā shall be the foremost of all mantras;
one should practice them either conjoined with Śakti and Rudra or alone. (4.153)
By this, everything is accomplished; therefore, one should place these [seeds] and recite them.
Regarding the garland-mantra:
"O best of sages, listen as I shall explain the procedure for the garland-mantra. (4.154)

"Yam-rvāṃ-ba-gakhaṃ-tryam-va;
this mantra beginning with Tryambaka bestows the fruit of all desires.
O Goddess, at the beginning of creation, the power of Śiva (Śivaśakti) is divided in many ways. (4.155)
Ādiśakti belongs to Śiva; Manonmanī belongs to Sādākhya; and Bhavānī belongs to Maheśa—thus the Śakti is considered to be threefold. (4.156)
One should fashion the mantra beginning with the letter *kha* (the sky) and the syllable *mā* (the beginning), which is white;
it consists of the mind (*ma*), the mind-born (*na*), the sky (*kha*), and fire (*va*), combined with the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*). (4.157)

The mantra of Bhavānī is remembered as [the syllable] with the visarga (HḤ), while for Gaurī it is likewise; for all other Śaktis, the first letter of their own name is said to be their mantra. (4.158)
The mantra for the Śaktis has been declared; now listen to the Melā-mantra:
Tāra (Oṃ), Khaṃ, the Kūṭa ending with Ṣa, Ha-ra-la-ya-va-ra-yū preceded by Tāra, the Bindu, Nāda, Huṃ Phaṭ, the emission (Ktasarga), Vaṣaṭ, and Vauṣaṭ for the Wind at the navel. 159.

The white *vāṭ* [is] the moon, the drop (*bindu*), the sound, the *śa-ṣa-ṣa-paraṭ*, the two parts, the white, the resonance (*nāda*) with the *sarga*s (visargas), the Lord of the World together with *amā* (the new moon) and *preṃsa-bhau*, the *sarga* and the resonance.
Speech is the drop; the drop of resonance is the letter of the mind-born [god]; and there is the pair of the drop and the resonance.
It is said that on the Śukla [tithi], the *bindu* and *dhvani* are indeed the mantra; on the Vālikā [tithi], the *visarga*.
The end of *ṣa*, *kha*, the *vāc* [mantra], the *bindu*, and the *dhvani* are the mantra; the end of *ṣa* on the Śukla, together with the *sakāma*, is *hrīṃ*.
The *bindu*, *nāda*, *dhvani*, and the supreme are the *bindu-nāda*, which is stainless (*vimelā*).

In the recitation of the *melā* mantra, one should first recite the fifty letters of the *mātṛkā*, and then, having joined the mantra to it according to the rules for recitation, recite the mantra from that point onward—
whether it be in the middle of this mantra or at its end.
Whatever unsurpassed realms he causes himself to traverse, he attains those very incomparable desires. (4.162)

Those mantras known as *mālā-mantras* consist of more than twenty syllables; those mantras consisting of more than ten syllables [are *sādhyamantras*], while those fewer than that are designated as *bījas*. (4.163)

A rosary bestows the fruit of old age, while mantras bestow the fruit of youth; those consisting of more than one hundred and eight beads bestow the fruit of childhood, and those with fewer always yield diminished results. (4.164)

Svāhā, Namaḥ, and the remaining [mantras] consist of feminine, neuter, and masculine natures; [mantras] consisting of masculine forms are used for subjugation, eradication, poisoning, and so forth, as well as for minor rites. (4.165)
Women are for the removal of disease, while eunuchs are for other tasks;
thereafter, it is predominantly fiery, characterized by the sky, fire, peaks, lamps, and oceans. (4.166)
The gentle and the remaining [deities] are both praised for gentle and cruel rites respectively;
through the application of "namaḥ" and "phaṭ," the gentle and cruel [mantras] are distinguished from one another by others.
A mantra that is merely slightly awakened will not grant success;
those two qualities are considered to belong to the periods when the left and right breaths flow. (4.168)
The mantra of the Fiery [element] should be thus; for the Gentle [element], these are reversed.
However, in the flow of the two enclosures (puṭa), there is the awakening of the Gentle and the Fierce.
One should avoid the Manus beginning with Aniṣīti and Narāśaṃsa. [The following are the durations of the Manvantaras: two, four, three, four, one, two, two, two, and five. (4.170)
The [number of] eyes is the sky (0), the eyes are the sky (0), the hands are the moon (1), the eyes are fire (3), fire (3), sky (0), and fire (3);
the letters are sky (0), Ka (2), the sky (0), the eyes (2), the sky (0), the eyes (2), fire (3), and the vowels beginning with Aśva-yuja (the horse-sacrifice, i.e., the letter *ai*). 4/171.

At the end of the *jīva*, joined with *Revatī*, the sequence of days is thus by means of the letters: four, three, fire (three), fire (three), noose (four), eyes (two), eyes (two), elements (five), and five. (4.172)

The vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ta*, as well as the remaining letters situated in the sixth [row], are traditionally taught for the purpose of establishing the favorable arrangement of the collection of phonemes. (4.173)
That mantra which is favorable to a practitioner bestows success upon him.
Having written the syllables within a svastika, one should worship Śaṅkara with the sixteen-fold [mantra]. (4.174)
The *siddha*, *sādhya*, and *svasiddhāri* [of the practitioner] are derived from the first letter of the practitioner's name;
furthermore, they are determined by the letters from the beginning of the mantra up to its final syllable, through the conceptualization of *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth. (4.175)
Siddha-siddha, Siddha-sādhya, Siddha-svasiddha, and Siddha-ari;
likewise, in other cases such as sādhya and so forth, a fourfold classification is recognized. (4/176)

The *siddha* mantra grants one's desired object through recitation (*japa*) and other means; the *sādhya* is accomplished through recitation and libations (*tarpaṇa*); the *susiddha* grants its own success merely by being read; and the *ripu* (enemy) mantra brings about what is undesirable for the practitioner. (4.177)
A mantra that contains an abundance of syllables denoting enemies is said to cause destruction;
likewise, even a disciple endowed with good character or a son possessed of devotion to Śiva [may bring ruin]. (4.178)

Then the preceptor should give him a thousand [mantras]; the preceptor should cause him to recite them. [The mantra] cast upon the son was obtained through deception and grasped in the form of a book. (4.179)
If one recites [the mantra] obtained through another method, it causes destruction;
therefore, the best of practitioners, the master of mantras, should recite it for the sake of accomplishing the primary rites. (4.180)
And other mantras than that sādhana grant success everywhere; even the mantra of a single syllable grants success through ten hundred thousand recitations and so forth. (4.181)
Due to an excess of syllables, a reduction in the number of recitations must be made according to reason and in due order;
thus, the recitation of the seed-syllable (bīja) should be performed with a count that is double or triple that [of the mantra]. (4.182)
The number of recitations for a mantra consisting of a garland is prescribed;
for a mantra whose number is not specified, it is one hundred and eight thousand. (4.183)
In the ritual of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) is considered to be one-tenth of the recitation (*japa*).
For the limbs (*aṅga*) [of the mantra], worship, oblation, recitation, and so forth, are to be performed one-tenth of the root-mantra (*mūla*). (4.184)
That which is recited audibly (bhāṣya) is superior to the whispered (upāṃśu), and therefore the mental (mānasa) is indeed the most excellent.
The recitation of mantras and so forth should be performed while facing either the east or the north. (4.185)
"All mantras should be received during the day, or they may be beneficial when taken at that [specific] time.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the extraction of mantras, in the great tantra known as the *Kāminī*.
Oṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, whose form is the divine atmosphere,
who pervades all, the primordial principle; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, the Great God, who shines with the eightfold splendor of the sky and possesses manifold forms.

To the one possessing the three forms, whose foot is the word, who destroys all obstacles, who has a fierce form, who transcends all distinctions, *abhilipilikiṃśili līpi vaktadaṃṣṭrāya*, and whose eyes cause terror.

To the one with a licking, fierce tongue; to the one whose senses are the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāma*, and *Atharva* Vedas; to the infinite, the unmanifest, the unsupported, the fixed, the eternal—so it is said.
To Śiva, who is seated upon the Kailāsa mountain and the Lambaka-yoga-pīṭha; who is the eternal yogin whose food is meditation; who is both the support and that which is supported;
the sovereign Lord of the universe; and the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa.
Homage to Ghoraśiva, whose heart is eightfold; to the Indra of Śiva’s armor;
to him who has resorted to lightning; to the secret of Vāmadeva; to the one who cooks and cooks;
to the most excellent among the excellent; to the form of Sadyojāta, the bliss of the heroic ones who have completely conquered.

Salutations to the one who is the support of the powers beginning with Vāmā; to the destroyer of time and the remover of desire; to Bāla, Abāla, and Manonmana; to Rudra, who is both Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā; to the secret of power; to the one of manifold forms.
To sound, whose form is sound; to heaven, whose form is heaven;
to splendor, whose form is splendor; to taste, whose form is taste; to fragrance, whose form is fragrance; to the seed, whose form is the seed; to the root.
To the root-form, the sprout; to the sprout-form, the stalk;
to the stalk-form, the leaf; to the leaf-form, the bud;
to the bud-form, the flower; to the flower-form, the fruit.
To Him who is the form of the fruit, the infinite, the one whose form is the infinite; to the seed, the one whose form is the seed;
to the mind, the one whose form is the mind;
to the object, the one whose form is the object; to the ego, the one whose form is the ego.

Salutations to Sadāśiva, who is of the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti) and whose form is primordial matter; who is illusion (māyā) and whose form is illusion; who is purity (śuddha) and whose form is purity; who is knowledge (vidyā) and whose form is knowledge; who is the method (naya) and whose form is the method.
Obeisance to Śiva, whose form is Sadāśiva; Oṃ Hauṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
Salutations to Kālāgnirudra, adorned with the eight forms, eternal yet non-eternal; salutations to the golden-armed one, to the wind,
to him whose splendor is like the wind, to the causal cause, to Tripura, who transcends the three cities.
Salutations to Ananta, from Nāda; you who are peaceful, beyond the peaceful, terrible, more terrible than the terrible, most auspicious, and the most auspicious of the auspicious.
Oṃ, homage! Homage to you, who are more secret than the secret, the protector of the protectors.

O Lord of all sciences, whose form is light, who is devoted to the Supreme Lord, who pervades the conscious and the unconscious, the sky, and all space; O formless one, the first of the first, whose nature is the light of fire and fire; O Fire, smokeless!
Abhasma, beginningless, by the beginningless, manifold, manifold, dhū-dhṛ, dhū-dhū, Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ suvaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ,
Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam, many, many.
O Vāmā, O Vāmā; O Avyaya in prosperity, O Avyaya in peace;
O Śāsana, O Śamana; O You who have transcended the abode; O Anidhana, O Source of dissolution;
O Śiva, O Sarva, O Sarva Sadāśiva; to the Lord of Yoga, and to Śarva—[salutations].

Release first the splendor! Bhava, of all beings, non-existent, existence, source of existence, by power, O possessor of power, knowledge, ignorance, Puruṣa, unborn, space! Oṃ klīṃ ślīṃ oṃ hlīṃ glīṃ oṃ phaṭ phaṭ oṃ huṃ huṃ.
Oṃ drīṃ drīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ hrūṃ tri namaḥ.
Svasti svāhā svadhā vaṣaṭ vauṣaṭ huṃ phaṭ!
O Anantānanda, self-blazing, svāhā! To the one who holds the golden embryo!

Svāhā! O bestower of happiness upon all beings, O maker of all things present, O Supreme Brahman beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; you who are unworshipped and unstudied by those previously praised; you who abide from before, the witness of the primordial half, the witness—turu, turu, O Pataṅga!
O Pataṅga, O Jñāna-jñāna, O Śabda-śabda, O Subtle, O Gross, O Śiva, O Sarva, O Sadāśiva, obeisance! Oṃ Āṃ Īṃ Ūṃ, to the one who pervades the sky, Oṃ Yāṃ.
RĀṂ LĀṂ VĀṂ GĀṂ ṢĀṂ SĀṂ HĀṂ LĀṂ KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢŪṂ KṢAIṂ KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ, homage to the Lord of Peace!
Homage to the Source of the World!
Oṃ svāhā! Homage to the Lord of the End; homage to the Self of Reality;
homage to the Self of Śarva.
Salutation to the one whose nature is nectar;
salutation to the Lord of the Rudras.
The classes of mantras are twofold, distinguished by the division of mantra and vidyā.
Mantras are known as those whose deity is male, while Vidyās are remembered as those whose deity is female.
All mantras are declared to have the nature of male, female, or neuter. Male mantras should end in *huṃ phaṭ*, while those considered female should end in *svāhā*.
The three types of *mantras* have been described as ending in *namaḥ* and being neuter:
*sarvātmane parāya parameśvarāya yogāya yogasambhavāya karakara kurukuru sadya bhava bhava bhavodbhava*.
O Destroyer of all gods and all undertakings, O Sadāśiva, be gracious; salutations unto you, Svāhā!
Oṃ Sa-Śiva Śi-namaḥ! Oṃ Maṃ, the flames from the heart of Śiva, Svāhā! O Great Splendor whose essence is Śiva, O Omniscient One, unconquered!
O most terrible one, turn back Piṅgala, who has the luster of armor!

Come, O Piṅgala! By the command of Śiva, bind, bind my heart with the great armor; O you who are subtle through devotion, wielder of the thunderbolt, wielder of the thunderbolt-bolt, whose body is adamantine, having entered this body!
Paralyze, paralyze all evil ones—huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ prasphura prasphura, O you of terrible and most terrible form, caṭa caṭa, pracaṭa, kaha kaha, vama vama, slay, slay, hūṃ phaṭ— oṃ jūṃ saḥ.
Oṃ, may we know that Great Lord; may we meditate upon Mahādeva;
may Śiva impel us.
Oṃ, may we know Gaṇāmbikā; may we meditate upon Mahātapā.
May Gaurī inspire us.
Om, svāhā to Nidhanapati Antaka!
Salutation to Water; salutation to you, the Water-liṅga.

Salutation to Rudra; salutation to you who are the *liṅga* of Rudra. Salutation to Bhava; salutation to you who are the *liṅga* of Bhava. Salutation to the Upward One; salutation to you who are the upward-pointing *liṅga*.
Salutation to Śiva; salutation to you, the Śivaliṅga.

One should avoid the letters *ṇ*, *y*, *ś*, *s*, and those ending in *m* or *t*, as well as the letter *v*, except when they occur with speed (as part of a rapid succession).
Furthermore, in the case of the divisions of *su-sāṭa* and *tata-bheda*, one should avoid the letter *ś* and those ending in *t* within the *paṅkti* meter.

then *napūrvaḥ*, *tasvarādyaśca*, and *rūpāniti* followed by *uḥ*.

likewise bhaverū with the bindu, ha, vidha, and vaitya.

the letter Ā, Rūpikāṇe, and the twenty various forms.
Then *sū*, *dhau*, and *ta*; likewise *rū* with the *visarga* and the letter *ma*;
*prekhakṣāṃ* ending in the *visarga* and the letter *ma*; and again the letter *ma*.
And while performing it, one should go; the knower of the heart should write [the sequence] in the eighteenth [position].
Indeed, *ava*, *asu*, *lagu*, *ru*, *pi*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *idaṃ*, *rāgu*, and *huda* are [the syllables].
In that very place, one should meditate upon the self-nature of the syllable Śakāra arising from Vāk-bhava;
Śa, Kṣu, Tadīpa, Rakāra, and likewise Ekāraja.
The letters *laṃ*, *daṃ*, and the letter *ya* are situated in the nineteenth [tattva], *Vistatha*, in the form of pervasive *mavistha*; they are likewise kindled by Śivā.
In the twentyfold [vision], one should perceive the rivers, the peaks, the letter *śa*, the letter *ā*, the mountain, the dust, the thought, the breath, and the nose.
In the same way, when the *rākā* vowel (*ā*) is joined with the nasal (*m*), it becomes the name of the elephant (*gaja*); when joined with the vowel *u*, it becomes the name of the sun (*sūrya*).
When joined with the letter *v* and the visarga, it becomes the star (*tāraka*).
Śā-var-va-rū and svā-har-ci-sa-kā-ra, along with kṣai joined with the bindu;
mar-vā-ra and pra-ma, preceded by the letter ra and followed by va.
Bhañca, vañca, vasupsuśca, and cakāra are in the twenty-first [case];
likewise māpateśca, apiśca, and ṇethapāca preceded by ṣa.
The syllable *sa* is the hero, the syllable *na* is the fierce one;
the syllable *ka* is the bull, and the syllable *ru* is the two trees; the syllable *ne* is the self, and the syllable *ku* is the kusha grass.
One should place the twenty-two syllables in the second row: *ṛ* preceded by *ja*, *ā* and *pa*, those preceded by *na*, *jña*, *ca*, *va*, *ra*, *da*, *u*, and *ta*.
The letter *jña* preceded by *bhū*, as well as those formed with *nare* and *arddha*, likewise with *ādara*;
the letter *cha* with *pa* and *visarga*, and the letters *dī*, *pā*, *na*, *añ*, or *svarā*.
Bha, va, u, kṣa, na, ś, ca, ma, na, ca, ru, mau, va, śī;
ma, ś, ca, yā, ca, ta, thā, ya, ś, ca, śa, śva, du, ś, ca, ta, thā, ca, yoḥ.
One should write the letters *pra*, *va*, and *ma* in the twentieth [square] of those two; likewise, *se*, *ca*, *ra*, *āp*, and *a* are for the one whose form is the day (*vārarūpiṇe*).
The letters *ra*, *ma*, *tha*, *ya*, *śca*, *dyo*, *kāre*, *hu*, *śca*, *śca*, *pra*, *jā*, *ca*, *yā*, *ya*, *stu*,
*śi*, *ca*, *pra*, *kāra*, *ca*, *ma*, *kāra*, together with the *visarga*.
One should add *pañcu*, *rasa*, *saniṣṭhā*, *rac*, *bhuḥ*,
*śabhā*, and *tathāyā* into the twenty-fourth [position].
Biya, uca, caṣva, caṣva, rūru, pītārāgya, and likewise Anana;
Paścati, ending with the Visarga, and the two groups va and ga—these are said to be for the sake of darkness (tamas).
And likewise, Paścañca, Svātavāgāntiśa, and Śāsya;
then Roviṃśa, Pūrvaska, Yoṭa, Ṣaṭva, and Hetāraya, in sequence.
There, the wise one should place them in a row of twenty-five:
Na, Ra, Ru, Śa, Vī, Ņa, E, Bha, Au, Śa, Va, Ā, Tu, Ma, Sa, and Visarga.
The letter *ra* at the beginning of the first [group] is long, as is the letter *na*; likewise, *tha*, *cha*, and *bha*.
Furthermore, *ta*, *va*, *ya*, *sa*, *da*, *ha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, and *ja* are also [long].
One should place the *harauka* and *dīpa* as the *nāpāna* in the twenty-sixth [position];
likewise, one should place the *viśvaṇi*, the *viśivā*, and indeed the *moca*.
The Tāra, Meru, Svaḥ, Śaiva, Mā, Vāk, Bhavanta, Śac, and Cau;
the emission of the entire path, the Śapadī, Arc, Śic, and Ca.
In that battle, he was pursued by her; then, with his [remaining] forces, he went toward the sky.
Jaṅkāra, Yaśa, Caṇa, and Madhaśvāra were among the twenty-seven [who followed].
Maśca, praśca, as well as ādyāca, pāvethenaśca, and pārśa;
likewise, oṃkāra, ādijate, and vaṣaṭkara joined with the letter ra.

Tāraka with the visarga, dhīcavi, and likewise hinasta.
One should place *naḥ*, *śakuḥ*, and *ca* in sequence within the twenty-eighth [position];
likewise, *kūḥ*, *thaḥ*, *yakāraḥ*, and *ca* at the beginning of the vowels, joined with *raḥ*, *meḥ*, and *vay*.
The origin of speech, the vessels of honey, the syllable Oṃ, and indeed the elements;
the letter A with its bindu, by which one is not defiled and by which one truly transcends.
One should place *jara*, *bhāca*, *karabhāśca*, *tabhauddha*, *vai*,
*oṃkāraḥ*, *śa*, *makāraśca*, *kātapāḥ*, *śa*, *tathācamau*, *drākāraḥ*, and *tathāteca* in the twenty-ninth [position].
Pi, śca, na, and likewise ca, eva, śu, va, and tathāca na;
the letter ha with the visarga, and yāvo—these indeed are the lamps.
The letter *bhu*, *ta*, and likewise *va*; *kha* with the *visarga*; *va*, *bha*, and *sa* with *li*; and the letter *ti* joined with the letter *ra*.
Ka, bha, and the vowel i; ya, and likewise tu; patohi indeed;
na, dva, and ñca joined together; and the letter da, as well as candathau.
One should place the letter *na* and the letter *va* in the thirtieth row;
likewise, the letter *ka*, the letter *i* preceded by it, and the letter *ū* with the *bindu*.
Vyoja, hṛpau, bhaścanasvādyāḥ with the bindu,
kauśaphaṭ, bhava, bhenna, and ma preceded by ta, and niścaka.
The letter *li* joined with the *bindu*, as well as *mecabha* and *tathācabhāḥ*, and the letter *bha*—
these one should place in the thirty-two rows, along with *gāpa*.
Bhya, ca, mā, and ca; pradīpaṃ and bhaktaṃ, as well as pradīpakāḥ; those beginning with the letter na, and likewise da, ca, va, and ya.
The letter *pra* preceded by *ta*, the letter *ma* preceded by *ka*,
the two lamps *ya* and *ca*, *ma* and *ca*, *vāc*, *kṣu*, and [the letters] beginning with *ra* and *bha*.

|| The commencement of the ritual for bathing. ||
Now I shall describe the procedure for bathing as revealed by the Supreme Lord;
it removes all defects, is meritorious, and is supremely pleasing to the mind. (5.1)
The sixfold bath is declared to be the Cāruṇa, the Āgneya, the Māntra, the Mānasa, the Vāyavya, and that called the Mahendra. (5.2)

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, [one should meditate upon] Śiva, who resides within the heart-lotus, who is unwavering, like a lamp, consisting of the syllable *praṇava*, and imperishable. (5.3)
Meditating at the clear dawn, Daṇḍapāṇi, accompanied by his companion, went from his dwelling to a secluded place near a body of water. (5.4)
In that place, the best of practitioners must certainly perform a bath;
he should avoid ground covered with urine, thorns, insects, bones, excrement, and the like.
In the mud of the Mārgaśīrṣa river, in pits, water, cow dung, and ashes; in cremation grounds, gardens, cow-pens, solitary trees, crossroads, and the like. (5.6)

One should not perform the obligatory rites (āvaśyaka) while facing women, cows, Brahmins, the sun, or ascetics (liṅgin), nor while facing the moon, nor during the transformation of living beings. (5.7)
During the day or at the two twilights, a man should have a gentle countenance and keep a sacred thread over his ear;
having covered his head, he should avoid both [of these]. 5.8.
At night, facing south on ground covered with grass and the like, remaining silent, concealed by shrubs and such, with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose. (5.9)
One should not cast one's gaze toward the directions of excrement, urine, or the genitals;
one should avoid pressing the nose, spitting, belching, yawning, and similar acts. (5.10)
One should remove impurities that have come onto the body with blades of grass, clods of earth, or fragments of clay;
one should avoid using wood, cow dung, stones, bones, and the like. (5.11)
Having taken up earth with his left hand while still wearing his garment, a man should fetch pure, grit-free, and soft earth for the purpose of purification. (5.12)
For the purpose of purification, one should avoid earth found near trees, water, bridges, anthills, or in the middle of a village, as well as earth remaining from a previous application. (5.13)
On the bank of the washed water, he should place [the earth] to his own right;
he should perform purification with one application of earth for the cleansing of the organ of generation. (5.14)
In the same manner, one should cleanse the anus with the left hand seven times;
the left hand [should be washed] ten times, and both hands seven times. (5.15)
Having thoroughly cleansed both his feet and hands with earth once each,
he should apply a single lump of earth the size of an *āmalaka* fruit.

Having performed his necessary duties at home or at the site of Mitra, the wise man, wearing the sacred thread, should rise and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) on another part of the bank.
One should perform purification by bathing in the temple according to the previously prescribed rules;
having taken up a tooth-stick, one should remove the impurity residing in the teeth. (5.18)
The wooden staff for both the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) and the householder (bhogin) should be eight finger-breadths long;
it should be fresh, covered with bark, straight, cut evenly, and held upright.
Both [types of tooth-sticks] for men should be the size of the little finger. [The trees from which they are taken are:
karañja, ciribilva, khadira, and likewise arjuna. (5.20)
For the sake of liberation, one should use Apāmārga, Jambu, Āmra, Kakubha, and so forth; for the sake of enjoyment, Dhava, Dhātrī, Mākulī, and that which originates from Nimba. (5.21)
