One should avoid tooth-sticks made from the *śigru*, *śleṣmātaka*, *eraṇḍa*, or *piśāca* trees; likewise, one should avoid those made of metal. (5.22)
The rivers flowing to the ocean, as well as lakes, streams, ponds, bathing-places, and confluences that are sacred pilgrimage sites. (5.23)

For one who has been initiated, [drinking from] a lotus pond here is excellent; from a medium-sized pond it is middling; from long ponds and the like it is inferior; and from a well it is the lowest of the low. (5.24)
One should fashion the fourfold Vāruṇa [image] from pure clay;
having dug a pit measuring eight *aṅgulas* deep and extracted [the clay], one should do so while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Having taken earth with his heart, he should fill the dug-out pit with it;
having placed it on the bank of the water, he should sprinkle it while touching it with his head alone.

Having purified the grass and other materials with the *śikhā* mantra, one should divide them three times with the *kavaca* mantra; then, reciting the *astra* mantra, one should place another portion below the navel.
The wise man should wash all his limbs seven times thereafter, covering his mouth, eyes, nose, ears, and other openings with both hands. (5.28)
Having restrained the vital breaths, one should immerse oneself in the heart and meditate on the one who has the splendor of the sun;
having thus bathed in the water and emerged, one should be endowed with initiation and the three-fold coloring.
Previously unattached, the practitioner should worship the Brahma-sandhyā; at its conclusion, he should resort to the Śiva-sandhyā, following the abbreviated rite. (5.30)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, the wise one should recite the *melā-mantra*;
however, the other, whose nature is dispassion, turns his back on worldly aims. (5.31)
One who has been initiated should perform the Brāhmī initiation nine times, or the Śaivī initiation according to the rule;
if he belongs to the Gaṇa caste, he should perform the twilight rite (saṃdhyā) with the Astra-mantra.
Having taken a portion of the remaining earth from the midst of the water,
one should stand facing north and place a third part in the left hand.

One should consecrate [the disciple] seven times with the *caturaṅga* mantra, once with the *dakṣa*, seven times with the *hetin*, ten times with the *mūla* mantra while he stands upon the moon, and likewise for each respective portion.
Having cast [the water] consecrated with the *dik-astra* mantra, one should place that consecrated with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) into the water;
by merely rotating it around the arms, one should imagine it as the sacred ford of Śiva (*śivatīrtha*).

Having smeared all the limbs starting from the head with a portion of the mantra recited over the unguent, and having immersed himself while keeping his senses closed, he should meditate upon the flawless Śiva. (5.36)
Joining the hands, which consist of the sun and moon, with the *ghaṭamudrā*, the consecration (*seka*) should be performed once each with the mantras beginning with the root mantra. (5.37)
One should bathe with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances according to the royal ritual;
like a king, well-seated upon a golden throne and the like, one should be bathed with golden jars.
Having bathed, one should perform the act of immersion with auspicious sounds;
then, having withdrawn the mantras placed at the sacred site (tīrtha), one should deposit them within one's own heart. (5.39)
Alternatively, in one's own home, one should perform the bath while seated on a seat placed upon a smeared floor, using either pure cool water or warm water. (5.40)
With nine, eight, or five jars consecrated with the Śiva-mantras,
[he should bathe] the body with a pure, white cloth.
One should properly remove the bath water by rubbing [the body] very gently;
the rite pertaining to Agni, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be performed with pure ashes.
The bath with ashes is of four kinds, according to the distinctions of *kalpa* and so forth: *kalpa*, *anukalpa*, *upakalpa*, and *akalpaka*. (5.43)
Among those, the first is superior to the others because of its absence [of defects];
it is a cow free from disease and the like, whether black or tawny. (5.44)
Having taken cow-dung from that [place], while standing in the *kha* [posture], one should take the cow-dung with the *sadyojāta* mantra and form a ball with the *vāmadeva* mantra. (5.45)
Having dried it in a pure place, one should burn it with the fierce fire of Śiva;
likewise, cow dung that is dry, forest-grown, and powdered [should be used]. (5.46)
That which is called the "subsidiary rite" (anukalpa), consisting of ashes from a river or similar source that have been burnt,
wrapped in a cloth, and formed into a ball bound with cow's urine— 5/47.
That which has been burnt according to the previously mentioned procedure becomes "prepared ash" (kalpaka); ash brought forth by others is known as "unprepared" (akalpaka). (5.48)
O best of sages, bathing with that which is free from defects such as birth and devoid of diseases and the like is commendable; it is not so with anything else. (5.49)
Taking one of these [substances] in vessels such as bowls or jars,
one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day, or otherwise as circumstances permit.
Having first assumed the form of Brahmā at the morning twilight, the twice-born devotee of Śiva should perform the Śaiva Sandhyā, or otherwise the obligatory [Sandhyā] first. (5.51)
Having first performed the ritual bath in water, one should practice the Āgneya [rite] in the morning;
likewise, during the intervals between the *saṃdhyās*, one should perform either the Āgneya alone or that accompanied by the Vāruṇa.
For those who are capable, the rule is thus; for those who are incapable, it may be according to their desire.
The Āgneya bath yields incalculable fruit compared to the Vāruṇa bath.
Therefore, having abandoned the water-based bath, one should practice the fire-based bath;
being free from attachment, one should purify the object to be purified for the sake of purification. (5.54)
Just as the water of the Gaṅgā is pure, so too is the sacred ash purifying;
for that which is called "ash" (bhasma) illuminates, and it makes auspicious things shine.
Because it consumes all sins, it is celebrated as "ashes" (bhasma);
it is auspicious, purifying, and likewise serves as a necklace and an ornament. (5.56)
The daily ash-bath brings merit that brings the world under one's control;
those afflicted by fever, epilepsy, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas [are freed]. (5.57)
Merely by the application of this ash, mortals become healthy;
even after drinking liquor, approaching the wife of one's guru,
committing theft, or having committed the murder of a Brahmin.
Covered in ashes, lying upon a bed of ashes,
and reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.
The ash-bath possesses ten million times the merit of a water-bath;
therefore, an ascetic should always bathe by smearing himself with ashes while facing north.
Just as a householder, having taken [the ashes] by touching his limbs with *tilaka* marks or triple lines (*tripuṇḍraka*), should grasp a handful of ashes with his right hand. (5.60)
Having purified [the elements] through the yoga of retention and meditation and rendered them supreme,
one should likewise purify them by means of the root-mantra and the mantras of the Brahma-aṅgas.
Having placed the ashes on the left hand with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should perform the cleansing of impurities from the head downwards using the right hand and the Astra-mantra.
Having performed the ritual bath once more, one should carry out the consecration;
one should dust the body with ash using the Īśāna mantra, and the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.

The heart [should be consecrated] with the Ghoramantra, the secret [part] with the Vāma mantra, all the limbs with the Sadyojāta [mantra], and the six limbs beginning with the heart with the [respective] six limbs [mantras]. (5.64)
One should gently shake off dust from one's body with both the right and left hands,
but not in the presence of the Guru, fire, or deities, nor on a path.
On an impure ground, the wise man should perform an ash-bath;
for it is indeed recommended in certain cases when in the presence of a deity or near a fire.
The procedure for smearing [ashes] has been declared for a Brahmin in the teaching of Śiva;
if one is unable even to smear them, one should at least apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). || 5/67 ||
Brahmins and other householders should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rules;
for those of the royal, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, a single stripe (paṭṭapuṇḍra) should be placed on the forehead.
It is prescribed at the five, eight, two, eight, and eight joints:
the head, the forehead, the two ears, the two eyes, and likewise the two nostrils. (5.69)
The mouth, the neck, the two shoulders, the two upper arms, the two elbows, the two wrists, as well as the heart, the navel, the genitals, and likewise the anus. (5.70)
The thighs, the knees, the shanks, and likewise the buttocks—these belong to the eight forms (mūrtis) as well as to the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas). (5.71)
One should assign the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and the Vasus to the head and other parts:
the forehead, the two ears, the two shoulders, the two upper arms, and the wrists. (5.72)
The heart, the belly, the navel, the two sides, and likewise the back—these are to be known as the sixteen joints (sandhis) in sequence, beginning with the letter *ka*. (5.73)

In the same manner, the visualization of the forms beginning with Śiva and Agni, as well as those beginning with Vāmā, and the beloved [forms] of the two Aśvinīs, should be understood as being conceived starting from the head. (5.74)
The head, the forehead, the two ears, the two arms, the heart, the navel, and the back— these should be known as the eight joints in their respective order. (5.75)
In due order, it should be pleasing to Brahmā and the sages;
or it may be located at the five joints: the forehead, the arms, the heart, and the navel. (5.76)
For the sake of attaining the favor of Śiva, Īśa, Rudra, Kṛṣṇātman, and Bhūvan,
one should duly apply the Tripuṇḍra with the middle, index, and ring fingers.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for Brahmins should be six finger-breadths in measure;
for kings it should be four finger-breadths, and for Vaiśyas it should be two finger-breadths. (5.78)
All Śūdras as well, and likewise women, should apply the Tripuṇḍra with a single finger; however, those of other castes should avoid it. (5.79)
For women, however, the *tilaka* may be either in the shape of a cloth-strip (*paṭṭākāra*) or in the form of a lamp; it may also be a half-moon or a forehead-mark (*lalāmaka*). (5.80)
It is prescribed for all—men, women, and those of neutral gender—either ground with sandalwood or combined with water. (5.81)
Or rather, the ash-bath alone should be performed every single day—at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight—at all times. (5.82)
Whether three times a day, twice, once, or even just a single time, whoever performs the ash-bath as is appropriate; (5.83)
Freed from all sins, one shall accomplish the desired fruit by means of copper, lotus, coconut, stone, bamboo, gourd, or leather vessels. (5.84)
One should sip water with one's own hand; by that act alone, one does not become impure.
One may even take two *prasthas* of water provided it is sufficient for one's own needs. (5.85)

Then, having made the *tāla* mudrā, he should put on his loincloth; as for the garment, it may be very white, yellow, or dyed with decoction (kaṣāya), and he should wear the sacred thread (*upavītaka*). (5.86)
A loincloth is said to be one or two cubits in width and long;
the waist-string should be threefold and secured with two knots. (5.87)
The thread made of cotton should be tripled and then twisted three times over;
however, for Śūdras, the single thread should consist of two strands.
For Kṣatriyas, the thread should have three strands, while for Brāhmaṇas it should consist of seven;
alternatively, it may have five strands or even nine threads.
For Brahmins, it should be worn as an upper garment (*sottarīya*); for Śūdras, however, it is worn only in that manner.
As for the sacred thread (*upavītaka*) prescribed for the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes: [it is worn over the left shoulder and under the right arm]. (5.90)

At the time of reciting mantras for worship and other rites, one should consider whether the letters, in their forward order and so forth, are to be retained or indeed not retained, having deliberated upon what is appropriate and inappropriate.
According to the rules prescribed for the different castes, it should not be worn [in some cases], yet it must indeed be worn [in others];
the cord, tripled in length, should measure four finger-breadths.
Having multiplied that thread threefold according to the number of the sun’s rays (twelve),
one should, facing eastward, wind it out— sprinkled with water, level, and auspicious.
Then, having folded that [cloth] three times and evenly gathered its ends together, one should hold it above the right hand and avoid letting it touch the ground. (5.94)

Having placed that [offering] upon a tree or similar object, just as they had previously reached the ground, the satisfaction of the sages occurs through that delusion; then, after giving grass, there is purification.
One should contemplate all of that within the heart by means of the heart-mantra;
one desiring long life, however, should wear many double-stranded threads.
But one desiring other benefits should wear an odd number [of strands] and a very short thread;
thereafter, taking that thread, one should double it and place it around the neck.
Having brought the thread up to the tip of one's own breast, it is tripled by that very [hand];
having made three windings around the knot, the thread is thus prepared. (5.98)
If the measurement of the upper garment should increase by one barley-corn at a time, that same measurement is prescribed for the sacred thread as well. (5.99)

The sacred threads for the Brahmin and the other castes, in order, are to be worn with the *puruṣa*, *aghora*, *vāma*, and *ājama* mantras respectively, each according to the mantra prescribed for its own caste. (5.100)
For householders, the Vāruṇa rite is prescribed, while for ascetics, it is performed with ashes;
following these two types of bathing, the occasional (naimittika) bath is declared. (5.101)
One should perform the *aindra* [rite] during sunshine or rain, facing east with upturned palms, while recollecting the *mūrdhaja* mantra as one takes seven steps. (5.102)
One should perform the most excellent of all baths by means of the dust raised from the movement of herds of cows by the wind, using the very mantra of Puruṣa. (5.103)
Washing with water consecrated by the recitation of the *sadyojāta* and other mantras is prescribed as the ritual for the *māntra* bath,
which is also part of the procedure for the *vāruṇa* (water) bath.

Accompanied by the recollection of the *praṇava* and performed mentally through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), this is prescribed as that which should be done in all ablutions, or it may be performed alone. (5.105)
As long as there is no purification of the body, those who do not perceive [the truth] will have no purity;
he who is purified by the purity of his inner disposition is always pure, and no other. (5.106)

[One should avoid] donkeys, crows, vultures, outcastes, dogs, village pigs, cocks, ghosts, contact with the ground, corpses, those in a state of birth-impurity, and those who have committed sins. (5.107)
If one is touched by Śākyas, Nirgranthas, those who consume discarded offerings, those of other sectarian marks, or others who are censured, one should perform a bath. (5.108)
When two parts have entered the water and reached above the navel, purification occurs through washing below and bathing, with the exception of the hands. (5.109)
Bathing is prescribed in six instances: after vomiting, when the sun has risen, after shaving, after sexual intercourse, after a bad dream, and after touching a wicked person. (5.110)
Having washed his feet up to the knees and his hands up to the wrists,
he should assume the cock-posture (kukkuṭāsana), with his palms joined between his knees.
Having properly tied his topknot and facing either the east or the north, he should form his hand like a cow’s ear and drink water in which a single *māṣa* bean has been submerged. (5.112)
Having drunk three times from the root [of the thumb] using the Brahma-tīrtha—[the water] being free of living organisms, froth, bubbles, and the like—one should wipe the mouth twice. (5.113)
With the root of the thumb and the little finger joined together, one should touch the lips, the eyes, the nose, the ears, the arms, the chest, the navel, and the head. (5.114)

Afterwards, having performed the sipping of water (ācamana) along with mantras, one should drink water ending with the word *svadhā* using the auspicious seed-syllables (*śivāṇu*) of the Self-knowledge, and then wipe the lips with the *hetin* mantra.
Touching his eyes with the heart-mantra, he should perform [the rite] by moving to the left and right;
or else, the wise one may perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in another manner.
One should take water that has soaked a black gram (*māṣa*) and drink it three times without fault;
one should wipe the mouth twice with the *astra-mantra*, and having wiped the face once, one should gently cleanse it. (5.117)
Having sprinkled water on the feet and the head with the ring finger and the thumb, one should touch the left eye with the index finger and the thumb. (5.118)
Having touched both nostrils by joining the little finger with the thumb,
one should touch the ears and the two upper arms with the thumb moistened with water.
Having touched the region of the heart with the thumb and all the tips and joints of the fingers, one should then touch one's own head with all the fingers. (5.120)
Satisfaction from drinking is desired for the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas after three sips; likewise, there is satisfaction by wiping the lips twice for the Atharva Veda and the Itihāsas. (5.121)
By wiping the mouth, one pleases Gaṇeśa here;
by sprinkling the heart and the head, one indeed pleases the sages. (5.122)
By the mere touch of the two ears, Soma and Sūrya will be pleased;
by the mere touch of the nose, Aśvinī will likewise be pleased. (5.123)
By the mere touch of the ears, there shall likewise be joy in the directions;
and [joy] in the arms, the navel, and the heart of Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
Upon sneezing and when phlegm has been produced, one should immediately perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Then, having touched the ears, one should wipe the mouth with the thumb. (5.125)
The *tīrtha* at the base of the little finger is established as that of Prajāpati;
the *tīrtha* at the tip of the hand is divine (*daivika*), and at its base is the supreme *tīrtha* of Brahmā.
The *paitṛka* [mantra] is on the base of the little finger; the *ārṣaka* is at the joints of the fingers;
the *saumya* is on the palm of the left hand; and the *āgneya* is on the palm of the right hand. (5.127)
Having thus made his body complete with the ritual assignments (sakalīkṛta), he should then perform the twilight worship (sandhyā).
During the time of Brahmā, he should contemplate the Brāhmī Sandhyā, which is endowed with the qualities of Brahman. (5.128)
At midday, one should meditate upon the Vaiṣṇavī [form], characterized by all the attributes of Acyuta;
at evening, however, one should meditate upon the Raudrī [form], marked by the characteristics of Rudra.
That power of the Supreme Lord which governs the three forms and is the witness of all actions is called Sandhyā. (5.130)
Having entered into the midst of its radiance, one should accomplish the rites in the morning;
then, according to the sequence of the *melā* mantras, one should again recite the *śambhuśakti*. (5.131)
Then, that salutation should be performed preceded by the recitation of the great mantra;
immediately thereafter, the ritual action following the sprinkling (of water) should be carried out.
Having placed water in the left hand, one should apply it to the dripping head daily with the right hand, using the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the Brahma mantras. (5.133)
Furthermore, having drawn in with a pūraka through the right nostril the remaining water held in the right hand, like the lightning of the sun; 5.134.
The right hand, together with water, should be placed near the right nostril;
by that water, the black-colored sin within the body is utterly consumed. (5.135)
One should contemplate [the breath] as it issues forth from the right nostril during exhalation;
then, by casting water held in the right hand, one should perform the rite with the Śiva-weapon (śivāstra).

Having thus performed the cleansing and other rites, one should then commence the libation (tarpaṇa), which consists of the offering of water to the gods and others with appropriate materials. (5.137)
The libation with both hands is prescribed; it is remembered as the libation for three:
the mantras, the deities, and Speech (Vāṇī), as well as the directions and their respective lords. (5.138)
Then the sages, as well as humans, the Siddhas, the planets, the spirits, the ancestors, and others—relatives and teachers alike—[were present]. (5.139)
Those seeking success should offer libations according to the rule, with the word *svāhā*, to the deities of the mantras as well as to Sarasvatī. (5.140)
For the lords of the directions and the sages, one should append "namaḥ" at the end; for humans, "vaṣaṭ"; and for the Siddhas and the hosts of planets, one should arrange "namaḥ" at the end. (5.141)
For the spirits (bhūtas), the mantra should end with *vauṣaṭ*; for the ancestors (pitṛs) and others, it should end with *svadhā*.
Everything should be preceded by the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*); the flower is for the propitiation of the deities. (5.142)
Kusa grass is prescribed for the sages, and sesame seeds for the ancestors and others;
for the remaining [deities], one should perform the rite with unbroken grains (akṣata), wearing the sacred thread (upavīta) as appropriate. // 5.143 //

O best of sages, the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder and under the right arm, then over the right shoulder and under the left arm—this constitutes the triad; the mantras for these are the Mūla-mantra, the Brahma-mantras, and the Aṅga-mantras.
Śiva, Īśa, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Abjabhū are proclaimed as the gods; Vāgvādinī is Vāṇī (Speech), and Indra and the others are remembered as the directions.
Indra and the other lords, ending with Brahmā and Ananta,
as well as Atri, Viśvāmitra, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu— 5/146.
Vasiṣṭha and Marīci are proclaimed as sages;
from them came the humans: Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana. (5.147)
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Bhṛgu, and Pañcaśikha; likewise Śiva, Rudra, Bhavānī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Vāyu. (5.148)
Dharma, Sūrya, Candramas, and the Siddhas are proclaimed as these; likewise Āditya, Soma, Aṅgāra, Budha, and Bṛhaspati. (5.149)
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are known as the planets (grahas).
One should apply [the principle] "from the elements (bhūta) [arise] beings (bhūta) of innumerable number. (5.150)
Soma, Pitṛmān, Aṅgiras, Aryaman, Agni, Kavyavāhana, and others are proclaimed to be the Pitṛs (ancestors). || 5.151 ||
Having understood everything, beginning with the father’s wives, in due order, one should perform the rites;
having sipped water (ācamana), one should offer the arghya to the Sun with the three-syllabled mantra.
The procedure for that will be explained in detail in the worship of the Sun:
having meditated upon the Sun according to the rule, one should perform the ritual attendance through the six limbs. (5.153)
Then, having recited the *melā-mantra* according to the division of Śiva and Śakti, O lords of sages, one should stand in the morning and remain seated in the evening. (5.154)
Whether sitting or standing, one should perform the ritual at midday;
then, having performed the worship (upasthāna), one should likewise recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra. (5.155)
One should recite the *udutyam*, the *citram*, and the *haṃsaḥ śuciṣad* mantras;
then, having performed a circumambulation, one should offer prostrations like a staff. (5.156)
One should always perform the twilight worship; if it is omitted, one should fast for a day.
If one is healthy but becomes afflicted by disease, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times immediately.
Having carefully wrapped the washed bathing cloth and other items around the staff,
one should worship Gaṇeśa, Rudra, and Vāgīśa with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having dispelled obstacles and protected his body by means of mantras at the path and the site, he should proceed either to a temple or to his own excellent home. (5.159)
Then, through the sequence of purification, one should conceive of the lower principles (tattvas) beginning with earth;
the temple, consisting of the principle of Vidyā, bestows the fruits of both worldly accomplishment and liberation. (5.160)

Having concentrated upon the tantras and mantras near an auspicious ivory peg, he should wash his feet and hands and likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules. (5.161)

With his body armored by mantras, holding the general *arghya* in his hand, and being pure, the wise practitioner, casting off the portion of the remaining path, should enter the temple (*prāsāda*). (5.162)
O best of sages, thus has the bathing and other rites been briefly described, which are the support for all mantra arts and the impeller of all powers. 5.163
"A wise person should practice by collecting what has not been stated from other tantras.
Thus ends the third chapter, the ritual for bathing, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The beginning of the chapter on the ritual procedure for worship.
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That [worship] is proclaimed to be of two kinds: for the sake of others and for one's own sake. (6.1)

At the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā), when the emblem (liṅga) or the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and so forth have been bestowed by the Guru, worship for one's own sake is prescribed, because it bestows the desired fruits upon oneself. (6.2)
Whether in a village, a hamlet, a city, or the like; by a river or even on a mountain; in the sixty-eight great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) or elsewhere in a delightful place. (6.3)
In a temple of Śiva endowed with a self-manifested (svayambhu), divine (daiva), arrow-born (bāṇa), or ṛṣi-liṅga,
as well as in a liṅga installed by men for the sake of others, worship for the benefit of another is prescribed.
For the increase of the king’s lifespan, health, victory, and prosperity, and for the sake of expanding villages and other domains, let worship be performed for the sake of others. (6.5)
The Śiva-brahmins must constantly perform sacrifices for the sake of others;
the righteous and foremost of the twice-born, who is a true devotee of Śiva, performs this daily. (6.6)
But others, if they perform [the rite] other than for their own sake, would bring about the destruction of the performer;
those, however, who are born from the mouth of Brahmā without the creation of Śiva [are exempt]. (6.7)
They are equal [in status], yet they have no entitlement to perform sacrifices for the sake of others;
if, out of delusion, they should do so, it would bring about the destruction of the king and the kingdom. (6.8)
If ordinary Brahmins worship Śiva for the sake of gain, they fall from their status within six months; therefore, one should avoid them. (6.9)
For the wise Śiva-brahmin who has been consecrated by the initiation of Śiva, performing sacrifice for the sake of others under the authority of Śiva’s command incurs no fault. (6.10)
The Agnihotra rites, the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees—even all these together—are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga. (6.11)
He who, though born as his own son, has not worshipped the Blessed Lord Śiva, wanders for a very long time in this saṃsāra, an ocean of suffering. (6.12)
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head than to eat without having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord.
Knowing this, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped with diligent effort;
having washed the feet up to the ankles and the hands up to the wrists.
The task consists of the removal of the three kinds of obstacles from the temple;
they are traditionally held to be of three types: celestial, those moving through the sky, and those on the ground. (6.15)
But according to the true view, one should remove from the temple the divine offerings of flowers suspended in the sky by three strikes of the heel, as well as those on the ground. (6.16)
The best linga faces west; in the absence [of that], it is traditionally taught to face east. However, facing south or north is not approved by the wise for the sake of accomplishment. (6.17)
Alternatively, in rites for pacification and the like, it is desired that [the deity] face the north;
this rule applies to the Niṣkala [form] in palaces with a single entrance.
(Verse 6.19) At Meru and other such sites, as well as at the four-faced Liṅga,
a four-gated [mandala] should be constructed; there is no fixed rule regarding this.
One should designate as the east that direction in which the door is located;
however, that door which faces the liṅga is considered to be the east. (6.20)
In that case, the Tatpuruṣa face should be facing upwards, and the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), the bull, and the trident should be facing toward that face. (6.21)
One should worship Gaṇapa and Bhāratī above; on the right branch, Gaṅgā and Nandin;
and on the left branch, Yamunā and Mahākāla. (6.22)
O Four-faced One, Nandī and Kāla, as well as Bhṛṅgī, Vighneśa, Vṛṣa, and Ṣaṇmukha, along with the Goddess and the two Caṇḍas, are stationed on the two sides of the doors. (6.23)

These [deities] are to be worshipped in due order with their heart-mantras and so forth ending in "namaḥ," and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to their respective forms, postures, and dispositions. (6.24)
Then, having offered the general arghya and taking hold of the left branch,
the Guru should enter the interior of the temple with his right foot.
Having placed a sword in the udumbara post for the purpose of warding off obstacles, one should worship the Self-born Lord (Brahmā) with the mantra "vāstoṣpate" and also with "brahmaṇe. (6.26)
Having circumambulated the Liṅga with devotion and praised Maheśvara, all the perfumes, flowers, and other offerings brought by his attendants were presented. (6.27)
Having surveyed the collection of materials, the wise one should place the jars;
these, having been inspected with the vision of reality, are then sprinkled with the weapon-mantra.
Having taken up jars that have been struck and sprinkled—jars with beautiful necks and mouths, very stable, and free from cracks—one should go outside. (6.29)
One should pray, "I worship you," in whatever manner is appropriate;
having reached the sacred site of Śiva (śivatīrtha), one should consecrate it with the six-limbed mantra (ṣaḍaṅga).
Having washed the water-pots and the cloths with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
one should fill them with water dripping from the cloth while reciting the Rudragāyatrī and the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Then, having wiped the full jars with their respective cloths,
he should hold them two by two, joined by a yoke, with each hand individually.

Having taken it, one should bring it either to the front of the inner sanctum or to the pavilion, taking care not to let it touch the door-frames or other parts situated at the sides of the thighs. (6.33)
The wise man should act in such a way that the water does not spill upon the ground;
having smeared the ground, he should spread kuśa grass, flowers, and so forth, while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra. (6.34)
One should place there the *vardhanī* jar and eight jars, or alternatively, fifty-five jars corresponding to the fifty-five syllables of the *kṣamāloka* mantra. (6.35)
Alternatively, having installed [the deity] according to the number of transformations, or twice that number,
or by means of the rite of bathing (snāna), one should perform the daily consecration (nityābhiṣecana).
The purification of oneself is the first; the purification of the place is the second;
the purification of the ritual materials (dravya) is the third; and the purification of the mantra is the fourth. (6.37)
The fifth is the purification of the ritual implement; these are said to be the five purifications.
Whether in a consecrated abode, one that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, or elsewhere, the wise man [should proceed]. (6.38)
Then, having assumed a comfortable posture upon a seat well-prepared with *kuśa* grass, a *bṛsī*, or a black antelope skin, one should sit with the body straight and facing north. (6.39)
One should purify those two hands, which have been smeared with sandalwood paste, by means of the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
while touching the palms, the backs of the hands, and the fingers against one another.
Having rendered them immortal with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should meditate upon the supreme nature of those two as the body of the Vidyā, up to the end of their power (*śakti*).
Having invoked Śiva with the root mantra, one should assign the Brahmāṇīs as the limbs;
a householder, moreover, should perform the ritual assignment on the hands (karanyāsa) according to the path of emanation.
For forest-dwellers and ascetics, the dissolution-nyāsa (saṃhāranyāsa) is taught:
beginning from the thumb and ending with the little finger, starting from Īśāna and concluding with Sadyojāta. (6.43)

The *sṛṣṭinyāsa* (creation-assignment) is fully described as beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna; the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-assignment) is said to proceed from the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) to the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*).
In this context, the sequence is indeed the same as the process of the creation and dissolution of the universe.
Having placed the eye upon the palm of the hand, one should subsequently perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).

From the thumb to the little finger, and from the little finger to the thumb; the placement on the index finger and the thumb should likewise be performed with the thumb upon all [the fingers]. (6.46)
The wise one should place [the mudrās] ending with the index finger; he should place the index finger on the head.
Alternatively, he should place them starting from the thumb on the armor, crest, heart, and weapon. (6.47)
For those desiring liberation, the placement [of mantras] in reverse order is the dissolution;
that which begins from the head is called creation, while that which begins from the feet would be dissolution. (6.48)
One should again place the seed-syllables of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) on the thumb and the other fingers;
having rendered them nectar-like through meditative absorption, one should enclose them with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Thus, the hands, having been made auspicious (śivīkṛta), are capable for all rites:
for the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, at the time of twilight prayers, and likewise for the sipping of water (ācamana). (6.50)
The ritual placement (karanyāsa) should be performed according to its specific rules, having restrained the mind pervading the body by means of the mudrā of withdrawal (saṃhāramudrā). 6/51.
In the base of the hollow of the heart-lotus, or in Śiva, or in the stainless void;
[the centers are] the heart, throat, palate, brow, the conch, the rodhinī, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Kuṭilā, Vyāpinī, Tanvī, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā;
a person should unite [the breath] with that Śakti which is above them, or with her. (6.53)
Having first performed the visualization, one should immediately burn the body;
this yoga must be performed by the teachers for the sake of protecting the karma that is to be experienced. (6.54)
The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes in an instant;
however, O God, regarding action pertaining to liberation, there is no dissolution of it by the power of divine command. (6/55)
The power of concealment belongs to Śiva, the Supreme Lord;
it is fully established as the cause of the world's creation, dissolution, experience, and so forth. (6.56)
Just as gold mixed with impurities, when purified by fire, remains as something stainless with all defects destroyed; so too does this [Self] remain. (6.57)
Thus, with the flood of his sins destroyed by means of the *dhāraṇās*, the person becomes stainless; yet, by the force of his residual *adhikāra*, he again assumes embodied existence. (6.58)
The man who has been initiated is said to be truly liberated while living; having performed this union, he should thereafter contemplate the principles (tattvas). (6.59)
Whether it be the three principles, the five principles, or even the nine principles;
or twenty-five, thirty-six, or even one; or indeed the internal principle. (6.60)
Whatever has been taught regarding initiation, one should perform that here as well;
I shall now describe the purification according to the sequence of the five principles for the sake of purifying the body. (6.61)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti belong to the ether;
by these very kalās, this entire world is pervaded. (6.62)
In this world, mantras are pervaded on all sides by words and letters;
letters are pervaded by worlds, and those [worlds] are pervaded by the principles (tattvas). (6.63)
In this world, those principles (tattvas) are pervaded by the kalās in sequence;
having thus contemplated them as containing the fivefold paths (adhvan), they are to be purified. 6/64.
That meditation which, accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma), is performed at each lunar phase (parvan) according to the color, signs, forms, and qualities of the mantra and its presiding deity.
Therefore, in this context, dhāraṇā is said to be like the extraction of poison and so forth;
the earthly [element] is square, golden-hued, and marked with a thunderbolt. (6.66)
The seed-syllable *la* has Brahmā as its deity and consists of the unborn heart;
it is endowed with the kalā called Nivṛtti and the five protracted vowels (*uddhāta*) of the syllable *haṃ*. (6.67)

The element of water is marked by the moon, the white lotus, and the conch; its presiding deity is Viṣṇu, its seed-syllable is *va*, it is joined with the vowel *vāma* (the first vowel *a*), and it is endowed with the digit of *pratiṣṭhā*.
One should perform [the visualization] joined with the four *uddhātas* preceded by the utterance of "Hrīṃ":
the fire is triangular, seven-flamed, red in appearance, and has Rudra as its presiding deity. (6.69)
It is joined with the *rārṇa* [mantra] and the *aghora-śikhā*, endowed with the digit (*kalā*) known as *vidyā*, and conjoined with three *udghātas* together with the utterance of "hrūm. (6.70)
The northwest is the corner of taste (rasakoṇa), followed by six black dots;
the letter Ya presided over by Īśa is joined with the Tatpuruṣa and Kavaca [mantras].
Accompanied by the *śānti* [mantra], preceded by the utterance of "haṃ," one should visualize the sky as circular, devoid of marks, and smoke-colored. (6.72)

Having uttered the letter *ha* together with its location (*sadeśa*), its presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhita*), and its union with the transcendent Lord (*atīteśa*), one should apply it to its proper place by means of a single upward expulsion (*ekodghāta*). // 6.73 //
The earthly element resides in the heart; the watery element is located in the throat; the fiery element is at the root of the palate; and that which arises from air is between the eyebrows. (6.74)

The space-element (vyoman), joined with the Brahma-knot, is situated at the crown of the head, or it is considered otherwise; the earth is to be known as extending down to the knees, and that which is above the navel is declared to be the water-element (āpya). (6/75)
The fire [element] is from the region of the throat up to the circle of the mouth;
above that is the station of space (gagana), which is proclaimed for the purpose of concentration (dhāraṇā). (6.76)
I shall describe breath control (prāṇāyāma) in brief and in detail:
one should practice it in three ways—exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka). (6.77)
The syllables *a*, *u*, and *m* are proclaimed as the phonemes;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are proclaimed as their presiding deities. (6.78)
The principles (tattvas) known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva should be [visualized] in their respective order.
The lowest [form] is devoid of twelve mātrās; the middle one is considered to have double that amount.
The time for each of the [three], beginning with exhalation (recaka), is three units (triguṇa).
One should exhale the impure air residing within the body and situated in the ether. (6.80)
Having slowly drawn in pure air by means of inhalation (pūraka),
one should remain like a completely filled jar (kumbhaka) and then exhale it.
Having bound the uvula to the palate through the practice of uttering the syllable *phaṭ*,
one should cause the [knot] to burst by means of the *pāśupata* weapon, thereby releasing the bondage.
Then, at those various times, the piercing of the knots must also be meditated upon;
for by that upward progression, this individual soul attains one station after another. (6.83)
Having performed the subtle prāṇāyāma, one should act as if the body were a flute;
together with Śiva, it reaches its end through the bursting of the knots by means of the upward thrust (udghāta). (6.84)

Having visualized the tree of saṃsāra as having its roots above and its branches below, the wise one who knows what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted should, by means of half the inhalation, [place it] upon the earth element. (6.85)
It is nourished by the power of Varuṇa from the latter part of the inhalation;
it is endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and is made glossy by the sword of dispassion.
Having cut [the body] and then dried it with the *kumbhaka* breath in the southeast, it is completely consumed by the fire of knowledge from the big toe up to the end of the head. (6.87)

Then, by means of the *recaka* [exhalation], one should contemplate the ten directions as reduced to ashes; by the final [breath], one should meditate upon the pure, stainless void into which everything has dissolved. (6.88)
Having agitated Mahāmāyā, one should fashion the body consisting of Śakti;
then, having flooded it with nectar, one should install the limbs of the Vidyā.
Having invoked the Self there— whose eyes are the powers of will, knowledge, and action, and whose essence is Mātṛkā— with the flower-mantra and the mudrā.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts. (6.91)
One should place Sadyojāta on the feet, accompanied by its respective mudrā;
one should then assign the Mālā-Brahmāṇi from the head down to the feet.
The wise one should place [the mantras] starting from Īśa in the faces facing upward, south, north, and west;
or he may place the seed-syllable Brahmās, or he may place the thirty-eight kalās.
"Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," ending with "namaḥ," is on the upper head;
"Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām," ending with "namaḥ," is on the eastern head. (6.94)
"Brahmaṇe adhipatiḥ brahma" ending with "namaḥ" is for the head of Yama;
likewise, "śivo me astu" ending with "namaḥ" is for the head of Kubera. (6.95)
One should place Sadāśiva, ending with "namaḥ," upon the head in the water-element; one should likewise arrange the five kalās of Īśāna, preceded by the Praṇava.
Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Iṣṭā, Marīci, and Jvālinī are likewise [the deities] of the Īśāna-kalās; they may be worshipped by those very names alone. (6.97)

One should first place the digit (kalā) upon the upward-facing mouth with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ); then, ending with "salutation" (*namaḥ*), one should place [the mantra] "tatpuruṣāya vidmahe" upon the eastern-facing mouth.
One should contemplate Mahādeva, ending with "namas" for the southern face; and for the northern face, one should arrange it ending with "namaḥ," saying "tanno rudra namas. (6.99)
And ending with "pracodayāt" and "namaḥ," it should be assigned to the western face;
there should be four kalās on the face, and the unmanifest (avyakta) kalā should be at the head.
Peace, knowledge, stability, and cessation—these are the kalās.
One bows even to those who are not terrible (aghora) within the sphere of the Heart. (6.101)
Then, one should place *natyanta* at the throat; one should place *mohāṃ* followed by *ghoranamaḥ* for protection upon the right shoulder.
One should place "niṣṭhāṃ" and "ghoratarebhyaḥ" on the left shoulder,
and one should place "mṛtyuṃ" and "sarvataḥ sarva-namaḥ" at the navel. (6.103)
Having uttered "Salutation to all," one should place Māyā in the belly;
with "Salutation to you, O Rudra" up to the end, one should place Abhayā on the back.
One should offer salutations preceded by the *praṇava* to the forms [of the mantra] ending with *jarāmaraḥ*;
then, one should assign the eight digits (*kalā*) of the manifold form (*bahurūpa*) to the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).
One should place the syllable *ra* ending with "salutation to Vāmadeva" in the secret organ;
one should place the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) ending with "salutation to Jyeṣṭha" upon the *liṅga*. (6.106)
One should place [the mantra] ending with "salutation to Rudra" upon the right thigh for Rati; one should bring [the mantra] ending with "salutation to Kāla" upon the left thigh for Pālī.
One should place "Kāmāṃ kalanamontāṃ" on the right knee,
and "Vikaraṇāya namaḥ" on the left knee.
One should place the mantra "Kriyāyai balanāya namaḥ" on the right shank,
and "Buddhyai vikaraṇāya namaḥ" on the left shank.
One should place the mantra ending with "balanamaḥ" on the right hip,
and the mantra "dhātrīṃ pramathanāya namaḥ" on the left hip.
One should place the word "namas" at the end of the name of a Brāhmaṇī woman, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*;
then one should formulate a single word for the purpose of subduing all beings. (6.111)
Having bowed with "natyantam" to the one called Manas on the right side, and having bowed with "unmanāya" to Bhava on the left side; 6.112.
Thus, the thirteen kalās of Vāmadeva have been proclaimed;
one attains success by taking refuge in Sadyojāta on the right foot. (6.113)
One should place "Sadyojātāya vai namaḥ" on the left foot, and one should place "Bhavāya namaḥ" ending with "namaḥ" on the right arm.
Having uttered "Abhave Namaḥ," one should place Lakṣmī on the left hand;
one should place Medhā with "Natyambhave" ending in "Namaḥ" at the tip of the nose.
One should place *bhava* ending with *mām* and *kāntim* upon the head; one should place *svadhā* ending with *bhavanam* on the right arm.
One should place "Udbhavāya Namaḥ" on the left arm,
and then assign all eight Sadyojāta-kalās with their respective mudrās.
Having fashioned the body of the Vidyā through the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās,
and having invoked the root mantra, one should subsequently perform the placement of the limbs (aṅgas).
Having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head;
having placed the crest-mantra on the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
Having placed the weapons upon the two hands, one should then perform the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa):
the lamp (dīpaka), the vāgbhava syllable, the bindu, and then the word "to Śrīkaṇṭha."
One should place [the mantra] "Oṃ Pūrṇodarīyai namaḥ" at the region of the hairline;
then one should again place "Oṃ Āṃ Anantāya Virajāyai Natiḥ. (6.121)
One should place the mantra "Dīpādyam" on the forehead; then, for the sake of the subtle [deity], one should likewise place the mantra "Śālmalyai namaḥ" on the right eye.
One should place "Oṃ Īṃ, salutation to Trimūrti Lolākṣī" in the middle of the left eye, followed immediately by the syllable Oṃ. (6.123)
Then, one should assign [the mantra] "to Amareśvara" and again "salutation to Vartulākṣī" to the right ear; immediately following this, one should assign the syllable *Om* and the syllable *Mūm*.
Then, one should place [the mantra] "Arghīśāya" and also "Dīrghaghoṇāyai namaḥ" on the left ear; furthermore, one should install the syllable *oṃ* there. (6.125)
And again, one should place "namaḥ" to the long-faced one for the sake of the success of one's burden;
immediately thereafter, one should place the syllable *oṃ ṛṃ* in the right nostril.
One should place the foot [of the mantra] for the Lord of the Treasury (Nidhaneśa), namely "Oṃ, salutation to the foremost of cows," in the left nostril, followed immediately by the syllable *ḷ*.
Salutation to Sthāṇu and Dīrghajihvā on the right cheek;
first the word "Oṃ Ḷṃ," and then the word "Harāya. (6.128)
One should place "Salutation to Kuṇḍodarī" on the left cheek;
first the word "Oṃ," and then the word "Caṇḍīśāya."
One should perform the placement [of mantras] on the upper lip with "ūrdhvakeśyai namaḥ";
then, having extracted "oṃ aiṃ", one should again place the word "bhautikāya".

The word *pada* should be placed at the beginning of the modifications and the principal [mantras], but not on the lower lip. Then, having extracted the syllable *oṃ*, there is the word *sadyojātāya*. (6.131)
One should place [the mantra] "Jvālāmukhyai namaḥ" on the upper teeth;
and again, "Oṃ auṃ anugraheśāya ulkāmukhyai namaḥ. (6.132)
The supreme practitioner should place [the mantra] upon the lower row of teeth;
having extracted the syllable *oṃ*, he should then add the word *krūrāya*. (6.133)
Having placed "śrīmukhyai namaḥ" upon the head, one should meditate;
then, having extracted the syllable "oṃ," [one places] the word "mahāsenāya. (6.134)
One should assign these vowels to the mouth with the mantra "Salutation to Vidyā"; then, having extracted the syllable *oṃ-kaṃ*, one should again utter the word "to Krodhīśa. (6.135)
One should place [the mantra] "Salutation to Mahākālī" on the right arm;
then, having extracted the syllable *khaṃ*, one should again utter the word "Caṇḍeśāya. (6.136)
One should place [the mantra] "Salutation to Sarasvatī" on the right elbow;
then, having extracted the syllable *Gaṃ*, one should utter the word "to the Destroyer of the Five" (*pañcāntakāya*).
That which follows the salutation to Sarvasiddhigaurī should be at the right wrist; there should be the syllable *oṃ*, followed by the syllable *ghaṃ*. (6.138)
Having extracted the word "padaṃ śivottamāya" according to the prescribed rule,
one should place the salutation "namas trailokyavandyāyai" upon the surface of the right palm.
Having extracted the syllable *ṅaṃ*, one should place [the mantra] "to Ekarudra, to the state [of that], obeisance to the power of the mantra" at the tip of the right hand. (6.140)
Having extracted the syllable *caṃ*, followed by the word *kūrmāya* and then *ātmaśaktyai namaḥ*, one should place it upon the left arm. (6.141)
Having extracted the syllable *oṃ chaṃ*, one should place the mantra "to Ekanetra" and "salutation to Bhūtamātṛ" on the left elbow. (6.142)
Oṃ jaṃ, for the four-faced one; ending with "namo lambodaryai.
On the left wrist, however, there should be oṃ followed by jhaṃ. (6.143)
One should assign "Ajeśāya padam" and then "drāviṇyai namaḥ" to the palm of the left hand, followed immediately by the syllable "Oṃ Ñaṃ."
There should be a prostration with the tips of the left hands toward the city of Candra; then, having uttered "Oṃ Ṭaṃ," the word "Someśāya" follows again. (6/145)
One should perform the placement [of mantras] with "Khecaryai namaḥ" at the base of the right thigh; then, having extracted the syllable "Oṃ Ṭhaṃ," [one recites] the mantra "Lāṅgaline namaḥ. (6/146)
One should place "namaḥ mañjaryai" on the right knee;
then, having uttered the syllable "ḍaṃ," one should again utter the word "dārukāya. (6.147)
One should place [the mantra] "Oṃ Rūpiṇyai Namaḥ" on the tip of the right calf; and that which is the word consisting of the syllable "Ḍhaṃ" is for Ardhanārīśvara. (6.148)
And with the mantra "vīrāyai ca naḥ," one should place [the seed-syllable] on the sole of the right foot;
having extracted the syllable "ṇaṃ," one should utter the word "umākāntāya. (6/149)
Saying "khādiryai namaḥ," [he should place it] thus on the tip of the sole of the right foot;
having extracted the syllable *taṃ* (*oṃ taṃ*), he should utter the word "ṣaḍīśāya. (6.150)
Saying "Salutation to Pūtanā," one should place [the mantra] at the base of the left thigh;
then, having extracted the syllable *thaṃ*, one should again utter the word for Ḍiṇḍin. (6.151)
One should place [the mantra] "Salutation to Bhadrakālī" on the left knee;
then, having extracted the syllable *daṃ*, one should again utter the word "to Atri. (6.152)
One should place "Gomatyai namaḥ" on the tip of the left calf;
then, having extracted the syllable "Dhaṃ," one should again utter the word "Īśānāya. (6.153)
One should place "śaṃkhinyai namaḥ" on the sole of the left foot;
having extracted the syllable "oṃ naṃ," one should utter the word "meṣāya. (6.154)
"Salutation to Garjinī"—with these words [one should touch] the tip of the left sole;
"Oṃ Paṃ, salutation to Lohitāya and to Kālārātri"—this is the mantra for the foot. (6.155)
One should place "Oṃ Phaṃ, obeisance to Śikhinī" on the right side, and likewise one should place "Obeisance to Kubjinī" on the left side. (6.156)
Having extracted the syllable *oṃ baṃ*, one should place the mantra "to Chagalaṇḍa, obeisance to Kāminī" on the back part. (6.157)
Having extracted the syllable *Bhaṃ*, one should place the mantra "Oṃ Bhaṃ Dviraṇḍāya Vajrāyai Namaḥ" in the region of the navel. (6.158)
Oṃ maṃ mahākālāya, and likewise jayāyai namaḥ—one should place these at the region of the heart; and [the mantra] oṃ yaṃ, which is the word for that, belongs to the self of the skin. (6.159)
One should place [the mantra] on the skin with "Salutation to Pālinī Sumukheśvarī.
Then, [one should place it] with "Oṃ Raṃ, to the one whose essence is blood (raktātmane)," followed by the word "bhujaṅgāya" (to the serpent).
The phrase "Revatyai namaḥ" is for the sphere of blood;
and the phrase "Oṃ laṃ vasātmane pinākine" is for Pinākin.
One should place the word "mādhavyai namaḥ" pertaining to the flesh;
then again, "Oṃ vaṃ medomayāya khaḍgīśāya. (6.162)
One should place this phrase, "vāruṇyai namaḥ," upon the fat;
and one should utter "oṃ śaṃ asthyātmane ca" for the sake of the bone. (6.163)
One should place this word, "vāyavyai namaḥ," upon the bone;
and one should utter the word for Śveta as "oṃ ṣaṃ majjātmane. (6.164)

One should place the word *pada* for the one who wears protective armor; then, one should place the word *majjagataṃ* (situated in the marrow), followed by *oṃ saṃ śuklātmane* (Oṃ Saṃ, to the self that is white) and then extract the word *bhṛguve*. (6.165)
One should place the words "sahajāyai namaḥ" upon the semen;
and the word for Lakulīśa is "oṃ haṃ prāṇātmane. (6/166)
One should place this mantra in the heart:
"Oṃ laṃ, salutation to the Liṅga-self, which is the state belonging to that which consists of the form of darkness. (6.167)
One should place "Salutation to Vyāpinī" at the base of the liṅga;
then "Oṃ Kṣaṃ, to the Self of Wrath," and the word "to Vartakāya. (6.168)
One should place the word "māyāyai namaḥ" upon the tip of the *liṅga*;
one should then fashion the limbs of the Mātṛkā using the phonemes residing in the locations beginning with the heart. (6.169)

First, the line of the lamp (Dīpalekhā) and the two *hasas*; likewise, the final letter of *bhānta* (the letter *ha*) and the breast (*ku*), the two eyes (*cakṣus*), and the peak (*kūṭa*), joined with the heart-mantra and the other seed-syllables. (6.170)
O ascetics, this six-limbed [mantra] of Mātṛkā has been declared.
One should join the first [syllable] with the middle, or else join the first with that which follows the middle;
this is known as the *kīla* (the pinning), wherein one should write down the form of oneself as it moves about.

For the successful accomplishment of the mantra, one should recite the entire mantra in its written form according to the rules of phonetic combination (saṃyoga) and logical application; having joined and then dissolved the *kīla*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). (6.171)
Having understood this through the application of the *kīla*, one should perform everything in the proper sequence:
the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapons. (6.172)

*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are the [six] classes. Having thus performed the placement of the letters (*lipinyāsa*), one should place the ninefold set of principles (*tattva*). (6.173)
In the lunar orb and in the *nāda*, in the space between the eyebrows and the cavity of the palate, and in the regions of the throat, heart, and navel—that is, in the eternal seats. (6.174)
One should duly place the mantra as stated in the throat at the root location;
the three-syllable mantra, joined with the *melanā*, [should be placed] at the navel, the heart, and the forehead. (6.175)
Thereafter, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Vyomavyāpin mantra, beginning from the head and ending at the thumbs;
thus, having attained the state of a mantra, [the practitioner] comes to possess a divine body in due order.
One should designate the locations for worship, fire-oblation, and meditative absorption:
the rite of worship is to be performed in the heart, while one should arrange the fire-oblation at the navel. (6.177)
One should meditate on Īśvara, the bestower of boons, facing in all directions, upon the forehead;
one should conceive of him as the abode in the heart according to the procedure for the invocation of Īśvara.
One should prepare a seat here according to the procedure to be described;
having invoked the Lord, one should worship Śiva with mental offerings of fragrance and other articles.
Having kindled one's own fire by means of the restrained movement of the apāna, one should satisfy it with the supreme nectars arising from its own nature within the pit of the navel. (6.180)
One should meditate upon the Liṅga, brilliant like crystal and intensely radiant, in the place of the post;
having visualized Śiva situated within it, one should attain absorption into that oneness. (6.181)
Having filled [the body] through the *iḍā*, worship is performed; one should shake the nectar through the *piṅgalā*.
Having caused the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to enter the foundation (*ādhāra*), one should bind the knot along with its root.
Having filled [the body] through the *devanāḍī*, one should practice meditation upon the bow;
or else, one should perform the mental sacrifice (*mānasayāga*) with devotion in detail.
Having meditated upon the deity residing there— whose own essence consists of the principles (tattva) from Śiva down to the earth and who is the life-force of all— one should arrange the three sides.

One should meditate upon the fourfold group of principles (tattvas) as residing within the three groups: the seat (āsana), the side of the embodied form (mūrtipakṣa), and likewise the side of Śambhu. 6.185.
In this expansive body, having conceived the seat called Śakti,
and having conceived the form of Śiva as the body of Mūrtividyā, one should then invoke Him. (6.186)
In the pericarp, one should worship the God surrounded by the Brahma-mantras and the limbs [of the deity],
as well as by the Gaṇeśas, the world-protectors, and the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt.
One should worship according to one's ability with either three obstructions, or a single obstruction, or twenty-seven obstructions. (6.188)
With substances fashioned by the mind, in a temple fashioned by the mind, one should constantly worship the Supreme Lord while contemplating him with the mind. (6.189)
Just as a teacher who meditates upon the state of Garuḍa obtains the fruit of being free from poison, so too in this case one shall obtain the desired result. (6.190)
Just as one performs a sacrifice by means of the cessation of the vital breath (prāṇa-vṛtti), so too should one cause the reversal and expulsion of all those who act unrighteously. (6.191)
Having worshipped the five Brahmans with the Śaktis, as well as the limbs of Śiva, the Mūrti, Maheśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva, one should then perform the exhalation (recaka).

Likewise, in the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara), as well as in the enclosure of the Lords of the Gaṇas, in the enclosures of the World-Protectors (lokapāla) and the two [others], and also in the enclosure of Rudra and the rest. || 6.193 ||
Having dissolved [the deities] once more, one should perform worship toward the enclosure;
worship from the rising of the moon until the rising of the sun will be a fruitless hardship. (6.194)
Through worship during the disappearance of the moon and sun, one shall accomplish the desired fruit;
when the vital breath is situated in the center of the Suṣumṇā, one should worship all the deities. (6.195)

Alternatively, the practitioner, whose body is composed of power (śakti), should offer the collection of principles known as the eightfold worship beginning with the earthly element to the one whose body consists of the six qualities.
All fragrance is the earthly element; water is the consecration;
those same waters are the drink and the food offering; and the metallic element is the lamp and the garland.

Having likewise offered the wind-related [substances] such as the palm-leaf fan, those originating from space such as music, and the other principles (tattvas) as appropriate, [one should proceed]. // 6.198 //
Having meditated as taught by Śiva himself, one who is free from the pairs of opposites attains immortality.
Having thus performed the purification of the self, one should then perform the purification of the place. (6.199)
Having formed the three *tāla* mudrās, one should visualize a rampart with the weapon [mudrā];
then, having meditated on the crossbar outside of that, by means of the armor mantra.
One should place that net of missiles (astrajāla) on the outside for the removal of obstacles;
then, having meditated upon the divine abode, one should perform the purification of the ritual materials.
Then, having filled the *vardhanī* vessel with scented water by means of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
he should sprinkle that water for the sake of purification using the *hetimantra*.
Then, one should wash with water the vessel for the *arghya*, the conch, the vessels for the *pādya* and *ācamana*, and whatever else is required for use. (6.203)
Then, having gazed upon it with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should envelop it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
[The vessel may be] made of gold, silver, copper, or conch-shell, and adorned with a playful necklace (kelihāra).

A vessel made from the leaves of the *palāśa* or *padma*, one made of wood, one made of clay, or any other [vessel] placed upon a stand (*yantrikā*) and so forth, is prescribed for the worship of Śiva. (6.205)
Then, having filled the *vardhanī* vessel with scented water while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), all the perfumes,
flowers, and other offerings were brought by the attendants.
Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle [the vessel] with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
having washed the water-offering vessel (*pādyapātra*), one should fill it with scented water.
One should provide *uśīra* and sandalwood for the water for the feet;
likewise, one should prepare that vessel for the purpose of the water for sipping. (6.208)
The three myrobalans, camphor, cardamom leaves, and costus should be employed for the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the Hṛdaya mantra. (6.209)
Afterward, one should place another vessel of scented water into the *arghya* vessel;
[it should contain] water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice, flowers, and sesame seeds.
The *arghya* is said to consist of eight ingredients; having prepared the special *arghya* with barley and white mustard seeds, one should place the groups of mantras therein.
Having rendered it supreme with *sudhā* and having covered it with the *varman* [mantra], one should worship it;
likewise, one should sprinkle it along with *kuśa* grass using those waters while reciting the *kavaca* [mantra].
One should sprinkle the perfume, flower, incense, lamp, water offering, and the food offering, as well as the curd, milk, ghee, and so forth, with the heart mantra. (6.213)
One should consecrate each individual substance intended for worship with mantras,
together with three palas of *uśīra* root, as well as camphor and high-quality saffron.
And they are joined with sandalwood, agallochum, leaves, and fragrant flowers. || 6/214 ||

Water is prescribed for the act of immersion; whatever has been obtained from among the groups of substances mentioned according to one's means should be accepted here by both the wealthy and the poor. (6.215)
One should cast a drop of water from the *arghya* vessel, together with a flower, into all the bathing jars with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, for the sake of their purification. (6.216)
Whether with the heart, or with the purifying limbs, or with those [limbs] which are their very nature;
likewise, [one offers] fragrance, clothing, ornament, food offering, and flower. (6.217)
One should consecrate [the materials] with the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna mantras;
the remainder, however, one should consecrate with the Gāyatrī for the purification of the substances.
One should prepare curd, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and scented water;
or, for the purpose of bathing, one should consecrate them with the purifying mantras beginning with the *hṛdaya*. (6.219)
Having worshipped the pure mantras and substances in sequence with perfumes and other offerings,
and having rendered them nectar-like by means of the mudrā, one should meditate upon them under the name "Nectar."
One should worship oneself with such substances in the proper sequence:
having applied a tilaka of sandalwood, one should place a flower upon the head. (6.221)
Having adopted the desired silence, one should then purify the mantras;
indeed, the various nets of power, such as those of the garland-mantra and others, have been proclaimed for the mantras.
Their awakening power is remembered as the command of Śiva: "Oṃ, obeisance.
One should recite the mantras in their entirety, beginning with the syllable Oṃ and ending with the day's conclusion. (6.223)
Having formed a handful of joined palms with flowers and being permeated by the true nature of Śiva,
one should proceed through the three measures in immediate succession until reaching the end of Nāda.
In this way, the purification of the mantras occurs by relying upon the pure reality;
one should employ the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and its ritual procedure is now described here. (6.225)
In an auspicious part of the pavilion, having divided the site into nine squares and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five elements, one should arrange five vessels.

O Śivā, at the time when [the principle] called Sādākhya is being taught, the teacher [should contemplate] the individual soul (puruṣa) as well—[the soul] which is well-established, perfectly tranquil, like radiant energy, and of the nature of nectar. (6.227)
Having consecrated the water with the *ratnodaka* mantra, one should place milk, curd, ghee, cow dung, and cow urine, consecrated respectively by the mantras beginning with *Īśāna*. (6.228)

Having consecrated the water of kusha grass as nectar by reciting [the mantra] one, two, three, four, or five times—thus in six ways—and having worshipped it, one should declare its identity with Śiva. || 6/229 ||
One should consecrate with mantras such as the *pavitra* and the *hṛdaya* [mantra] the milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and fragrant water for the purpose of bathing. (6.230)

Whether it be for daily rites, occasional rites, or rites performed for specific desires, one should perform the bathing of the Lord according to the prescribed rule; indeed, that bathing may be of many kinds. (6.231)
One should purify the ground with the Astra mantra and smear it with the Vāmadeva mantra;
the laying out of the lines (sūtranyāsa) should be performed with the Aghora mantra, at intervals of one palm's breadth as appropriate.
The measurement of the pericarp is said to be three *tālas*, which is common to all;
when there are four petals, there is the installation of five jars in each direction.
In the intermediate directions as well, there should be one called "the new," surrounded on all sides;
that which is numbered twenty-five is likewise surrounded on all sides. (6.234)
O twice-born ones, forty-nine are renowned, one hundred and eight are [renowned], and twenty-five kalaśas are situated in the center. (6.235)
Having avoided [the center] on all sides, one should construct two outer enclosures connected by eight gates, using either two or one path. (6.236)
In the center, there should be nine triangles situated according to the number of lunar days (tithis).
One should abandon the central triad known as the "middle lunar day. (6.237)
Indeed, this [measurement] is one hundred and eight, or one thousand and nine;
one should lay down two threads running from east to west and from south to north.
The enclosure on the outside, formed by a circumambulation, should be fourteen in number, with an interval of one and a half cubits, or even just one cubit's measure.
Having entered the inner path, the ritual procedure is proclaimed in the scripture as follows:
there should be four or eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) surrounding the central arrangement.
For a mandala of forty deities, there should be twenty-five [perimeter lines] each;
however, the Guru should discard the outer enclosure from the one thousand and eight [lines]. (6.241)
In that regard, one should perform the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) situated in the corners beginning with the southeast;
everything else shall be the same, and it shall consist of five hundred and eight [verses]. (6.242)
In the middle, one should take two hundred bricks joined with the number eight;
on the outside, one should take sixteen bricks located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Furthermore, this [altar] should consist of eight arrays (vyūhas) and possess the aforementioned number;
the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the Puruṣa-mantra should measure four prasthas at most.
Starting from that, the measurement should double with each increment up to ten times;
this is the measure for the *śivakumbha*, while half of that is considered the measure for the *karaka*.
When the pitcher is filled to the measure of four, three, two, or one *prastha*, it should be wrapped with two, three, or [up to] three threads of sky[-colored silk], respectively. (6.246)
Varāla, truṭi, karpūra, nyagrodha, and uśīra—water mixed with these, consecrated by the recitation of Śiva-mantras, becomes auspicious water (śivāmbhas). || 6/247 ||
With that very [water] one should fill the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī* jars;
then one should place therein the *kuśa* grasses, numbering three or more, up to the limit of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*).
One should install the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī, wrapped in a pair of cloths, with the Kūrcāneśa mantra and the root-mantra of the ritual substance. (6.249)

One should place the ninefold jewel upon Śiva and Śakti; and in the four directions, the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then there shall be kuśa-water, milk, curd in the corner, and ghee;
this is declared as the second ablution, and the third is now described. (6.251)
Honey, parched grain flour, fried rice-flake powder, turmeric, bhūtika, the essence of sugarcane, plantain, sesame, mustard, and pānasa fruit; 6.252.
There should be a coconut and two oranges, as well as a citron;
however, among these twenty-five, one should exclude that which is enclosed within.
When this is done, there shall be sixteen water-pots here;
and in the four directions and the corners, the eightfold set beginning with the foot-washing water (pādya) is prescribed.
In the interval, however, it is said that there are as many [mantras] as the number of the Vasus (eight), beginning with Madhu;
and these three previously mentioned [groups] are specifically for the daily obligatory rites (nityakarman). || 6/255 ||
Even the number twenty-five is praised for the permanent [daily] rite;
for the most excellent worship, it extends up to one hundred and eight.
That which is occasioned (naimittika), as well as what was previously stated for the positions above that, is also prescribed;
one should install all these materials with the root mantra.

Having covered [the vessel] with the primary seed-syllable using either shallow bowls or sprouts, and having offered various garments with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra), [one should proceed]. (6.258)
Having prepared a seat in this jar, one should meditate upon the deity in embodied form;
having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the Brahma-mantras, one should deposit its constituent parts (*kalā*) therein. (6.259)
Having meditated upon Śiva as possessing that particular form with the body of the Vidyā installed,
the Guru should perform the installation and so forth, offer water for the feet and other honors, and then bestow [the mantras] with the heart-mantra.
Having presented perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the water-offering (arghya), and having displayed the liṅga-mudrā, one should conceal [the deity] with the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 6/261 ||
Having worshipped Gaurī with the *vardhanī* vessel and having displayed the *yonimudrā*,
O best of the twice-born, one should omit the Brahmāṇīs and worship Īśāna during the fivefold arrangement (*pañcakḷpti*).

In the arrangement of the nine [deities], the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) should be placed externally in the directions, while the Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśvaras), beginning with Vāmadeva, are within; thus, there are twenty-five in number.
Likewise, outside are the eight lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Aṅguṣṭha;
then the Krodhas and others, numbering eight, or else the Śatarudras and so forth. (6.264)
In the fifty-fold ablution, however, the deities are considered as follows:
the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are to be worshipped in the center, while the hundred Rudras are considered to be on the outside. (6/265)
In the ablution known as the "One Hundred and Eight," the deities are considered to be the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) in the central [vessel], while in the others, it is indeed Śiva alone.
And that [text] is recited specifically by means of thousands of names. ||266||
[In the bath known as the one with one thousand and eight [verses], the deities are considered [to be as follows]:
Joined with the seed-syllables (kūṭākṣara) and so forth, ending in the dative case, followed by *svāhā* or concluding with a salutation (*namaskāra*), and preceded by the *praṇava* (OM). (6.267)
Having recited [the mantra], one should worship the Lord; then, the mere name of Śiva is to be uttered according to the sequence for the purification of the liṅga, as it is duly explained.
The *liṅga* is declared to be of three kinds— manifest, unmanifest, and consisting of both— and is manifold, such as the *svayambhū*, divine, *bāṇa*, *ārṣa*, and human types. (6.269)
Whether it be a fixed linga or a mobile one, likewise the three types of mandalas,
or a cloth painting, a mural, or a pedestal consecrated with mantras— 6/270.
Alternatively, there may be a seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) consisting of fire, water, a guru, a tree, and so forth;
or specifically, a stone that is self-manifested, or even a jewel.
Or whatever else is prescribed in the Liṅga-kalpas, especially that made of sand and so forth—
one should arrange all this for the sake of worshiping Śiva, according to what is appropriate.
Having taken up the general offering (sāmānyārghya), one should worship the bull at the front of the door;
one should worship an image made of metal at the door, but one made of stone in the surrounding area.
The fourth letter from the seventh group, adorned with the seven musical notes (svara), joined with the bindu and nāda, preceded by the praṇava at the beginning. (6.274)

After offering salutations to Vṛṣabha at the end, one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs of Brahmā upon him; having sprinkled the doorway with the Astra-mantra, one should worship the door-keepers in their proper order.
One should worship Gaṇapa and Bhāratī above; Nandin together with Jāhnavī on the right, and Mahākāla together with Yamunā on the left. (6.276)
One should worship Vimala and Subāhu on the two cushions in sequence;
these are to be worshipped with their heart-mantras and so forth, ending in "namaḥ," according to the proper order. (6.277)
Having sequentially assigned the three types of obstacles through the forms, shapes, and substances such as incense and flowers, one should place the sword upon the Udumbara tree.
At the conclusion of the door-worship, at the end of the ritual bath, after the food offering,
and at the close of the twilight prayer, the excellent concealed cloth should be set aside.
Having worshipped the Self-born (Brahmā) with the mantra "O Vāstoṣpati, [belonging] to Brahmā," one should perform the worship situated within the *liṅga* that was previously arranged.
Having worshipped with the Gāyatrī, one should offer the general arghya;
then, having recited the five Brahmans and performed the worship, one should dismiss [the deity] from the liṅga.

Having cast the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) into the northeast direction upon the altar-base (*pīṭhikā*) and so forth according to the rule with the *hṛnmantra*, [one should do so] while reciting "to Caṇḍeśa" and employing the *astra-mantra*.
Having purified it with the right hand, one should cleanse the Śivaliṅga;
having thoroughly cleansed the Śivaliṅga along with its pedestal using the water of the Astra-mantra alone.
Thereafter, one should perform the consecration with the general offering waters;
for the rite of bathing, the lotus seat, Ananta, the invocation, and the seat [are required]. (6.284)
One should know that the pure [seat] is for worship, yoga is for the food offering, and the āsana is for the garments and other rites; one should arrange these on the lion-throne.
Thus, when the purification of the self, the station, the substance, the syllables, and the liṅga has been performed, the Śaiva worship should be carried out; otherwise, it is not prescribed. (6.286)
One should worship Gaṇeśa in the northwest of the pedestal with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
and one should worship the lineages of gurus in the northeast with the heart-mantra.
Having understood the true nature of the seat and the sitter, one should begin the sacrifice.
The seat is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the body and the living soul. (6.288)
