The seat beginning with Ananta and ending with Śuddhavidyā is proclaimed;
one should contemplate the divine body ending with Mahāmāyā. (6.289)
In this [body], the individual soul (jīva) must indeed be Śiva himself, because of these threefold conceptualizations;
for that which is light and all-pervading is indeed pervaded by, and presided over by, Him. (6.290)
That sustaining power (adhāra-śakti) by which the visible world is supported and produced, like grass by the wind,
should first be placed upon the seat of the Tortoise-stone (kūrma-śilā).
Pure as the rays of the moon, gentle, four-faced and four-armed,
with a form resembling the ocean of milk, she is visualized as residing within the heart-lotus.
Infinite, resembling the color of the blue sky, adorned with many hoods, with hands joined in *añjali* at the heart, having one face and four arms. (6.293)
The practitioner of mantra should, with the heart-mantra, place upon that support a seat consisting of the form of a lotus arisen from the ocean of milk. (6.294)
The auspicious factors beginning with Dharma, which constitute that vigor, are like sandals placed at the four corners;
they resemble a lion, white, the rays of the sun, yellow, and black. (6.295)

Surrounded by many lions who gaze at one another, those [qualities] are indeed known as unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya). (6.296)
One should visualize the limbs in the various directions as having variegated colors; one should contemplate the lower garment as red and the upper garment as white. (6.297)
The two [lines] consisting of the two powers—the cause for bondage and liberation and so forth—are joined above and below the girdle in the directions from the southwest to the northeast. (6.298)
A lotus provided with eight petals, endowed with the eight supernatural powers (siddhis),
distinguished by the power (śakti) of the filaments, and joined with the power of the pericarp.
One should especially prepare an offering with bilva leaves at the base of the liṅga while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then follow with Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Kālī.
The goddess Kalavikaraṇī, likewise Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī as well. (6.301)
From the east to the northeast, one should place [the goddesses] upon the filaments and the petals;
then, with the heart-mantra, one should place Manonmanī upon the pericarp.
The powers beginning with Vāmā are red; Manonmanī has a white luster.
The triad of mandalas known as Sun, Moon, and Fire exists according to its own essential nature. (6.303)
One should fashion [the design] up to the tips of the petals, the tips of the filaments, and the pericarp;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the deities of the three mandalas. (6.304)
Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, four-faced, adorned with four arms, red in color, holding a water-pot and a staff in his hands. (6.305)
Having meditated upon the divine one, who holds a rosary, has a lotus in his hand, and possesses beautiful eyes, and having placed him upon the petals, he destroys all sins. (6.306)
Resembling the flax flower, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, wearing divine yellow garments, and adorned with a forest garland. (6.307)
Having meditated upon the Great-Souled Viṣṇu, adorned with a network of tiny bells from the rubies of his shimmering crown, one should place him upon the filaments.
White as a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon, holding a trident in his hand, three-eyed, clad in a lion’s skin, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (6.309)
Having meditated specifically upon Rudra, who is blue-throated and mounted upon a bull, one should place him within the pericarp; this destroys even the greatest of sins.

Having assigned the three selves (ātman) in that very place, one should thereafter assign the three qualities (guṇa) and the three fires (vahni) in that same location, according to their respective divisions.
Having thus contemplated the pervasion of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), one should again place the Śakti within their midst.
Thus, from Śakti up to Śaktyanta is the seat of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
Here, Ananta, in the form of the agent, abides as the very soul of the pedestal (pīṭha). (6.313)
Thus, O Brahmins, the arrangement of the seats (pīṭhas) is here described in brief:
Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya—this is the tetrad. (6.314)
Ananta and Śakti—these indeed are the six limbs of the seat.
The seat of Śambhu consists of the six paths; the worship should be performed with the heart-mantra. (6.315)
Alternatively, the conception of the sacred seats (pīṭha) is described in another way:
the seat is constructed from all the paths (adhvan), with the four ages as its great feet.
The bulbous root is the Earth, while its upward-stretching stalk consists of the principles situated within Time;
it is adorned with thorns differentiated by the fifty states of being.
The principle of Māyā is the great knot; the lotus of Śuddhavidyā has the Vidyeśvaras as its petals and is adorned with the filaments of Śakti. (6.318)

One should meditate upon the seat (pīṭha) as being thus constituted, arising from the syllables of the Mātṛkā, and resplendent with the seed-syllable at its pericarp, which is produced from the two, Śiva and Śakti. (6.319)
One should conceptualize Dharma and the other [elements] by means of the neuter syllables alone:
Ananta by the first of the emanation [vowels], and the great lotus by the one preceding that. (6.320)
One who is most pure should fashion [the lotus] ending at the pericarp with the final vowel;
those beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *a*, excluding the six neuter vowels and the nine [long] vowels. (6.321)
There are nine filaments, corresponding to the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā, arranged both in direct and reverse order;
these twenty-four are contained within the letters from ka to bha.
One should visualize nine seed-syllables beginning with *ma* and ending with *ha*;
right here, one should likewise visualize the three mandalas as previously described.
Having thus brought about the sacred seat (pīṭha) born from the Mātṛkās, one should worship her who has arisen from the three mandalas, resembling a pillar of fire.
One should place the form (mūrti), ending with the principle of Īśvara, within the measure of the *liṅga*.
Indeed, the form-mantra (*mūrtimantra*) is declared to be the unborn [syllable] enclosed by the heart [syllables]. (6.325)
In the same way, this mantra called Sadākhya is said to be at the root itself;
one should place the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), which is Sadāśiva, upon the head and in the middle. (6.326)
Upon the mounting of the Śiva-liṅga, one should contemplate this Lord, who consists of the pure abode,
is endowed with the thirty-eight kalās, and has formed His body from the limbs of Brahmā.
The form of Sadāśiva is described here for the purpose of meditation;
indeed, meditation is for the sake of attaining all perfections, whether performed upon a cloth-painting or otherwise created. (6.328)
Five-faced, with ten staff-like arms, brilliant as crystal, and three-eyed;
peaceful, with the crescent moon upon his crest, and his matted hair bound and adorned with serpents. (6.329)
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, resting on a white lotus,
adorned with earrings, pendants, necklaces, a waist-cord, and a belly-band.
Adorned with armlets, bracelets,
and beautiful anklets, he was sixteen years of age, lovely, very gracious, and possessed a smiling countenance.
In the right [hands], he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a vajra, and fire;
and likewise, [in the left hands] he holds the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a noose, another [object], a bell, a serpent, and a goad. (6.332)
One should meditate on [the attributes] held in the left hand; otherwise, it is described differently:
the *prasāda*, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the *khaṭvāṅga*, the spear (*śakti*), and the trident (*śūla*) are on the right side. (6.333)

One should meditate on him as being joined with the three eyes— the powers of will, knowledge, and action— [and] with the left [hands] holding a hand-drum, a serpent-eyeball, a rosary, a blue lotus, and a vessel for filling.
The moon is the form of all the sacrificial stars; the ten hands are the ten directions.
The trident is said to be the three qualities (guṇas), and the axe is called pure existence (sattā). || 6/335 ||
The sword is the majesty of the Lord; the thunderbolt is impenetrability.
The power of withdrawal is external, reducing fetters to ashes. (6.336)
She is the illuminator of the categories of existence that abide above Mahāmāyā;
she is the power that cannot be assailed even by the serpent-king, and the ordainer of all things. (6.337)
One should know the noose to be the threefold noose consisting of māyā, karma, and impurity (mala);
the bell is the form consisting of resonance (nāda), which makes known the body of the mantra.
Fearlessness for all the worlds, and indeed the power that protects them;
the attainment of what is to be enjoyed by the Self, and here itself, the restraint which is the goad. (6.339)
Indeed, the weapons are remembered as having such forms:
the Lord (Īśa) is like crystal in the center, while Nara is like saffron in the east.
The face in the south is as terrible as collyrium; the one in the north is lovely like saffron;
and the face facing the western direction is as pure as a ray of the moon. (6.341)
On the forehead in the east is the auspicious eye with a lion’s roar face;
it is devoid of eyebrows, possesses a prominent nose, beautiful cheeks, and a smiling lower lip. (6.342)
The right [hand] has a terrifying form, rough with jagged fangs,
with its mouth wide open, a large nose, round eyes, and a tongue lolling out.
Adorned with serpent ornaments, having a skull as his crest-ornament,
his matted locks are wreathed with flames and entwined by a coiling serpent tied into an upward-pointing topknot.
Yellow, belonging to the water element, serene, with a beautiful nose and a handsome forehead,
three-eyed, adorned with a crown and auspiciously decorated with earrings.
With a mass of hair like a swarm of bees, adorned with golden ornaments,
endowed with a tilaka on the forehead, and possessing a brilliance fixed upon a mirror.
There, Īśāna stood with his face upward, adorned with the ornament of Alakā, gentle and endowed with a beautiful form; yet he who stood upon the crown of the head was exceedingly terrifying.
Adorned with earrings, three-eyed, and wearing a crown with a young moon, he is thus remembered;
having thus conceived the faces, one should worship the form of Sādāśiva.
Just as one performs the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) upon the body, so should one perform it upon the deity;
having thus fashioned the body of Śakti, [one should place] the Supreme Cause within it.
Śiva is indeed eternal, true, consisting of the bliss of knowledge, all-pervading among all principles, immeasurable, and incomparable. (6.350)
One should specifically manifest that which is devoid of the expressed and the expresser, beyond the reach of speech and mind, unmanifest within the manifest, partless within the whole. (6.351)
Thus, by means of the root mantras preceded by the invocation, [the deity] is constrained;
just as fire residing within wood is manifested through friction and other such means. (6.352)
Likewise, Śiva is manifested through devotion by the power of mantra;
having placed one's hands joined in añjali at the heart adorned with flowers, one should recite the Prāsāda mantra. (Page 38)

The practitioner, having attained a state of aesthetic oneness (*samarasībhāva*) with that which is beyond parts through devotion, should meditate upon [the deity] in the abode of his own power (*svaśakti*), first in the *nāda* and then in the *bindu*. Having thus emerged sequentially by means of the rays of his own power, this indeed constitutes the invocation (*āvāhana*). (6.353)
The sages said:
"O Lord, how can there be an invocation here of Śiva, who is omnipresent?
If an invocation were desired, his omnipresence would be contradicted. (6.354)
Īśvara said:
Just as the manifestation of fire situated from root to tip occurs in a tree, so too the manifestation of consciousness in one place does not contradict its all-pervasiveness. 6/355
Just as one's own coming and going may occur here through the medium of the body, so too are the desired coming and going of Śiva effected through the medium of the mantra-body. (6.356)
Because he is endowed with inconceivable power, Śiva is both all-pervading and non-pervading; he possesses a body or is devoid of a body, and he is the creator of all and omnipresent. (6.357)
In this way, one should meditate upon the Lord residing in the *bindu* as being present in the flower held in the hand;
and that [meditation] should be performed via the path of the vital breath through the channel whose nature is light. (6.358)

Therefore, having taken that which resides in the *liṅga*, one should deposit it within one's own body by means of the *sthāpinī* [mudrā], so that through this capacity, Śambhu may possess His own lordship over oneself. (6.359)
The manifestation of that power through one's own mudrā is "proximity" (sannidhāna).
That which occurs at the conclusion of the time of worship, without abandoning this proximity, is [the state of] "abiding" (sannidhi). (6/360)
The cessation of even the pervasive [consciousness] is clearly perceived by the pervasive power of cessation;
just as in the world, an object that is essentially pleasant must be concealed. (6.361)

Its veiling should be performed with the veiling mudrā, so that [the deity] becomes capable through its own respective splendors, just as fire, the sun, and others are capable through their own lights. (6.362)
In that same way, Śiva, the creator of all, is invincible through his limbs arising from his own nature;
his existence is the heart, and his head is the position of the crest-lock (śikhā).
His crest-lock is sovereignty, and his armor is protection;
for that power by which he casts away worldly existence is indeed his weapon.
The eye is the power of omniscience, which illuminates all objects;
thus are the six qualities of Śiva, the creator of the world, described here. (6.365)
One should assign these six limbs, beginning with the heart, to one's own mantra upon the heart, head, crest, body, eyes, and hands. (6.366)

The realization of the non-difference between the limbs and the possessor of limbs, even though they are distinct, is declared to be the "rendering immortal" by means of the Lord’s Amṛtamudrā. (6.367)
There should be an incitement for him, which increases the delight of his limbs;
one should perform that by means of the Mahāmudrā, for the purpose of gladdening and melting.
The God, whose form consists of the six paths, stands face-to-face, united with Śakti, whitening the quarters of the sky with a mass of supreme bliss. (6.369)
Having meditated, one should offer water for the feet at the [deities'] feet, then water for sipping (ācamana) into their mouths;
likewise, the respectful offering (arghya), consisting of dūrvā grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, should be given upon their heads.
The water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamana) should be offered with the Heart-mantra ending in "svadhā";
the water for the guest-offering (arghya), consisting of dūrvā grass and other items, should be offered with the Heart-mantra ending in "svāhā" and "vauṣaṭ."

Having thus performed the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one should worship with ritual offerings (upacāras). These offerings for worship— such as bathing and so forth— should be performed according to one's means, whether they be very few or extensive.

In the case of a mandatory rite (nitya-vidhi), it is prescribed with all [the offerings] such as garlands and so forth; in the case of a rite for a specific desire (kāmya-vidhi), it must certainly be so. (6.372)
Bathing, clothing, and ointments; flowers, incense, and lamps;

sacrificial oblation, betel leaf together with mouth-perfumes and fragrances; song, great dance, and the fire-sacrifice accompanied by offerings to the spirits; or the daily festival, or the bali offering.
And all this music was proclaimed when Śambhu’s manifestation occurred.
Fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offering—these are the five modes of worship; alternatively, it is also accepted that they may consist of only those ending with the lamp. (6/374)

Those fit for bathing are those to be bathed, such as Citrā and others; those devoid of that [reflection] are [the objects themselves]. Or [they are seen] reflected in a sword, a mirror, or a gem. (6.375)

Worship ending with the lighting of lamps is proclaimed [as one type], while worship ending with the offering of food (naivedya) is another; that ending with the ritual oblation (bali) is called the propitiatory rite (śāntika). Indeed, worship is said to be of three kinds. // 6.376 //
Having worshipped in this manner in the evening and the morning, one should offer the oblation at midday;
having purified two *prastha*s of food at that time, one should present it. (6.377)
There is one lamp at both times, but here at night there are two lamps;
in this manner described, one should perform the lowest of the low rites.
At both morning and midday, one should offer two *prasthas* of rice as an oblation;
indeed, having worshipped [the deity] in the evening and morning, there should be exactly four lamps.
One should then specify two *prasthas* for each of the three times;
there should be four lamps, but at evening they should be doubled.
During the three lowest periods, the wise one [should offer] accompanied by the sound of musical instruments;
during the lowest of the middle periods, and at midday, an *āḍhaka* measure of oblation.

In the morning and evening, the twice-born should offer two *prasthas* [of grain] accompanied by twelve lamps; at the three times of day, he should perform the offering of flowers and the presentation of oblations (*bali*). (6.382)
At midday, one should likewise offer a middling portion, and at the three times of day, an āḍhaka of sacrificial oblation;
during the half-watch, half of that amount, and twenty-four lamps.

Three times a day, accompanied by offerings and flowers, one should present the *arghya* and the sequence of oblations (*bali*) together with the sound of musical instruments and the resonance of conchs and *kāhala* drums. (6.384)
At midday, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) conjoined with the Śiva-mantra;
for the highest among the middling [practitioners], two āḍhakas [of grain] are required at all three times of day.
An āḍhaka measure [of offerings] accompanied by seventy lamps should be provided during the half-watch;
there should be the offering of bali three times a day, and one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) three times a day.
One should play it well at the six times of day, joined with all musical instruments;
where one performs the sixfold [practice], there no counting of time exists. (6.387)
Where the lowest [measurement] for the highest [deity] is one *droṇa* at the three joints (*trisandhi*), there shall be eight hundred lamps at the half-*droṇa* price-point. (6.388)
There should be an offering of oblations (bali) three times a day, and one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) three times a day,
accompanied by twenty-four musical instruments and all varieties of musical accompaniment.
There should be thirty-four, twenty-four, or ten courtesans, endowed with beauty and youth, who should perform dance at the appropriate time. (6.390)
It is joined with five preceptors and provided with the watches of the night;
it is supreme or middling, wherein there are four oblations at the three times of day.

One should prepare milk-rice and other offerings according to the prescribed rite, using one *droṇa* of rice for each; having cooked them separately, one should prepare one *droṇa* of pure boiled rice.
Furthermore, at the half-watch (ardhayāma) for Droṇa, there should be two hundred lamps;
the offering of oblations and fire-sacrifices performed at the three times of day is called the Śītāri-dīpa. || 6/393 ||
With thirty-four musicians and accompanied by fifty courtesans, one should perform dance for two watches of the night at the three junctions of the day. (6.394)
With reference to the most excellent [rite], the sequence of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya) is now declared:
the uncooked preparations, beginning with *pāyasya* and others, are each made from five *droṇas*.
At midnight, half of that [time], there should be five hundred lamps;
and at the three periods of the day, there should be offerings and fire-oblations accompanied by fifty musical instruments.
Accompanied by one thousand six hundred courtesans,
he should perform a dance at the three junctions of the day, when the time is joined with the watches (yāma).
In this rite, the five-colored oblations, beginning with milk-rice (pāyāsa) and so forth,
are prepared in sequence from one *droṇa* of rice, then half of that, and then half of that again.
One should especially offer one, two, three, or even all of these at a single time. (6.399)
Pure food is said to be of two kinds; this is declared to be the general rule.
Thus it is stated regarding the ninefold [classification], and for each one, a specific procedure is prescribed.
Having bathed and worshipped the water-vessel, which has been perfumed with fragrant bathing-water, consecrated with Saṃhitā mantras, adorned with flowers, incensed, and auspicious; || 6/401 ||
With oil prepared by means of hand-machines and the like, fresh, cooked, or scented, or else with pure cow-ghee; || 6/402 ||
Having anointed the liṅga together with its pedestal, one should immediately fumigate it with auspicious rice flour mixed with turmeric.
Having rubbed [the body] with powdered black gram (māṣa), one should then perform immersion.
In that case, bathing with fragrant myrobalan and other such substances is prescribed.
(Verse 6.405) With colored clay, shards, or substances such as vajra originating from cow dung;
or with well-prepared nourishing [substances], or even with black mustard and salt.
One should perform an ablution with lukewarm water, scented waters, and decoctions, as well as with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, according to one's capacity. (6.406)
From one *kuḍupa* up to an *āḍhaka*, increasing by one *kuḍupa* at each step;
in the absence of sugar, sugarcane juice may be used, and in the absence of honey, ghee may be used. (6.407)
If one has the means, the consecration should be performed with water mixed with incense, or with the water from coconut fruits, or with other flavorful liquids. (6.408)
Then one should perform the consecration with flowers and other offerings, with water from golden vessels, with gifts of jewels, and with fragrant waters; one must not leave the head bare. (6.409)
Taking flowers with the *hetin* [mudrā] by joining the index finger and the thumb, one should cast away the flower that has reached the head and join another there. (6.410)
One should employ eight flowers, three fragrances, and seven waters for the invocation, the water-offering (arghya), the foot-bath (pādya), the ritual bath, the incense, and the unguent.

One should employ flowers in eight instances: in the offering of food (naivedya), in the dismissal (visarga), in the water for honor (arghya), in the unguent (vilepana), and in the bath (snāna). One should apply fragrance in these three [latter] instances.

In the offering of flowers, the arghya, and the pādya, as well as in the bathing, the sipping of water (ācamana), the washing, and the sprinkling—one should employ water in these seven instances. (6.413)
Incense should be offered everywhere; having understood what remains, one should employ it at the conclusion of the door-worship, at the end of the bath, and during the presentation of offerings.
At the conclusion of the twilight rite, having set aside the excellent concealed cloth,
one should subsequently perform the consecration with the jars that have been placed there.
Having placed the *gaḍuḍuka* on the palm of the left hand, one should remove the flower previously deposited upon the top of the *liṅga* with the *astra-mantra*.
With hands washed and with water that is not moving, consecrated by mantras and poured from the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā), one should bathe the Lord upon His head.
One should not wave the hand upward, nor should one form a mudrā below;
furthermore, one should not consume those substances with water that has been drawn up [from a lower level]. (6.418)
Having lifted up the auspicious pitcher (*śivakumbha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel accompanied by shouts of victory,
one should lead them and place them upon the tripod over the divine fire.
Having offered the triad of water for the feet (pādya) and so forth to the deity and the goddess residing in the jar,
and having presented perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the water of honor (arghya).
Removing the lid with his right hand, the preceptor,
while recollecting the Śiva-mantra, should perform [the rite] with water and flowers.
Having gathered his mind upon reality, he should place the mantra on the top of the *liṅga*;
he should also install the Goddess of the Gods to the left of the God.
Reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should bathe Śiva with the water from the pitcher;
immediately thereafter, one should bathe the Goddess who is in the form of the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
In that rite, bathing with fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances is prescribed;
having performed the consecration with scented water upon the *liṅga* together with its pedestal, [one should proceed]. (6.424)
Having offered water for sipping (ācamana) at the [five] faces, he should wipe it with a clean cloth;
then, having anointed the Śiva-liṅga together with its pedestal using fragrant substances.
Having covered the deity with various kinds of pure garments and materials,
and having offered the eight flowers to the god, one should then present the mantra-oblation.
Or one should offer mung-bean rice or pure rice accompanied by side dishes and the like,
and worship with pure flower garlands or cut leaf-patterns.
With golden bands and crowns made of gold,
with many sprouts of golden dūrvā grass and golden lakṣmī-flowers.
The practitioner should adorn [the image] with a crescent moon, with numerous golden flowers, with an upper garment of three threads, and with a waist-belt. (6.429)
Indeed, with a golden garment, a golden lower cloth, and other items such as crowns and flowers, along with golden spheres; 6.430.
And one should adorn [the image] according to the rule with various kinds of gems:
a ruby on Sunday, and a pearl on Monday. (6.431)
On Tuesday, coral should be used; on Wednesday, it should be emerald;
on Thursday, it should be topaz; and on Friday, diamond is prescribed.
Sapphire is suitable for Saturday; all these and whatever other gems there may be are considered appropriate for ornaments on every day of the week. (6.433)

Having offered water for the feet with the *ajāta* mantra upon their feet and in their mouths, and at the conclusion of the sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should cause the respectful offering (*arghya*) to be presented upon the head and other parts of the body. (6.434)
During the consecration with the five products of the cow and other rites, one should offer incense accompanied by the great sound of a bell and joined with the subsidiary ablutions.
At the conclusion of the veiling, there must certainly be a ritual bath accompanied by incense;
one should cause either the chanting of mantras or the sound of a lute to be performed.
After the study of the Vedas and whatever else such as the recitation of the Śāstras,
one should perform the singing in Gauḍīya and other dialects, ending with the offering of incense.
The song, which is a constituent part of the Drāviḍa language, may be accompanied by dance; it is free from corruption of the Sanskrit language and endowed with various musical notes. (6.438)
One should also imagine a song arising from the eighteen languages, and having imagined a dance produced in various regions. (6/439)
And one should hang garlands of flowers and the like all around below;
[and] within the interior of a vessel filled with smokeless, blazing coals, intensely.
Immediately thereafter, one should fumigate [the image] with burning incense,
while holding a bell of beautiful form and deep resonance in the left hand.
While playing [the instrument], he should always offer incense impelled by the *astra-mantra*,
using wicks made of camphor and *agaru* wood soaked in ghee from a tawny cow.
And with lamps that do not go out, with lamps for the wheels and archways,
with trident-lamps, and indeed with garlands of lamps.
One should cause various other kinds of lamps to be lit on all sides;
likewise, one should perform the gift of cows, the gift of sesame seeds, and the gift of gold. (6.444)
And one should provide grass and other fodder for the cows according to worldly custom, using many steady lamps filled with oil and set ablaze. (6.445)

Afterwards, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with a fine wick while being awakened [by music], touching the various limbs with ashes, or marking them with *tilaka* or triple-crested *tripuṇḍra* marks. (6.446)
Then, having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya), as well as the bali within the enclosure,
and having given the ācamana once, the subsequent rite should be performed.
Having prostrated and made a formal request, and having received permission, one should worship the outer enclosure;
one should then worship Īśāna in the pericarp with flowers and other offerings.
One should worship Puruṣa on the eastern petal, Aghora on the southern, Vāma on the northern petal, and Sadyojāta from the western petal. (6.449)
One should place five petals, each endowed with five faces, along with ten arms and moon-adorned crowns. (6.450)
One should meditate upon their true forms as bearing excellent weapons,
and worship them as situated in the four directions— namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
The Tree-head, the Crest, the Armor, the Eye, and the Weapon follow in due order;
the Heart has the luster of the moon’s color, and the Head has the radiance of yellow orpiment.
One should properly contemplate the crest-lock (śikhā) as resembling a flash of lightning;
one should assign the armor (kavaca) as smoky-grey and the weapon (astra) as tawny-colored.
One should meditate upon the eye situated in the center as having the radiance of the form of light;
all [the faces] are endowed with five faces, ten arms, and adorned with the crescent moon.
Adorned with various ornaments, decorated with diverse garlands and perfumes,
they have the appearance of sixteen-year-olds, possessing beautiful forms and eternal youth.
With serene faces, gentle, three-eyed, and seated in the svastika posture—
these [forms] of the Lord are to be brought forth from the head and other parts, as well as from the heart and other centers.
Or the practitioner should worship Īśāna as the Eye in the northeast;
in this manner, he should worship the inner enclosure surrounding Hara.
Alternatively, in this place, the nine powers beginning with Vāmā are to be worshipped;
or the primordial power Manonmanī, mounted upon the [central] digit, is to be worshipped by the Lord.
One should worship these [deities] in sequence with their respective mantras, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth;
however, there is no veiling (nāvakuṇṭhana) for them, except for the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa).

The wise have prescribed this very group of eight preparatory rites for each [deity] individually; the bathing and the arrangement of lamps are not separate from them, as they are constituent parts. (6.460)
On the second [ring], however, are the Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Ananta, in their proper order:
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetra. (6.461)
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍika—
these gods have four faces and ten arms like Hara.
They have gentle faces with crescent moons as their crowns; they stand upon lotuses and hold various weapons—carrying swords, shields, bows, arrows, water-pots, and rosaries.
Endowed with hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding tridents and lotuses in their palms,
resembling the sun at the end of an eon, they were impelled by Śiva to join together in union.
Ananta is to be worshipped in the east; one should sacrifice to Sūkṣma in the south;
Śivottama in the west (vāruṇī), and likewise Ekanetra in the north.
Likewise, one should place Ekarudra in the northeast (Īśāna), Trimūrti in the southeast (Agni),
Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest (Nairṛta), and Śikhaṇḍin in the northwest (Vāyu).
In the third [circle], however, are the lords of the Gaṇas starting from the direction of Kubera in sequence;
Ambikā, mounted upon a lion, three-eyed, yellow-hued, and holding a mirror. (6.467)
And Caṇḍa is situated in the northeast, possessing the luster of pure lapis lazuli;
he wears a tiger-skin garment, has three eyes, and holds a trident, a staff, and an axe.
Caṇḍa, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, is adorned with a crescent moon and a serpent;
he stands in the eastern quarter, possessing a radiance like that of a ruby, [attending upon] Nandin.
[One should meditate upon] Mahākāla, who has three eyes, holds a trident in his hand, is gentle, wears a serpent as a sacred thread, has a greenish luster, and possesses three eyes. (6.470)
One should worship the fierce Nāga, who wears a sacred thread, in the south-eastern direction.
Gaṇeśa is short of stature, elephant-faced, and holds his own tusk. (6.471)
He holds a water-pot and a winnowing-basket, with his sprout-like hands marked by three lines;
he carries a *laṅḍuka* fruit, an axe, and a rosary in his hands, and possesses three eyes. (6.472)
Resembling a lotus leaf, he is indeed worthy of worship and is situated in the direction of Yama;
he is a bull, bull-shaped, three-eyed, and possesses the luster of the kunda flower, the moon, and snow.

The one who is the foundation, whose nature is Dharma, who is worthy of worship, and who dwells in the realm of Nirṛti; Bhṛṅgī, whose body is fleshless, who is white, and who is situated in the direction of Varuṇa. (6/474)
He has six faces, the appearance of a youth, twelve eyes, and likewise twelve arms;
he bears a spear, a sword, a banner, a lotus, a javelin, a cock, and a staff.
Possessing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a bow, arrows, and a great axe, he may have four arms or two; for the sake of prosperity, he has but one face.

Holding a spear and a cock, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, he who has the luster of coral in the northwest should be worshipped by those seeking fruits [of their actions]. (6.477)
Alternatively, the lords of the Gaṇas may be worshipped in another manner:
the Goddess, Caṇḍeśa, Mahākāla, and likewise Vṛṣa. (6.478)
One should meditate, without agitation, upon Nandīśa, the leader of the Gaṇas, Bhṛṅgī, and Skanda, who possess a luster equal to that of rubies.

In the fourth [circle], one should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) in their respective directions in due order; and [in the southeast] the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin), yellow in color and mounted upon the king of elephants.
One should worship Indra, the thousand-eyed, situated in the eastern quarter;
and Agni, who is seated upon a goat, surrounded by garlands of flames and holding a spear.
To the south, Yama, dark-hued and seated upon a buffalo, holding a staff in his hand;
and in the southwest, Nirṛti, blue-colored, seated on a man, with a mace in his hand.
In the western quarter, one should worship Varuṇa, who is white, seated upon a fish, and holding a noose;
and in the northwestern quarter, Anila (Vāyu), who is brindled, seated upon a deer, and holding a banner.
In the north, one should visualize Kubera, yellow in color, holding a sword in his hand and seated upon a treasure-trove;
and [one should visualize] Śiva, tawny in color, three-eyed, mounted upon a bull, and holding a trident in his hand.
One should worship Īśāna, who has a serene face and is joyful, in the Śāṅkara [mandala];
but Viṣṇu, who is dark-complexioned, seated upon Tārkṣya, and holding a discus in his hand, in the lower [mandala].
The wise one should worship Brahmā, who has the luster of the dawn, is seated upon a swan, holds a lotus in his hand, and is positioned above, using the initial syllables of their respective names.
In the fifth [section], one should worship the Astra-saṃghāta as prescribed;
in the eastern part, one should worship the yellow-colored six-cornered Vajra.
In the southeast (Agni), one should place a spear of deep red luster; in the south, a black staff;
in the southwest (Nirṛti), a blue sword; and in the west (Vāruṇa), a white noose.

The variegated banner is in the northwest; the golden-hued mace is in the north; the blazing trident is in the northeast; and the discus, with a radiance equal to the sun, [is in the southeast]. (6.489)
The wise one should worship the white lotus situated below and [the other] above;
thus, the worship of the five enclosures has been succinctly proclaimed.
The single-enclosure worship may be performed with both the limbs (aṅga) and the Brahmās, or alternatively, with the limbs alone or with the Brahmās alone. (6/491)
There should be three enclosures consisting of the limbs of Brahmā, the world-protectors, and the weapons;
or one should worship the world-protectors together with their missiles.
Then, one should worship the eleven Rudras, who are the embodiments of the Lord of the Brahma-aṅga-vidyās,
with the mace and other weapons, according to the sequence of the intermediate enclosure.
And they know that the worship of the outer enclosure is performed according to the ritual for the retinue;
having thus worshipped the enclosure, one should offer the supreme food offering (naivedya).
The food offering (naivedya) should be made to the five faces, or alternatively, to the upper face alone;
furthermore, for all the limbs as well, there should be a separate food offering consisting of half [of the total].
The cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru) should be performed in separate vessels if possible;
otherwise, it may be done in one purified vessel, consisting of sacrificial food consecrated with mantras. (6.496)
The worship of the deities of the outer enclosure is performed individually with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, preceded by the presiding guardians of the gates. (6.497)
One should offer the *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*) and others, and then perform the offering with the mantra;
at the conclusion of that, one may either perform the daily fire-sacrifice (*nityahoma*) or enter once again into the inner sanctum.
Upon their satisfaction, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth, preceded by the wiping of the hands;
then one should cause to be offered betel-leaf as an oral fragrance, fit for the deity. (6.499)
Then one should honor him with the glorious five great sounds, the mirror, the parasol, and the fly-whisks, as well as with songs, dances, recitations, and hymns of praise. (6.500)

Having meditated upon [the deity] seated joyfully with the Goddess, together with his attendants and having the form of Śakti, one should place the purifying thread that completes the rite upon his head.
Because it protects one daily from falling due to the excessive activity of speech, mind, and body, it is therefore called *pavitraka* (the purifier).

Immediately thereafter, for the sake of fulfillment, one should utter the "Supreme End" (*paramāntika*)—which signifies the state of supreme absorption within the primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—and then install the Prāsāda mantra as before. (6/503)
One should first perform an act of encouragement using the previously acquired mudrā;
having made the request, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (japa) with a rosary.
That restraint which is produced regarding the senses—which are like dice—resulting in the attainment of fruits both seen and unseen, is called the "rosary of the senses" (akṣasūtra). || 6/505 ||
The rosary for recitation should be made with one hundred and eight beads, or half of that, or half again; it must be consecrated with the *śarva* and *śambara* mantras.
From the drawing together of the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, the highest accomplishment is attained;
from the joining of the thumb and forefinger, the middling accomplishment is desired. (6.507)
Through the joining of the little finger and the thumb, the least degree of accomplishment is said to be attained.
Here, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation of the Brahma-mantras and the limbs [of the deity] ten times for every hundred [recitations] of the root mantra. (6/508)

A wise person should perform the recitation neither too slowly, nor indistinctly, nor without formal commitment, nor too hurriedly, nor with mental confusion that fails to count the repetitions. (6.509)

Having performed the recitation as prescribed for the various daily rites and so forth, the practitioner should offer it for the sake of accomplishing his goal; others may do so until they cease. (6.510)

With three handfuls of water, together with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and so forth: "Oṃ! You are the protector of that which is more secret than the secret; accept this recitation performed by us. (6/511)
May success be mine through your grace while you remain present;
for whatever action there may be, O Lord, whether always good or evil—6/512.
O Śaṅkara, enjoy this and consume it for me, who am established in the state of Śiva;
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire universe. (6.513)
"Śiva worships everywhere; he who is Śiva is indeed I myself.
Having thus offered one's own self, one should perform recitation and worship with devotion. (6.514)
One should remain meditating upon Śiva afterwards, as previously described;
having praised him with various hymns, one should prostrate again and again. (6.515)
One should perform the daily fire-ritual in the chamber for the perpetual fire,
or in the sacrificial pit situated toward the direction of the kitchen fire, according to the prescribed sequence for the fire rites.
One should perform a perpetual festival, and immediately thereafter, the *tāṇḍava* dance;
then, one should worship the *liṅga* in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (6.517)
One should offer the *arghya* with the face turned away and display the *mahāmudrā*;
then, with the *saṃhāramudrā* and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [one should dismiss] the deities stationed in the enclosure.
Having raised them with the Mūrti-mantra, one should unite them with the embodied forms;
having uttered the root mantra accompanied by the heart-mantra, [one should perform this] while free from mental constructs.

One should contemplate [the Self] as liberated from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and having attained a state of partlessness (niṣkala), by means of the division of the Śiva-principle, while it resides within the heart. (6.520)
This emission without expectation is considered common to all liṅgas;
however, that which involves expectation regarding a specific, chosen liṅga has been demonstrated previously. (6.521)
Even in the case of a mobile linga, [the worship] is dependent; it is never independent in the case of a sthaṇḍila (altar).
However, in every instance, that which is independent is prescribed for daily practice.
One should worship Caṇḍa in the northeast with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order;
one should offer all the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) to him—that is what is proclaimed.
Some say it is located at the top of the liṅga; others say on the pedestal (piṇḍikā);
or situated on a throne in the northeast, or else in the outer chamber of Caṇḍa. (6.524)
The portion of the Supreme Lord's wrath is celebrated as Caṇḍeśa;
whatever substance arises over time, such as food offerings, perfumes, flowers, and the like, [is for him]. (6.525)
That garland which has been used is called *nirmālya*;
likewise, that which remains on the dust or on the pedestal of the *liṅga*, having been enjoyed by Śiva, is indeed *nirmālya*. (6.526)
The food of a Caṇḍāla, which is difficult to overcome, should be avoided with great effort;
as should canopies, umbrellas, garlands, and so forth, as well as clothing, ornaments, and vehicles. (6.527)
Cows, land, houses, clothing, and so forth—these are called the property of the deity;
likewise, any other substance offered to Śiva is also such. (6/528)

One should not employ the property of the gods or food intended for fierce deities for one's own enjoyment; however, contact with canopies and garlands, as well as the fragrance of incense, does not constitute a fault.
Likewise, having arranged the rows of lamps for Śiva’s vision and so forth, one should release the Lord's *liṅga* independently and purify it as before. (6.530)
Having projected the form identical with that [deity] upon the Yoga-pīṭha in the Praṇava,
and having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) with the purificatory mantras, one should worship it with the Gāyatrī.
Then, having adorned the liṅga along with its pedestal with flowers and other offerings according to one's ability for the sake of enjoyment, one should say: "Forgive me. (6.532)
Having washed the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, one should place them upon a wooden board or similar surface;
then, having cleansed the interior of the temple with three balls of cow-dung, one should proceed. (6.533)
One should cast food for the Caṇḍas outside into the vessel for leftovers;
however, if it has been sprinkled with water from bathing, drinking water, milk, or the like, then [it should not be discarded]. (6.534)
One should bathe or wash oneself above and below the navel;
then, having sipped water (ācamana) and become pure, one should bow down to the God of gods.
One who has fallen or slipped should practice the collection of mantras for the sake of purification;
this same rule is ordained even for a movable linga in the sacrificial hall.
One should withdraw the worship from the sacrificial ground using three balls of cow-dung;
then, having washed one's hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.
Having prostrated on the ground like a staff, one should say, "Please forgive me.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Ritual of Worship, in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Limbs of Worship (Arcanāṅgavidhi)
(Verse 45) I shall explain the ritual procedure for the ancillaries of worship, preceded by the characteristics of the junctions [of time],
beginning from one sunrise until the next sunrise.
A watch (yāma) measuring seven and a half ghaṭikās is called a junction (sandhi). Sixty breaths constitute one prāṇa, and six prāṇas constitute one ghaṭikā. (7.2)
Sixty *ghaṭikās* constitute a day and night, which is said to have eight junctions (*saṃdhyā*).
Worship performed during these eight junctions shall be the most excellent of the excellent. (7.3)
The ninefold worship, performed during the periods of seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, and half a watch (yāmārdha), shall be of nine kinds. (7.4)
One should perform the ritual from the commencement of worship until the end of the dance, concluding at the twilight (saṃdhyā).
There is a fault in exceeding the twilight period, but one incurs no fault if it is deficient. (7.5)
This procedure has been proclaimed for the worship consisting of the service to the Guru:
two *ghaṭikās* should be spent on bathing, and one *ghaṭikā* on worship. (7.6)
The offering of food (nivedya) is for half a ghaṭikā; the bali-offering is equal to that.
The daily fire-ritual (agnikārya) is for half [a ghaṭikā], and the daily festival (nityotsava) lasts for two nāḍikās.
One *ghaṭikā* is proclaimed as the time for dancing;
thus has the rule for time regarding the three great *saṃdhyās* been declared. (7.8)
If the twilight rite is performed with abbreviated materials during the twilight, it is not defective;
however, at whatever time it is possible, it should be performed for as many nāḍīs as are available. (7.9)
One should perform a sacrifice for one's own sake according to one's capacity, at the time of dawn, or even before half a watch has passed. (7.10)
One should produce the five great sounds that cause all living beings to tremble;
at that time, one should worship the God for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (7.11)
The worship should take place at the end of the evening service, or at the half-hour mark; it should be performed with abundant perfumes, flowers, fragrances, and aromatic substances.
Having especially adorned the goddess Umā as she reclines upon her couch with incense rich in fragrance and with offerings such as those customary in the world, [one should worship her]. (7.13)
One should cause [the deity] to enter the presence of the God with various dances and songs;
thereafter, for the sake of the increase of sons and grandsons, one should worship Śaṅkara. (7.14)
One should worship Śiva at midday and at the end of the twilight with [mantras] ending in *vauṣaṭ*, for the sake of attaining long life, health, and victory for the king. (7.15)
In this manner, worship should be performed every day provided one has the means;
however, the worshipper should first perform the ritual procedures, such as bathing, at the junction of the day (dawn).
At the conclusion of the bath, let the necessary materials, such as water and the rest, be gathered for the sake of the sacrifice by the attendants wearing clean garments and so forth. (7.17)
[Water] originating from rivers such as the Gaṅgā, or arising from lotus ponds and the like, sweet-tasting and scented with flowers, filled in new earthen jars. (7.18)
[The water] is strained through clean cloth, pure, and infused with the fragrance of cardamom and other spices;
it is combined with cardamom, ginger, and the three fruits (triphalā), along with camphor, fine saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, cinnamon leaves, and fragrant flowers. (7.19)

Water is prescribed for the act of immersion; from among the groups of substances mentioned according to one's means, whatever is obtained here should be accepted by both the wealthy and the poor. (7.20)

One should prepare the water for the purpose of consecration—that water which is the ocean of saṃsāra—ranging from one *bhāra* up to nine *bhāras*, in the lowest of the low [form of] the nine *liṅgas*. (7.21)
But here, by increasing the load by one, there is a distinction according to the number nine;
or else, with eight *droṇas* of water, or with double or triple that amount. (7.22)
For it has been stated regarding the rites taught in the *Svāyambhuva*, *Aṇaliṅga*, and other [tantras] that the desired result is attained;
indeed, for one's own sake, the quantity of water for bathing may be according to one's wish. (7.23)

One should prepare the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), water with kuśa grass, and water from a ritual jar, according to the prescribed measurements, for the purpose of the ceremonial bath.
It should be made from gold thread, woolen thread, cotton, or fine silk, and it must be endowed with the dimensions suitable for the ornaments of a deity. (7.25)
Cotton cloth is declared to be the best; linen is said to be middling; and cloth made from cotton threads is proclaimed to be the lowest. (7.26)
Alternatively, it may be one cubit long and two cubits wide;
such a cloth, which is pleasing to the mind, very smooth, and excellent, is prescribed. (7.27)
It should have a length eight times its width, be provided with a fringe, and possess the proper characteristics;
however, one should avoid cloth that has been bitten by rats, burnt by fire, or pierced by hair. (7.28)
One should accept such clothing as is useful;
likewise, saffron, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, sidhārtha, and uśīra [should be accepted]. (7.29)
Water for the feet (pādya) combined with sesame seeds alone is considered the best;
that which is joined with white mustard, uśīra, and dūrvā grass is called middling. (7.30)
Uśīra combined with sandalwood is said to be the lowest grade of water for washing the feet;
it is further joined with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and excellent nutmeg. (7.31)
O best of the twice-born, water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana) should be prepared with uśīra, sandalwood, three palas of camphor, cardamom, and tamāla leaves.
In the case of *ācāma*, however, one should employ it either combined with *elā* and *uśīra*, or with water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, barley, white mustard seeds, and rice. (7.33)
The eightfold *arghya* is said to consist of water combined with rice grains; [the eight components are:
water, milk, tips of *kuśa* grass, rice, flowers, and sesame seeds. (7.34)
The *arghya* is said to consist of eight ingredients: barley together with white mustard seeds;
or alternatively, rice, *vrīhi* grain, sword-blade grass (*sidhārtha*), sesame, and water. (7.35)
The *arghya* is declared to consist of water mixed with flowers;
likewise, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron are said to constitute the fragrance. (7.36)
One, two, three, or even four [parts] may be prepared with camphor; or one may fashion them with saffron, fragrance, camphor, and sandalwood. (7.37)
For each [image], it should be one *niṣka*, or half of that, or half of that again; for the highest of the high *liṅgas* and so forth, it should range from one *pala* up to a maximum of one *pala*.
For those who are extremely weak, the measurement of the water for the feet and other substances is according to what is available; thus has the measurement of these items been proclaimed. (7.39)
O best of sages, I shall describe the characteristics of flowers in brief:
the white lotus, the punnāga, the śaṅkhapuṣpa, and the mallikā. (7.40)
The *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, the *bahukarṇikā*, the *dvikarṇi*, the *kurava*, the *jātī*, the *lakṣmī*, and likewise the *vakula*. (7.41)
White arka, mālatī, droṇa, atasī, white lodhra, viṣa, kāsīsa, kusuma, bhadrā, and that which is mahatī. (7.42)
Vyāghrī, the campaka flower, karavīra born from the aśoka tree, hālikā, the śatapatra, unmatta, and the kuśa flower. (7.43)
Indeed, these white flowers possess both primary and secondary status:
the red lotus, the palāśa, the red water-lily, and the pāṭalī. (7.44)
Mausalī, dhuttūra, bṛhatī, karavīraja, vyāghrī, raktamandāra, paṭṭikā, and likewise vaijikā. (7.45)
And that *munipuṣpa* which is red—one should designate these as the red flowers;
likewise the *śonakya*, the *karṇikāra*, the *campaka*, and the *hemadhuttura*. (7.46)
Āragvadha, koraṇḍa, śairīṣa, and girikarṇikā—these have yellow flowers; for the dark rite, the blue lotus is best. (7.47)
The bilva leaf, the ascetic (tapasvin), the mahābhadra, and the dhātakī;
the apāmārga, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, the five bilvas, and likewise the śamī tree. (7.48)
Tulasī, candrapo, dānta, jambuka, nāganandikā, ekapatra, aravinda, and likewise viṣṇukrānti. (7.49)
The mango tree, as well as the black tulasī and the fragrant-leafed plant—leaves such as these increase one's progeny. (7.50)
Indeed, the families of plants beginning with uśīra and hrībera bestow auspiciousness;
a single bakapuṣpa flower is superior to a thousand arka flowers. (7.51)
A golden *dhuttūraka* flower is superior to a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers; a *śamī* flower is more distinguished than a thousand *dhuttūraka* flowers. (7.52)
(Verse 47) Among all varieties of flowers, the glorious blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is the best. [In another manuscript of the *Mātṛkā*,
there is a variant reading:]
The karavīra flower is superior to a thousand arka flowers;
the padma flower is superior to a thousand karavīra flowers.
A single *bilva* leaf is superior to a thousand lotus flowers;
a single *baka* flower is superior to a thousand *bilva* leaves.
Dhuttūraka is superior to a thousand *cakra* flowers;
and *bṛhatī* is superior to a thousand *dhuttūraka* flowers.
A *droṇa* flower is superior to a thousand *bṛhatī* flowers;
an *apāmārga* flower is superior to a thousand *droṇa* flowers.
A single *kuśa* flower is superior to a thousand *apāmārga* flowers;
a single *śamī* flower is superior to a thousand *kuśa* flowers.
Among a thousand *śamī* flowers, the glorious blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is superior;
according to another reading: "Among a thousand lotus flowers (*padma*), the *baka* flower is distinguished."
A single *bilva* leaf is superior to a thousand *bakapuṣpa* flowers;
among all species of flowers, the glorious blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is the best.
The *jātī*, *vijayā*, and *pāṭalī* should be known as equal to the *karavīra*. (7.53)
The white mandāra flower and the hundred-petaled lotus are equal to that;
the nāga, campaka, and punnāga flowers are recorded as being equal to the dhuttūraka.
One should avoid the ketakī, the atimukta, the yūthī, the fresh mallikā, as well as the flowers of the śirīṣa, sarja, and bandhūka. (7.55)
One should discard the leaves and flowers of the *aṅkola* tree, and one should avoid the leaves and flowers of the *vaibhītaka* tree. (7.56)
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or have a pungent odor;
one should also avoid flowers that, though fragrant, are impure.
Even if it lacks fragrance, sacrificial grass (kuśa) and other such items that are pure should be accepted;
golden kadamba flowers should be offered to Śaṅkara at night.
Flowers other than these [are suitable] during the day; the *mallikā* is suitable both by day and by night;
the *jātī* is said to be suitable for half a watch (one hour and a half); and the *karavīra* is suitable day and night. (7.59)
One should discard flowers that are infested with hair or insects, those that are withered or stale, those that have fallen off on their own, and those that are otherwise defiled. (7.60)
One should not worship the deity with buds, nor should one offer unripened fruit;
even in the absence of flowers here, one may offer leaves as well. (7.61)
If leaves are not available, one should offer fruits;
if fruits are not available, one should offer even grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs. (7.62)
If, however, medicinal herbs are unavailable, he becomes worshipped through devotion;
for each individual flower offered, the fruit is ten pieces of gold. (7.63)
A jewel originating from the nine sources, such as ruby and the like, is ten times more meritorious than gold;
one enjoys double that fruit when those very jewels are strung together in a garland.
One should worship with flowers produced from one's own garden, or those grown in the forest, or with blossoms and such purchased for the purpose; one should not worship otherwise.
Black aloe-wood should be one part, resinous exudate two parts, and sandalwood is said to be three parts, mixed with a small amount of camphor. (7.66)
This incense, known as Śītāri, is celebrated when mixed with honey, along with one, two, three, four, or five parts of nakha, sandalwood, and milk-rice (pāyasa). (7.67)
Combined with *turushka* and gradually increased, this incense of *śītāri* should likewise be thoroughly saturated with honey. (7.68)
Alternatively, one should offer incense mixed with honey, blended with *turuṣka*, camphor, *nāgara*, *agaru*, *candana*, *muruā*, and *māṃsī*, along with sugar. (7.69)
The incense known as *uśīrādi*, which consists of *uśīra* and sandalwood, combined with light ingredients and sprinkled with honey, is declared to be the "medium" incense, beloved by Śiva. (7.70)
Guggulu mixed with clarified butter is called the lowest type of incense;
likewise, agarwood alone or mahiṣākṣa may also be used for the purpose of incense.
Lamps numbering from one up to ten are of the lowest-of-the-low quality;
those from a hundred up to a thousand, ten thousand, and ending at a hundred thousand [are progressively better]. (7.72)
Lamps numbering in the millions, tens of millions, and so on up to hundreds of billions, may be lit in a single night; at that time, it shall be double that amount. (7.73)
Half of those would be without extinguished lamps, and half of those again would be so;
such is the calculation regarding lamps and the like—this is the enumeration that has been proclaimed. (7.74)
Furthermore, a lamp with ghee from a tawny cow is said to be *sāttvika*;
that with sesame oil mixed with goat's ghee is *rājasa*. (7.75)
Flames of one, two, or three finger-breadths are considered superior, middling, and inferior respectively;
however, a lamp made with buffalo ghee is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
A lamp made with oils produced from tree seeds is called Paiśāca;
the Paiśāca lamp is also considered Tāmasa and unfit for ritual use.
The food offering (naivedya) is said to be of many kinds, perfected according to the rules for sacrificial oblations (haviṣya);
likewise, the fire sacrifice (homa) and the bali-offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) are performed with substances prepared according to those same rules.
Likewise, one should arrange for a perpetual festival according to the constant rite,
including the *tāṇḍava* dance as described in the *Tāṇḍava-adhyāya*, along with the characteristics of dance, song, and so forth.
I shall explain its divisions; let that now be attentively grasped.

The embodied soul who, endowed with faith, performs the rite of worshiping Śiva through these constituent parts of such worship, becomes honored by the best of gods in the three worlds, revered by his master, and one whose every direction is illuminated.

In the end, he shall go, as it truly is, to the city of Śiva— his nature being knowledge and bliss, the cause of the origin and transmigration of all things— and be utterly liberated from the bonds of impurity, māyā, and so forth.
Thus ends the rule on the ancillaries of worship in the Kriyāpāda of the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Ritual for the Offering of Food (Naivedya)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite for the offering of food (naivedya).
One should prepare the naivedya with devotion, according to one's means. (8.1)
One should never consume a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, drink, or medicine without first offering it to the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva. (8.2)
By offering to Śiva edible substances such as cakes and the like, one's grain increases, as do fruits, flowers, and so forth. (8.3)
But if one enjoys wealth without having given it away, that fortune is exhausted;
whether the amount be small or great, the result for both the wealthy and the poor is the same. (8.4)
One should perform [the rite] according to one's ability; devotion alone is the cause here.
Having offered the food-offering (naivedya) to Śiva, the wise person should bring about auspiciousness.
But that auspicious deed which is performed without having given [as a gift] indeed leads to misfortune;
even an auspicious act, O Goddess of Auspiciousness, perishes if it is done so. (8.6)

Therefore, during a great festival such as the raising of the thread or the consecration [of an image], a wise person should avoid performing his own auspicious rites, such as the tonsure ceremony or marriage. (8.7)
The rice of the *śālī* variety is the best; that of *yava*, *veṇu*, and so forth is middling;
and the rice of the remaining *vrīhi* varieties is considered inferior. (8.8)
Those which have white grains are all known as *śāli*; the others are called *vrīhi*. Their fruits are distinct from one another. (8.9)
Hemaśāli, Mahāśāli, and likewise Ratnaśāli;
Sitaśāli, Atiraktā, and Saugandhi are considered the most excellent. (8.10)
The bamboo, as well as the remaining grains such as śāli and mādhurī, along with kustumbara and nīvāra, are proclaimed as the middling [grains]. (8.11)
The *biḍālavrīhi* is similar [to the others], being slightly blackish and having six grains;
likewise, the *sūkarīvrīhi* has a short beak and is the smallest. (8.12)
Among these, rice grains are considered the best for the Lord’s food offering (naivedya).
As many as the rice grains are used there in the preparation of the naivedya, [so many merits are gained]. (8.13)
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of years as there are grains of rice and other seeds dried by the rays of the sun upon a pure ground. (8.14)
Having sprinkled water upon the mortar, the practitioner should place the rice grains therein with the Astra mantra;
then, grasping the pestle, he should strike it with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should perform the pounding three times, or five times, or even nine times;
one should have it struck by women or men born of the four castes.
One should remove the husks and chaff from them using winnowing baskets and other such tools.
That which is filled with two hundred and twenty-five measures of rice— || 8.17 ||
One should know that the measure is merely a *śukti*;
by that very [unit] one should calculate the *tala*, the *prakūrca*, the *prasṛti*, and likewise the *kuḍupa*. (8.18)
Likewise, the añjali, prastha, pātra, āḍhaka, śivaka, droṇa, and khārī are declared in sequence; thus is the measure proclaimed. (8.19)
One should know that two guñjās make a māṣaka; twenty māṣakas make a dharaṇa;
eight dharaṇas make a pala, and a pala is here called a muṣṭi.
Four times that [prastha] shall be a *prastha*; vessels and the like are as before.
A *bhāra* is said to be three *khārīs*; thus is the measure proclaimed. (8.21)
The food offering (naivedya) is of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and for specific desires (kāmya).
Among its eight components, it is prepared with four parts of fire, one part of the sun, and one part of the moon. 8.22.
In the daily rite, the sacrificial offering (havis) consists of nine measures of an āḍhaka of rice;
one should not prepare the food offering (naivedya) with less than an āḍhaka of rice grains. (8.23)
Two *prasthas* are declared to be a *caru*; an oblation (*havis*) is said to be one *āḍhaka*.
One *prastha* together with a *kuḍuba* is called the food of the *piśācas*. (8.24)
However, for all [the deities], the food offering (naivedya) should be more than two prasthas;
beginning from two āḍhakas, it increases by that same measure up to nine times.
The measurement for the occasional oblation (*naimittika-havis*) is according to the three types of lingas;
however, the measurement for the optional oblation (*kāmya-havis*) shall be as much as is desired. (8.26)
Just as a cooking vessel is pure every day, at the end of a fortnight, or at the end of a month—
being respectively superior, middling, or inferior— so too is it ordained today according to the prescribed rule.
One should prepare a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or the like, or one consisting of pure clay, at every juncture of the day. (8.28)
Having first bathed according to the previously mentioned procedure, the attendants then put on white garments and white sacred threads.
Those with purified hands (pavitra-pāṇi) should prepare the cooked sacrificial oblation (caru) in the prescribed manner;
and one should fill the water-vat with water filtered through a cloth.
Then, having purified the vessel, one should wash the rice with water six times while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, squeezing it repeatedly. (8.31)

Having performed the cleansing with the six limbs, one should cast [the tooth-stick] into water with the *sadyojāta* mantra, having correctly understood through reasoning whether it is one and a half times or merely one time the length of the water. (8.32)
Having meditated upon the middle vessel, one should tie *darbha* grass around its neck;
then, in that kitchen which has been smeared with cow dung and other substances and sprinkled with water, [one should proceed].
One should worship the hearth of those who consume merit and demerit with rice while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra;
having lifted it up with the *Vāmadeva* mantra, one should establish it with the *Hṛdaya* mantra. (8.34)
Having installed the fire with the *aghora* mantra, one should kindle the fire with the *astra* mantra;
[one should avoid wood] infested by ants and the like, or joined with hollows and insects. (8.35)
One should not kindle the fire with wood that emits sparks; nor [should one eat food] that has a smoky odor, that is excessively moist, overcooked, or cold. (8.36)
One should discard food that is infested with hair or insects, as well as that which has been kept overnight;
thus has pure food been described, and now milk-rice (pāyasa) is being discussed.
The milk should be twice the amount of the rice, and the mung beans should be half the amount of the rice;
if these are unavailable, one should use half or even a quarter of that, and fill the remainder with water. (8.38)
Cooked milk-rice is called *pāyasa*; now *gulānna* is described.
Having prepared the *pāyasa* as before, one should add jaggery (*gula*) equal to one-fourth [the amount of milk]. (8.39)
One should add half a *guḷa* of clarified butter, or half of that, or half of that again;
when combined with plantain fruit, it is known as *gulānna*. (8.40)
Half a grain of rice is known as the measure for sesame; kṛsarā-rice is highly commended.
In its absence, half that amount, or even half of that again, is now prescribed as mung-bean rice.
Half a measure of rice, or half of that, or mung beans, is called *mudgānna*;
or one may use any of these according to availability. (8.42)
Having mixed together black pepper, turmeric, cumin, and mustard seeds, this is cooked; it is indeed celebrated as *haridrānna*. (8.43)
The characteristics of the sacrificial offerings have been declared; now I shall describe the side-dishes (upadaṃśakas):
mung beans, black gram, horse gram, peas, and flat beans. (8.44)
Rājamāṣa and āḍhakī, both husked and unhusked; likewise, kūṣmāṇḍa, panasa, alābu, kāliṅga, and the two types of bṛhatī. (8.45)
The cucumber and the karkarī, likewise with husk and without husk;
the plantain, the kāravī, the vyāghrī, the mango, and the urvāruka. || 8.46 ||
The root of a creeper, a bulb, and a root from another source combined—
each one of these should constitute one pala for a prastha of pickles.
Indeed, they should be fresh, pure, and free from all defects;
they should be ground, mixed with ghee, along with coconut fruits and the like. (8.48)
That which is prepared with black pepper, cumin, and other such ingredients is highly praised;
indeed, those side dishes should be served with salt and clarified butter. (8.49)
These should be prepared with sour condiments and combined with black pepper and other spices;
twenty palas of salt are prescribed, along with one prastha each [of the other ingredients]. (8.50)
Marica is prescribed at one-third or one-fourth the measure [of the other ingredients];
however, the measure of ghee is praised as being twice that of the marica. (8.51)
A portion equal to one-sixteenth part of a split mung bean, or even half of that, should be used for the rice;
it is taught that the split mung bean should be equal [in quantity], or perhaps even greater, in terms of its quality.

One should cook [the substances] combined with a paste (*kalka*) and prepared with *marīca* and other ingredients, as well as those mixed with a paste of white mustard (*siddhārtha*), making them flavorful.
Some of those very same items were prepared with pieces of cake, along with the flour of *kuluttha* grain and pepper ground together in succession. (8.54)
Having cast it into the churned [mixture] and made it smooth, one should cook it over a gentle fire, combining it with jaggery and flavorful fruits. (8.55)
In this manner one should cook the soup, as well as other similar dishes, and various kinds of cakes prepared with appropriate ingredients. (8.56)
Accompanied by the sound of conch shells and provided with umbrellas, lamps, and the like,
one should present the well-prepared food offering along with side dishes and other accompaniments.
On a pure ground smeared and adorned with the five powders,
one should perform the heated sprinkling with clarified butter using the purifiers.
One should offer three oblations with ghee into the fire called Śītā;
one should purify the vessels with water and apply the Tripuṇḍra mark.
Having placed them upon a tripod and covered them with clean cloths,
accompanied by the sound of a conch shell and provided with parasols, lamps, and other offerings.
When the people occupying the obstructed sections of the path have departed, one should wash away [the remains] with water;
having lifted all the vessels, one should place them in the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa).
One should also collect water from this very spot in due order, once the locations have been identified by the characteristics established in the chapter on instruments (karaṇādhyāya). || 8.62 ||
Or [the offerings] may be placed in small bowls and the like, or on pure plantain leaves and such,
upon clean cloths, using a ladle endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should place [the syllable] *oṃ*, which has the luster of the full moon, and mutter the three-syllabled mantra;
one should place all types of side-dishes upon the food offering (*naivedya*).
Fresh cow’s ghee, fruits possessing the essence of candied sugar, young mango fruit, and blameless curd and other such items [should be offered]. (8.65)
In front of Śiva, in a pure pavilion spread with white cloth and other materials,
one should place the sacrificial offering (havis) contained in a small vessel or similar receptacle upon a three-legged stand.
Having sprinkled [the offering] with the Heart-mantra and purified it with the Weapon-mantra,
and having rendered it nectar-like with the Cow’s Milk-mantra, one should place a flower upon the food offering (naivedya).
Having offered [the oblation], one should give excellent water with the right hand,
separately for each of the deities stationed in the intermediate enclosures.
Having divided the oblation into four parts, one part is for Śiva;
the portion below that is for the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and the portion below that is for the bali-offering.

One should cause the portion of the oblation that has adhered to the vessel to be given to the worshipper, as well as whatever sacrificial offering remains from the fire-ritual and from the *bali* offering. (8.70)
All of that has been explained here for the worshipper as it is now;
however, the food offering (naivedya) should be presented mentally if it is unavailable.
The food offering for the deities of the outer enclosure should be presented individually;
in their absence, an oblation (bali) should be offered, preceded by the presiding deities of the gates.
Outside of that, on the seats of the elements (bhūtapīṭha) established in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
one should offer to the Rudras in the east and likewise to the Mothers in the south.
One should offer the bali to the Gaṇas in the western part, to the Yakṣas in the north,
to the Planets in the northeast, and to the Asuras in the southeast.
To the *pālāśī* [direction], to the serpents who feed on flesh, to the sphere of Vāyu, to the groups of constellations and zodiac signs, and likewise to the host of the Viśvedevas; || 8.75 ||
There should be an offering of bali in the northeast for the Kṣetrapāla;
one should cast the bali for the Kṣetrapāla in the direction between the northwest and the west.
In these eight seats, one should offer the bali to the guardians of the directions;
first to the gatekeepers, and secondly to the spirits.
One should offer [oblations] starting from Vṛṣādi up to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) according to the sequence of the enclosures (āvaraṇa):
eight, twelve, sixteen, and thirty-two attendants. (8.78)
Standing in the hall where the inner necklaces and other ornaments are kept, one should offer them individually to each of them;
having especially worshipped Gaṇeśa there with the full set of ritual services (upacāras).
When it is possible, there should be worship through symbolic offerings for all;
thereafter, one should especially offer the bali-oblation upon the seat already established.
The yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, gandharvas, and kinnaras;
the pitṛs, dānavas, and nāgas; and those beginning with Brahmā, ending with Īśāna and Antaka. (8.81)

One should employ the formula for the offering of bali by placing one's own name between the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and the dative case ending at the end, concluding with *svāhā*, and appending the word "to all" (*sarvebhyaḥ*). (8.82)
Then, one should offer the *bhūtabali* (offering to the spirits) accompanied by the *balidāna* ritual,
in a space measuring three, two, or one *aśāvakāśaka*, provided with doors on all sides.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities from Indra to Īśāna during one's own rites;
then, having gone to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Having brought the *nirmālya*, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
because by this [offering] it attains purity, it is celebrated as *nirmālya*. (8.85)
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth to Caṇḍa and then discard the remains of the offering (nirmālya);
one should cast it either into deep water, into fire, or even present it to cows. (8.86)
Because the body is bound by impurities, one should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya);
thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual preceded by the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the ritual for food offerings, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of the Fire-pit (Kuṇḍa)
(Verse 52) Now, for the sake of accomplishing the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) are described:
the abode of the fire is of two kinds—either a pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*). 9/1.
One should lay down the initial thread according to the sequence for establishing the directions;
by that very means, one should subsequently establish the thread running from south to north.
Then, by taking half the measure of the site from the cardinal lines toward the intermediate directions,
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall be either square or circular, constructed with a span (hasta).

The rites that are obligatory, occasional, and those performed for specific desires, as enjoined by the ritual manuals, should be performed with well-baked bricks; in the absence of these, with unbaked ones.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as prescribed in the scriptures, in accordance with the specific mantra-homa;
for mantras dedicated to Varuṇa, it is ordained that the pit be shaped like a water-jar (kumbha).
The banner is prescribed for those of Vāyu, while the thunderbolt is for those of Mahendra;
the form of the seven-tongued [flame] is declared for those of Agni by the best of gurus. (9.6)
For those of middling and superior vigor, it yields a square fruit;
for those of little vigor, it is triangular; and for those of female form, it has the shape of a vulva. (9.7)
The crescent moon shape belongs to the fierce deities, while the circular shape indeed belongs to the gentle ones;
the five-cornered shape belongs to the Mūrtis as well as to the Kinnaras. (9.8)
The seat of the Vidyās and Vidyēśvaras is said here to be lotus-shaped;
