for the rite of immobilization (stambha) it is square in the direction of Indra, and for the rite of scorching (tāpa) it has the form of a vulva in the southeast.
A half-moon [is used] for killing in the south; an eight-cornered [figure] in the southwest;
a circle for pacification in the west; and a six-cornered [figure] in the southeast for driving away.
In the north, for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), there is a lotus; in the northeast (raudrī), an eight-spoked wheel that grants liberation.
For a fire-sacrifice of fifty or a hundred oblations, the width [of the altar] should be doubled respectively.

In a homa of one thousand or ten thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit shall be one cubit or two cubits respectively; in a homa of one hundred thousand or one million oblations, it shall be four cubits or six cubits.
For a *koṭi-homa*, the pit should be eight cubits; above that [number], it should not be larger, nor below.
For a minor *liṅga*, one should place a pit measuring only one cubit.
The increase for those two at the edge is half of two fingers (one finger) respectively;
having placed a fifth part in front, according to the measurement of four parts (a square) at the corner.
By mistake, the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is said to resemble the leaf of an aśvattha tree;
in a square house divided [into parts], having omitted the first and last portions, that portion [remains]. (9.15)
By means of a measurement equal to seven middle parts, one should draw a circle like a half-moon through rotation;
thereafter, one should place [the marks] in the desired directions and then lay down the thread toward the north.
By increasing [the side] by one-third, three fish-tails shall be formed;
by discarding half the neck and one-eighth [of it], the circular *kuṇḍa* is here described.
By increasing six parts, a hexagon is formed from four triangles;
in the square, the pericarp (karṇikā) should occupy two parts out of eight.
Outside of that, one should fashion the filaments with one part;
the centers of the petals in the third [part], and the tips of the petals in the fourth.
From the rotation [of the cord], there shall be a lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa), which should display the tips of its petals externally;
it may be equal to a circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) or otherwise according to another method.
Having first prepared a circular pit, one should divide the girdle into four parts;
having likewise established the height, the pericarp shall be one and a half [parts].
The remaining portion may be four-petalled or eight-petalled;
it should occupy one-tenth of the area of the field, extending in the four directions and further toward the north.
One should mark it according to that measurement and lead it toward the fourth corner;
one should also mark its arms according to the measurement of its diagonal.
In that case, by joining eight cords, the pit is said to be octagonal;
its depth is equal to its width, or it may consist of the remaining parts for the girdles.
The neck is one *aṅguṣṭha* in measure, and from that, it increases by one *yava* up to two *hastas*.
This is declared to be the measurement of the neck; O twice-born ones, now hear about the girdle (*mekhalā*). (9.25)
For a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one fist in size, the girdle (mekhalā) should indeed be two finger-breadths wide;
two girdles should be made, following the sequence of half a finger and one finger [in width].
The rim of a sacrificial pit measuring one *ratni* in size should be three finger-breadths wide;
its other two rims are considered to be half a finger-breadth each.
For a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*), the rim (*nemi*) should be four finger-breadths wide;
likewise, another girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made, measuring three and two finger-breadths respectively. (9.28)
For a pit measuring two cubits, the first rim shall be six finger-breadths;
the second shall be four finger-breadths, and the third shall be three finger-breadths.
For a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits, the rim (nemi) should be made eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) wide on the eastern side,
six finger-breadths on the other [two] sides, and four finger-breadths on the western side.
The first girdle should be made six cubits long with a width of ten finger-breadths;
the second should be eight finger-breadths, and the third six finger-breadths.
Of the eight-cubit [stūpa], the first girdle is twelve finger-breadths;
the second is ten finger-breadths, and the third is considered to be eight finger-breadths.
The form of the girdles should be like that of the pit;
or else, the measurement of the girdles is stated in another manner.
One should divide the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) into twenty-four parts;
that which consists of a single part may be [multiplied] by two, three, or four times that amount.
In this context, the girdles (mekhalās) are formed according to their width and height;
if there is to be a single girdle, it should be six finger-breadths in both breadth and elevation.
The navel is considered to be half the measure of the *kuṇḍa*’s diameter, or one-third;
the *yoni*, situated in the middle of the girdle (*mekhalā*), is joined with a height of two finger-breadths.
The measurement of the *yoni* is declared to be one fist for a pit of one cubit;
in pits of two cubits and more, it is increased by two finger-breadths for each additional cubit in width.
The height [of the altar] should be one finger-breadth more than its length;
from that, the *yoni* of all *kuṇḍas* is fashioned with a measure equal to half of its own [height]. (9.38)
Or it may be like the leaf of the aśvattha tree, or like the lip of an elephant;
it should be provided with a channel and measure one hundred thousand cubits.
Starting from the *yoni* up to the navel, it should be beautifully adorned by Gonanda;
the navel, however, is fashioned in the center of the *kuṇḍa* with a measurement equal to half [the height] itself.
The altar, which should be shaped like a lotus and have a height equal to one-fourth [of the total],
shall consist of eighty-one squares and be situated outside the pavilion.
Outside of that, one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in three sections, with the middle section being the altar (vedikā).
Having divided the altar into four parts, the altar is situated in the center of the pits.
One should arrange the array of fire-pits so that they occupy a single portion, or one may conceive them otherwise;
[the officiant] should face eastward at the primary pits of Vāyu, Soma, and Īśa.
The eastern face should be the northern one, and the Śiva-face should face the northeast.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Fire Sacrifice (Agnikārya)
(Verse 10.1) Hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the fire-offering (*agnikārya*).
The fire-offering is traditionally known to be threefold: Vedic, Mixed (*miśraka*), and Śaiva.
That which is performed with exclusively Vedic mantras is called Vedic;
that which is performed with both Vedic and Śaiva mantras is called mixed (miśra). || 10.2 ||
That which is performed with the Śiva-mantras alone is called Śaiva;
such is the procedure ordained for its production in the teaching of Śiva. (10.3)
That which is provided with three enclosing rings and two upright fuel-sticks is designated as the Vedic fire; the mixed fire, however, possesses the nature of both.
In this scripture, the Śaiva rite is proclaimed as having four boundaries;
that which is performed with the Brahmakūrca is known as Vaidika. || 10.5 ||
In the same way, there is the mixed fire (miśravahni), or indeed the Śaiva fire joined with that;
O twice-born ones, hear now the essential nature of the two fires, the mixed and the Vedic.
Endowed with a single body, he has two faces and two nostrils;
he possesses six eyes, is girt with a belt, and is provided with three feet. || 10.7 ||
He is considered to be endowed with four horns, two heads, and matted hair; he wears the sacred thread, possesses a girdle of muñja grass, and is seven cubits in height.
Endowed with seven tongues and mounted upon a bull,
his tongues on the right side are Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and Kṛṣṇā.
Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā are on the left;
thus the tongues are designated in the mixed fire of the Vedic hearth.
The tongue of Varuṇa is golden; the middle one is yellow;
the northern tongue should be red; and the one situated in the southern direction is black.
Suprabhā is at the front of the tongue, and Atiriktā is situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast);
Bahurūpā is the tongue itself—thus is the locus of the tongues proclaimed.
O Brahmins, listen with concentrated minds as the Śaiva fire is described:
it is red, endowed with five faces, and resplendent with seven tongues of flame.
Ten-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments, clothed in red garments, and seated upon a lotus. (10.14)
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana) and endowed with the ten weapons;
then [the goddesses] Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā follow thereafter.
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and another, Raktā, which is golden—these three are situated with their faces upward; the remaining ones are situated starting from the east.
The meditation on the Śaiva fire has been taught; fire is proclaimed to be threefold.
The Vedic fire is also threefold: it may be the Gārhapatya, or the Dakṣiṇa fire. (10.17)
Then, the wise preceptor should cause the Āhavanīya fire to be used for them here, arising from the fire mixed with the Śiva-fire.
Having procured a secondary substitute, the Guru should accomplish the Śaiva rite;
or he may accomplish it there with mixed materials, for a specific rule is also prescribed in this regard.
The Gārhapatya fire belongs to householders, the Dakṣiṇāgni to the ancestors, and the Āhavanīya fire is declared for the gods and others as well. (10.20)
The child, the youth, and the aged are described in sequence;
for the sake of the installation of the Śiva-fire, one should collect [the materials] for the sake of prosperity. (10.21)
One should designate youth for the "child-fire" intended for festivals;
one should employ the "old" fire in the perpetual fire, and may also employ it elsewhere.
The sequence is considered for the purpose of generating the secondary Śiva-fire;
however, the oblation for generating the primary Śiva-fire is proclaimed as the most excellent. (10.23)
The homa performed with the production of mixed fires is proclaimed as the middling one;
however, one should not employ the Śiva-mantras in either a Vedic fire or a solitary (non-mixed) fire. (10.24)
Vedic mantras or others that have been proclaimed for the Śiva-fire,
as well as those for the mixed fire, are likewise said to be for the Vedic fire. (10.25)
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the lords of the world, and whatever other gods are present;
Vyāsa, Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and Āśvalāyana. || 10/26 ||
Satyāṣāḍha and whoever others besides me [desire] the Vedas along with their meanings, other treatises, the Purāṇas, and likewise the Smṛtis—[let them listen]. (10.27)
However, for the sake of clarification, the Sūtras provide both detailed and concise treatments; that Vedic fire which is recited according to their doctrine has not been performed [by me]. (10.28)
It is said that Brahmins and others who are uninitiated have authority only over the Vedic fire; however, those who are initiated are qualified for everything.
However, those who follow both [traditions] should first separately perform the Vedic rites,
beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and thereafter accomplish the Śaiva fire.
Thus has the mixed fire been described as suitable for both seasons and both stages of life;
or else, immediately after the Vedic *homa* has been completed.
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as prescribed by the Śaivas, and having previously [established] the fire,
one should rest within the fire situated at the navel by means of the downward-moving breath (apāna) through the activity of the upward-moving breath (udāna).
Then, by means of the *tarda* [mantra], one should successively cause Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and Nareśvara,
as well as Nityāgni and Śivāgni, to enter the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍaka*).
Having thus prepared the mixture, one should offer oblations with all the mantras;
this is for the purpose of unifying both [the deceased] at the commencement of the funeral rites and other ceremonies.
Or, at the outset, one should perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the Vedic or Śaiva rites;
or, having completed the Vedic fire-ritual, one should then prepare the Śaiva fire.
Having established the Śiva-fire elsewhere, one should lead it to the union [with the other fire];
thus, in rites such as the funeral ceremony (antyeṣṭi), such a commingling is indeed accepted here.
Furthermore, in other cases, it should be performed separately according to one's faith and wealth.
I shall now fully describe the Śaiva fire, preceded by the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Likewise, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square, circular, or lotus-shaped;
it bestows all desires and is always constructed to measure one cubit.
The three [sections] should be four, three, and two finger-breadths [in width] respectively; the girdle is one [finger-breadth];
the vulva-like opening in the middle should be twelve finger-breadths long and resemble the trunk of an elephant. (10.39)
Having a height and width of one thumb-joint, situated above the cavity of the womb;
in the absence of that, one should establish the consecrated fire upon a brick-pavement.
Indeed, the Śiva-fire is not established in an unrefined fire-pit;
and if the Śiva-fire is not established, the oblation becomes fruitless. (10.41)
The inspection should be performed with the Śiva-mantra, the sprinkling with the Astra-mantra, the sprinkling around with the Varma-mantra, and the striking with the Astra-mantra. (10.42)
One should perform scraping, scattering, filling, and likewise sprinkling; then one should carry out pounding, and after that, sweeping. (10.43)

The smearing [of the site], the fashioning of the pit (kuṇḍa), the encircling of the pit, the worship of the pit, and the placement of the enclosing sticks and the sacrificial grass-bundle. || 10.44 ||
The wise one should fashion the four lines, the arrangement of the vajra, and the design of the śṛṅgāṭaka— all of this— using the weapon mantra.
Having mentally prepared a seat there, one should install the goddess Vāgīśvarī, and likewise Vāgīśvara, who is Śiva whose body is space. (10.46)
Having meditated and united with another woman who desired pleasure according to the prescribed rule,
he then performed for those two the ritual of churning and the oblation of fuel-sticks.
One should cast fire produced by the friction of pure wood, or fire generated from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta), or fire born from the abode of the twice-born (a fire-drill). || 10.48 ||

One who knows the ritual procedure should employ [the substance] purified by mantra according to the secondary rule; or else, having brought an unsuitable material from a magnet-stone or similar source, he should do so.
One should purify [the vessel] by means of the rites of inspection and so forth in a copper plate or a clay bowl;
having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters, one should sprinkle it with water empowered by the weapon-mantra.
Then, having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) with "aim namo'ste.
One should then effect the union with Fire by means of the seed-syllable of Fire and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).

Having rendered [the materials] nectar-like with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* accompanied by the *dhenumudrā*, and having performed worship, one should circumambulate the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having divided [the mantra] into three parts, one who has gone to the ground should place them with both knees,
so that they face oneself within the central channel of Vāgīśī. (10.53)
Having cast [the offering] with the root mantra, one should contemplate oneself as Śiva;
then, having offered a drop of water, one should cover it with excellent fuel. (10.54)

Having consecrated a darbha bracelet with the Astra mantra and tied it upon the hand of the goddess with the Hṛdaya mantra for the sake of protecting the fetus, this is performed on account of the *garbhādhāna* rite. (10.55)
Having invoked Sadyojāta with the heart-mantra and offered three oblations of sesame seeds for the sake of the *puṃsavana* rite, one should worship Vāmadeva.
Likewise, at the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), one should offer an oblation with the head [mantra];
having worshipped with the Aghora mantra, one should offer three oblations with the crest-mantra (śikhā).
Having offered [the oblation] with *darbha* grass and performed the ritual arrangement of the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the limbs of the face,
and having then performed the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should then proceed to the birth-rite (*jātakarman*).
Having performed worship with the *puruṣa-sūkta*, one should then offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *kavaca-mantra* for the sake of removing the impurity of birth (*sūtaka*). (10.59)

Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit with water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should spread darbha grass around the pit with its tips pointing eastward and northward, using the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Then, for the sake of protection, one should open the faces of the fire of Śiva;
or else, with three oblations, for the nourishment of those faces.
And for the purpose of removing saliva, one should offer twenty-four pieces of fuel-sticks, each sixteen finger-breadths in length, as oblations.
Having invoked Īśāna during the naming ceremony, one should perform the fire-oblation with the Astra-mantra;
preceded by the root mantra, one should say: "Thou art the Śiva-fire. (10.63)
One should perform the dismissal of the parents and worship the girdles;
one should also worship Indra and the other guardians of the world within the enclosures.
And on the seat, one should worship Brahmā and Rudra in due order, as well as Viṣṇu and Īśvara in the four directions starting from the east.

Having taken the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, having sprinkled them with water using the *astra-mantra*, having enveloped them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and having heated them in the fire or whirled them before it; || 10.66 ||
Having touched it with the tip of a blade of darbha grass and whirled it around the middle from the center, and having whirled it again from the root and touched the root of those two; 10.67.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of those five faces upon the *sruc* ladle, one should place the Śakti [therein].
Having worshipped Śambhu upon the *sruva* ladle, one should place it to the right of oneself.
One should worship upon the darbha grass with the Heart mantra;
having sprinkled the clarified butter with the Astra mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca mantra.
Having heated it in the fire with the Śiva-weapon mantra and then removed [from the fire] with its armor-mantra,
one should lead it three times clockwise around the very top of the sacrificial pit.
Having placed it in the *yoni* and grasped it, one should take up the *prādeśika-pavitra* made from two tips of *darbha* grass, using the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger. (10.71)
Having performed the triple immersion with the *kavaca* mantra facing the fire, and likewise having performed the immersion with the *hṛdaya* mantra facing oneself; 10.72.
Having cast the purifier into the fire and illuminated that clarified butter with the Astra-mantra,
the wise one should then gaze upon the ghee and perform the lustration rite (nīrājana).
Having cast the firebrand into the fire, one should sprinkle it with water and consecrate it with the limbs [of the mantra];
then, having rendered it nectar with the root mantra accompanied by the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having worshipped a blade of *darbha* grass measuring a span with the root mantra,
and having placed it here with the syllable *oṃ*, one should fashion the triad of channels.
Having taken clarified butter from the center, one should perform the oblation to the north with the mantra "To Agni Svāhā" and "To Soma," joined with the Praṇava. || 10/76 ||
One should perform the oblation in the center, joined with Agni and Soma;
one should offer the fourth oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the words "Svāhā. (10.77)
By casting a drop of that clarified butter, one should purify other [offerings] from the clarified butter;
this division applies to the bright fortnight, while in the dark fortnight, one should perform the solar oblation.
One should perform the consecration of the faces of the fire with three oblations of clarified butter, accompanied by their respective mantras; one should join Sadyojāta with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should join the left [vowels] with the Terrible (Ghora), and that with Tatpuruṣa;
having joined that with Īśāna, one should join it with Śiva himself.
Having thus performed the joining of the faces and their unification, one should proceed from Sadyojāta onwards, each accompanied by its own respective mantra. (10.81)

One should fashion the mouth and the size of the sacrificial pit according to one's desire, for the successful accomplishment of the sacraments such as the first feeding of solid food and the tonsure ceremony.
Then, one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) upon the tongue situated in the center,
specifically using the root mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ" with the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva).
For the sake of the sacrificial oblation, incense, lamps, and boiled rice,
one should carefully extract fire from the hearth and take separate portions for each purpose.

In the eastern direction, the offerings of cooked rice (caru) and sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are made into the fire that has been consecrated with the five purificatory rites (pañcasaṃskāra), even if Śiva has not yet been invoked; however, the oblation (homa) is performed only when Śiva has been invoked.
O Agni, since you are the sovereign splendor and the supreme purifier,
I therefore place you within the lotus of my heart and satisfy you.
Having thus made the request, one should place his seat of yoga within the lotus of the heart and then conceive of his form as radiant, excellent, and supreme.
Having brought that [deity] into presence by means of invocation and other rites, one should worship the causal [form] within her and then assign the limbs of enjoyment upon her exterior.
Having meditated upon the luminous [elements] individually by means of their respective supports,
and having made them pleasing and supreme, [one should offer them] into the fire-mouths of Śiva and Agni.
Having established a connection with the fire, one should clearly contemplate its light emerging through the nostrils and becoming unified with Śiva at the place of sacrifice. (10.90)
Having performed the union of the channels (nāḍīsandhāna) and requested permission, one should satisfy Śiva;
O best of the twice-born, one should then satisfy the limbs [of the mantra] with a tenth part of that [offering] to Śiva.
One should perform the fire-oblation every day for one's own sake or for the sake of others, [offering] a hundred, half of that, half of that again, twenty, or ten. (10.92)
One should perform the fire-oblation once, twice, or thrice a day;
in the absence of clarified butter, the oblation should be performed with black-seeded sesame.
Either with rice grains, or with sacrificial fuel-sticks, or with curd, or likewise with barley;
or with the three myrobalans, or with bilva leaves, or with auspicious flowers fit for sacrifice. (10.94)
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed by others according to their faith and wealth, having assumed the form of a deer, a boar, or a conch-bearer. 10.95.

Or one may offer separate substances with the mantras known as the *mātrās*, in whatever manner is appropriate; the oblation of well-refined oil, honey, and milk should be poured in a continuous stream.
One should offer an oblation with a handful of curd from a bower, and from a *pala* of both solid food and milk-rice;
alternatively, all kinds of food may be offered, as well as sesame seeds with five fingers extended.
One should offer fried grains (lāja) with the fist, fruits in their natural form,
vegetables in a handful measured by the hand, and varieties of tubers in an eighth part of that measure.
For bitter substances, oil-cakes, and their like, there is no requirement for the ritual procedure of *abhicāra*;
however, the roots should be divided into three segments, and those of the creeper species should be two finger-breadths in length.
One should offer grains mixed with parched rice, all types of food in a quantity equal to a single mouthful,
and then, at the end, one should present sacrificial food (haviṣya) and betel leaf.
Having circumambulated, bowed, and praised with devotion,
and having worshipped, offered, and delighted [the deity], one should then dismiss them.
Having afterwards gratified the Śiva-fire with the vyāhṛtis,
one should restrain it right there and protect it every day.
One should meditate upon the threefold fire in the sacrificial pit according to the threefold rite;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods there and not dismissed Him, one should touch one's own limbs.
Afterwards, when the deity has been dismissed, there will be fierce ashes;
or else, one should dismiss the fire into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and preserve it elsewhere.
If the protected fire is extinguished, one who has fasted should mutter the Ghoramantra;
or else, for the sake of pacification, one should mutter or offer oblations with the Bahurūpamantra.

In that very place, one should offer the inner oblation (antarbali) after having prepared a small mandala on the ground, or else on a consecrated wooden board purified with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Rudras in the east, likewise to the Mothers in the south,
to the Gaṇas in the western part, and to the Yakṣas in the north.
Likewise, [offerings] to the planets in the northeast, to the Asuras in the southeast,
to those who eat raw flesh from the Palāśa tree in the southwest, and to the Nāgas in the northwest.
(Verse 10.109) To the constellations, the zodiac signs, the groups [of deities], and likewise to the Viśvagaṇas,
offerings should be given within the maṇḍala to them according to one's desire.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla in the northwestern direction;
this same procedure is prescribed for one's own sake in houses and the like, as well as in temples.
One should offer the bali-oblation separately for each of the attendants, beginning with Nandin;
at the conclusion, one should likewise perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) and the bali-oblation.
Having sipped water and become pure, with his body consecrated by the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite,
he should then go to the vicinity of the *liṅga* and perform the subsequent ritual action after offering libations.
One should further gratify Śiva with offerings such as songs and the like;
thereafter, one should perform the perpetual festival, concluding with the dance known as the "Pure" (śuddha).
The wise teacher should cause a festival and pure dancing to be performed for the sake of others at the temple; however, he should not perform them in front of his own house. (10.114)
And at the conclusion, one should have songs performed so that Maheśvara is pleased;
having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and having offered the arghya, [one should dismiss him] with his face turned away.
Having displayed the supreme mudrā and raised the limbs with the weapon [mudrā],
one should meditate on Śiva as the Withdrawer and unite him with the form within the image.
Having worshipped Śiva and further uttered the mantra that follows from the heart,
one proceeds through the abandonment of causes until reaching the state of partlessness (niṣkalatā).
Alternatively, one should meditate by means of oneself through the non-differentiation from the supreme reality;
one should conceive of oneness with that [deity] abiding in the heart-lotus by means of that mudrā.
In this manner, one should dismiss the deity, whether with or without further expectation;
having performed the worship beginning with the drop (bindu) and ending with the sound (nāda), one should finally worship Caṇḍeśvara.

[The rite is performed] when the arrow, the iron [image], the moving [image], the consecrated [image], and the self-manifested [image] are present, but not for Caṇḍeśa, nor at the end of all [other] images, nor upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 10.120 ||
Outside the temple, in the northeast direction within the shrine,
whatever substance has been given to the deity is designated as being for Caṇḍeśa.
One should not employ food intended for Caṇḍa—the invincible one—for one's own enjoyment;
one must avoid stepping over the remains of an offering (nirmālya), giving it away, or eating it. (10.122)

Just as there is no discarded offering (nirmālya) belonging to the Guru, the scriptures, the Nāgas, the fire, the assembly of yogis, Pārvatī, the Yakṣas, or the Mothers that is not [considered sacred] for Śiva; || 10/123 ||

In the case of lingas made of jewels, gold, and the like, as well as in mobile lingas, there is no discarded offering (nirmālya) at every moment; this also applies to gurus, in discourses, and in images. 10.124.
Whatever is offered to one's own chosen deity (iṣṭaliṅga) is equivalent to an offering of sacrificial porridge (caru); of this there is no doubt.
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be given to one's brothers, sons, and sisters.
If he should be sprinkled with bathing water, milk, or other such substances,
then he should bathe or wash himself above and below the navel.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and become purified, and having bowed down to the God of gods,
one should practice the collection of mantras for the sake of purifying what has been dropped or faltered.
One should depart from the ālaya with the left foot, without touching the threshold.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the procedure for the fire-ritual, in the great tantra known as the Kāmākhyā.
The Ritual of Time.
(Verse 11.1) Now I shall declare the time that brings happiness to all:
with the exception of the month of Māgha, the northern course of the sun is auspicious.
The two months of Kārttika and Āśvayuja, as well as Śrāvaṇa, are prescribed for the southern course when it is swift; others besides these are considered censurable.

The bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is auspicious, while the other (the dark fortnight) is considered favorable up to the seventh day. In the bright fortnight, one should avoid the first third [of each lunar day], but in the dark fortnight, one should avoid the last third. || 11.3 ||
The two middle parts are considered middling, while the other two are proclaimed to be excellent;
this is excluding the ninth and fifteenth lunar days, as well as the odd-numbered tithis.

The first among those [conception days] is on even nights; likewise, the second and the tenth, as well as the sixth in the dark fortnight—those remaining ones are all irreproachable in this world. (11.5)
Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, Hasta, Svātī, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Śravaṇa, Śatabhiṣaj, and Maghā. (11.6)
Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, and Pauṣṇa are praised among men;
likewise, Śatabhiṣak, Viśākhā, and the Pūrvās (the three Pūrvas) are to be honored. (11.7)
All this that was told among the gods regarding Raudra is considered auspicious for Śiva;
however, among humans, the Pauṣya and Pauṣṇa [nakṣatras] and others besides them are censured here.
Having excluded the days of Mars and the Sun, the day of the gods (Thursday) is praised;
humans should also avoid the day following that of Venus (Saturday).
When the sun has entered the sign of Pisces (Jhaṣa), one should avoid commencing the construction of a house;
likewise, wise men should not perform any auspicious rite when Jupiter has set.

One should not perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and other rites at the time of Venus's setting; the installation of the image (garbhapratiṣṭhā) should be done by day, and the construction of the temple site (vāstukarma) by night.
Entering [the site] at night is said to cause all kinds of defects;
one should never, under any circumstances, perform the Vāstu-bali offering with fire in a village at night.
A fixed sign (sthira-rāśi) is excellent, while a dual-natured sign (ubhayātman) is middling;
a movable sign (cara-rāśi) should be avoided, unless it contains a living planet (sajīva), in which case it bestows auspicious results.
The rising of Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon is highly commended;
for Brahmins, the rising of Jupiter is auspicious, while for kings, the rising of Venus is so. (11.14)
The rising of Viśāmbudha is most excellent for a Vaiśya, and it is ordained as such even for a Śūdra;
moreover, malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses are auspicious at night. (11.15)
Excluding the expenditure (Vyaya), all auspicious planets are considered to bestow auspicious results everywhere;
however, in the case of a square (Caturaśra), the malefic planets should be especially avoided.

The wise preceptor, established in the five-fold range of observation (*pañcagocara*), should avoid the moon situated in both [the fifth and seventh houses] as well as when it has reached the sixth or seventh house. 11.17.

The best of teachers should avoid a place that is thorny, or where a Brahmadaṇḍa has been cast, or where a pillar has been uprooted by a planet, as well as a place that is occupied or desired by another. 11.18.
Vidhi, Tārakṣa, Vyatīpāta, Vajra, Śūla, as well as Viṣkambha, Parigha, Gaṇḍa, Vaidhṛti, and Harṣaṇa. (11.19)

Likewise, [one should avoid] the *atigaṇḍa* yoga, a weak lunar mansion (*mandarkṣa*), the commencement of the six-eighths (*ṣaḍaśītimukha*), a month devoid of planets (*māsaśūnya*), a day pierced by malefic planets, and similarly a "burnt" day (*dagdhavāra*). // 11.20 //
One should avoid that which is afflicted by planetary defects, such as flaming asterisms and so forth, as well as everything from the lunar day and asterism up to the month, year, and solstice.
A wise guide should especially avoid an intercalary month;
rather, he should act when the lunar mansion is favorable to the patron, when defects are minimal, and when qualities are predominant. (11.22)

Either in the forenoon or at midday, when the ascendant is endowed with the strength of the planets, one should have this rite for the building site performed for the sake of the increase of all prosperity. (11.23)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the rules of time, in the great tantra called the Kāmika.
The Procedure for Examining Omens.
(Verse 12.1) Having first examined the time, one should perform auspicious deeds at the end;
having first recognized the omens and signs, one should perform the ritual action.
The architect who knows the site, the artisan, the astrologer, and the patron—having become pure, dressed in white garments, and adorned with ornaments. (12.2)
When setting out on a journey, when departing, and when entering a dwelling site, one should contemplate Sadāśiva and observe these signs and omens. (12.3)
A learned man, or even a Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by his wife and son, being strong, adorned, possessing excellent sons, and especially filled with joy; || 12/4 ||
A beautiful maiden, a pregnant woman, and especially children at play;
as well as food, edibles, drink, meat, and likewise a lamp—(12.5).
Unction, garlands, and other fragrant substances; ghee and curd;
the Śrīvatsa mark, a full water-pot, a conch, and likewise gorocana pigment.
A mirror, a banner, white mustard seeds, and water again—whatever other auspicious things there may be, the sight of them is indeed favorable. (12.7)
The cucundarī, the śivā, the gaulī, and the tawny pig,
as well as the cuckoo on the left, are auspicious during a departure and for all undertakings.
Those whose rivers flow nearby, those who travel swiftly from afar to distant heights, and those who dwell in auspicious and delightful places such as mansions and palaces; || 12/9 ||
The best [milk] is that from trees bearing sweet sap, milk, fruit, and flowers;
a wild cow should not be taken from a village, nor a village-dwelling cow from the forest. (12.10)
One who wanders by day should not be taken at night, nor one who wanders by night during the day;
those moving in pairs and seeking their desired object are to be captured, as are the crows that desire the sacrificial bricks.
Intoxicated birds separated by a river should never be accepted;
a sneeze is undesirable everywhere, but a cow's sneeze portends death. (12.12)
Seeing jujube seeds, black grains, cotton, charcoal, cattle, and fuel—these sights of the provisions of destiny bring intense sorrow. (12.13)

The sight of a leather-worker, one with disheveled hair and so forth, those emaciated by hunger and thirst, shaven-headed mendicants, those who are filthy, those who have not eaten, or those who are naked, brings about suffering. (12.14)
There will be verbal abuse and weeping, as well as quarrels that bring further sorrow;
likewise, there will be the sight of boars, buffaloes, camels, and other such animals. (12.15)
One should avoid all ritual action when there is an unfavorable omen;
for by performing it once, twice, or thrice, one incurs the fault of the threefold omen.
The wise preceptor, endowed with the five spheres of perception, should avoid [these].
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the procedure for examining omens, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for Examining the Ground.
When an auspicious omen has been obtained, one should perform the examination of the ground;
[namely] the Śaiva, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, and Aindra [examinations]. (13.1)
The Aukṣa, the Bhautika, the Āsura, the Piśācaka, the Rākṣasa, the Vāyavya, as well as the Vāruṇa and the Āgneya. (13.2)
One should recognize the qualities of the earth by these characteristics:
the Karṇikāra, Arjuna, Aśvattha, Kapittha, Aśoka, and Ghātakī trees [should be present]. 13.3.
The earth is pervaded by land-lotuses, tulasī, and dūrvā grass;
or by viṣṇukrāntā, ākhukarṇa, śālmalī, giriśā, and ariṣṭa.
That auspicious earth belongs to Śiva when it is frequented by pigeons, parrots, and swans;
likewise, when it abounds with bilva, palāśa, darbhā, kuśa, and hariṇa grasses. (13.5)
The earth, when offered with fragrant sacrificial materials, is considered to bestow auspiciousness;
likewise, it is so when offered with *tinduka*, *tintriṇī*, *karaja*, and *veṇu* wood. (13.6)
And that ground which is filled with cotton plants, arka, and japā flowers, as well as with swans, birds, and deer, and likewise with thornless trees. (13.7)
This land is declared to belong to Viṣṇu; it bestows valor and heroism upon men.
It is adorned with plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, punnāgas, and likewise with vakulas. (13.8)
The earth is considered to belong to the Vaiśyas through *pāṭala* and *sindhuvāra* flowers as well as *āmalaka* fruits; it is considered to belong to the Śūdras through *indīvara* lotuses. (13.9)
Rich with the fragrance of *pāṭalī* and *agaru*, it bestows abundance of wealth and grain;
likewise, it is graced by *aṅkola* trees, as well as by cats and mongooses.
A land abounding in hares, iguanas, cakora birds, wolves, and bulls is considered auspicious;
it bestows valor and heroism, as well as the prosperity and abundance of progeny. (13.11)
Nirguṇḍī, mādhavī, dūrvā, tvak, kola, kiṃśuka, as well as mallikā, karavīra, and madhūka—these are considered the bhautikī [offering]. (13.12)
It bestows food and nourishment upon men and is permeated with the scent of ashes;
it abounds with marking-nut trees, great trees, wicked creatures, and onions.
The ground was filled with Kirātas, Kakubhas, vultures, and all manner of rogues; it was demonic, conducive to battle, and permeated with a foul stench. (13.14)
Likewise, the ground was covered with *śālmalī* trees, *vakula*, and *vibhītaka* trees;
it was further filled with *śleṣmātaka* trees, as well as donkeys, camels, jackals, and boars.
It is inhabited by Caṇḍālas and Pulindas; it is foul-smelling and barren, and according to the scriptures, it is known as Paiśācī, fraught with total destruction.
Abounding in the pungent scent of black pepper and garlic, that Rākṣasī brings about destruction through Caṇḍālas, poison, thieves, and diseases such as ailments of the head. (13.17)
That which is crowded with packs of jackals, filled with crickets and gravel, and situated in the northwest is called Vāyavī; it bestows suffering and poverty. (13.18)
The land surrounded by groves, belonging to Varuṇa, which bestows all perfections,
is joined with *snuhi*, *śleṣmātaka*, and other such small pebbles.
The saline, waterless land is fiery and destructive of all;
that which is in the region of Śiva is declared to be Śaivī, and that in the region of Viṣṇu is Vaiṣṇavī. (13.20)
The land of Brahmā is Brāhmī, while Śaivī is suitable for Brahmins and the other castes; Śaivī is distinguished by Brahmins, and the land of Viṣṇu is Vaiṣṇavī. (13.21)
The earth of kings is said to be Vaiśyā, that of Śūdras is remembered as Bhautikī;
while the earth of Piśācas is Āsurī, and that which is considered the earth of Rākṣasas is Paiśācī. (13.22)

The land that has been long occupied by outcastes here, even if it has been cultivated by them in hundreds of ways, may be taken back from them after a year, provided it was previously broken up by oxen.
According to the nature of the terrain, the earth is said to be of two types for those who follow the natural order:
the marshy (anūpā) and the arid (jāṅgalā); thus the ground suitable for building sites (vāstu) is twofold. (13.24)
A *jāṅgala* soil is firm, heavy, abounding in gravel, and extremely mixed with alkaline water,
even when dug to a great depth. (13.25)
It was strewn with *kaśeruka* grass and white water-lilies, filled with blooming fragrant lotuses and blue lotuses, possessed fine sands, was marshy, and its waters surged due to irrigation.
That which possesses qualities mixed with both the *jāṅgala* and *anūpa* types is known as *sādhāraṇa*.
That which originates from trees such as the plantain (*kadalī*), the palmyra palm (*tāla*), and the breadfruit (*panasa*) is considered *jāṅgala*. (13.27)
The marshy region (ānūpa) is considered suitable for all crops, a source of happiness from trees bearing flowers and fruit, providing comfort in all seasons, and beneficial to all. (13.28)
The combination resulting from the union of these two is declared to be common, and it is of four kinds: Padmaka, Bhadraka, Dhūmra, and Pūrṇa. (13.29)

The *padmaka* site is characterized by even contact, being smooth, fragrant, resonant with pleasant sounds, and stable; it has water rising to the height of a hollowed palm (*añjali*) when the hands are joined. (13.30)
Water from the east or north is excellent for crops; that from the south is for the lord [of the city];
and that from the northeast is most essential, being accompanied by vīraṇa grass.
It is a place of excellent substance, delightful, and auspicious as a dwelling for the virtuous;
it is full, smoke-colored, eternal, and floats in the direction of wind and fire.
It is of four kinds— excellent, middling, inferior, and constant—
and it measures ten *daṇḍas* in length, being bent by six *mātrās*.
The best [well] should be two spans in depth, the middling one a cubit, and the lowest one should be half a cubit; it should be provided with a slow, moderate, or rapid flow of water.
A site that is deeper than a cubit is declared to be censurable;
however, that which is square and level is suitable for deities and the twice-born.
If an octagonal, hexagonal, or square [mandala] is prescribed for the king and the Vaiśya,
the best of teachers should likewise arrange it for the Śūdra according to the respective order.
A site extending eastward is the best; one extending south-north is middling.
White, red, yellow, and black are the colors corresponding respectively to the Brahmin and the other castes.
Accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, flutes, lutes, and kettledrums, and with the fragrances of puṃnāga, jasmine, lotus, grain, and pāṭala flowers. (13.38)
The best [soil] is equal to the scent of cattle, causing all seeds to sprout;
it is uniform in color, dense, smooth, and endowed with a pleasant touch. (13.39)
The sky is devoid of crooked limbs; when covered by the low, it is supreme bliss.
It is indeed bitter, pungent, astringent, sweet, and sour. (13.40)
Salt, combined with the six flavors, brings all happiness when used appropriately;
it should be accompanied by water that flows clockwise, with the water rising to the height of the forearm.
Free from skulls and stones, devoid of anthills and worms, without hollow bones, and filled with fine sand. (13.42)
It should be free from charcoal and husks, devoid of the roots of trees, abandoned by any remaining mud, and free from pits, caves, and clods of earth. (13.43)
However, [a site] devoid of sugar and ashes, located near an assembly hall or a shrine, situated close to wicked creatures, or dependent upon a royal palace; || 13/44 ||
Situated near a temple, surrounded by thorny trees, belonging to a Caṇḍāla, or located within the premises of a workshop. || 13.45 ||
One should avoid that sacred field which is obstructed by one, two, three, or four roads, where the path is indistinct, and which is joined with the grove of Śaṅkara. (13.46)
Any other site of this nature would be productive of all defects; yet, out of delusion, one might perform the prescribed rite upon such a site. (13.47)
Since that bestows great harm, one should avoid it in every way;
it is prescribed for those of low birth, but not for the superior. (13.48)
What is prescribed for the superior is not for the inferior; it is appropriate among all the gods.
Or rather, the mixed-caste [temple] may be suitable for those born of that mixed caste, provided it is the most excellent. (13.49)
When a pit is dug into the earth and filled with its own very dust, such is the fruit obtained when the dust is respectively greater, less, or equal [to the original amount]. (13.50)
If a pit is filled with water from a flower-pot, the merit from holding its dust, according to the discernment of fruits, is one hundred and sixtyfold. (13.51)
Water that flows clockwise, possesses calm bubbles, and has flowers facing upward is praised as excellent; however, water with flowers facing downward is not so. (13.52)
That ground upon which sprouts of sown mustard or sesame seeds emerge within three nights shall be auspicious. (13.53)
A site sloping toward the northeast is excellent; one sloping in all directions is mediocre.
That [latter] may also be accepted for houses and the like, provided it is endowed with abundant qualities. (13.54)
Or that which has been lawfully obtained as a royal capital for a prince;
having thus examined it, one should accept land endowed with many virtues. (13.55)
Furthermore, one should properly offer the oblation for the entry of the *vetāla* and other spirits.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Procedure for Examining the Ground, in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Entrance Offering (Praveśabalividhi)
The "offering upon entry" is prescribed for all villages and the like, for palaces and dwellings, and indeed for all other [structures]. (14.1)
At an auspicious moment and under a favorable lunar mansion, during a night free from defects, one born of a pure Śaiva lineage and established in the five spheres of perception [should act]. (14.2)
Adorned with the five ornaments, wearing a turban and an upper garment, and enriched with white unguents, he should begin the offering for entry.
One should first feed the Brahmins and then cause them to pronounce the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha).
Then, having divided the ground into nine parts starting from the central position of Brahmā, one proceeds in order.
The one who knows the Vāstu-ritual should offer the bali-oblation in the nine directions with this mantra:
"O Bhūtas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas dwelling here upon this earth! (14.5)
"May these go wherever they wish; I quickly take this ground for the sake of the site.
With food consisting of curd, clarified butter, and cakes, one should offer them the bali-oblation.
One should cause it to resound with the sounds of songs, musical instruments, and the like, as well as the chanting of the Vedas;
first, one should worship the preceptor, and thereafter, worship everyone else.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Ritual for the Entrance Offering, in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for Taking Possession of the Ground.
Then, at dawn, having bathed and adorned himself,
wearing a new garment together with an upper cloth, he should perform the formal acceptance.
In the center of the well-smeared earth, situated upon all kinds of grain, its limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste and adorned with mango and *aśvattha* leaves. (15.2)
A pitcher filled with the waters of rivers containing all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs, its mouth covered with fine cloth, and adorned with a white thread.

Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with fragrances, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), the Guru [should worship] that which is presided over by Śiva, together with his teaching and his body.
Then, having lifted up the water-pot, he should place it upon the head of the Brahmin,
accompanied by the auspicious sounds of the Vedas, musical instruments, and women of noble family. (15.5)
Then, while meditating on the welfare of all beings, he should quickly sprinkle [the area] clockwise with an unbroken stream of water flowing from the *karaka* vessel. (15.6)
Having led [the thread] to the eastern boundary and having paused there for a moment, [he should proceed] from that fire toward the southeast, the east, and the northeast.
Having led [the thread] through the directions, one should then lead it toward the east for the demarcation of the ground;
then, having honored the preceptor and the others, the performer should give the sacrificial fee.

For the purpose of entry, the sacrificial offering (bali), the examination of the ground, and its acquisition—these are not performed separately for the deities and other entities that constitute parts of the village by those who are wise. (15.9)
In that regard, one should first perform the plowing; one should carry out everything according to the independent [tantras].
One should do everything from the independent [tantra], in accordance with one's faith and wealth. (15.10)
In that matter of establishing a fortress, however, a certain distinction is prescribed:
having dug a pit one cubit deep in the center of the ground on an auspicious day. (15.11)
In the evening, he should fill the pit with water infused with sandalwood;
having drunk milk near it upon a bed of *darbha* grass, the preceptor should sleep there. (15.12)
O Earth, prosper upon this site with wealth and grain;
exerting your supreme power, salutations be unto you—be auspicious.
Having spoken thus and fasted with purified limbs, one should examine the pit in the morning;
seeing that the water has a residue remaining, that [earth] should be taken for the sake of all prosperity. (15.14)
If it is wet, there will be the destruction of the dwelling; if dry, there will be the loss of grain and wealth.
Or, having filled it during the day, one should perform the examination. (15.15)
Having gone a hundred paces inward and then returned, one should examine it;
if the water therein has not diminished, that ground is praised as excellent.
If it is deficient by one finger-breadth, it is proclaimed as "middling";
if deficient beyond that, it is "inferior," and if excessively inferior, it brings about misfortune.
This examination must be performed beforehand for the strength of the site intended for entry; indeed, it is considered common to all types of dwellings. (15.18)
Having thus performed the ritual appropriation (*parigraha*), one should then begin the plowing.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the procedure for the appropriation of the ground (*bhūparigrahavidhi*), in the great tantra named *Kāmika*.
The Procedure for Ploughing the Ground.
Hereafter, I shall explain the cultivation of villages and other lands. [One should employ] two bulls that are very white, well-tamed, young, and endowed with strength. (16.1)
The two bulls should have uncut noses, be intact in their testicles, and be endowed with auspicious marks;
likewise, one should adorn them with humps, tails, hooves, and horns. (16.2)

Having taken two bulls— one of which is endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and colors— and adorned them with golden ornaments, fragrant flowers, and other such items fashioned in their respective forms.
Having satiated [the deity] with juices and milk, one should then begin the plowing;
the materials for that [plowing] should be made of khadira wood by both the god and the brahmin.
For kings, the royal tree should be made of khadira wood; for vaiśyas and śūdras, it may be made of nimba, vakula, gavākṣī, or likewise kaṭphala.
Among all trees, the *tinduka* and the *karavīra* are [foremost]; its plowshare, handle, grip, and yoke are thus proclaimed. (16.6)
The ploughshare should be four spans long and its width at the base should be two spans and six finger-breadths; this is declared for ploughs. (16.7)

A plough is praised for its construction when it is three times as long as it is wide at the base, with a circumference of eight finger-breadths at the root and four finger-breadths at the tip. || 16/8 ||
The *haladīrgha* is specified as being three or two finger-breadths in thickness;
its width is twice its thickness, just like the flag-staff of a banner.
At the front, it is four cubits long and one span in circumference;
in the middle, at a distance of three times seven finger-breadths from the navel, it is shaped like a ring.
It should be four *vitastis* in length and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in width; the space between two *śamyās* is correctly called a *vitasti* here. (16.11)
In the middle, the wedge (kīla) should be two mātrās; on the left of the middle, however, it should be six barley-corns (yava).
The space between the pins (śamyā) should be equal, and the support of the pins (śamyālambana) should consist of yugas and so forth.
In this world, that which is made of clay or iron is considered to contain dust;
however, that which is made of gold and contains dust is prescribed for the gods.
For the twice-born and kings it is silver; for Vaiśyas and Śūdras it is copper.
Or else, whatever [the area] is, such as that measured by a ploughshare and so forth, one takes half of that when divided by eight.
Beginning with one part and ending with four parts,
one may construct it either less or more, according to the desire of the builder.
A rope made of cowhide, or one made of muñja grass, tāla fibers, or bark;
or even a rope made of coconut fibers—such a rope is prescribed for all purposes.

Likewise, those originating from the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* trees, as well as the *halā* and others, are considered suitable for all [liquors] such as *surā* everywhere. (16.17)
Having thus completed everything, the preceptor, born of Śiva and a Brahmin,
having made his body consecrated by mantras, and having put on a turban and an upper garment, [proceeded].
Having donned the five-fold ornaments, he should worship the two bulls;
he should worship the bull with the Tryambaka mantra and the plow with the Astra mantra.
Having summoned the farmer and given him a garment, that best of the twice-born,
meditating upon him as his own self, should send him forth to the work of cultivation.
The most excellent of teachers, having first touched it himself, should draw [the lines];
it is said that for the gods, the elder brothers, and the kings, this should be done thirty-two times. (16.21)
For a Vaiśya, fifteen [times] is prescribed; for a Śūdra, seven.
Or else, for all [castes], it may be seven times or even five times. (16.22)
One should begin the work of plowing while facing either east or north;
having thus plowed and leveled the ground, one should turn it over six times in succession.
Having washed sesame, mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, rice, and barley in succession with milk, one should sow them while recollecting the Netra-mantra.
One should give the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of five niṣkas of gold;
and one should also give him a cow and a bull, together with all necessary implements.
Leading two bulls by their backs, excessive running while on them, sleeping upon them, and other such misdeeds—all these bring about every kind of affliction for one's offspring. (16.26)

Likewise, in the event of a break in the *hala* and other parts, or indeed upon the snapping of the rope, the twice-born devotee of Śiva should then perform the expiation and the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*). (16.27)
Likewise, here too, when the farmer falls, it is exactly the same;
for by the plowing, both the crops situated there and those that have already grown are affected. (16.28)
The wise and most excellent of teachers should cause the cattle-herds to graze [the site];
he should have it remain for three nights, five nights, or seven nights. (16.29)
By the sprinkling of the dung and urine of cows with their calves and bulls, by the trampling of hooves, by sniffing, by wandering about, and by the cow-paddles; || 16.30 ||

Let a village and its surroundings be accepted, wherein the center of the earth has been purified by the falling of froth from the chewing and belching of calves as they emerge from their mothers' mouths. (16.31)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for plowing the ground, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Installation of the Śaṅku (Sacrificial Stake)
(Verse 17.1) For the gods, for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who follow the natural order,
and for those who have constructed houses, villages, and so forth, whose souls are endowed with the initiation of Śiva.

I shall now describe the installation of the *śaṅku* (the ritual peg), which brings auspiciousness to villages and other settlements for others who, though uninitiated, possess souls endowed with devotion to Śiva. (17.2)
One should determine the location for the peg (śaṅku) to the southwest of the site of Brahmā;
if the peg is placed elsewhere, it will destroy the village and other settlements. (17.3)
One should prepare a mandala for the eternal deities and for the sake of the ritual stake (śaṅku), measuring one staff in length and breadth, and six finger-breadths in height.
It was endowed with eight, six, and four morae, rising for two morae, captivating to the mind,
free from flaws, ageless, smooth, pleasant to the touch, perfectly level, and auspicious.
Three and a half cubits, three cubits, two and a half cubits, and two cubits—
these should be applied by the wise to the twice-born and the other classes respectively.
Having filled it with water there, one should properly dig many stakes of equal height, set at equal intervals. || 17.7 ||
There, one should make it firm with blooming clay, fine sand, and cow dung,
mixed with curds, ghee, and milk, along with earth from an anthill.
One should draw the mandala with the sūtra-instrument so that it is even, free from cracks, without high or low spots, very smooth, and like a mirror. (17.9)
Dānta and candana are for gods and brahmins;
khadira and tiniśa are for kings; and śāka and khadira are for merchants. (17.10)
The Śāka, Tinduka, and Kṛṣṇasāra trees are for those born as Śūdras; all milk-yielding trees, Śamī, and Sāla are declared suitable for everyone. (17.11)
The gnomon (śaṅku) shall be six finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in length;
its tip, however, may be one finger-breadth wide, which is suitable for all castes.
In all types of building sites, the peg (śaṅku) should be fourteen aṅgulas in length, with a base circumference of the same measure, and a width of three aṅgulas at its tip. (17.13)

The circumference at the tip should be half a cubit (hastārdha), and it should be joined with feet [projections] each measuring one-quarter of that; the circumference at the base is prescribed by decreasing the tip measurement by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each successive foot.
One should fashion it according to the sequence of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas;
for the gods and others it should have a pointed top, while for the twice-born it should resemble an umbrella.
For kings and those of the Vaiśya caste, the sword-blade should resemble the leaf of the Kuśa or Kīcaka grass;
for Śūdras, the maṇḍalāgra sword should have a point like the tip of a plantain bud.
The stake for the gods should be made of *bailva* wood; for kings, it should be of *khadira*, *sāla*, or *āgraja* wood; the seat should be of *vākula*, *tinduka*, or *khadira* wood.
The wise preceptor should fix a wooden peg for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, or one that is common to all, at the ancient well-known *śaṅku*.
The village and other areas should be demarcated by the drummers, free from confusion, using nine maṇḍalas provided with stakes situated at the center, the beginning, and the end. (17.19)
A peg provided with a needle, placed at intervals of one span (vitasti), should be used for villages, fields, and mountains; for a needle, it should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in length.

Having likewise cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or again with pure water a vessel made of barley, with its opening facing upward, and fashioned from gold, silver, or copper; || 17.21 ||
Then, one should sprinkle it with water from the *astra* [mantra] while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra;
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should call to mind the prosperity of the site (*vāstuvṛddhi*).
In the center of the altar within the pavilion, which measures five cubits, one should perform this rite to the north of the location of the ritual stake (śaṅku). || 17.23 ||

Having performed the tying of the *kautuka* (protective thread) and being completely enveloped in two new, unwashed garments, one should worship [the deity] situated upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should properly perform the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice for the former site upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Then, at dawn, on a clear and auspicious day with favorable stars, || 17.25 ||
Having washed the ritual peg (śaṅku) with water, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra;
and having worshipped the deities of the directions with perfumes and other offerings using their respective names.
Adorned with ornaments on his five limbs, wearing a turban and an upper garment,
he was accompanied by Brahmins who had received their sacrificial fees and by the artisan.
Having reached the site for the sacrificial post (śaṅku), one should then cause the auspicious day to be proclaimed;
having worshipped Indra and the other deities all around, one should commence the installation of the sacrificial post.

Having drawn a circle by rotating it with a cord equal in length to the gnomon, increased by half the diameter of the gnomon, one should place [the gnomon] in its center at the time of sunrise or sunset.
Just as the line of the shadow of a gnomon falls during the forenoon and afternoon, the thread passing through those two points is considered to be the east-west direction. (17.30)
The movement during the morning and afternoon sessions is one-fourth of a barley grain;
it wanders between two drops, having the face and tail of Śambara.
It has been stated that [the directions are] south and north; alternatively, they may also be described otherwise:
the north or the east may be determined by the piercing of the Pole Star (dhruva) using the star Dhruva.
One should accomplish this during the asterisms of Puṣya or Śravaṇa, at the rising of the equinox;
one should then construct a square using half the measurement of the limited field.
Equality with the arms is achieved through the ears when stability is maintained by trembling;
equality with the palms occurs through water, whether in the middle or at the pericarp.
In the eastern quarter, or rather, having determined the established points from the original site, any location further to the east than that would cause all manner of defects. (17.35)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the ritual peg (*śaṅku*), in the great tantra known as the *Kāmika*.
The Procedure for Measuring the Vessel.

I shall describe the measurement of the implements for all [deities] in particular; it is traditionally taught that the "measurement finger" (mānāṅgula) is defined by an increase according to the sequence of atoms (paramāṇu). (18.1)
That which is known as the atom (paramāṇu) is within the range of vision for yogins; likewise are the chariot-dust particle, the tip of a hair, a nit, a louse-egg, and a barley-corn. (18.2)
The eightfold qualities are said to increase progressively by six, seven,
and eight barley-corns respectively, according to the divisions of the smallest and the other sizes.
In the teaching of Śiva, as many fingers as there are are said to be of three kinds:
by means of three grains of rice, or four, along with half [a grain]. (18.4)
In this context, those arising from rice are declared to be three types of finger-breadths (aṅgula):
namely, six and a half barley-corns, or seven and a half barley-corns.
Fingers are said to be of three kinds, or indeed with eight and a half [units];
that which is the length of the joint situated in the middle of the middle finger [is the standard]. (18.6)
The best [measurement] is declared to be the *mātrāṅgula*; that which is reduced by one-quarter is the middling;
and that which is reduced by half is declared the lowest, according to the distinctions of the *mātrāṅgula*. (18.7)
The measure is declared to be ninefold, or even from the big toe of a human;
thus is the *mātrāṅgula* described, which is recommended for sacrifices and other rites.
A span (vitasti) is here said to consist of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula);
two of those are designated as a cubit (hasta), which is recognized here as a forearm-measure (kiṣku).
A length of twenty-five *mātrās* is known as a *prājāpatya*;
with twenty-six *mātrās*, it is proclaimed to be a bow-grip (*dhanurmuṣṭi*). (18.10)
The bow is declared to consist of twenty-seven *mātras*; in this treatise, the *hasta* is proclaimed to be derived from the *mānāṅgula*. (18.11)
The *pauruṣa* measure is born from the person (*puruṣa*); here it is derived from the right thumb.
Extending the palm with the four fingers together with the thumb [constitutes the span]. (18.12)

By means of the little finger and the others in successive order— known respectively as the barley-grain (*yava*) and the cow’s ear (*gokarṇa*)— the span (*vitasti*) is thus described, and immediately after that, the fore-arm’s breadth (*prādeśa*).
Thus has the hand been described in its various forms for all types of building sites,
according to the measurement of Prajāpati, as well as for pavilions and images.
One should employ [these measurements] for the garland-like assembly hall, the vast council hall, the capital city and so forth, the royal palace, and the lake. (18.15)
One should cause the fortification to be constructed with bow-grips and hand-holds;
one should especially provide a carriage-way for the seizing of bows.
One should measure the wall, the vehicle, and the bed by the *kiṣku* unit;
indeed, one should perform everything that is undertaken according to the measurement of the *kiṣku*. (18.17)
The vehicle, as well as the bed,
the linga, the image, the doorposts, the pillars, and the pinnacle, should be fashioned with a span (vitasti).

Whatever his implements may be, all of them are [measured] by the finger-breadth; however, those who are the best among men should understand that even this is very small when measured by the barley-corn. (18.19)
The characteristics of the *āya* (income) and so forth are likewise agreed upon by these very [authorities]:
a *daṇḍa* is declared to be four *hastas*, and a *rajju* is eight of those.
One should measure a village, a city, a town, or the like with a staff; one should measure a road by tying a rope, and likewise measure a field. (18.21)
A wise person should prepare the cord from cotton cloth, thread, and so forth, or else from the bark of the *nyagrodha* tree, or from the bark of the *tāla* and *ketaka* trees. (18.22)
The circumference of the ring finger should be three times that of the thread, free from knots;
it is for gods, Brahmins, and kings, but excluded for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
The tāla, the ketakī, the nyagrodha, the dhātakī, and likewise the śaṇaka are praised in sequence for the gods and the other [deities]. (18.24)
A rope made from coconut fibers is praised for all [practices];
measuring with a leaf of the coconut grants all accomplishments. (18.25)
The breaking (of the ground) is said to be of two kinds, according to the sequence of odd and even [days].
At the commencement, the breaking should be performed facing either the east or the north. (18.26)
One should perform the measurement with that very [unit], especially in the case of images and the like;
or one may measure with its leaf-vein or its small stalk. (18.27)
The hand-staff, made from *sāradāra* wood, should be free of knots; it should be well-proportioned, long, and half a finger-breadth (*mātrā*) in width. || 18.28 ||

It may be three times as wide as its height, or it may be well-proportioned with a width of one *aṅgula*; it should be endowed with a thickness that is half of those dimensions, or otherwise equal to its width.
That which is square in shape is declared to be the human staff;
at its base is the form of Svāyambhuva, and in its middle is the essential form of Lakṣmī.
One should then imagine the form of Viśvakarman before it;
this staff, which is two finger-breadths in width, shall be suitable for the gods.
It may be three-quarters of a cubit, or even one and a half cubits; it should be well-rounded and decorated, made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
The measuring rod, equipped with a base, a tip, and a ring, is for the determination of human proportions.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Rule on the Measuring Instruments, in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for Placing the Footsteps.
(Verse 69) Now I shall explain specifically the characteristics of the arrangement of the steps:
the first step shall be *sakala*, while the second is *pecaka*.
The *pada* is the seat (*pīṭha*), the third is the *mahāpīṭha*, after that the *upapīṭha*, and beyond that the *ugrapīṭha*. (19.2)
One should know the seventh to be Sthāṇḍila, and likewise the eighth is called Maṇḍūka;
the ninth is proclaimed as Parameśapada. (19.3)
The tenth is called the seat (āsana), and the eleventh is said to be the station (sthānīya).
The twelfth is declared to be the regional (deśīya) position, while the [thirteenth] step (pada) belongs to both Caṇḍikās.
The auspicious fourteenth position is known as the Great Seat (Mahāsana);
the fifteenth is proclaimed as the Lotus-Womb Position (Padmagarbha). || 19/5 ||
The sixteenth [digit] joined with three is the seventeenth, which is the portion of the circle;
and the eighteenth position here is known as the "eight ears. (19.6)
The section on calculation (*gaṇitapāda*) should be known to consist of nineteen chapters; the twentieth chapter is by name the *Sūryaviśāla*. (19.7)
There may be one with twenty-one feet called Susaṃhita,
and here there is also one with twenty-two feet called Supratikrāntaka.
The twenty-third is declared to be the site named Viśāla;
the twenty-fourth site is known as Vipragarbha. (19.9)
The twenty-fifth station here is declared by the wise to be named Viśveśa;
that which is the twenty-sixth shall consist of abundant enjoyment.
The twenty-seventh step may be one that is transgressed;
however, the twenty-eighth step is known as the step of Viśālākṣa. (19.11)
This twenty-ninth word is known as Viprabhuktika;
the thirtieth word is declared to be the ancient Viśvasāra. (19.12)
That which consists of thirty-one syllables is known as *īśvarakānta*; that which consists of thirty-two syllables is here called *indrakānta*. (19.13)
In all cases, Brahmā is to be worshipped at the central thread; one should worship Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma with perfumes and other offerings on the threads starting from the east.

In this [place], the gods and others are to be worshipped, and one should perform the fire-ritual and take one's meal; however, one should do so at the "pecaka" point, which is marked by two ear-lines.
The world-protectors are situated within the eight threads, with Prajāpati in the center;
in the middle of that, the best of teachers should install the formless image (niṣkalabera).
The pedestal (pīṭha) for all auspicious rites, including those for small villages, houses, and so forth,
is desired to be joined with two ear-threads (karṇasūtra).
Those deities previously mentioned who are established in positions are proclaimed as being in their respective stations;
this station belongs to the monasteries and such, and it is suitable for villages and the like.
In small villages and the like, one should likewise fashion a *pecaka*;
however, for a great seat (*mahāpīṭha*), one should have it made equipped with two ear-threads.
In the center, O best of sages, the four-footed Brahmā enjoys his portion here;
[the others are] Īśa, Jayanta, Āditya, Bhṛśa, Agni, Vitatha, and Yama.
Bhṛgu, Pitṛ, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, Śeṣa, Māruta, Mukhya, Soma, and Aditi—these are the external deities situated in the Sūtra. (19.21)
The site of the great seat (mahāpīṭha) is declared to be suitable for small villages and the like;
and in the site of the secondary seat (upapīṭha), the Grandfather (Brahmā) alone enjoys the center.
Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthivīdhara—these gods, who each enjoy a single quarter, have gone to the four directions. (19.23)
The deities born of Savitṛ, Indra, Rudra, and the Waters likewise enjoy their respective stations in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneyī). // 19.24 //
Īśa, Satyaka, Mahendra, Āditya, and Vahni;
likewise the Gandharva deity, Gṛhakṣata, and Yama. (19.25)
The Pitṛs and the Asuras, Puṣpadanta and Jaleśvara, Vāyu and Gaja, as well as Bhallāṭa and Soma. (19.26)
Each square is provided with two ear-lines;
this is known as the *upapīṭha* square, which brings auspiciousness to villages and other settlements. (19.27)
This Ugrapīṭha is in the center, provided with two ear-threads;
in the middle is the four-pada Brahma-square, and then the inner enclosure.
Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthivīdhara—the gods beginning with the east—enjoy the two-footed [directions] excluding the corners. (19.29)
Savitṛ, Indra, Rudra, and likewise the Waters—
these deities enjoy their respective positions, beginning from the south-eastern corner.
I shall now describe the outer enclosure within the four [squares] beginning with Pāvaka;
in the corners, the gods consume half a square each in sequence. (19.31)

In the eastern half of the Āgneya [quarter] there is Vahni, while in the western half there is Bhṛśa; in the eastern half of the Nairṛta [quarter] there is Gṛha, and in the western half there is Svayaṃ. (19.32)
In the western half, however, Śeṣa is in the northwest, while Vāyu is in the east;
in the eastern half of the northeast, Diti is located, while Īśa is in the west.
In the eastern direction, beginning from the north and proceeding in a clockwise sequence,
there are Jayanteśa, Mahendra, Āditya, and likewise Satyaka.
In the south are Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, Yama, and Gandharva; these four gods are the enjoyers of the quarters.
In the west are Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, the lord of the waters;
and likewise in the north, the Asura and the Deva—these four are considered [the guardians]. (19.36)
Mukhya, Bhallāṭaka, Soma, and Bhṛgu are the presiding deities;
this is the seat named Ugrapīṭha, which is highly honored by villages and other settlements. (19.37)
The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) is divided into seven parts each way and provided with two diagonal lines;
in the center is the nine-square Brahma-pada, and then the inner enclosure.
Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthivīdhara—these gods enjoy three quarters [of the earth] according to the sequence beginning with the east. (19.39)
In the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), there are the deities beginning with Sāvitra:
Sāvitra, Indraja, Rudraja, and likewise Āpaja.
Beginning from the station of Īśāna, the deities in the outer enclosure are Īśāna, Jayanta, Mahendra, Āditya, and Satyaka. (19.41)
Bhṛśa and Vahni are declared to be the deities in the eastern direction; likewise Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, Yama, and Gandharva. (19.42)
Then Bhṛṅgarāja and Nirṛti are the deities in the south; Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, Asura, and Śeṣaka [are the deities] in the west.
It is called Vāyu; in that western quarter, the deities are considered to be Mukhya, Bhallāṭaka, Soma, Ṛbhu, and Aditi. (19.44)
In the northern direction, the deities worthy of the bali offering are proclaimed;
this place called the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is honored in houses, gardens, and other such locations. (19.45)
The [altar] called Maṇḍūka consists of sixty-four squares and is provided with two ears;
in the center is a four-square area for Brahmā, and the four gods are situated at its mouths.
The sixteen lords of the two-pada sections—beginning with Tripada, Apavatsa, and the others—who each enjoy half a share (an ardhaṃśa), are situated outside in the four directions. (19.47)
On both its sides, there are eight [plots] each enjoyed by a single person;
that plot here, known as Maṇḍūka-pada, is suitable for endowments such as agrahāras.
This station of the Supreme Lord (Parameśa), consisting of eighty-one stations and provided with two ear-threads, should be conceived by the wise. (19.49)
In the center is a nine-square area which the four-faced Brahmā enjoys;
it is taught that four deities are intent upon enjoying six squares each.
The eight two-footed deities reside in the corners, while those who have reached the single goal are on the exterior;
here, the gods situated upon the frog are described in their proper order. (19.51)
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya, Satyaka, Bhraṃśa, and Antarikṣa are those who go in the east. (19.52)
Vahni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are likewise situated in the south. (19.53)
Nirṛti and Dauvārika, Sugrīva and Puṣpadantaka, Varuṇa and Asura, as well as Śeṣa and Roga, are in the west.
Vāyu, Nāga, as well as Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, and Soma;
Gaja and Aditi, and likewise Diti, are in the north. (19.55)
These are said to be the external deities; furthermore, in the inner enclosure are Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthivīdhara. (19.56)
The gods situated in the four directions and in the corners beginning with Īśāna are Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, and Sāvitra. (19.57)
Indra and Indrajaya, as well as Rudra and Rudrajaya;
Brahmā is said to be situated in the center, and Maṇḍūka is beyond that.
