Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the sinful Rākṣasī are stationed on spikes in the corners beginning with Īśāna, devoid of [specific] footprints. (19.59)
O best of the twice-born, Skanda, Aryaman, Jambha, and Pilipiñcha are stationed in the four directions, beginning from the east. (19.60)
One should prepare a supreme seat, suitable for a village, a land grant, or a residence,
which is provided with excellent bedding and equipped with two ear-threads.
Brahmā occupies sixteen parts; occupying his face are those who possess eight parts each:
Āditya, Yama, Karuṇa, and Soma. (19.62)
The *dvipada* measures, such as the *apavatsa* and others, are indeed proclaimed as being two feet long; the *śatapada* measure is used for fields, forts, cities, watchtowers, and grounds. (19.63)
It is said that [the term] *nagarī* applies to cities, market towns, villages, houses, and so forth;
however, one should designate a *sthānīya* as being provided with two ear-threads (*karṇasūtra*). (19.64)
In the center, however, one occupies twenty-five of the outer squares;
Brahmā resides in the square of Īśāna and the others, while Īśa, Agni, Pitṛ, and Vāyu occupy their respective positions. (19.65)
But others, beginning with Parjanya, are to be known as occupying a single lunar mansion each in due order;
however, the four beginning with Aryaman are the sharers of ten lunar mansions starting from the east. (19.66)
The eight [deities] beginning with Āpavatsā occupy the corners, each sharing two squares;
and the eight beginning with Carakī are proclaimed to be in the outer [corners], each according to their respective positions.
This site known as *sthānīya* should be understood as suitable for a village and the like;
one should determine the site known as *deśīya* by means of two ear-threads.
Brahmā enjoys a thirty-sixth part; those stationed in the mouth each receive a twelfth part:
namely Āditya, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma. (19.69)
The two-footed deities such as Carakī and others, situated on the outer path, are as described before;
this place called Deśīya is honored by agrahāras and other such institutions. (19.70)
The *caṇḍita* is called "both" (ubhayākhya) and is provided with two ear-lines;
in its center, Brahmā stands upon forty-nine squares. (19.71)
Outside the enclosure wall (āvaṇa), in the east, the deities beginning with Āditya occupy three parts each;
those situated in the corners—Īśāna, Agni, Pitṛ, and Vāyu—are to be known as occupying three squares (tripada).
The four beginning with Aryamā are situated in the fourteenth square;
as before, those beginning with Cāpa and Vatsa are proclaimed to be located on the outer edge.
That site, suitable for a land-grant (agrahāra) and other purposes, should be marked on both sides as "Caṇḍita.
One should first lay out fifteen lines, fifteen to the east and fifteen to the north. (19.74)
Provided with two ear-threads as before, one should determine the dimensions for the enjoyment [of the temple];
this square is suitable for an agrahāra and other such purposes, and is known as the Bhadrāsana.
This other [mandala] is the Lotus-womb (Padmagarbha), provided with two ear-threads;
there, in the center of the eighty-one squares, the Grandfather of the World (Lokapitāmaha) resides. (19.76)
The deities beginning with Āditya occupy three parts each; those beginning with Āryaman are proclaimed to occupy eighteen parts each, while the lords of the corners are the five leaders.
The remainder is as previously described, honored with agrahāras and so forth;
one should lay out seventeen threads extending eastward and northward.
Provided with two ear-threads and the enjoyment of the ground as before, it is proclaimed as "tri-yuta" (three-united), being fit for agrahāras and other such purposes. (19.79)
Another [portion] consists of twenty-one hundred square plots, including the square plots of the circumferences and provided with two ear-threads; Brahmā enjoys this in the center.
The world-protectors beginning with Indra, the eight [deities] of the five regions,
and the twenty-two gods who enjoy [the fruits of their merit] are proclaimed to be situated in the mouth. (19.81)
Indeed, the eight [meters] beginning with Āpavatsa are proclaimed to be two-footed;
this is called Vṛttābhoga, and one should employ it at the beginning of a musical mode (grāma) and so forth.
There should be nineteen [squares] facing east and as many facing north;
one should know this as the "Eight Corners" (karṇāṣṭaka), which is honored by those who bestow land-grants and the like.
The square known as *gaṇita* (calculation) is joined by two diagonal threads;
within its center, there is the *brāhmaka* (Brahma-square), which consists of sixty-nine squares.
The deities situated at the mouth are proclaimed to occupy thirty-six squares;
the world-protectors (lokapālas) shall occupy three squares each, while those situated in the interior consist of two parts.
The eight attendant deities, beginning with Āpavatsa, are proclaimed as the side-deities; one should assign the Gaṇitapāda [section] to the villages and other such locations. 19.86.
Then, one should fashion the *sūryaviśāla* as before;
one should arrange it with well-joined lines and provided with the ear-lines (*karṇasūtra*). || 19.87 ||
In the center are twenty-five words and elements;
for each of the four [groups] beginning with Aryaman, there are thirty words each. (19.88)
For the four [deities] situated in the corners beginning with the northeast, five squares are prescribed;
for the four beginning with Āditya, however, three squares are proclaimed. (19.89)
One should assign two feet each to Parjanya and the others individually;
and as before, one should assign two [feet] each to the group of eight beginning with Apavatsa.
Likewise, the group of eight beginning with Carakī is proclaimed on the exterior;
this is the well-composed [mantra] called Pada, honored by villages and other settlements. (19.91)
The square known as Supratikrānta is provided with two ear-lines;
according to the previously mentioned method, this square is honored by the Grāma and other [musical scales]. 19.92.
Let the lords among scholars design a spacious layout joined with the *karṇas*;
there shall be two hundred and eighty-nine *brahmapadas* in the center. (19.93)
For each of the four beginning with Aryaman, there are thirty-four [deities];
there are fifty world-protectors (lokapālas), and everything else is the same.
This is declared to be the one named Viśāla, honored by agrahāras and others; it contains brahmins within its womb, just as before, and is honored by agrahāras and others. (19.95)
One should arrange the station called Viśveśa together with Karṇa;
there are three hundred and sixty-one Brahma-stations in the middle.
The deities beginning with Aryaman, as before, are the three-part sharers of the outer [space]; this site named Viśveśa shall be fit for agrahāras and other such purposes. (19.97)

Formerly extensive wealth that was honored through gifts of land and other offerings, as well as a position attained by overcoming adversaries, endowed with the two earrings and the sacred thread. (19.98)
There are forty-one words here, and four hundred [syllables];
Brahmā enjoys them, while Aryaman and the others should be assigned as before. (19.99)
The corners shall consist of five parts, while the others shall consist of three parts each; this is known as the *vipratikrānta* layout, honored by agrahāras and other such establishments. (19.100)
One should fashion the large-eyed [image] with ears as before;
one should likewise lay out thirty threads extending eastward and northward.
In the center, Brahmā enjoys five hundred and twenty-nine [parts], while the four beginning with Aryaman enjoy forty-six parts each. (19.102)
There should be fifty world-protectors, beginning with Parjanya, who share in three parts;
this is to be known as the "Brahmin’s meal" (viprabhukti), a site suitable for a village and the like. (19.103)
This Viśvasāra, worshipped as before by the villagers and others,
is the station beloved by the Lord, endowed with two ear-threads.
Six hundred and twenty-five [yojanas] are assigned to the center of Brahmā;
fifty [yojanas] are declared for each of the four [gods] beginning with Aryaman. (19.105)
Three portions each are assigned separately to the eight world-protectors (lokapālas),
while four portions each are declared for Parjanya and the others.
This [place] called Īśvarakānta is honored by agrahāras and other [endowments];
Indrakānta is likewise honored by agrahāras and other [endowments], as previously described. (19.107)
In this same manner, it should be understood that the sequence continues upwards until the *parārdha* is reached;
[the divisions] are sixty-four-fold, pertaining to the divine, the human, and the supreme lord (*pārameśvara*). (19.108)
The station of the Supreme Lord (Parameśa) should be assigned for all four castes,
or one may do so for the three twice-born castes in the case of agrahāras and other dwellings. (19.109)
For a Brahmin and a Kṣatriya, especially, sixty-four steps are prescribed;
likewise, for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, forty-nine steps are declared.
Everything desired everywhere has been fully proclaimed in this treatise;
the postures (āsana) are considered to be of three kinds, namely those called the sixty-four and the eighty-one. (19.111)
In all cases, such as for the *sakala* and other types, these three specific positions among all the sites are recommended for construction work, whether for villages, houses, and so forth. (19.112)
Alternatively, the *sakala* and other [forms] are prescribed in another manner:
either devoid of the ear-line, or possessing two ears in the middle. (19.113)
Alternatively, every single word should be performed as if endowed with threads fixed to multiple ears; one should thus conceive it through the intellect. (19.114)
Now I shall explain, according to the rule, the placement of the lines for the Vṛtta-pada, which, like a wheel, consists of five equal lines with equal intervals between them. (19.115)
Thirty-two, twenty-four, twice eight, eight, and one;
this is to be known as the eighty-one squares of uneven arrangement. (19.116)
One should arrange this sixty-four-square grid within the four circles according to twenty-eight, twenty, twelve, and eight-and-a-half divisions.
One should perform the placement of the *kumbhaka* by mixing it with both;
this sixty-four-square *vāstu* diagram is the supreme *vāstuka*.

The village and so forth should be considered the *upavāstu*, while the house and so forth should be the *vāstavya*; the wise should apply this analogy just as one applies it to the union of a man and a woman. (19.119)
In Meṣa (Aries) the sign is established; in Aryaman (Yama), the station is Vṛṣabha (Taurus);
one should know that Mithuna (Gemini) is in Bhṛśāṃśa; and Kulīra (Cancer) occurs in Vitatha.
In the *vyañjaka* [month] there is Leo; in the *bhṛṅga*, Virgo; in the *sugrīvaka*, Libra;
in the *mitra*, Scorpio; in the remainder, Sagittarius; and in the *mukhya*, the position of Pisces. (19.121)
In the *pṛthivīdhara* [navāṃśa] it is Kumbha, and in Aditi it is called Mīna;
these are to be known as both moving and non-moving, and one should place them in their respective divine portions (*devāṃśaka*).
All the lunar mansions, beginning with Aśvinī, follow in their proper sequence, moving clockwise through the divisions starting from Aries and the other signs. (19.123)
On Āditya [the southeast], Sunday is assigned; on Agni [the south-east], Tuesday is considered appropriate;
on Yama [the south], Thursday shall be; and on Nairṛti [the southwest], Wednesday. (19.124)

Śukra should be in the northwest (Varuṇa), and likewise the son of the Sun (Saturn) in the northwind (Vāyavya); Soma-day (Monday) should be in the north (Soma), and Rāhu's station is in the northeast (Īśāna). || 19.125 ||
In this Vāstuśāstra called Kāmika, Ketu shall be situated in the center;
everything prescribed according to its influence bestows the fruit of all accomplishments. (19.126)

The feminine gender is to be known as uneven (viṣama), while the masculine gender is even (sama). Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning the rules for the placement of words, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Fabrication of the Thread.
(Verse 74) Hereafter, O twice-born ones, I shall explain the fashioning of the thread:
first, one should place the thread along with an offering upon the site of Brahmā. 20/1.
The second [line] should be the north-south thread; one should also offer an oblation upon it.
The third [line] should extend from the corners of the square to the corners of the oblong.
The fourth should be the ear-thread (karṇasūtra), the fifth the half-fifth;
the sixth should be its immediate neighbor, and the seventh the central pericarp (madhyakarṇika).
The eighth should be the half-ear, and the ninth the interval between the ears;
in this manner, the others are to be understood up to the thirty-second square.

The first thread should be the boundary-thread (paryanta-sūtra), then the placement-thread (vinyāsa-sūtra), and another would be the measurement-thread (pramāṇa-sūtra); thus there shall be two threads.
That measurement which begins from the water-pot and ends at the peak-chamber is the measurement of the final cord;
that cord is the supreme authoritative standard. (20.6)
The thread, suitable for the divine station, is for the purpose of measuring the womb, the walls, and so forth;
for that indeed shall be the layout-thread, and the arrangement of the thread must be understood. (20.7)
Now, one should divide the field into three hundred and sixty parts;
one part among those is the measure of the thread, and that is called its "vital breath" (prāṇa).
For the sutras are to be performed facing east, while those to be performed in imitation are indeed facing north;
these have been proclaimed in this scripture according to the measure of the vital breath (prāṇa). 20/9.
These forms of males and females have been described in sequence;
however, the secondary lineages (anuvaṃśakas) are twice the measure of the vital breaths (prāṇavāyu).
The great bamboo (mahāvaṃśa) situated at the side of the center of the site is proclaimed;
the great bamboo in the middle of the site is proclaimed to be threefold [in size]. || 20/11 ||
The channels associated with the three qualities (guṇas) are considered to extend from the vital breath (prāṇa) toward the ears;
the great vessels (mahāsirā) situated there are also considered to extend toward the middle of the ears. || 20/12 ||
By the measure of the vital breath (prāṇa), they are proclaimed to be threefold;
the great vessels (mahāsirā) and the secondary vessels (anusirā) are to be known as neuter.
In the center of the site (vāstu) there should be the Ketu; that is called the great vital point (mahāmarman).
At the end of the great veins and the great vital points, a joint (sandhi) is prescribed.
Pain arising from the entanglement of the bamboo-fiber-like cords and the sinews is so designated.
Great pain (mahāśūla) consists of four prāṇas, while secondary pain (anuśūlaka) is threefold. || 20/15 ||
The pure square (śuddhapada) is the vital point (marman), while the plough-shaped area (lāṅgala) is joined with the corners.
A group of four is formed by four lines, and a group of six by the application of six lines. || 20/16 ||
The eightfold [measurement] is proclaimed through the application of the eight sūtras;
the measurement of the vital points (marmans) is proclaimed to be one-eighth of a pada.
In the eight directions and the intermediate quarters, the Blessed One, the knower of the Sūtras and the Smṛtis,
[establishes] a cord measuring one barleycorn within a field fashioned to three cubits.
One should bind it with a single hair against others at every joint;
likewise at the heart, the bamboo-joint, the spike, the junction of the threads, and the vital point (marmaka).

In the eight, six, and four-finger widths of the *sīrā*, as well as in the *lāṅgala* measurement, it is not prescribed to construct temples and the like; if such a thing is done, it leads to the destruction of the lineage.
The best of teachers, having set aside one-eighth or one-ninth of the actual measurement of these [dimensions], should have the walls, pillars, houses, and so forth constructed.
A wise person should not cause affliction to the house using the *padasūtra* (foot-measure cord), for whichever limb of a mortal is afflicted in any ritual act [will suffer accordingly]. (20.22)
"Therefore, one should subsequently remove any obstacles pertaining to its constituent parts.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the "Ritual for the Manufacture of the Thread," in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Offering to the Deity of the Site (Vāstudeva)
(Verse 75) Now I shall explain specifically the ritual offering to the deities of the site (*vāstudeva-balikriyā*).
A wise person should perform the offering at night for the site of a village and so forth during the day.
Whether by night or by day, in his own home, a temple,
or similar places, he should be well-bathed, wearing new garments, a turban, and an upper cloth.
Adorned with the five ornaments and anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents, and joined by such a performer, one should carry out this rite. (21.3)
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, the wise man should then cause them to recite the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha);
then, having prepared a mandala in that place with cow dung.
Having placed the *kūrca* there, and having uttered his own name ending with the word "Sambuddha" followed by "I invoke you," he should perform the invocation and then carry out the worship.
Having uttered one's own name in the dative case, joined with the word "namas" at the end,
and having offered all [substances] beginning with water for the feet (pādya), one should cast the bali offering as prescribed for each respective deity.
One should first worship Brahmā and offer milk-rice mixed with ghee;
one should give fruits to Aryaman, as well as rice mixed with sesame and black gram.
One should offer a cake to Vivasvat and cause curds to be given to Mitra;
with a well-concentrated mind, one should cause fine fragrances to be offered to Pṛthvīdhara.
One should especially offer fresh butter to Parjanya;
one should offer clarified butter to Jayanta; Mahendra becomes a sufferer of leprosy [if he does not].
One should likewise offer the madhuparka especially to Āditya;
and to Satyaka, the fruit of the badarī tree accompanied by honey.
One should cause a powder of black gram (māṣa) combined with turmeric and cooked rice to be given for the purpose of causing a fall;
and one should offer the *tapana* oblation with milk and clarified butter to Antarikṣa.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer rice mixed with milk to Agni, and cooked food together with *śiva* to Pūṣan and Vitatha.
One should give food consisting of pods mixed with honey to Gṛhakṣata;
one should give milk-rice (pāyasa) to Yama, and for Gandharva, fragrance is prescribed.
The wise man should offer sea salt to Bhṛṅgarāja, fish and rice mixed with fish to Mṛga, and oil and oil-cake to Nirṛti.
Curd is prescribed for Dauvārika, while barley-food is for Sugrīva;
flour-cakes are for Puṣpadanta, along with flowers and water.
Milk-rice mixed with ghee should be offered to Jaleśvara;
one should cause the flesh of a boar to be given as an oblation to Asura.
With a concentrated mind, one should properly offer sesamum and rice to Śeṣa;
dry meat to Roga; and a yellow banner to Vāyu.
One who offers oblations should properly present parched grain (lājā) to Nāga Madhumukhya,
and indeed should properly give rice cooked with jaggery (gulānna) to Bhallāṭa.
One should especially offer milk-rice, incense, and a lamp to Soma;
to Gaja, sugar-cake (śarkarāpūpa); and they know that sweetmeat (modaka) is for Aditi.
One should offer an oblation according to the sequence of the outer deity offerings;
one should present milk-rice mixed with ghee to Īśāna.
One should offer parched grain (lāja) to Savitṛ, fragrant water to Savitṛ,
black gram (māṣa) food to Indra, and mung bean (mudga) food to the Son of Indra.
Meat should be offered as food to Rudra, and foam indeed to the son of Rudra;
one should cause curdled milk and meat to be given to Āpa and to Cāpavatsa respectively.
Clarified butter and meat should be given to Carakī; those who have resorted to Śūlasthā should be given to Bidārikā; and salt should be given abundantly by the wise man to Śivāśritā. (21.23)
One should then especially offer a ball of sesame seeds to Pūtanā;
to the sinful Rākṣasī, boiled grain with sour gruel; and to the Grahas, meat and rice.
The specific bali offering should be thus; however, the general offering consists of rice with ghee.
A bali accompanied by curd should be given to all of them as well.
Such would be the most excellent bali offering, especially in places such as villages;
now, that which is for houses, temples, and so forth is described as the middling one.
A bali offering of pure food mixed with curd, ghee, and molasses is for Brahmā;
however, a bali of milk-rice (pāyasa) is prescribed for the four [deities] beginning with Aryaman. (21.27)
In the intermediate directions, the offering for the eight deities beginning with Āpa is kṛsara;
for the eight deities beginning with Īśāna, the offering is said to be mung-bean rice.

An offering of rice cooked with molasses is prescribed for the deities beginning with Hutāśana; however, for those situated in the western direction, an offering of rice with clarified butter is said to be required.
For the deities mentioned starting with Vāyu, curd-rice is said to be the offering;
for the eight external deities, meat-rice is said to be the offering.
If the aforementioned items are unavailable, pure food mixed with curd, clarified butter, and fruit should be offered, preceded by perfumes and flowers. (21.31)
It is prescribed that sacrificial food (haviṣya) be offered at the temple of a god, meat and rice at the palace of a king,
fish at the house of a Śūdra, and elsewhere one should provide honey.
For the sake of curd or for the sake of meat, one may prepare flour;
or even in a village and such places, that offering should be performed with pure substances.
In a hurry, however, it may be without a wound, provided it is accompanied by fragrant flowers;
O best of Brahmins, in a large site, many preceptors are considered suitable.
Those born from the five spheres of activity are proclaimed as Śiva-brāhmaṇas;
due to the absence of the original Śaivas, the Brāhma ones there are the Śiva-dvijas.
In a temple or in a village and such places, a Śiva-brāhmaṇa is distinguished;
however, in one's own home, those who are Anuśaivas or Mahāvāntaraśaivas [are preferred].
The wise preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice either in the four directions or in a single location. (21.37)
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, provided with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, combined with sesame seeds and rice grains, either in a pavilion or at a water-shed.
One should construct a pavilion measuring between five and ten cubits;
this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in size, or even the measure of a span (ratni).
One should lead the pavilion to the boundary of the site or to the place of Brahmā;
[the trees] Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa are to be placed in order starting from the east.
The types of sacrificial fuel (samidh) have been described in the scriptures; let one of them be selected as desired.
One should worship the deities of the site (vāstudeva) either in a water-pot or in a vessel made of udumbara wood.
Provided with a golden cloth, equipped with a tuft and a lid, having established his base upon a prepared sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), wearing a turban and an upper garment; || 21.42 ||
Having performed the five-limbed prostration along with such image-keepers (mūrtipas) who were likewise devoid of turbans, accompanied by the sound of the Vedas.
Accompanied by the sound of hymns and joined with the recitation of mantras,
having received the sacrificial fee, being tranquil and endowed with mental satisfaction.
In all auspicious rites and in the purification of mandalas and the like,
the Vāstuhoma, which includes the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), serves as the regulating factor.
A Brahmin devoted to Śiva should especially perform the bali offering;
for if the worship of Vāstu is omitted, the very site of the dwelling perishes.
The preceptor should perform this every year for the removal of all defects,
in the villages and so forth, in houses and halls, or in a temple.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Offering to the Deities of the Site," in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Rule for the Characteristics of Villages and Other Settlements.
(Verse 22.1) With a concentrated mind, I shall describe the characteristics of villages, cities, and so forth;
for when a site is constructed according to the rules, the deities do not abandon it.
Piśācas, pretas, and rākṣasas will not be able to cause harm there;
one should perform the examination of time and other rites in that place according to the previously mentioned procedure. (22.2)
It is proclaimed as auspicious and fit to be enjoyed by learned brahmins;
that very thing, O lords of brahmins, is called an *agrahāra* in the scripture known as the Kāmika. (22.3)
A village is said to be one that may be enjoyed by Brahmins or by other castes, wherein there is a single village headman together with his servants and attendants. (22.4)

One should know that to be a *kuṭika* (hut), yet it is for the sole purpose of one's own enjoyment; however, when it is surrounded by people engaged in the buying, selling, and so forth of goods, [it is no longer a hut]. (22.5)
That which is joined with many births, endowed with the performers of karma,
and associated with all the deities is called a city.
That which is the abode of the Brāhmaṇas is likewise declared to be the enjoyment of merchants; while that which is for the city-dwellers is called a *kharvaṭa*.
Their very forest site was described in that same manner;
it was engaged in buying and selling and situated upon the shore of the ocean.
That city is renowned as being inhabited by Vaiśyas and filled with people of various castes who have arrived from other lands. (22.9)
That which is the turning away from the city is declared to be the *kharvaṭa*;
it is found in the forest and in the countryside, inhabited solely by Śūdras.
Karṇaka, kheṭaka, and grāma are declared to be the three types [of settlements] in order; that which is the residence of prosperous feudal lords (sāmanta) is known as a śibira.
That very place was indeed a military encampment equipped with elephants and horses,
containing the royal palace and populated by all classes of people.
The "military headquarters" (senāmukha) mentioned here is connected to the secret region; it is the dwelling place for all newcomers as well as those who are lifelong residents. 22.13.
A monastery (maṭha) is considered to be either provided with food and drink or entirely [unfurnished];
likewise, a center of learning (vidyāsthāna) shall be provided with a large army.
That which is joined with a royal residence is called a capital city (rājadhānī). A location near villages and the like is known as a *kubja*. (22.15)
That very place is called Cerikā, the birthplace of the city weavers;
and for all these villages and so forth,
the measurement of their width and length has been declared as eternal.
And that is proclaimed in this treatise and is set forth in due order.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, concerning the rules for the characteristics of the *gāma* and so forth, in the great tantra named *Kāmika*.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of Width and Length.
The measurement of the width and length of villages and other settlements is stated here:
beginning with five *daṇḍas*, one should increase it by two *daṇḍas* in succession. (23.1)
The wise do not accept it as extending beyond twenty-nine thousand [yojanas];
however, in the lowest [type], it is above that, while in the highest, it would be equal to that. || 23.2 ||
Thus has the extent of villages and so forth been described in brief; now follows the measurement of family lands, excluding gardens and fields. (23.3)
The measurement is stated in the scripture; outside of that, the enclosure ground is considered to be one-fourth, or even one-eighth, of the area.
It may be three-quarters or two-quarters [of the width], or three or two parts in its breadth;
or it may consist of five, six, or seven parts according to the sequence of the mūrti-angles.
Starting from fourteen cubits, one should increase by two cubits at a time;
one should determine the length according to a measurement ending in three times that [base] amount.
For Brahmins, a square shape is prescribed; for others, it is a long quadrangle.
In this world, all [offerings] made to a deity and to a Brahmin are declared to be equal.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, concerning the rules for the characteristics of the extensive Āyāma, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Rule for the Characteristics of the Vowels and Other Phonemes.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the dimensions (āyādi) and so forth.
One should practice by taking the width, multiplying it by three, and dividing by eight. (24.1)
The remaining [signs], beginning with the banner (dhvaja), are declared in the scripture as the eight wombs (yony-aṣṭaka):
the banner, smoke, dog, lion, bull, donkey, and the two excellent elephants. (24.2)
The eight birth-classes (yoni) beginning with the crow are as follows: the banner, the lion, the bull, and the elephant are auspicious; the others, beginning with smoke, are censured here.
Having multiplied that very [number] by eight, one should divide it by twenty-seven;
the remainder is declared here to be the lunar mansion beginning with Aśvinī. (24.4)
Starting from the birth asterism of the performer, three days, five or seven days, thirteen days, as well as fifteen asterisms, should be avoided. (24.5)
The seventeenth day, the eighteenth day, and the twenty-second day;
the twenty-seventh lunar mansion (nakṣatra) should be avoided; others are remembered as auspicious.
In this matter, that which is not in conflict with the birth asterism of the kings, the village, and the builder should be accepted; one should reject what is contrary. (24.7)
Or one who is learned in the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra) may have [the temple] constructed in conjunction with the birth asterism;
the compatibility between the name and the birth asterism is said to be the most excellent.
The one less than that is declared to be middling; the opposite should be abandoned.
Whatever the fruit of a lunar mansion may be, that is proclaimed to be its age.
Then, one should determine the age there by means of the banners and other [elements];
one should multiply the total by eight, and that [result] is also stated otherwise.
Having divided the total by eight, the Guru should divide it by twelve;
the remainder is declared to be the Āya, and therein the Vyaya is proclaimed.
Having established the obtained nakṣatra, the wise man should divide it by eight;
the remainder is declared here as the expenditure (vyaya), though it is also described otherwise.
Having tripled the entire [measurement], one should divide it by the measurement lines; an excess in length brings good fortune, while equality and deficiency should be avoided. (24.13)
A wise person should multiply the aggregate of breadth and length by eight;
he should divide that by thirty, or else by the remainder consisting of lunar days, serpents, and pits (eighteen).
Having performed the *sakala* rite three times, it is declared by the Sage that one should then designate the day (*vāra*) with the final *avaṭaka*. Thus the wise man should determine the day.

Those zodiac signs and degrees which are considered to be under the influence of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras)—among them, the eighth and twelfth signs are to be avoided; the remaining signs are excellent.
The portions belonging to auspicious planets are praised, while others here are censured;
one should practice the expansion [of the mantra] according to its length, or likewise again.
Or one should observe a heap endowed with width and length;
for those that are square or oblong, one should apply the measurement using the entire [diagonal] cord.
For other shapes, however, the wise man should not apply the width and height; rather, he should set the half-height of the *kumbhaka* at half the width.
The complete *kumbhaka* has been described; by means of that, one should assign the *āya* and so forth.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of *āya* and so forth, in the great tantra named *Kāmika*.
The Ritual of the Lunar Mansion Wheel (Nakṣatracakra)
I shall describe the circle of constellations for the sake of accomplishing the constellations associated with names;
first, having drawn a hundred-squared grid, starting from the northeast corner at the end.
Beginning with Dakṣa, one should assign the phonemes in their proper sequence;
likewise, the five principles (pañcatattva) [are assigned] starting from the south-east corner, following the western path.
One should thus place twenty syllables in sequence: by way of the northern path from the father (the letter *ka*) and by way of the eastern face of Vāyu (the letter *ya*). 25.3.
Apahakaṭa, likewise Avatapara, Nayabhajakhavarṇa, and Gajadacala. (25.4)
One should fashion the Īśāna-maṇḍala within a grid of twenty-five squares;
it is the third among those previously described, facing westward.
One should place the vowels conjoined with their own [consonants] for the fifth lunar mansion;
thereafter, one should place eleven, and at the end, one should place thirteen.
The letter *a*, the letter *i*, the letter *u*, and the letter *e*—these are said to be Kṛttikā; likewise, the fourfold group *vā*, *vo*, *vū*, and *va*. (25.7)
Rohiṇī is declared in the scripture, as well as Ve, Vo, Kā, and Kī;
Candrabhaṃ and Ku are Ārdrā, situated in the midst of the twenty-fifth [nakṣatra]. (25.8)
Ke, ko, and ha, as well as the syllable hī, are proclaimed as Punarvasu;
likewise, hu, he, ho, and ḍa are proclaimed as Puṣya. || 25.9 ||
Then, one should assign names by means of the remaining [syllables] through conjunction;
by this sequential method, one should perform everything here.
One should assign the letters gha, ṅa, cha, and na to the Kuṣṭha square conjoined with Ārdrā;
and one should arrange the letters pū, ṣa, ṇa, and ṭha in the Koṣṭha square conjoined with Hasta.
The Guru should place *dha*, *pha*, and *ḍhā* in Pūrvāṣāḍhā and the water-stall;
likewise, he should lead *dū*, *thā*, *jhā*, and *ña* into the constellation Uttarābhādrapada. (25.12)
By the very inclusion of the letter *na*, the letter *jña* is here accepted; by the very inclusion of the letter *a*, the letter *ā* is here accepted. (25.13)
By the very mention of the vowel *i*, the vowel *ī* is here included;
by the very mention of the vowel *u*, the vowel *ū* is here included. (25.14)
By the mention of the letter *e*, the five [vowels] beginning with *e* are included.
In the same way, this should be inferred elsewhere through the conceptualization of names and asterisms. (25.15)
In matters concerning villages, service to Kṣatriyas, warfare, and legal proceedings,
a wise man should employ a lunar mansion other than one's own name by adopting an alternative name.
Whether it be the birth asterism or both for the rite of laying a foundation—thus has the circle of asterisms been described by me to you. (25.17)
By this very [method], the wise should understand the state of favorability in times of calamity, in opposition, and in death, respectively. (25.18)
Except for the first and third parts, the remaining ones are auspicious;
moreover, in the third cycle, the best one is recited.
In the second and middle [categories], the first is considered inferior;
one should avoid an Asura or human *gaṇa*, otherwise it is auspicious.
In this manner, one should determine [the ritual] for both the birth asterism and the name asterism.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the "Ritual for the Name Asterism," in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Staff-Bearer and Others.
I shall describe the rules for the *daṇḍika* and other [arrangements]; listen, O seekers of knowledge!
There is the *daṇḍika*, the *svastika*, another called *prastara*, and the *prakīrṇaka*. (26.1)
Sampatkara, Parāka, Padmaka, Śrīpratiṣṭhita, Śrīvatsa, Vaidika, Nandyāvarta, and Kumbhaka. (26.2)
Thus, the twelvefold configuration of the villages and so forth has been described here;
specifically, the Vaidika and Daṇḍika types of Kumbhaka.

A wise man, having laid out a street in a town or similar place with its length oriented toward the east or the north for both sides, should know that this is auspicious; of this there is no doubt. (26.4)
One should construct houses on both sides or even on a single side;
it may be provided with a single pathway or joined with two pathways.
One should construct the staff-marked line (daṇḍika) joined with three paths, extending either toward the east or toward the north, appearing like a pair of scissors or a staff.
Having made two rows each with their tips pointing east and north,
it should be joined by nine other paths whose tips point toward the north.
Facing south, there is an exit from the eastern street;
and facing west, there is an exit from the southern [street]. (26.8)
Facing north, there is an exit toward the west;
then, facing east, there is an exit toward the northern path (saumyavīthī).
Thus, whatever is constructed in this manner is called a *svastika*; in this very same way, the layout for all villages and other settlements is determined.
It is joined with fifteen [lines] starting from the third and ending with the fifteenth, directed toward the north;
however, the "prastara" (spreading) here is said to consist of three lines directed toward the east.
Beginning from the four crossroads and extending up to seventeen squares,
it is joined with four northern [lines] facing eastward.
This is declared to be the *Prakīrṇaka* (Miscellaneous) section by the five northern [schools],
along with the twenty-one [sections] and the five facing east.
I have described here the Sampatkara; now I shall speak of the Parāka, beginning from six recitations up to twenty-three.
Increasing by one street at a time toward the north,
and with six streets facing east, this is proclaimed here as Parāka.
Beginning from the seventh path and extending up to the twenty-ninth,
it is joined with northward-facing paths and eastward-facing routes.
The lotus-diagram (*padmaka*) is said to consist of seven [lines]; let that which is desired among these be adopted.
Starting from the beginning, it consists of eight paths facing east and eight facing north. (26.17)
It is joined by eight [faces] facing eastward, numbering thirty-six parts; this is called "Śrīpratiṣṭhita," and let that which is desired therein be accepted. (26.18)
Endowed with desirable paths whose tips point both eastward and northward,
this is designated as the Śrīvatsa, which is suitable for all types of building sites.
Having made it either square or oblong, [one should place it] in the corners or in the center;
or else, starting with Puṣpadanta and the others, one may place it as desired, measured according to the door.
Whether on both sides or on only one side, provided it is joined with a house and a street, this is called a Vaidika [house]. // 26.21 //
That very [temple], surrounded by the houses of Brahmins, kings, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—
whether it be principal or secondary— is indeed prescribed here in all cases.
It should be made either enclosed by a field or enclosed by a grove and so forth;
this is declared to be the Vedic [temple], according to the internal and external divisions. || 26.23 ||
It is also said to be Vedic when joined with many rows,
having been made level all around by paths facing east and north.

Having first constructed that Vedic [mandala] according to one's desire with single or multiple [lines] as previously described, one should fashion the path called the *nābhi* (navel), provided with exits.
Outside of that [central space], it is provided with a great thoroughfare characterized by auspicious forms;
three, five, seven, or nine [circles] are fashioned around the navel.
It is traditionally taught that the Nandyāvarta should be constructed using only pairs [of lines],
endowed with circular paths that are either single or multiple.
It is joined by many paths facing east and north, and it is provided with a central area;
it is designated as *kumbhaka* and is endowed with many corners.
Kumbhaka is said to be joined with external paths having eight points;
it is prescribed here in the Kāmika for cities, towns, and the like.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, concerning the ritual for the staff and other implements, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The measurement of the street, the gate, and so forth.
I shall now describe, in due order, the measurements of the streets, gates, and so forth.
The street that surrounds the Brahma-section is called the Nābhivīthī (the navel-street). || 27.1 ||

That which is renowned as the Royal Road (rājavīthī), situated outside of villages and other settlements, is likewise called the Auspicious Road (maṅgalavīthī) and the Chariot Road (rathavīthī). (27.2)
All the streets facing east are known as "nārāca"; those same streets are considered "janavīthī" when they are narrow and run transversely. (27.3)
In this scripture, the measurement of the path (vīthi) begins from one pāda-ḍaṇḍa and increases by one pāda at each step, ending at eleven ḍaṇḍas.
While searching for it, one should not find the door at the tip of the street;
having avoided the tip of the auspicious street, one should never fix the center-line (nābhi) there.
At Bhallāṭa, Puṣpadanta, Mahendra, and Gṛhakṣata,
a four-gated enclosure should be constructed for all types of dwellings.
An excellent eastern gate should be placed in the Mahendra and Satyaka squares,
and an auspicious southern gate in the Gṛhakṣata and Gandharva squares.
The western gate is said to be at the location of Asura and Puṣpadanta;
the northern gate is said to be at the location of Mukhya and Bhallāṭa. || 27.8 ||
The stations for Parjanya, Bhṛśa, Pūṣan, Bhṛṅgarāja, Jaleśaka,
Śeṣa, Nāga, and Aditi are proclaimed to be in the northern doors.
Starting from three staffs and increasing by one staff at a time, the extent of the house and field reaches up to fifteen staffs. (27.10)
In that very place, the wise man should construct the house according to the measurement of a cubit;
or rather, the width of the house is said to be measured by the cubit. (27.11)
Beginning from five cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time, the width of a house site shall extend up to sixty-one cubits. (27.12)
The length should be measured by the village-rod, excluding the hand-span;
a house with four wings is excellent, while one with three wings is middling. (27.13)
A temple with two wings is declared to be of inferior quality, while one with only a single wing is the lowest.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, concerning the rules for the measurement of pathways, doors, and so forth, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Sites of Village and Other Deities.
I shall describe the eternal locations for all deities in villages and other settlements.
The station of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be in the north-west (vāyavyā) direction from the station of Brahmā. (28.1)
Brahmā is the deity of the site (vāstu) in the west; Śiva is considered the deity in the northern part of the thread, in the center of the village, in its northeast, and in the eight directions.
The sacred site may consist of both Hari and Hara, or of Hara alone;
all else may remain as desired, for their station here is now declared.

The position of the Sun, or the abode of the Lord of Śacī (Indra), may be located in the western quarter, in the eastern quarter, or between the directions of Indra and Īśāna (the northeast). || 28.4 ||
The station of Ṣaṇmukha is said to be in the northwest, the east, the south, the southeast, the southwest, or even in the west. (28.5)
The location of the Teacher is proclaimed to be in the western, southwestern, or eastern quarter;
or alternatively, in the west or southwest, or between the northwest and the north. (28.6)
Furthermore, in this scripture, the location for Gaṇeśa is stated elsewhere:
in the south, or in the southwest, in the northwest, or in the center of Indra's [direction]. (28.7)
The location of Durgā is proclaimed to be either in the southwest or at the end [of the western direction];
the locations of Śrī and Sarasvatī are said to be in the west, O you who take refuge in Śiva. (28.8)
The Mothers are located in the northeast, in the portion of Soma, or between those two;
the place for Moṭikā and indeed for Kāmadeva is in the southeast.
Jyeṣṭhā should be established on the bank of a lotus pond, or elsewhere outside;
the site for Kāma and Bhāskara is said to be the location of Ṣaṇmukha.
But for the Mothers of the Six-faced One, there is another location as desired;
O Brahmin, it should be on a site larger than a thousand [cubits], or in the middle of a temple of Viṣṇu. (28.11)
The firm conclusion of this scripture is that there is nothing superior to the worship of Śiva;
through the constant worship of the Lord of Śrī, there shall be an increase in progeny. (28.12)
Through the constant worship of the Sun, domestic afflictions perish;
the worship of Indra bestows power upon men. (28.13)
The daily worship of Subrahmaṇya brings benefit to the forces;
the worship of the Teacher (Śāstṛ) enjoins the inhabitants of the site (Vāstuvāsins) to their respective duties. (28.14)
The worship of Kāma bestows beauty upon those dwelling in the house, while the specific worship of Umā grants victory. (28.15)
If Mahāmoṭī is worshipped, she destroys diseases of children;
all success is attained without obstacle through the ritual service of Vighneśa.
The special worship of Jyeṣṭhā destroys the diseases of those dwelling in their homes;
the worship of Lakṣmī bestows prosperity and drives away misfortune. (28.17)
O twice-born ones, the worship of Sarasvatī constantly bestows the power of speech,
while the worship of the Mothers always brings about all forms of prosperity.
Whatever fruit Maheśvara may grant through the worship of all [deities], therefore Maheśvara should always be worshipped by those who seek results. (28.19)
The supreme Liṅga is proclaimed to be that established in the northeast;
O twice-born ones, any other Liṅga established elsewhere is said to be middling. (28.20)
The location of Hari in the center of the village is proclaimed to be the most excellent;
one should know that in the west it is middling, and in any other place it is inferior. (28.21)
The form of Īśa and Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be twofold: fierce (ugrā) and peaceful (śāntā). Of these, the former is considered to be intent upon fierce activities. (28.22)
The peaceful forms are devoted to peaceful rites and are situated within; the fierce form (raudrī), however, is located on the outside.
The peaceful form is said to be in the center in all dwellings, such as villages and the like.
Karikāmāpurāri, Kālāri, and others such as these are declared to be the fierce (ugra) forms; the remaining ones are cited as the peaceful (śānta).
One should know Viśvarūpa, Nṛsiṃha, Vaṭaśāyin,
and Jāmadagnya as the fierce forms of Viṣṇu.
The fruit of installing the fierce deities (raudra) in places outside of villages and the like, such as forests and so forth, is now declared. || 28.26 ||
If there is destruction of the village in the east, women of immoral conduct will perish in the fire;
but in the southern region, there will be severe destruction by spirits, demons, and the like.
One should know that there is destruction through diseases in the Nairṛta [quarter], sorrow in the portion of Varuṇa,
a state of distress in the Pāvaka [quarter], and the condition of the kingdom in the Saumya [quarter].
In the northeast, there is the attainment of all prosperity and the increase of sons and grandsons;
this is declared for the village, and is likewise considered applicable everywhere else.
In a village, it is recommended that [the image] be placed in locations behind walls even in all eight directions;
however, one should especially not install an image of Rudra in the center of a village.
If the form of Rudra is situated at the beginning of a village or similar location,
the most excellent preceptor should perform the consecration of a peaceful form in front of it.
One should have a tank or a pond constructed; by that, peace is ordained, even in places other than agrahāras, such as in local settlements and other inhabited sites. (28.32)

In the four directions beginning with the east—namely, Vāyu, Īśa, Śiva’s abode (the northeast), and likewise in the remaining region, the portion of Parjanya, and Jayantaka—[the temples should be situated]. 28.33.
Beholding that left eye there bestows the abundance of all prosperity;
indeed, its vision brings about both worldly and otherworldly fruits for all.
One quarter, half of that, three-quarters, or even a full quarter;
beginning with one staff and ending with five staffs. (28.35)
Having led [the image] there, one should place it outside in the abode of the form of Rudra.
Thus has been described the fruit of the installation of the forms of Rudra.
Today the fruit of the installation of the Śāntamūrti is declared:
the Liṅga situated in the Brahma-sthāna is auspicious for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. (28.37)
The Aindra Liṅga bestows everything; the Yāmya likewise grants increase in longevity;
the Vāruṇa Liṅga brings health; and the Saumya shall be the bestower of wealth. (28.38)
Śiva bestows happiness in the southeast, victory in the southwest,
prosperity in the northwest, and everything in the domain of the northeast.
In all the intermediate directions, one should likewise designate the fruit; whether in the north (Soma), in the northeast (Īśāna), or in the space between Soma and Īśāna.
If a Śiva-liṅga is situated in the space between Indra and Īśāna,
there will indeed be prosperity for the village and so forth, as well as for the king and the kingdom.
Good fortune, long life, and health will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, concerning the procedure for the installation of deities in villages and other locations, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Rule for the Number of Twice-born Men.
(Verse 84) O twice-born ones, listen as the number of the twice-born and others is here declared:
they are of four kinds—superior, middling, inferior, and lowly. (29.1)
Each is said to be ninefold according to the measurements to be described hereafter;
from fourteen thousand down to six thousand, ending with the twice-born.
O twice-born ones, among the four types, the group of nine minus one thousand is the best;
then, from five thousand down to one thousand, they follow in order.
The wise declare that the lowest [type] consists of five hundred, the middle of nine thousand, and [the highest] ranges from one thousand less one up to fifteen thousand. (29.4)
It is held that for the *kanīya* and *kṣudra* [types], it is done by fifty [verses] in due order;
or else, O twice-born ones, listen as another method is being described. (29.5)

One should further increase another hundred and eight by a factor of ten; up to a hundred thousand repetitions should be collected, and among those, one should perform at least one according to one's capacity.
If one is unable, one should increase [the number] from ten up to one hundred and eight by increments of five;
if it is too deficient, one should increase it by only one.
Or else, one should perform [the ritual] up to ten [fingers]; among those, one should carry out the desired [practice].
It may be thirty-two, twenty-four, sixteen, or even twelve [fingers]. (29.8)
Or they are proclaimed to be fifty-four in number.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the "Ritual for the Number of Twice-born," in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Layout of Villages and Other Settlements.
This specific arrangement of the *grāmas* and so forth is now described here:
the *grāma* is the body, and its limb is that which is occupied by gods and mortals. (30.1)
The secondary limbs (*upāṅga*), such as the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and abodes, should be understood [to be drawn] either on the *padaprastara* grid or on both of the two middle lines. (30.2)
One should not even cause a secondary limb (upāṅga) to be made at the two ear-threads; nor should there be an extension of the thread at the boundary of a street, a row of houses, or a limit. (30.3)
One should act according to what is appropriate; one must not cause distress to the sacred thread.
Neither the breaking of staffs nor the demolition of houses should be carried out, whether in a village or within a residential compound. (30.4)
In cases involving minor limbs, whether in length or breadth, even the amputation of a limb may be applied;
however, elsewhere one should not cut off a limb, especially in the case of the body itself. (30.5)
In the outer rows there is prosperity, while in the streets there is the cutting off of punishment;
the house will have its foundation remaining, and the dwellings and such will have their structural supports severed. (30.6)
The desired measurement for the streets is recommended in the work of architecture;
there, one should complete the remaining space within the rows of buildings.
Small paths are recommended for the entry and exit of Caṇḍālas, as well as for the discharge of impurities and the drainage of water. (30.8)
Whatever fault has been committed by the king throughout the village, and whatever fault has been committed against the people of the village within its own domain. (30.9)
If a defect has been made in a secondary limb [of the site], a person should dwell elsewhere, specifically avoiding all the vital points (*marmans*) and other such parts of the *vāstu*. (30.10)
In the trident (triśūla) there is loss of the fetus; in the square (catuṣka), the loss of servants;
death is to be known in the vital point (marman); and at the joint (sandhi), the failure of a friend's request.
In the *catuṣka* there will be constant illness; in the *lāṅgala*, the loss of friends;
in the *brahmasūtra*, death; and in the *karṇasūtra*, the destruction of wealth. (30.12)
And in the *Padaprastara-sūtra*, the destruction of the city is certain;
various types of arrangements are recognized according to the division of even and odd [syllables]. (30.13)
Those situated on the lines follow the even paths, while those in the middle of the squares follow the odd paths;
because there is a mutual confusion between them, it would result in misfortune for the people. (30.14)
This division has been described for the site known as Daṇḍaka;
a wise man should construct the assembly hall and other structures in the Brahma-sthāna according to the prescribed rule.
A thread should be drawn between Īśāna and Yama, and between Nairṛta and Yama;
leaving that aside, it should be done on both sides for the prosperity of the assembly hall.
Having set aside the middle portion for the pond, the well, and the pavilion,
one should construct the temple of the deities in the north-west, the south-west, or the north-east.
One should arrange the seat of Īśa in the northeast, that of Viṣṇu in another [direction], or the seat of Brahmā in the central portion. Alternatively, one may fashion a pedestal.
To the west of the village and other such places, specifically along the Brahma-thread,
the wise man should install Viṣṇu in the northern human region.
In the eastern sūtra of Yama, there should be Mānuṣa and Skanda;
to the north of the sūtra of Indra, the wise man should establish Sūrya.
Then, to the east, one should construct a Soma-sūtra, and in the human region, a Vināyaka;
or Durgā should be placed there, or she may be situated at the side of Skanda.
Or one may arrange it in the Paiśāca [direction] outside the street of auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the layout of villages and so forth, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Brahma-Deva-Pada and Other Positions.
Hereafter, I shall explain the positions of Brahmā, the gods, and so forth;
[measuring] from the village, either by a tenth or ninth part, or indeed by an eighth or seventh part.
Having performed the Paiśāca externally, it is said to be Mānuṣa internally;
that which is internal is declared to be Daivika, and the remainder is remembered as Brāhma. (31.2)
Having divided the village land into four parts, with one part for the Vasus, Agni,
and the Sages (the priests), the preceptor should increase that single portion on all sides.
It should be known that the "outer path" is indeed external and belongs to the Piśācas;
however, within the divine and human portions, the residence of the social classes (varṇas) is prescribed.
In the Brahma-Paiśāca portion, however, a temple for the deities is desired;
yet, those who live by their work (craftsmen) must not make their residence in the Paiśāca portion.
Alternatively, O best of scholars, it is stated in another way:
when "the dwelling of the castes" is mentioned, it refers to the portion belonging to Brahma and the Piśācas.
In the Paiśācika Pāda, one should construct the houses of astrologers and physicians;
the houses of other professionals are considered to be in the Vāstu-paiśācika.
The house of physicians should be either in the middle of the village or outside it; however, the house of the priests should be beside the temple. (31.8)
In the outer Paiśācika [region], the Teacher, Rudra, and the Mothers [are located];
for the other Vāstu-deities, their position is in the Padapaisācika.
Whether outside or inside, there shall be a temple for Gaṇeśa and Skanda.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, concerning the ritual for the positions of Brahmā and the gods, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for Determining the Location of the Limbs of the Village and Other Sites.
(Verse 32.1) Now I shall fully describe the stations of those who subsist on the [astrological] limbs:
the astrologer, the calculator, the physician, the *ambaṣṭha*, and the dispenser of medicine.
The poison-remover, the artisan, the divine worker, and the eight components of the village:
the merchants, the potters, the barbers, and those who live by flowers. (32.2)
Those who live by playing musical instruments, those who live by killing living beings, those who live by means of the wheel, merchants, weavers, laborers, and even washermen— (32.3).
Even these Caṇḍālas, who subsist on the twelve limbs [of trade], have their station in the west (the direction of Varuṇa), or it may be in the direction of Indra (the east). (32.4)
The site for potters should be in the northeast;
that for barbers should be in the north or the east; and for both [potters and barbers], it may also be in the southeast or the east.
In the northeast, however, the place for those who live by flowers is desired here;
and the place for those who live by musical instruments is ordained in the region of Soma.
The station of those who live by living beings is desired in the southwest;
that of those with wheels is desired in the south and the north. (32.7)
In the Śivāgama, the location for the Vaidehakas is declared to be in the northwest; the location for the Tantuvāyas is declared to be situated in the southern direction. (32.8)
One should determine the position according to logic based solely on the excellence of one's caste:
it should be near those who are superior, but far from those who are inferior. (32.9)

Then, having cleared a space of one hundred daṇḍas in the south-eastern and north-western directions, there shall be the residence for those engaged in manual labor; beyond that shall be the area for washermen.
But for the Caṇḍālas, [their dwellings] should be constructed in the eastern intermediate directions;
one should designate huts for the Caṇḍālas outside the distance of one krośa.
The cremation ground (śmaśāna) should be in the northeast or the northwest, or in the east or the north;
however, if a river or similar body of water is present, the cremation ground should be located on its bank.
One should have a pond or a well constructed in the east, the west, the northwest, the northeast, or the direction of the Moon (the north); one should avoid other directions.
A cowshed should be in the southern region, and a flower garden likewise in the north;
or else, in all directions, there may be ponds, wells, and tanks.
The dwelling of Vaiśyas should be all around [the city], while that of Śūdras should be near the ancestral cemetery;
the dwellings of Caṇḍālas and laborers should be at the cremation ground and in the northern region.
And there is the transformation of inferiority regarding the constituent parts of a village, especially those such as temples and houses, and particularly regarding the roads. (32.16)
When there is doubt regarding those to be purified, one should cast them onto a path in a desolate place—
namely, upon a śleṣmātaka tree, a vaṭa tree, a kaṭaka tree, or an udumbara tree.
One should plant the āragvadha, the aśvattha, the nimba, and the plakṣa;
these should be arranged in a clockwise sequence in the eight directions starting from the northeast.
These sacred trees (caitya-vṛkṣas) should be planted outside the site; they are said to remove defects, especially those of the earth and so forth. (32.19)
When there are more than a thousand Brahmins, there is no fault according to the capacity of the Brahmins;
however, outside the boundary of the auspicious enclosure (bhaṅgalavīthī), it increases by one-quarter, one-half, and so on.
The celestial abodes are separated from one another by intervals of different colors, houses, and gardens;
furthermore, they consist of four, five, four, and two-and-a-half quarters respectively.
Having brought it under the control of the house, one should construct the temple in its various forms;
in this manner, one should fashion the celestial chariot (vimāna) for the fierce deities.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the procedure for determining the locations of villages and other constituent parts, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Deposition of the Embryo (Garbhanyāsavidhi)
(Verse 33.1) I shall now describe the procedure for the deposition of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*) for villages and other dwellings.
When accompanied by the embryo, it leads to all prosperity; without the embryo, it results in destruction.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should establish the embryo;
for the establishment prior to the installation of the deity would be most excellent. (33.2)
At the conclusion of the installation of the deities, the central installation should take place;
this occurs after one year has passed from the commencement of the layout of the village.

The establishment of villages and other settlements is declared to be the "lesser" [rite]; it is traditionally taught that this should be performed during the previously mentioned auspicious time, especially during the bright fortnight. (33.4)
For villages and the like, [the ritual] may take place at night; for a dwelling, it may be during the day as well.
However, in the case of the Nāga-yoga, one should deposit [the materials] within the interior of the village even during the day. (33.5)
One should perform the ritual placement at night for men, or even during the day for the gods; this is done in order to make a housewife pregnant, provided that one does not cause an abortion.
A wise person should have a bowl made of copper in the shape of a lotus bud,
starting from a size of four finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
In the *Caturviṃśatikā*, the width is proclaimed [to be twenty-four units];
its height should be half of that, or three-quarters, or equal to it. (33.8)

The height of the pinnacle (phelotsedha) should be three-fourths [of the height of the dome], and the height of the covering (pidhāna) should be one part, or two parts, or two parts out of eight parts. (33.9)
Beginning with one barleycorn, one should increase by half a barleycorn;
thus, one should determine the thickness of the walls to be four and a half barleycorns.
The increase of the core (koṣṭha) should be half of that, or one-third of the whole, or even one-eighth; this applies both to the height and the thickness. (33.11)
The *phelā* is said to be five finger-breadths wide; it should not exceed that for houses.
It may consist of five-by-five squares or be joined with nine squares.
The best of instructors should fashion [the vessel] either circular or square;
or it may be a vessel made of stone, measuring half a barleycorn or one finger-breadth in size.
The wise one should prepare half of the thick paste in a conch shell or a casket; gems, minerals, and so forth, should be placed in a small and narrow vessel. (33.14)
Knowing the specific locations for each deity, one should install them accordingly;
having understood this, the wise man should begin the rite of depositing the embryo (garbhasthāpana).
Having scrubbed away the external impurities, purified it, and washed it with acidic water,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
A wise person should cause the rite for the auspicious sprout to be performed according to the rules;
the consecration of the embryo (garbhādhivāsana) should take place either in the womb, in the house, or in the village.
The consecration of other [deities] should take place to the north of the vimāna and in the direction of Indra;
or one should lead the procession to a pavilion (maṇṭapa) measuring ten, nine, or four cubits in width.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar occupying one-third of its area;
its height should be one *tāla*, and upon it, in the four directions—
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should each be one cubit square,
or they may be shaped according to the specific rite, or there may be a single pit situated in the east.
It was provided with canopies and banners, encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass,
adorned with flower garlands, and equipped with arches at the gates.
Having thus adorned the pavilion, which is joined with auspicious sprouts and surrounded by a great lotus, one should again perform the rite for a meritorious day (puṇyāha).
One should feed Brahmins there for three days prior to that day;
and with ten *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using rice grains and sesame seeds.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with filaments and a pericarp,
and having strewn it with *darbha* grass, the Guru should worship the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
On the western side of the altar, which has been smeared with cow dung and made auspicious,
one should draw a square on all sides using rice flour.
The Earth, endowed with its seven continents, possessed of its seven oceans, joined by the mountains and the elephants of the quarters, and supported upon the hoods of the nāgas. (33.26)
Having drawn [the deity] together with the sequence of the paths of the worlds using white foam,
and having washed the skull-bowl (*phelā*) with products of the cow (*gavya*), one should place it within the variegated mandala. (33.27)

The preceptor, having adorned himself with garments and ornaments for the five limbs, his body consecrated by the ritual application of the limbs (sakalīkṛta), and decorated with perfumes and flowers; || 33.28 ||
Facing the east and becoming purified, one should indeed arrange the syllables;
one should place the peak-syllable (kūṭa), endowed with the bindu and nāda, in the central square.
One should place the letters from *ya* to *ha* in the eight corners starting from the east;
one should place the letters from *a* to the *visarga* in the outer corners.
Three-eyed and four-armed, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
bearing a trident and an axe, gentle, adorned with matted hair and the moon.
Having thus meditated upon the vessel, one should afterwards arrange the ritual substances;
facing either the east or the north, one should place the clay and other materials.
In the intermediate enclosure, one should place earth from the ocean in the east, as well as earth from a river, from a lake, and even that found at the roots of *darbha* grass.
One should also place these earths in sequence: that from an anthill, that from the horn of a bull, and that from an elephant's tusk, as well as that covered by crabs.
Having joined those eight portions of clay according to the sequence starting from the east and so forth, placing them in the eight directions, one should deposit them all in the station of Brahmā.
Then, one should also place five types of earth in successive order: from the horn of a bull, from the tusk of an elephant, from the root of *darbha* grass, and from within water. (33.36)
And on the bank of the river, one should place these five types of earth in the center and in the cardinal directions:
the roots of the lotus, the blue lotus, the white water-lily, and indeed the kumuda lily.
Furthermore, in that very enclosure, there are red lotuses, white lotuses, kaśeru grass, and blue water-lilies.
One should place all the central *kandas* in the mandala of the Lord of All Worlds in their proper sequence, and outside of that, the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgala*).
The Śrīvatsa, the full water-pot, the kettledrum, and the mirror;
likewise, the pair of fish, the goad, the conch, and the lion.
One should install Indra and the others in their respective order with the mantras of Indra and the rest, [visualizing them] as diamonds, coral, sapphire, emerald, pearl, and topaz.
One should place [the gems] while recollecting the radiant Śakti, namely ruby, lotus-colored stone, and lapis lazuli as previously described;
or else, one should arrange the five jewels in their proper sequence.
Recalling the five Brahmans, one should place a ruby, a sapphire, lapis lazuli, coral, and a pearl in the center and in the four directions.
One should place the minerals—haritāla, śilā, kāṅkṣī, tālamūta, and gairika—which are known as the fragrant peaks and consist of the nature of stability (dhṛti) and vigor (vīrya). || 33.44 ||
One should place all the serpents— immeasurable, marked with golden-red [signs], and possessing a loud, joyous sound— in the center as they are described, while recollecting the power of the body.
On the outer enclosure, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate quarters, there are sixteen seeds: rice, wheat, sesame, and mung beans, arranged clockwise. (33.46)
And in the intervals between the mudga, yava, nīvāra, and śyāmāka,
one should place all these [grains] which consist of satisfaction, with mantras denoting the lords of the worlds.
Gold for śāli rice, silver for vrīhi rice along with kodrava, tin for kaṅku and lead for māṃsa, flowers for āyasa, and sesame seeds [for the same].
Mudga, iron, copper, the *nimitta* [seed], and the sequence of *kuluttha*;
*viṣṇukrānti*, *triśūlī*, *śrī*, *sahā* and its predecessors, and *bhṛṅgaka*.
One should place the medicinal herbs apāmārga, ekapatra, and abja in successive order from the east,
as well as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, cloves, cardamom, and nutmeg.
One should place the eight fragrances, beginning with the east, in their proper order.
Although these are common to all [the deities], they will be described according to their respective insignia.
One should place the skull-bowl, the trident, the khaṭvāṅga, the axe, the bull, as well as the Pināka bow, the deer, and the golden noose upon the Śiva [liṅga]. (33.52)
One should place the specific weapon belonging to whichever deity it may be in the center;
for the benefit of the Brahmins, one should also place a sacrificial thread and a water-pot.
And one should place a golden *sruva* ladle, shaped like the syllable *praṇava*, in the middle;
as well as a chariot, an elephant, a horse, a tiger, and a bow.
And one should place a razor made of gold in the region of the king, as well as a balance, a measuring vessel, a buffalo, and a pair of bulls. (33.55)
One should place a golden bull, a pair of ploughs, and a pair of fish made of śāli rice in the middle compartment, which is the portion for the Vaiśyas.
In the Middle Country, one should prepare a golden vessel in the place of the Śūdra,
along with its supporting stand, a ladle, rice, and a water-pot.
A staff made of *daṇḍaka* wood called *galā*, black iron in the kitchen,
and a jar filled with excellent rice and water in the southern chamber.
In a house of wealth, the *garbha* (central core) becomes a bolted key;
in a bedchamber with a couch and lamp, one should know it as a dwelling of happiness.
Beginning with a measure of māṣa and ending with a pala, these are the measures of substances;
and the four-footed animals and the gods should be established facing inward.
Beginning from the size of a toe and increasing by the measure of a toe,
the heights of the images are proclaimed according to the measurement of eight finger-breadths.
The height of the mounts should be half of that, whether they are seated or standing;
having thus arranged the materials and covered them with the Īśāna mantra.

Having wrapped it with a pair of garments and encircled it with *kuśa* grass, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. || 33.63 ||

Having lifted the *phela* with both hands, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipas*), should place it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and perform the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarman*).

Having performed the rite of the fire-mouth (agnimukha) with those adorned with garments, gold rings, and other ornaments, along with upper cloths, one should then offer the ritual substances into the fire according to the prescribed rule.
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha [trees] are assigned to the eastern direction and the others respectively;
[one should offer] sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.

Having offered libations according to the prescribed rule—one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five times for each with the Śiva-mantra—and having likewise offered libations for the limbs (aṅgas) at one-tenth the number of the Śiva-mantra; 33.67.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the *śivamantra* ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should install the three principles (*tattva*) together with their presiding deity, as well as the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*).
Then, one should worship the vessel with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, and satisfy it;
having consecrated it ten times with the root mantra along with the *saṃpad* [syllables].

Beginning from the ritual placement of the substances (dravyanyāsa) up until the final establishment of the embryo (garbhasaṃsthāpana), the recitation of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas should be performed; furthermore, the chanting of the Astra-mantra should take place in the corners.
Indeed, these are the locations for the central sanctums (garbha) of all dwellings, such as villages:
in the portion of Brahmā, Aryaman, Vivasvat, and likewise Yama. (33.71)
In Indra and Varuṇa, in Soma and Pṛthivīdhara, in Puṣpadanta and Bhallāṭa, and in Mahendra and Gṛhakṣata. || 33.72 ||
The wise man should also establish it in a village or similar place during the period of a gentle deity or planet;
having made a pit right there, he should lead [the image] by means of a distance of only one añjali.
One should fashion it ending at the head, or at the ears, or at the heart;
its measurement may be six finger-breadths up to twenty-four finger-breadths.
Around the vessel, however, it should be provided with space;
likewise, one should dig a pit in the shape of a basket using stones and bricks.
Having performed the smearing with cow-dung, one should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place eight types of earth in its center.

One should worship Śeṣanāga in the upper realms, along with the earth consisting of seven continents and oceans, together with the elephants of the quarters and the mountain ranges, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
the lowest [gift] shall be five niṣkas, while the middling shall be double that.
The fee for the preceptor is declared to be threefold and excellent,
consisting of cows, land, slaves, grain, and other household requisites.
Having caused [the offerings] to be given especially, one should then satisfy the preceptor;
thereafter, one should worship the students, the image-keepers (mūrtipās), and the astrologer.
Having honored the master craftsman there with garments and ornaments as well,
and having meditated upon the form of Sadāśiva, one should recite the root mantra.
Having discarded it, the primary Śaiva practitioner, facing the east, should place it;
he should fill the pit with earth and make it very smooth and very firm.
One should fashion an assembly hall, or one should fashion the image above; [this applies] to the gods beginning with Śiva and the goddesses on the right of the door. (33.83)
Likewise, one should cause the embryo to be deposited at the base of a pillar during the yoga, or in a pit;
[this applies] when the pillar possesses the *homastambha* [characteristic], beneath the covering of the pillar-base and the *kūrca*.
Therefore, a womb that is excessively elevated or depressed causes the destruction of prosperity;
alternatively, one should place the Brahma-garbha in the Brahma-sthāna.
One should place [the deity] at the right foot of the corner of the assembly hall, the water-shed, or the pavilion;
specifically, on the second pillar at the southern leg of the entrance.
If one should place the core at the mouth of the small chamber within the theater hall,
the wise man should establish the core at the base of the decorated pillar.
It is prescribed in the interior of the house, in the assembly hall area, or at the door-pillar; or its interior is prescribed upon a base shaped like a pinnacle.
For the purpose of the Tulābhāra consecration, it should likewise be performed in the pavilion;
indeed, the central sanctum (garbha-sthāna) is prescribed for all such pavilions.
Either at the right foot of the door, or on the left pillar, or in the courtyard,
or at the previously mentioned corner-foot, or in conjunction with the right side of the door.
One should place [the deities] at the base of the pillars of the pavilion in the first enclosure;
however, in the case of a *pādabandha* temple, one should place them above the interior of the shrine.
But in the Pratibandha Vimāna, one should place [the images] above the enclosure;
for the Brahmins above the enclosure, and for the kings above the lily-pool.
For Vaiśyas, it should be on a wooden seat; for Śūdras, on a footstool;
