for all others, it should be placed upon the ground, so that it may grant all spiritual accomplishments.
In Puṣpadanta, Bhallāṭa, Mahendra, and Gṛhakṣata;
and in the four houses beginning with Saumya, [one should place] Netrabhīta in the south.
Or it is also prescribed that the circumambulation of the pillars at the entrance should be performed;
however, for the shrines of the retinue deities, one should carry out the ritual as in the case of the main deity.
In the case of halls, however, it should be grasped at the corners or in a preferred location;
if the hall is provided with a garland-like structure, [it should be grasped] at the second corner pillar.
One should place [the deities] either in the first enclosure or in the second enclosure;
having stood outside, looking outward, and having conceptualized them on the left and the right.
One should employ the inner-outer-facing womb in the center of the site,
both in the temple and in the pavilion, following the circumambulation of the exit.
For all the gate-towers (gopuras), the measurement is for the entrance and the circumambulation;
for the halls devoid of the stage called "Svāmī," it is for the wall of the eyes.
One should place [the images] of all those associated with him at the feet [of the principal deity];
or alternatively, they may be on the middle wall, or on the right side of the door, or in the center.
There are five locations for dwelling, both in halls and in houses: in wells, ponds, lakes, and the like, as well as in oblong ponds and embankments. (33.101)
If it is the foundation-stone (garbha), one should place it in the northern or eastern part;
the worship of Vāstu and the fire-oblation (homa) are prescribed for the laying of the foundation.
The gateway, the surrounding enclosure, the examination of the primary site, and the front of the pavilions are proclaimed in every scripture. (33.103)
Having divided the width of the wall into eight parts, one should lead four parts outward and three parts inward, and thus properly deposit the inner sanctum (garbha).
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the procedure for the deposition of the embryo, in the great tantra called the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Installation of the Child Deity.
(Verse 91) Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the children's quarters;
without a place for the children, a wise man should not construct the main residence. 34/1.
The primary liṅga and so forth are indeed not devoid of the characteristics of the infant [liṅga] and so on;
this is the division at the beginning of the village, whereas elsewhere it is otherwise. (34.2)
One should perform [the rite] either devoid of the marks of a child and so forth, or endowed with them;
and [one should place the vessel] in the northeast of the primary site, or in the north, east, or south. (34.3)
The preceptor should construct the children's quarters either in the southeast or in a desired location;
having set aside nine rods' distance, he should build a spacious dwelling.
One should construct the main chamber with three, six, or seven cubits, or even with just two cubits. // 34.5 //
Then, the space for the vestibule (bālasthāna) shall be half [the width] of the inner sanctum (garbhageha);
the wall is considered to be two or three times the width of the base section (mūlabhāga).
The remainder of the sanctum, however, may be a pavilion or shaped like an assembly hall;
its size shall be half, or even three-quarters, less than that of the sanctum. (34.7)

The height of the liṅga is proclaimed to be eight parts of the [overall] superior and middling [measure], with the circumference being equal to the length; the diameter and the length are considered to be equal. (34.8)
One should have it made complete with the head of a variegated serpent, but devoid of threads;
beginning from nine finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at a time.
Whether the child-liṅga be thirty-three finger-breadths in length, one should install that liṅga at a measurement of three or four parts [of its height]. || 34.10 ||
The best [height] is equal to the root and the rise; the middling is less than that; and the lowest is even lower.
When divided by eight, nine types of liṅga heights are considered therein. (34.11)
Starting from seven finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step, the ninefold measurement for youthful images is thus declared. (34.12)
One should fashion the *sakala* [form] in the *sakala* [state], and likewise the *niṣkala* [form] in the *niṣkala* [state].
The measurement of half the size of the original image is excellent, according to the measurement of one-fourth [of the whole]. (34.13)

An image that is eight parts less than the standard is considered inferior, while one measuring nine parts is middling; however, for a formless (niṣkala) deity, the seat should be of the highest quality according to its width.
The inferior [pedestal] should be one-fourth [the size], and the medium one should be one-ninth;
one should fashion the pedestal according to the measurement of the *liṅga*.
An image of Bālaliṅga is fashioned from metal, stone, or wood;
the wood may be from milky trees, or from Palāśa, Vaṭa, Udumbara, or Pippala trees.
One should fashion the image of the Liṅga from Madhūka, Panasa, Plakṣa, Sāla, Candana, Khadira, Sarala, and Amaravṛkṣa wood.
When a mansion is under construction, when it is dilapidated, when it is broken, or when its parts are defective,
and in cases of such faults as bursting, one should cause a child’s chamber to be built.
Even before twelve years have passed, one should move the *liṅga* and the *bera*;
beyond that, it is not desired elsewhere, so the wise man should install them in that very same place.
In front of the entrance to the children's hall (bālālaya), a square pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed;
it may be equal in size to that [hall], half its size, or three-quarters its size. || 34.20 ||
One should construct it firmly according to the rules using baked bricks, stone, and other materials;
it should be enriched with a height equal to its width and provided with a pillar and a pinnacle (cūlikā).
The main temple and the youth-chamber (taruṇālaya) should have doors in corresponding positions;
the pedestal (pīṭha) is considered to be threefold in form, either with four corners or eight sides.
The width of the linga-nāha (the base) is considered to be half the height of the pedestal;
the linga may be made of well-baked bricks, or of lime and clay.
One should not perform the placement of jewels, nor the construction of the foot-mountains and so forth;
rather, the wise one should first perform the ritual sowing of sprouts according to the prescribed rules.
In front of the child's residence, a square pavilion should be constructed;
the pavilion may be ten, nine, eight, or seven cubits in size.
It should be joined with wide pillars or perhaps with pillars of the sun;
it should be provided with three rows [of elements], square in shape, and equipped with archways.
Adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and provided with canopies and other ornaments,
one should construct an altar in the middle portion, raised by one-fourth of that [dimension]. (34.27)
Its width should be eight finger-breadths and its height four finger-breadths;
one should arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around it in the eight directions.
One should fashion squares in the cardinal directions and lotuses in the corners;
between Īśāna and Śakra is the principal circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Alternatively, one should prepare a bathing pit with five compartments or even a single one, situated to the east or on the northern side of the pavilion.
Afterwards, having dismissed the artisan, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
then, one should construct a water-shed (prapā) in the middle of the water, endowed with all the required characteristics.
Having washed the *liṅga* with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) using the Astra-mantra,
the preceptor should bathe it with pure water, perfumes, and other offerings, and worship it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments and provided it with a long beard,
one should lay the liṅga upon kuśa grass in the water while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should perform the ritual for three nights, two nights, or one night, ending with the Veda-recitation;
or one should carry out a ceremonial bath using an abundant quantity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
On all sides, [he should place] eight jars presided over by the world-protectors (lokapālas),
provided with cloths, gold, threads, and lids.
One should feed the Brahmins there in the well-decorated pavilion;
then one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice in either the temple or the pavilion.
Having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) using the fire from the Vāstuhoma,
one should bring the liṅga from the water and place it upon the bathing pit.
Having removed the cloth from the *liṅga*, one should perform purification as before;
then the wise practitioner should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
The preceptor should wrap the liṅga with a cloth while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra;
in the center of the altar, he should prepare it with four *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
One should well-strew the bed with rice, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and flowers;
in the center, one should prepare a couch in due order using skins and other materials.
Accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and hymns of praise uttered by those reciting auspicious words,
the foremost Śaiva teacher, endowed with all auspicious marks, together with his disciples, [should enter].
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes, adorned with flower garlands,
wearing white garments, a turban, and a white upper cloth.
Endowed with the fivefold ornaments, his body fully consecrated through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
and possessing such characteristics as these, the Ācārya faces northward.
One should place the liṅga upon the altar with its head toward the east and facing downward;
having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings using the Heart-mantra alone.
Filled with water from a droṇa-measure, wrapped with thread, provided with a tuft of grass (kūrca), endowed with the five jewels, covered with a lid, and accompanied by cloth.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher upon his head with the *varman* mantra; having placed the *vardhanī* vessel to the left, equipped with the measuring cord and other implements.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva, the God of gods, one should place the Śiva-mantra and worship him with the root mantra, accompanied by the thirty-eight kalās.
One should worship the Vardhanī and Manonmanī with their respective mantras;
one should then display the Mukulī, the Padma, and the Liṅga mudrās.
On all sides, however, he should place eight jars filled with half-water,
provided with threads and other [ritual requisites], and accompanied by gold coins (taṅkas).
The most excellent preceptor should install [the deities] beginning with Indra in their respective order within the jars,
from Ananta up to Śikhaṇḍin, using their own individual mantras.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings up to the food offering (naivedya), one should worship with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should then place eight water-pots for the retinue upon the smaller altar (upavedī).
Those most proficient in the Vedas, being refined, should perform the study of the Ṛgveda and the others;
or one person, remaining in his own respective direction, may recite all the Vedas.
In their absence, however, those beginning with Sadyojāta should be recited by the guardians of the images;
Sadyojāta is remembered as the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva as the Yajurveda.
Aghora is the Sāmaveda, while Atharva is remembered as Puruṣa;
[the recitation should be] one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again.
Or one should recite it one hundred and eight times for the sake of Vedic perfection;
however, in the absence of a physical image or a stream [of water], the preceptor should perform everything [else]. (34.55)
One should perform all rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Likewise, [the wood of] the Khadira, Aśvattha, Bilva, Udumbara, and Vaṭa trees [should be used]. (34.56)
Madhūka, Arka, and Palāśa are proclaimed as the sacrificial fuels (samidh);
however, the Palāśa is the foremost and is said to be the fuel for all of them.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, grains, parched rice, and sesame seeds—
either one thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight times.
Then one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having offered ten parts for Śiva, one should assign the Brahmās in the other directions.
In the intermediate directions, one should place the heart-mantra and the others, along with half of the root-mantra, or all together.
Then, one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) using the root-mantra ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the principles beginning with the Self (ātmatattva), as well as the forms and the lords of the forms,
and having placed them all within the *liṅga*, one should invoke them into the fire and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Then he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and pass the night with auspicious rites.
On the following day, the wise one, having bathed well together with the guardians of the images, [should proceed].
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, he should worship the deities of the gates and their presiding lords;
having fully honored the deity, the pitcher, and the fire, he should worship the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra.
Having consecrated [the offerings] with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should worship Brahmā and the others at the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should invoke the mantras and satisfy them.
One should properly perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantras of the *prāyaścitta* weapons;
having offered one hundred oblations with the *aghora* mantra, and [further offerings] with the *jaya* and other mantras for the destruction of misfortune.
Then the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
he should honor the teacher there with garments, gold, and rings.

Alternatively, five niṣkas may be the lowest fine; double that (ten) shall be the middle, and triple that (fifteen) is declared to be the highest, according to the threefold classification of offenses.
In the middle kalpa it shall be double, and in the best [kalpa] it shall be triple;
however, the fee for one who bears the image shall be one-tenth of that.
Half of that is for those who mutter mantras; for Vaidikas, however, it is equal to that.
One should know it to be equal for an astrologer, or double for one who performs the Vāstu-homa.
The sacrificial fee for the artisan is considered to be one-fourth of that given to the preceptor.
One should begin the installation of the *liṅga* prior to the auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) and the *nāḍikā*.
Having raised the liṅga from its bed, one should place it within the Bālasthāna;
then, while reciting the Śiva-mantra, one should establish it in the center of the pedestal.
Having consulted with the three bonds while reciting the heart-mantra,
when the auspicious moment has arrived, one should present it to the Guru.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums, joined with song and dance,
endowed with the chanting of the Vedas, and attended by various devotees.
It was crowded with umbrellas, banners, and canopies, as well as incense and lamps;
it was accompanied by the flow from the *vardhanī* vessel and adorned with auspicious sprouts.
Having lifted the jars and carried them on his head, and having performed a circumambulation of the temple,
he should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) inside the inner sanctum.
One should prepare a seat there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having placed the purifiers upon the head, one should also apply the Netra-mantra.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās upon the liṅga;
having meditated there upon Sadāśiva, one should worship him with his body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
Taking the seed [of rice] from the water-pot while recollecting Śiva upon the top of the liṅga,
one should place the seed upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) in the gentle northern part of the liṅga of Śakti.
Having bathed the liṅga and the pedestal with the waters from the pitcher (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel,
one should place the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) upon the pedestal in the directions starting from the east.
Having worshipped [the deity] according to the procedure for worship, one should perform the remaining rites with due skill;
one should then place the seed-syllables (bījas) of the retinue in their respective locations.
One should cause a ceremonial bath (snapana) to be performed with waters and offer abundant sacrificial food (havis).
One should also perform all the daily festivals and other rites even at the location of the child.
One should also determine the location for the child-stage of other deities,
as well as their image, palace, and so forth, by means of the door and the path.

The opening of the eyes, the consecration with cow-products, the laying to rest, as well as the installation of the water-pot, worship, the fire-oblation, and the rites of installation and so forth. (34.83)
One should perform constant worship consisting solely of meditation with pure flowers and other offerings,
strictly according to the path prescribed for the installation of each respective deity.
This has been described as the general rule; however, there is indeed a specific exception:
O Lords of Sages, on the second lunar day, one who is worthy of installation should do so during the first part of the night.
There, at the front of the main house, the master of the ritual site should place a water-pot upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having worshipped the primary liṅga with perfumes and other offerings along with oblations,
and having prostrated before the Lord of the gods, the performer, who is skilled in ritual action, [should proceed].
Starting from one year up to twelve years,
I shall renovate them within that interval and establish them once again.
Having made this request, the performer of the rite, together with the preceptor,
should likewise invoke [the deity] from the *liṅga* and the guru should install it within the center of the water-pot.
Having invoked the Goddess from the pedestal, one should place her in the center of the *vardhanī* vessel;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) before it, one should perform the *agnimukha* rite as previously described.
The wise man should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, grains of rice, parched grain,
and sesame seeds with the root mantra, and perform the oblation for the limbs at one-tenth that amount.
Reciting the Mṛtyujit mantra while offering dūrvā grass soaked in honey three times, one thousand times, half of that, or one hundred and eight times; || 34.92 ||
Having performed it in this manner, one should then carry out the *kṣaṇahoma* at its conclusion,
[observing] the days beginning with Sunday and the lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī.
One should perform the oblation with a single offering for each month beginning with Aries (Meṣa) and for each lunar day beginning with the first; one should practice this every year.

This should be performed every year, or alternatively, one may perform it at the end [of the ritual cycle]. Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should dedicate everything to the Deity.
Having lifted the jars, one should place them upon the altar with all auspicious rites;
for all of them, without exception, an image of a child must be fashioned.
Whether in an image, or in a water-pot, or on a pedestal made of brick,
or likewise among the retinue, one should fashion the form of a child.
Everything else shall be the same as previously established.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Rite for the Installation of the Child (Bālasthāpanavidhi), in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
[Now follows] the Rite for the Layout of Villages and Houses (Grāmagṛhavinyāsavidhi).
The layout of villages and the like, as well as their initial settlement and so forth, is now described. First comes the examination of time; second is the determination of the site.
The third is the examination of the ground; then follows the offering for entry. The fifth is the formal acceptance of the land, and the sixth is said to be the plowing.
Next is the fixing of the pegs, then the eighth is the determination of the site;
the ninth is the laying out of the threads, and the tenth is the offering of bali to the deities.
The division of house-alleys and so forth is declared as the eleventh;
the twelfth is the arrangement of the interior (garbha), followed by the placement of the deities. || 35.4 ||
Immediately after that, for the twice-born, there is entry into the *dvādaśānta*;
at the end of that, however, the observation (*nirīkṣaṇa*) of the *bhūsurās* is declared.
Therefore, there should be a division of the site; having understood this, one should proceed accordingly.
Even before the commencement of the house, there must be a determination regarding the dwelling of the deities.

Having first established the deities, one should afterwards settle the Brahmins; the determination of the temple site is according to the procedure taught for the primary foundation and the abode. (35.7)
One should construct [the temple] for the gods and humans according to the rules for building halls;
likewise, the divine abode is considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (35.8)
If the celestial abode is superior while the human one is inferior,
then a person should strive to make the inferior state equal to or even superior to the other. (35.9)
All of this, however, one should perform according to the previously stated sequence, especially for villages and the like, houses and the like, and gardens. (35.10)
I shall now describe the entry into the kitchen for the pavilion and other such structures, as well as the entry of the patron for other objects.
Those who are always of good mind, self-controlled, endowed with compassion, firm in their vows,
accompanied by their wives and sons, and provided with all necessary utensils— || 35.12 ||

Those who are favorable to the village, who worship the gods, the fire, and their gurus, who know the truth of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who are learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas), and who are pleasant to behold. || 35.13 ||
Those who have studied the scriptures of Śiva, though poor, are free from faults, devoted to excellent deeds, and dedicated to the performance of religious observances. || 35.14 ||
Having summoned the Brahmins and reached a decision, one should then have the ten-limbed document written out,
specifying the kingdom and the village, the lineage and the boundary-line, along with the left and right markers.
Having written the lineage of learning, the father's name, and the ten pure limbs upon a copper plate fashioned as a primary casket, [one should proceed]. (35.16)
Or then, with faith and preceded by water, one should present the materials for a house, such as stone and so forth, beginning with the ground. (35.17)
A king endowed with faith should give to the Brahmins ornaments for women, grain, clothing, a milch cow, and male and female slaves. (35.18)
One should give land to Brahmins at an auspicious time accompanied by a libation of water;
however, at other times, one should give it with mere words.
All else, however, is common to the construction of every dwelling.
[One should avoid] atheists, backbiters, the cruel, and those who revile the gods, the sacred fire, and their gurus. (35.20)

The king should avoid such Brahmins in the act of giving—that is, those who have misappropriated the property of a Brahmin by force, or who are guilty of treason against the sovereign and similar offenses. (35.21)
On an auspicious day, having placed a full water-pot and lamps in front,
he should cause the excellent Brahmins to enter while accompanied by the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana).
From among the twenty-four medium-sized [liṅgas], one should install thirty-six excellent ones;
and in a small [shrine], one may install one, two, or even three.
And one should seat the Brahmins as before— even those previously selected—
along with their wives and sons, and likewise accompanied by the deities and the sacred fire.
Upon entering these, one should worship the site (vāstu) and perform a fire-oblation (homa);
[one should avoid] a house that is not walled, not fenced, not roofed, and where no offerings or food have been given.
Entering a house with such zeal, one surely steps into the path of calamities;
therefore, one should, according to one's own ability, provide shelter for Brahmins in their respective homes. (35.26)
One should first establish the divine and human portions within the house;
one should establish them under a lunar mansion or a zodiac sign favorable to the patron.
In houses, pavilions, towers, and the like, as well as in halls and kitchens,
one should cause the maker of that [image] to be seated in this very manner.
In a temple or similar place, one should worship the Lord of Gods together with the Goddess accompanied by Skanda,
or else the Goddess alone, or the Lord of Gods alone, or the pavilion.
One should first cause the king to enter the temple peak and other such structures by the eastern path,
accompanied by his chief queen, as well as the garland-makers and others.

One should have [the king] enter, either preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) or without it, surrounded by ministers and others associated with the Prime Minister (pradhānamantrin). || 35.31 ||
In houses, pavilions, peaks, and the like, as well as in halls and kitchens,
one should cause the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, to enter by this path.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the ritual for the layout of villages and houses, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Pacification of the Site (Vāstuśāntividhi)
(Verse 36.1) I shall now describe the ritual for the pacification of the site (*vāstu-śānti*), which brings auspiciousness to villages and other settlements;
it is known as the "Pacification of the Site" (*vāstūpaśamana*) and destroys all defects.
In the restoration of what is dilapidated, in renovation, as well as in cutting or breaking,
and likewise in distress caused by wind, fire, or water, or in affliction from kings, thieves, and the like.

And when there is an increase in the south and west, when there is a cutting off in the east and north, when there is a deficiency or excess in the measurement, or when there is a breach in the exit of the door; (36.3)
In the case of breaking through walls or defensive barriers, in the construction of a temple, in the presence of another patron, or when the site possesses deficient characteristics; (4)
When [the mantra] has been abandoned, rendered void, or likewise destroyed, or when it is in a state of reverse order;
and when there is the fault of performing malevolent magic (ābhicāra), as well as in the presence of disease, pestilence, or fear.
In the event of portents and ill omens, a wise person should immediately perform the pacification of the site (vāstūpaśamana) for the removal of all defects.
Or even in a place possessed of crooked streets, devoid of proper layout and so forth, or in other inauspicious locations such as houses and temples. || 36.7 ||
When a great marvel has occurred, or when any of the three types [of portents], beginning with the "excellent," have arisen,
one should apply this specific expiation that is about to be described.
Then the Guru, a Brahmin devoted to Śiva, having performed his ablutions and being of serene mind,
shall be clothed in two new, fine garments along with an upper robe.

Having worshipped all the deities of the site and its constituent parts according to the methods prescribed in their respective scriptures, and likewise having worshipped other gods according to the ritual injunctions; || 36.10 ||
One should construct a water-shed in the center of the site or in another pleasant location,
provided with garlands of *darbha* grass and endowed with all types of ornaments.
In the direction of Varuṇa (the west), or in the south or even the north of the direction of Indra (the east),
one should construct an altar five finger-breadths high with a staff-like measure in its center.
Upon that [ground], one should mark out the squares with a thread smeared with flour,
consisting of either nine times four (thirty-six) or twenty-five squares.
Or else, there are thirty-six parts, or forty-nine, or the square of eight times eight, or the square of the number of threads. (36.14)
The best knower of the site (vāstuvittama) should establish one of these suitable [measures];
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice mixed with sesame and husked rice.
Having placed there the sacrificial oblation (caru) accompanied by parched grain and darbha grass, and provided with flowers, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter.
Having sprinkled [the site] with water while reciting the Heart-mantra and covered it with a cloth and excellent *kuśa* grass,
one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with three tiers in the western region of the altar.
Having established a square hearth measuring one cubit and nine finger-breadths in height,
one should enkindle the fire there according to the path prescribed for fire-rituals.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial offerings, as well as with barley, black sesame seeds, and dūrvā grass mixed with honey, ghee, and milk.

One should perform one hundred or fifty oblations with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva, with the limbs of Vidyā preceded by Śiva, with the Aghora mantra, and with the aforementioned five substances.
An oblation of one hundred and eight *dūrvā* grasses shall overcome death;
then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should worship the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*).
Having placed a tuft of grass (kūrca) upon the footprints, one should perform the invocation and other rites;
having first worshipped Brahmā, one should then worship all [the others]. (36.22)
She was fully twelve years of age, born of the Brahmin caste,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with various ornaments.
Having worshipped that maiden, who wears white garments, is adorned with white flowers,
and has a white cloth as an upper garment, one shall find happiness through offerings of food and other gifts.
And having given her betel-leaf together with the offering materials,
the preceptor should then place the vessel of offerings into her hand.
Adorned with the five ornaments, wearing a turban and an upper garment,
and clad in new clothes, the Śaiva Brahmin shall present the bali offering within the city.
One should offer pure food combined with honey, clarified butter, and curd; or else, one should perform this rite using all these substances together. (36.27)
At night, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) in a temple or similar place as desired;
or alternatively, there may be a libation for the Vāstu-deities in four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the preceptor and the others in due order;
the lowest fee shall be five niṣkas, and the middle fee shall be double that.
Threefold is said to be the highest fee for the preceptor, whether in the case of a gift village and the like, a temple, or for kings and the twice-born. (36.30)
In the dwellings or pavilions of Vaiśyas and those of Śūdra birth, as well as in places inhabited by Caṇḍālas and others, and even upon the birth or death of such persons; || 36.31 ||
If the water has been defiled by asuras and other such beings, one should perform this rite:
one should cast all the water outside, whether it be from a well or a lotus pond.
Having poured in either water from a thousand jars or water from a hundred jars,
along with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the pacifying fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the ritual for the pacification of the site (vāstu-śānti), in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of the Hall.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme characteristics of temples for gods, for Brāhmaṇas, and especially for Kṣatriyas. (37.1)
Those [houses] are prescribed as suitable for the residence of Vaiśyas and those of Śūdra birth;
they are proclaimed to have one, two, three, four, or seven rooms. (37.2)
Beyond that, one may take as many as desired by increasing the number threefold;
these are called *mālikās* because they are formed like a garland (*mālā*).

First, the measurement (māna) is declared to be of two kinds according to the division of cubits (hasta), beginning from one and a half cubits and increasing by three finger-breadths (aṅgula) at each step. (37.4)
The width is considered to be up to one hundred and eight cubits;
the length should be three times that, starting from half a cubit.
Thus, by the power of devotion, it may be one cubit in measure;
starting from one cubit, it increases by three finger-breadths at a time.
The divisions (bhaktis) are proclaimed to have a width of up to nine cubits.
The length should be twice the width, increasing by one and a half finger-breadths up to that maximum. From a base width of one division, it increases by half a division [at each step]. (37.7)
The length is considered to be three times the measure of the width;
those divisions are laid out both across the width and along the length.
If all [the lines] are equal according to the measurement, or unequal as desired,
the divisions (bhaktis) in both width and length may be either even or odd.
Whether it be a measurement internal to devotion, or even external to devotion;
or a measurement within devotion, or likewise from the foot established therein. (37.10)
O best of the twice-born, that which is square is for the gods and also for the Brahmins;
likewise, it is prescribed for Kṣatriyas, while for the other two [castes] it is rectangular.
What is said for the inferior castes is not beneficial for those of superior birth, and vice versa.
The height should be equal to the width, or one-quarter greater, or even one-half greater. (37.12)
The length may be one and a half times, twice, or equal to the width;
or one may construct it according to the sequence of the dimensions to be described below.
For the sake of perfecting the proportions, one should bring it to complete perfection in its width, length, and height, measured in cubits.
Whether it be solely from the width, or from the length, or likewise from the height;
let the first [dimension] be taken from the combination of width and length. (37.15)
Having multiplied by eight, three, three, and eight, one should divide by eight, fourteen, twelve, and seven;
the remainder will be the Āya, Vyaya, Yoni, and Nakṣatra respectively. (37.16)
Let the lunar day reach its limit at thirty, while the weekday is determined by seven; or else, let the calculation of the remainder be undertaken according to another method. (37.17)
O sons of Nanda, one should calculate the length, the width, the circumference of the length, and the circumference of the width by means of the numbers eight, nine, three, and eight. (37.18)
One should divide [the figures] by twelve, ten, eight, seven, and nine respectively;
the results beginning with lifespan (āya) are declared as before, and a surplus of lifespan brings auspiciousness.
Having examined it so that it may be favorable to the birth asterism of the sacrificer, the rite should be performed; or else, it may be done according to the name asterism.
One should act after examining [the matter] in many ways, or one should examine both; for total conformity is not to be found everywhere. (37.21)
Therefore, one should accept that which has superior qualities and minimal defects;
namely, the base, the foot, the cushion, and the neck itself. (37.22)
The pinnacle (śikhara) and the finial (sthūpikā) are said to be the limb of the hall (śālāṅga);
[it should extend] from the knees of the patron (yajamāna), up to the navel, and reaching as far as the heart.
From the throat to the end of the head, it should be half a foot or one-third [of the total height]; or, according to the stated measurement, it may be greater by three to sixteen parts.
The measurement of the base shall now be stated;
it begins at one and a half cubits and increases by three finger-breadths for each subsequent quarter.
The heights of the pillars are proclaimed to range up to nine cubits,
beginning from three finger-breadths and increasing by half a finger-breadth.
The widths are proclaimed to end at thirty mātrās,
beginning from four parts up to sixteen parts according to the rule.
Having divided [the measurement] into parts, the width at the top should be less by one part; in this manner, one should determine the lengths of the stars for each successive quarter.

One should have the *prastara* (the base slab) made with a measurement equal to half the length of the foot; having divided that measurement into nine parts, [the various types] are formed by one and so on up to four parts.
A wise man should cause the pedestal to be made either less or more [than the prescribed size];
however, everything according to the dimensions stated for the pedestal is ordained for the neck (kaṇṭha).
All the measurements stated for the base (pāda) are also prescribed for the spire (śikhara);
or one may fashion the spire according to the method for the fixed measurement (dhruva). || 37.31 ||
The height of the stūpa is proclaimed to be equal to all the measurements stated for the neck;
it may be from twice the measurement of the base-width up to nine times that.
The width of the wall has been specified; one may proceed with it at two finger-breadths, or starting from eight finger-breadths, increasing by two finger-breadths each time. (37.33)
The width of the walls is proclaimed to be three cubits;
this measurement applies to the base wall, while for the upper portion it is reduced by half a foot.
The walls may be mutually greater or even lesser, or they may be equal; a single-winged temple (śāla) resembles a segment of a staff, while a two-winged temple consists of two such segments.
With three [units] there should be a three-winged hall, and with four [units] a four-winged hall;
with seven [units] there should be a seven-winged hall, and in this manner others are proclaimed.
In width, one should arrange [the measurements] starting from a single *bhakti* up to a limit of fifty *bhaktis*;
likewise, in length, one should calculate by increasing in the same manner up to a hundred [units].
In front of these, however, there may be porticos (alindas), especially in the case of the principal [shrine];
they may be joined by one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven porticos. (37–38)
Likewise, they should be on the back or the sides, or again in a desired location;
one should arrange broad gateways and other doors in exactly this same manner.
In the center, however, a courtyard (prāṅkaṇa) should be constructed, wide and consisting of a single row;
by increasing it by half a row at a time, it is intended to extend up to thirty rows.

The length should be from one row [of cells] up to three times that, and the width should be likewise; thus the Brahma-courtyard should be constructed, either provided with a water-fall or not. (37.41)
Or it may be made mixed with the water flowing from the circumambulation;
or it may be joined with external water, or one should fashion a cavity.
The width of the hall (śālā) is desired to extend from one row of large trees and so forth, increasing by one tree at each step, up to a limit of five parts.
One should likewise construct the wide doorway as spacious;
the vestibule (alinda) should be equal in size to the wide doorway, or half that measure.
The measurement of the door should be exactly thus; the door-pilaster (*daṇḍikā*) is half [the width] of the door.
The sequence for the placement of the womb (*garbhādhāna*) and the entrance is in the primary sanctum (*mukhyadhāman*), which has walls. (37.45)
The rite of conception (garbhādhāna) is proclaimed to be performed either on the southern wall of the eye or,
alternatively, it is prescribed to be performed on the Brahma-wall.
On the southern side of the wall, the residence of the master is recommended;
on the north, it is said that "raṅ" should be placed, which shall be the house of the wife.
One should construct two doors for one who maintains the foremost [position]; this is especially distinguished.
In that house divided into nine parts, the southern section consists of five parts.
Having set aside three parts on the left side, the door is prescribed in the middle;
thus the door shall be in the vestibule (alinda), and it is exactly the same elsewhere as well.
Alternatively, one may construct the door in the middle or on either side;
it should occupy one-twelfth of the wall's width, with an additional one-fifth part extending outward.
The middle of the *yoga* and the middle of the *pāda* are prescribed;
the middle of the wall or the middle between those two, or the middle of the *pāda*, should be equal. (37.51)
The water channel should be placed after leaving the corner and the central position;
the outlet of the water is desired at the third part from the corner.
In Gṛhakṣata, Mahendra, Puṣpadanta, and Bhallāṭa, as well as in the center, a door is prescribed for these [deities]. (37.53)
For men, the hand-stambha, the tulā, and so forth are measured by even numbers;
for the gods, both [odd and even] should be taken, while at the base, the middle door indeed [is used].
The outer, inner, and middle [sections] are located clockwise from the center of the site;
starting from the Ādityas and ending at the feet of Nanda, they proceed in increments of five finger-breadths.
From the center of the site, proceeding north-eastward and south-westward in sequence,
the divisions of Dharma, Nanda, and Aṣṭadhātu constitute the quarters beginning from the eastern section.
In that rite of erecting pillars, those situated at each individual part are known as the middle between the two legs of the house and the middle of the wall.
Thus, the four types of houses have been described; one should arrange nine [types] within a hall.
All of this is proclaimed as common to all halls.
[This applies] to the Taitila twice-born, even to those belonging to heretical orders,
and to the elephant-riders, cavalrymen, chariot-warriors, and combatants during rites such as sacrifices and fire-offerings.
For the gods, kings, and women who subsist on the stage, a single-hall structure is recommended for activities such as dancing and singing. (37.60)
For prostitutes and the like, a plow [should be used]; for those who live by fierce means, a winnowing basket; and in a place devoid of a hall, one should provide a door upon the wall.
Now, beginning from the upper floor, the arrangement is described:
the main hall is where the stage area is established. (37.62)
The layout of the master’s residence should be arranged in the form of a pavilion,
provided with a pinnacle and a palace-like structure above, and equipped with a principal entrance at the top.
It should be provided with the door of the site (vāstu), especially with the walls, joined on all sides with sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), and endowed with the door of the house.
It should be provided with painted walls, equipped with turrets and stairs,
furnished with upper chambers, or even provided with a pinnacle and a palace-like structure.
It may be joined with the primary ritual acts and provided with two ear-ridges (*karṇakūṭa*), or it may be devoid of the ear-ridges; this applies to all other types of buildings as well.
The middle courtyard area should be provided with a pavilion, or equipped with an assembly hall,
or otherwise consist solely of water and land.
It is known as the "Upper Level" (ūrdhvabhūmi), and it is also described otherwise:
the main pavilion building is devoid of a pinnacle and a turret.
Having thus prepared the residence for the Lord, one should construct the stage (raṅga) in a similar manner,
provided with the installation of the *lūpā* pillars, following the other procedures according to the path previously described.
Alternatively, there is the mounting of the *lūpā* upon the entire hall;
this is known as the *ūrdhvabhūmi*. O twice-born ones, now hear about the second [type].
In the area of the four-winged quadrangle, however, that ground below is described;
that ground is adorned with pavilions, houses, turrets, and palatial towers.
Below that, on all sides, it likewise possesses broad doors;
its arrangement is prescribed as being by means of two parts of that very same [structure].
In the four corners, there are four peaks constructed with the same width [as the main structure].
One should lead the assembly hall for the rear residence by means of two parts out of four. (37.73)
Between the two front peaks, there are halls like the rear assembly hall;
on both sides, the width extends to the end of the fourth part.

Two penthouses (pañjara) should be constructed, arising from the junction of the ear-ridges (karṇakūṭa); one should lead the two eye-ridges (netrakūṭa) situated at the eyes of the principal vestibule (pradhānāvāsana).
Above those two is the assembly hall; extending upward for the distance of two *tala*s, it contains the Hall of the Rear Quarters. Likewise, everything else is situated on the lower level.
This is declared to be the *tritala* (three-storied) type, joined with a *avasāna* (finial).
The *vāraka* (enclosure wall) is situated all around the *alinda* (veranda) by means of one part.
On both sides, according to the length of the front hall, and likewise on both sides of the main hall, [the side halls should be constructed]. (37.78)
Following the alignment of the porch (alinda), specifically at its eastern part,
there is an extension of two parts with a width of two parts.
One should arrange six sets of halls with six doors and windows outside the veranda,
extending from top to bottom and ending in four halls.
Below that, at the entrance to the earth, is the conclusion of its doorway;
and in the interval between the six Netra-shālās is the Vāstu-sthala.
It should be four parts in length and endowed with a width of two parts,
specifically on the south, the north, and the east.

One should arrange two in the front corner and five in their respective places; alternatively, one may place them in the southwest and northwest, provided they are endowed with the portion for the deities.
Alternatively, a water-platform (vāḥsthala) should be constructed above six talas;
below that, there should be two stories provided with cords, measuring lines, and pigeon-arches (kapota).
This is declared to be the seven-storeyed [palace] suitable for the residence of kings;
below that, on all sides, there should be a surrounding enclosure (vāraka) occupying one part.
This is declared to be the ten-fold level of the cord-line (rajjusūtra), which is the lower level;
beneath that is the level consisting of eleven and twelve stages.
In this very manner, one should construct [the mandalas] up to sixteen types;
the first is the Sarvatobhadra, and the second is the Vardhamānaka.
The third is declared to be the Svastika, the fourth the Nandyāvarta;
one should know the fifth to be the Caruka, which serves as the lid for the halls.
The *sarvatobhadra* has eight faces, the *vedāsya* has four faces, and the *vardhamānaka* has six eyes on both the right and the left; these are considered to be the *svastika*.
Adorned with four eyes on both sides and in front,
it is known as the Nandyāvarta when placed in the east, the south, and likewise the west.
In the north, the front of the Saumya-hall and other halls is prescribed;
one should know that the *niṣpaṭa* and *caruka* apply everywhere, especially in this case.
The first four [offerings] are praised for everyone;
however, the *caru* fit for the gods is especially recommended for kings.
This is prescribed for the twice-born as well as for those belonging to heretical orders;
it may be situated in a portion of the hall, on the veranda, or even in a spacious courtyard.
The desired arrangement has thus been declared for the pavilion on the aforementioned ground;
one should construct a pavilion in front of these rows of garlands.
Beginning from one part up to the limit equal to the length and breadth,
the length increases by increments of one part, while the width remains equal to the length.
By reducing the height by one part at a time, the width [should be] up to three parts;
it may consist of one, two, or three stories, or even four or five stories.
A pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed in the area in front of the halls;
one should lead the pavilion all around such a dwelling.
Starting from one part and increasing by a quarter-part each time,
one should construct the surrounding pavilion (āvṛtamaṇḍapa) up to a limit of five parts.
One should construct the surrounding pavilion (āvṛtamaṇḍapa) measuring one cubit, increasing by half a cubit up to fifteen cubits.
Alternatively, even without a pavilion, the wise should construct a pedestal (pīṭhikā) according to that same measurement, either as a Vibhadra or a Sabhadra Mālikā.
In the four directions of the halls, however, starting from one part and increasing by a quarter-part in sequence, it extends up to eight parts. (37.101)
The length of the exit [of the wall] and its width should be increased accordingly;
the distance between them should be made double [the thickness], and in this way, the middle enclosure (madhyavāraṇa) is formed. || 37.102 ||
O twice-born ones, such a dwelling may be provided with a middle enclosure or even without it;
indeed, there should be a threshing floor all around it.
Having divided the Vāsavyāsa into four parts, starting from one part and increasing by one up to sixteen parts on the exterior of the Vāsa; 37.104.
Having cleared away [the obstructions] on all sides, one should perform the rites starting from the first enclosure;
the *khalūrikās* (open spaces) should consist of one part up to a maximum of seven parts.
In the mouth, on the two sides, and at the back, there should be decorative divisions (bhaktis) according to one's desire;
they may be less or more than twice the measure of the *ojas*.
Whether it be *sabhadrā*, *vibhadrā*, or *khalūrī*, it may be according to one's desire;
the interval between these, however, may be either even or uneven. (37.107)
The center of the Khalūrī-dhāma is prescribed in exactly the same manner;
whether it be in the interior or the exterior, it may be either larger or smaller.
Or it may be excessive on one side, or excessive at the back;
likewise, it may be excessive at the front, at the mouth, on both sides, or at the rear. (37.109)
Whether by the measurement prescribed for the hall, or by one's devotion, or according to one's means—all that should be gathered here, or it may consist of the hall alone. (37.110)
By increasing the number of repetitions from a single offering up to half a bhakti, one attains the splendor of the quarters through devotion;
this is declared in the Khalūrikā ritual, and it applies to both cases.
Having divided the broad *khalūrikā* into three, four, five, or six or seven parts, and having set aside one part on the exterior; 37.112.
In the interval, having omitted the remaining portions, one should place the *sālaka* in the middle; it should be provided with one or more stories and extend in length according to the base.
It should be provided with a hall-like form and a pinnacle, or else shaped like a hall;
or alternatively, it may be adorned above the pavilion with a chimney and a turret.
It should have a measurement slightly less than that of the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) and the base (pāda),
or it may have an upapīṭha increased by that same amount, or a masūraka increased by that same amount.
Or it may be elevated at the base with an amūsuraka ornament; or it may be joined with a base floor that is as high as the height of the main chamber floor. || 37/116 ||
A wise person should construct this training ground (khalūrikā) for temples and other structures, either with its surface devoid of those [faults] or provided with level ground. // 37.117 //
Among gods and humans, and especially in the royal capital, [these are found] at Puṣpadanta, Bhallāṭa, Mahendra, and Gṛhakṣata. (37.118)
One should lead the door or the side-door into the middle of the enclosure;
likewise, one should construct the gateway (gopura) according to the prescribed rule, provided with a threshing floor (khalūrikā).

In this manner, one should construct the hall according to the prescribed dimensions of the hall; it may also be provided with an inner sanctum (garbhagāra) or divided into sections in the center. || 37.120 ||
As prescribed in the *Khalūrikā-vidhāna*, one should divide the area— comprising both the outer and inner paths—
into portions starting from four parts up to twelve parts, and then take a single part.

Having set aside the first part from the base upwards, the wise one should fashion the group of six beginning with the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) using the remainder; that measurement applies to the upapīṭhaka.
The height of the door should be made equal to or even greater than [the width];
just as it is prescribed for the surface of a threshing floor, so it is ordained here. (37.123)
One may perform [the construction] slightly less than the height of the base floor;
however, the height of the *sāla* and the *gopura* should be greater than that of the base.

One should also fashion the ornamentation of the gopura like the ornamentation of the hall (śālā), provided it is joined with a crest in the form of a pavilion (sabhā) or fashioned with a crest in the form of a hall (śālā).
It is provided with the form of a pavilion, adorned with turrets and palaces,
equipped with porticos in front, and possesses watchtowers within the rows of its towers.
One part out of three parts of the width of the gopura [is the measure];
likewise, one part out of four parts, and one part out of five parts. || 37.127 ||
The exit from the gate-towers (gopuras) should be located outside the enclosure wall;
both the gate-tower and the khalūrī must be aligned according to the primary site-plan (mūlavāstu).
In the interior, one should arrange the houses of the king's queens with their entrances facing inward, and the residence of the chief queen should be situated on the left side. (37.129)
One should cause other [enclosures] also to be constructed surrounding that house;
furthermore, others may be made outside of those, according to the builder's desire.
The eastern courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should be the most important; if the courtyard is in the east, there will be fever.
In the south, it brings victory to kings; in the southwest (nairṛta), it increases enemies.
In the west, there is prosperity through sons and friends; in the northwest, death occurs.
In the north, there shall be an increase of wealth; in the northeast, death is certain. (37.132)
One should construct a perimeter wall all around the royal capital; this has been declared to be suitable for gods and other classes of beings as well, and is eternal. (37.133)
However, at the time of commencement, these [planets] are said here to be considered individually:
one should begin the eastern house when the Sun is situated in Aquarius or in a pitcher (Kumbha).
When [the Moon] is situated in Aries, there is dexterity; in Taurus, it is watery; in Leo and Cancer, it is fiery; in Libra and Scorpio, it is gentle; and the other four signs are not desired.
A house facing inward is never auspicious in the direction of the sun;
if one should build such a house, it will perish within a year.
A house built in the place of the Sun will certainly cause suffering to that residence;
however, if it is situated in the place of Mars, the house or field established there will be destroyed. (37.137)
When Saturn arrives, there is fear of hunger for those residing there;
however, if it is in the house of Jupiter, it will bring about all prosperity for the home and field.
A house built in the field of Venus should always be declared auspicious;
it brings supreme happiness to Mercury, while the Moon causes wretchedness for men.
One should likewise provide happiness to women; such shall be the result for the zodiac sign (rāśi).
This should be understood for the divisions (aṃśaka) and so forth as well; having known this, one should act accordingly. (37.140)
In this very manner, one should lay the first brick in a dwelling situated in the shade of a mountain or a temple. (37.141)
It is obstructed by the current of a river and brings about the removal of grief;
likewise, when a house is cut, broken, destroyed, bent, or otherwise damaged, [this rite] shall prevail. (37.142)
The *aga*, the *karavīra*, the *nandyāvarta*, the *kiṃśuka*, the *arka*, and the *kārpāsaka*—these six are destroyers of the household. (37.143)
The Palāśa, Khadira, Plakṣa, and Cintāvaṭa trees should not be cultivated within a house; however, they are considered auspicious when planted in villages and similar locations. (37.144)
If the site in the assembly hall is immeasurable and equal in length to its width, yet exceeds it in expenditure, then that house is inauspicious.
A bed facing west brings misfortune, as does one facing south;
placing a foot at the doorway is not desirable, nor should the head point north or west.
The dining hall and likewise the bedchamber should not be situated along the lineage wall (anuvamśa); those seeking auspiciousness must never construct a house door along the lineage wall. (37.147)
While constructing a single-winged house, one should diligently place two rooms on the south and west; those two rooms should be constructed with vigilance.
Having constructed a corner hall, one who dwells there will quickly perish;
however, one should arrange the beam of the brahmin’s house so that it points toward the east.

The tip of the bamboo staff for Kṣatriyas should point south, for Vaiśyas it should point west, and for Śūdras it should be toward the north; this is the rule regarding the orientation of the tip of the bamboo.
For the twice-born, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, pillars with an even number of feet are prescribed;
for śūdras and those of other castes, an odd-numbered pillar is desired.
For the two kings of the twice-born (the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa), there should be Khadira, Khādira, and Śamī;
for the Vaiśya, the trees are Silindhra, Piśita, and Madhūka.
The *rājādana*, *nimba*, *silindhra*, or even meat may be used for the immobilization of Śūdras; however, the inner bark of trees is suitable for all [castes]. (37.153)
The width of the base (pādavyāsa) is said to be one-fourth or one-fifth of the house's total width, or it may be derived from the width of the house itself.
The width of the pillars for all houses is desired to be equal in number to the fingers on as many large hands as there are. (37.155)
In the north should be the house of the Brahmin; in the east, the house of the king (Kṣatriya) is prescribed;
in the south, the house of the Vaiśya; and in the west, for the Śūdra caste. (37.156)
The middle wall of the house is devoid of a central opening;
relying upon that [wall], two doorways resembling channels are desired here. (37.157)
In no way should one perform the rite of reconciliation between different schools; the installation of deities and the ritual offering of the *piṇḍa* are not prescribed for separate schools. (37.158)

The feet may be placed with one intervening space between each, or they may be set down without any gap; in other rooms and such places, there may be two or five [footprints] according to one's desire.
In the piercing by Mars (Manda), there is loss of wealth; it may be severe, involving debt and imprisonment.
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the [maximum] is three *cūlīs*; for kings, it is five or seven.
Likewise, for Brāhmaṇas, there should be eleven altars;
for those belonging to heretical orders or stages of life, an oven of even number is prescribed.
One should not construct stone pillars or stone walls within a human dwelling;
[a stone structure] should be covered with grass and the like, and an earthen structure should be covered with clods of earth. (37.162)
The elevation of the face, heart, and navel should be made in successive order;
furthermore, the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of four rooms starting from the south in the prescribed method.
If the interior of the door is depressed, there is prosperity for the master of the house;
however, an elevation on the exterior of the door should be known as increasing enemies.
The Bhallāṭa door should be desired for Brāhmaṇas, especially; one should know the Māhendra door for kings, and the Rākṣasa door for merchants as well.
The Puṣpadantapadadvāra is declared to be for Śūdras alone; having taken recourse to the lords of those directions, one should perform the rite for the door according to the rules. (37.166)
One should construct the door according to the prescribed rule on the left side of the central axis;
furthermore, I shall describe the placement of their water-door.
In Jayanta, Mahendra, Rākṣasa, Vitatha, Bhṛśa, Puṣpadanta, Sugrīva, Bhallāṭa, and Gṛhamukhyaka; (37.168)
Facing Brahmā, the supreme Brahman is established; [the deities] are barred from the divisions of one, three, five, and seven [parts], where the banner, lion, bull, and elephant reside. (37.169)
These [planets] are indeed auspicious when situated in the east and other directions in their direct order;
however, for those in the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth houses, they are like smoke, a horse, a donkey, and a crow.
These should be avoided in the intermediate directions, such as the southeast, by those desiring worldly enjoyment.
A house whose entrance faces a flag, a lion, a bull, or an elephant [is auspicious]. (37.171)
To its southwest is the house of the master;
the banner goes to the place of Hari, and the lion to the place of the elephant.
All go to the place of the bull (ukṣapada), yet those who are not pure (anukṣa) do not go anywhere;
one should not make a door for the bull, or it should be situated between the upper and middle sections.
For Brahmins, the north-facing door is best; for a Kshatriya, the east-facing; for a Vaishya, the south-facing; and for a Shudra, the west-facing. (37.174)
This is declared to be the door of the hall (śālādvāra) even in the four-house layout;
one should arrange the outer door of the southern residence at the location of Bhallāṭa.
The Māhendra [door] is in the western part, the Gāndharva in the northern house,
and the Puṣpadantapadadvāra is prescribed for the eastern house.
The cooking place for Brāhmaṇas is prescribed in the northeast;
the cooking place for Kṣatriyas is recommended in the southeast. (37.177)
The place for cooking is recommended for Vaiśyas in the southwest;
the place for cooking is highly recommended for Śūdras in the northwest. (37.178)
The dining hall is in the east, while the kitchen is in the southeast;
the sleeping quarters are in the south, and the armory is in the southwest. (37.179)
Furthermore, the chamber for the Maitra fire should be there, or else a water reservoir in the northwest;
the cow-pen should be in the northwestern quarter, and the treasury in the northern quarter. (37.180)
For the sake of the obligatory and occasional rites, one should construct the sacrificial pavilion in the northeast;
one should place vessels of fermented rice-water and salt in the north-eastern direction.

Or even in the intermediate space, on the hearth, on the mortar, in the sun, in the portion belonging to Āryā, in Indrāṇī, and in Savitṛ—[these are the places for] the first feeding of solid food. (37.182)
One should know that cooking occurs in the portion of Vivasvat, marriage in the region of Mitra, honey in Indrajaya, and it may also occur in the portions of Vāyu or Soma. (37.183)
And with a false alignment in the positions of Pitṛ and Dauvārika, as well as for Sugrīva and Puṣpadanta, the birth-chamber is desired. (37.184)
In the Āpavatsa [direction], there should be a water-pot; a bowl is also prescribed for that same place.
In the Mahendra portion, however, there is a mortar, and on the Mahīdhara [portion], a grinding stone.
In the quarters of Bhṛṅgarāja, Sugrīva, and Pitṛdauvārika,
there should be a desirable house for the Ariṣṭa tree, and there also a ground for its preparation.
The vehicle should be placed in the northeast (Īśāna), the bathhouse in the west (Vāruṇa),
clothing in the southwest (Asura), and weapons and the like in the southeast (Indra).
Likewise, in the portion of Mitra, there is clothing; in the portion of Mitra, a mortar is considered to be present.
In the portion of Bhūdhara, there is a treasury-house; and in the portion of Nāga, there is clarified butter and medicine.
In the Jayanta, Cāpavatsa, Parjanya, and Śiva [śakhas], respectively, there should be an antidote for poison, a well, and a temple of the gods. (37.189)
From Savitṛ to Antarikṣa, the kitchen shall be well-furnished;
in Vitatha, Pūṣan, or Sāvitra, or indeed in the dining hall itself.
In the quarters of Ṛkṣa, Bhallāṭa, and Soma, there should be a pavilion for the assembly;
at the entrance, one should place a mortar, and courtesans are highly recommended [there].
To the left of the vehicle, it bestows fame especially when placed there;
this is described as the "four-hall" type, provided it is joined with a central pavilion.
A waterfall on the top of the outer wall portends the destruction of the family;
its occurrence upon this house during such a violent transit is not auspicious. (37.193)
All of this, however, is common to both halls and houses.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of halls, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Special Hall (Viśeṣaśālā)
O twice-born ones, listen as I shall describe the specific characteristics of the halls, beginning from three or four cubits and increasing by two cubits at each step. (38.1)
The number of Rudras is said to extend up to twenty-four cubits;
it may consist of one hall, two halls, or is described as having two or three halls.
Starting from seven or eight *aratnis*, one should increase by two cubits (*hastas*) each time; thus, there are seven types for a temple with two or three halls, ending at nineteen *aratnis*.
Thus the width has been described in detail; now the length is stated here: it may be one-quarter greater, or one-and-a-half times, or likewise one-quarter less than double [the width].
The length is considered to be eightfold, ranging from double [the width], or half of that, or two-thirds, up to double, and ending at three times [the width]. (38.5)
The maximum height for the gods shall be two units, while for humans it is considered to be one unit;
all those dwelling in monasteries and hermitages should have heights starting from twice that [human measure].
In every structure possessing a connection (saṅgama), its length is considered to be double [the width];
its height is equal to its width, increased by one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters.
The height of the halls is proclaimed to be twice [the width] up to five times;
it subsequently bestows peace, nourishment, victory, and wealth. (38.8)
Thus has the fruit of height been declared as bestowing wonders;
moreover, halls situated to the south and west are especially beneficial for men.
If the plough is deficient in the south-west, death will occur;
however, if the plough is complete in that direction, it is proclaimed that there shall be prosperity and nourishment in the home. (38.10)
A hall situated in the south-western direction bestows all defects;
it may have one wing, or two large wings, or three wings, and possess two junctions.
Of heretics, mortals, Brahmins, kings, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others born between [the castes]. (38.12)
A single *śāla* should have the appearance of a segment of a staff, possessing two eyes and bearing a face;
likewise, it is considered that there should be two or three *śālas* in all villages and the like.
From thirteen cubits, one should increase by two cubits each time;
the width of the four-winged (catuḥśālā) structure ranges from six to seventy-six cubits.
The inferior, the low, the middling, and the superior— each of these has twenty-eight measures in a spacious four-winged monastery. (38.15)
Therefore, the hall for the umbrella and the assembly hall should be thirty cubits wide;
from that point on, they increase by two cubits each, starting from six and seven cubits respectively.
Ninety-eight cubits have been specified, multiplied by three, five, and eight;
starting from that point, one should bind [the cord] with both hands at the distance of one hundred cubits.
Endowed with six or seven *ratnis* in measurement, it has ten halls;
this is called "Variegated" (*citram*) in every respect, and by number it should be sixty-eight.
The inferior is said to be "birth," the base is called "desire," the middling is "conceptualization," while the supreme partakes in the name "appearance. (38.19)
By this name, one obtains fourteen and seven halls in sequence; [the horses] named Turaṅga, Avadhi, and Medhā obtain the long and short [forms]. (38.20)
In this case as well, one should determine the height and length as before;
however, that which is equal and square is declared to be for the gods and humans.
It is recorded as being suitable for sacrifice to heretics, gods, Brahmins, and others;
it consists of the Daṇḍaka, Maulika, Svastibhadra, and Caturmukha [arrangements]. (38.22)
The fourfold general [classification] of deities and so forth has been illustrated;
I shall now explain, in due order, the arrangement of the *daṇḍaka* meters and the rest. (38.23)
The width shall be three parts, while the length shall be four parts;
the width of the house shall be two parts, and at the front, there shall be a single part for the entrance.
Having two eyes and resembling a broken staff, it is suitable for the residence of all;
this is declared to be the *daṇḍaka* [plan], and the halls shall consist of six parts.
In width there should be four parts, and in length there should be six parts;
the width of the house should be two parts, and the projection should be two parts. || 38/26 ||
The remainder is designated as before; this is considered the second *daṇḍaka*.
One-third of the width of the house is desired for its length, which is intended to be double [the width]. || 38.27 ||
One should perform the division and the stepping-out (kramaṇa) provided with the Brahma-wall, joined with the two doors of the channels; all else, however, is as before.
The dwelling should be at the base of the bamboo, while the painted area is intended for the top of the bamboo;
on all sides there should be a wall, and the painted area should be provided with a base. (38.29)
One should decorate the *alindaka* (porch) in front, behind, or on the sides like a palace; this is considered the third type of *daṇḍaka*.
That same middle section is the cloth at the top and bottom of the bamboo;
the remainder is specified as before, and this is considered the fourth type of *daṇḍaka*.
The width of the house is six parts, while its length is twelve parts;
the width of the surrounding veranda and hall is one part, and two parts respectively.
That [central hall] is equal [in size], with a porch (alinda) in front and provided with internal pillars;
on both sides, the two side-wings (vivāsaka) have a length equal to two or three parts of the width (tārā).
The colored panel (raṅgaka) in the middle of the hall should have a width of two or four parts;
this is declared to be the fifth type of staff (daṇḍaka), and the remainder should be executed as previously described.

In the Vyāsa [plan], when there are one, two, three, or four [units] in front, there shall be an *alinda* (veranda) in a house consisting of one, two, or three wings, provided it is as pleasant as the Nandā river in the hidden netherworld (*pātāla*).
This very same type of pinnacle with a hall-like form is considered the *maulika* (original) style;
that same [pinnacle], when provided with a *bhadra* (frontal projection) at four and two parts, is approved as such. (38.36)
One should construct a porch (alindaka) at the front and on both sides, equal in length and breadth,
and provided with three eyes (netra) in its width.
This is called the *svastika*; now the four-faced (*caturmukha*) is described:
it is that same [design] provided with a *bhadra* at the back, just as it appears in front.
At the top of the hall of the bamboo pole of the *karkarī* drum, it is endowed with four eyes;
it is rich with the [architectural] sections beginning with the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and is adorned like a temple (*prāsāda*). || 38/39 ||

This four-faced [temple], endowed with parts such as the nose-gate (nāsikā) and the archway (toraṇa), as well as windows and other features, is known by name according to its sequence, bearing names such as Jāti and so forth.
The fourfold group beginning with the staff (daṇḍaka) and ending with the fifth ground is placed according to the will of the presiding deity, joined with the arrangement of the locations. 38.41.
Or [he may worship] each of the elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth, together with their attendants;
[an image] having six, five, or three limbs, with a beautiful neck, and provided with a couch. (38.42)
The height [of the pillar] is taken as one and a quarter, one and a half, or equal to that;
the *daṇḍaka* or *maulika* [base], or the elephant-head (*vāraṇa*), may be placed in any desired direction. (38.43)
This is declared to be the single-hall [temple], adorned with the sanctum and other features.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the specific characteristics of the single-hall [temple], in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of Two- and Three-Winged Buildings.
In a square structure with two wings, divided into ten parts,
the outer section shall be the entrance, and its width shall be twice that of the wing.
In the east-facing [mandala], one part shall be for the pavilion (maṇḍapa) consisting of nine divisions;
surrounding that, there shall be a single boundary line (kālinda), and the remainder shall be the circumambulatory path (kramaṇa).
The main hall and the outer gate, shaped like a ploughshare as appropriate, are here proclaimed to be provided with four entrances and two wings. (39.3)
One should design a two-winged structure (dviśāla), whether it be devoid of a courtyard for the citizens, or even without a pavilion, or likewise provided with a veranda. || 39/4 ||
That same [hall] extends to five parts in length for the front hall;
the door is prescribed as before, adorned with all ornaments. (39.5)
An oblong porch is constructed outside the pavilion;
that which is joined with three eyes is called the Svastika.
That very same [structure], when provided with two openings, is known as the *daṇḍavaktra*;
it may also be provided with an open space within, even without a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
One should likewise design it with a single wing or even with two wings; it may have a courtyard or be without one, and consist of one or more stories.
In a two-part division, one part; in a three-part division, two parts;
in a four-part division, three parts; or two parts in a five-part division consisting of three parts. || 39/9 ||
In a six-part [division], it may be two parts or one part;
in a seven-part [division], it may be five parts, or likewise from two parts up to five parts.
Having divided [the space] into nine parts, or from seven parts down to two parts, or again from eleven parts down to two parts, starting from three parts; || 39/11 ||
One should determine the width of the hall (śālā) up to the end of the ninth part;
this is declared to be the common rule for halls consisting of one, two, three, or four bays. || 39.12 ||
Having thus carefully examined it, the preceptor should perform what is appropriate;
he should divide the width of the foundation into eight parts.
The courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should consist of two parts, with an entrance porch (alinda) on three sides and on one side;
the width of the hall (śālā) is two parts, adorned like a palace (prāsāda).
It was provided with a six-faced structure, and even its courtyard was concealed;
it possessed both single and multiple stories and was adorned with pavilions and other such features.
Whether it be devoid of the *aṅkaṇa* or even lacking the *vāra*, this is declared to be "Merukānta," suitable for all [deities]. // 39.16 //
In the Vyāsa [plan], it is held that one should divide the width by twelve; one part is for the side walls on the west, one part is for the door, and two parts are for the width of the house. (39.17)
Facing east, one should arrange one part for the path on one side,
two parts for the courtyard, and one part for the sun-sector.
Or, if there is another principal Vyāsa on the two sides, it shall have two lalāṭas;
this is known by the name Maulibhadra, while the rest is declared to be as previously described.
In a three-winged house, there should be a courtyard provided with an open space;
one should construct the three-winged house either with or without a veranda.
In a place devoid of halls, one should employ walls and doors.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of two or three halls, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of a Four-Walled House (Catuḥśālā)
Now, the ornamentation of four-sided halls and other types of halls is described.
One should arrange [the measurements] from eight to twelve units for the lower [class of] halls. (40.1)
One should assign ten solar units (daśārka) as the deducted portions (nikṛṣṭa);
however, one should assign a single portion (ekāṃśa) of the two solar units as the middle portion (madhya).
On the excellent path, the seed portion is declared to consist of fourteen, two, eight, and eighteen parts, since the caste portion is increased by two parts. (40.3)
In this [mandala] known as Sarvatobhadra, one should conceive of it as having an increase of four parts,
an increase of six parts, and an increase of eight parts for the *ābhāsa*.
The seed-syllable (bīja), however, is square due to its nature as a dvandva compound and so forth;
the number produced from the seed-syllable and its class is traditionally known as sixty.
In the *nikṛṣṭa-sarvatobhadra* layout, the central courtyard occupies two parts;
there is one part for the path on all sides, and the width of the house is two parts.
