It should be provided with eight eyes (projections) and joined with auspicious recesses in the four directions; in the center of the auspicious area, there should be a quadrangular hall with a pinnacle on its corner.
In the middle [section], conjoined with the [proper] day, there should be a pinnacle (kūṭa) provided with a conch-shell and joined with a pair;
the residence of the master is praised if it is located either in the east or in the west.
It was enclosed on all sides by walls, with doors fashioned to resemble the walls themselves;
it was adorned externally with latticed walls, while the interior was provided with cobweb-like pedestals.
The door is praised when it is situated in the eastern wing-section;
one should have it constructed with equal pillars, an equal door, and an equal ridge-pole. (40.10)
One should construct a pinnacle joined with a staff-like door-post, serving as a lamp for the quarters,
with the top of its lattice-work made of bamboo and water-jars, or one may omit the small turret.
Having abandoned the inner door, it may instead have an outer door;
it may have a veranda or no veranda, or it may have an open space between.
The courtyard should indeed be constructed, adorned with all ornaments;
this is declared here for kings as the "Jātya" type, known as "Sarvatobhadra. (40.13)
That same [structure], extending two parts on all sides and provided with a large door, may be made known as the *karkarī*, the *vaṃśajāla*, or even without a pinnacle (*kūṭa*). || 40.14 ||
It has eight faces, with a neck above the surface and a well-proportioned ridge;
it is surrounded by eight-faced porticos and covered with well-formed limbs.
The *Bhadrordhva*, which is the primary form of the *kūṭa* structure and is endowed with all ornaments, as well as the variegated *Sarvatobhadra*, are praised for kings. (40.16)
That very same [structure], with two parts in front and provided with a large door,
has a pinnacle for the four halls shaped like a hall (sabhā).
The mandala should be designed as the Sarvatobhadra, provided with houses and palaces,
consisting of one, two, or three stories, and adorned with every ornament.
The residential quarters of the master consist of a palace structure lacking its pinnacle and crest,
yet endowed with a finial, a stūpa, a nose-ornament, an altar, and latticed windows.
A palace with a high hall and a low pinnacle,
or even the reverse of both, may be a middle-sized pavilion.
However, due to the combination of types such as *jāti* and so forth, four kinds are illustrated: the *ābhāsa*, the *gṛhamālika*, the *nikṛṣṭa*, and the *sarvatobhadra*. (40.21)
In the Sarvatobhadra layout, however, the courtyard in the center is two parts;
the path on all sides is one part, and the hall in the two-winged structure is two parts.
On the exterior, the door should extend by a portion all around and be divided according to the Viśva proportion;
it should be as high as the foot of the *masūrikā* and provided with a series of elements situated above the *prastara*.
One should construct that very same courtyard, provided with a pinnacle, a dome, a nose-ornament, a railing, and a lattice, and endowed with an inner enclosure.
The previously mentioned [layout] beginning with Bhadra, however, is suitable for a king;
that very same [layout], moreover, is provided with two doors on the exterior and two rows [of pavilions]. (40.25)
Alternatively, a large hall (mahāvāra) provided with a gabled chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) and a porch (alinda) may be constructed;
this is designated as an option (vikalpa), with the exits and so forth as previously described. || 40/26 ||
This is declared to be the abode for gods, the twice-born, and kings; in whichever direction it may be, it shall be auspicious in that very direction according to one's desire. (40.27)
One should lead the path of the courtesan and the porch according to the desire of the master;
this is designated as "conceptualization" (vikalpa), which is a manifestation arising from all yogic union. || 40/28 ||
The types known as Muṇḍaprāsāda, Harmyaprāsāda, Ābhāsa, and Sarvatobhadra are for gods, brahmins, and kings. (40.29)
The inferior *sarvatobhadra* is declared to be of four types;
the middling *sarvatobhadra* is provided with corners consisting of four parts.
The path should be covered by one part, and the hall portion should be double that;
outside, one should arrange the porch (alinda) as one part, just as previously described.
That same [design] would be the *sarvatobhadra* type if it were provided with a boundary line on the outside consisting of one part,
or joined with two parts, or indeed joined with a broad boundary line.
As before, one should provide it with a *bhadra* (central projection) for gods, brahmins, and kings;
or else, one may lead the courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*) to consist of two parts, provided it is devoid of an inner enclosure (*vāra*).
From that portion, one should lead it to the outer door or the great gate;
one should specify the alternative as being sixteen parts in width.
In that [layout], the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) shall consist of six parts, with a path on one side;
the division for the hall (śālā) shall be two parts, while the inner enclosure (antarvāra) shall likewise be on one side.
By means of one part, one should arrange the outer enclosure as previously described; the remainder should be fashioned as the "alternative" (vikalpa), wherein the manifestation is mixed.
The *muṇḍaprāsādaharmyāṅga* is desired to have the appearance of a garland; it is excellent, auspicious on all sides (*sarvatobhadra*), and provided with four corner-projections (*aṅkaṇa*). (40.37)
The path is surrounded by one part on all sides, and then on one side there is an inner enclosure;
the width of the hall shall be two parts, and then on one side there is an outer veranda.
Provided with a lattice-work for the nose and joined with arches and other ornaments,
one should arrange it either inside the enclosure or outside.
The courtyard (aṅkaṇa) shall be two parts, while the main hall (mukhyavāra) takes up the area of the porch (alinda);
it may be "with auspiciousness" (sabhadra) or "without auspiciousness" (vibhadra), and the gate (vāraṇa) is determined by the portion of the courtyard.
This sequence of castes has been declared as suitable for the residence of kings;
or else, a broad enclosure provided with paths may surround that very [site]. || 40/41 ||
For the *chanda* is auspicious on all sides; though not explicitly mentioned here, it is as described previously.
One should arrange that very same [pattern] around the edges with a partial portion, or rather, outside the enclosure. (40/42)

The "Sarvatobhadra" (all-auspicious) variety of *vikalpa* is proclaimed here for the lords of the stages (*bhūmīndra*); it consists of a mixture of various types of meters and *vikalpas*, characterized by its radiant manifestation.
The *harmyāṅga*, the *mālikāṅga*, and that known as the *muṇḍaprāsāda*—these are declared to be the types of reflected forms suitable for the dwellings of kings. (40.44)
The placement of the five limbs of the Lord (svāmipañcāṅgavinyāsa) not explicitly mentioned here is as previously stated;
thus, the excellent Sarvatobhadra is declared to be of four kinds.
Thus, the Sarvatobhadra is intended through this variety of modifications.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the four-hall Sarvatobhadra, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Vardhamāna Śāla.
The hall known as Vardhamāna consists of six, eight, and ten parts; and the Nikṛṣṭabhāginī consists of eight, ten, and twelve parts. (41.1)
A length of ten or twelve finger-breadths is proclaimed as middling;
however, that which is in the proportion of two, six, seven, or eight is proclaimed as excellent.

Thus the root has been fully explained; likewise, the *jāti* increases by two parts, and in that which is increased by two parts, the *chandas* and so forth are combined with those not yet joined. (41.3)
In this context, the three beginning with the low (nīca) are also endowed with nine subdivisions;
they are said to extend from the manifestation of caste (jāti) up to the beautiful (kānta), and are accompanied by their roots.
In number, it extends up to forty-five births and so forth;
and here, the highest birth is that which has its beginning and end as long as a kalpa.
Twelve added here make fifty-seven, which is declared for the inferior [type]; however, when increasing, the middle courtyard consists of two parts.
The central section of the hall consists of two parts, while the remaining portion is for the portico; it is joined with a water-channel attached to the middle wall and provided with two doors.
Others may have long halls, two-eyed and endowed with height;
the eastern hall should be slightly low, and the long hall should be two-eyed.
The two wings, however, are like two halls, sloping toward the bamboo-beams and having two faces;
they are joined with outer walls and provided within with pillars.
A central hall is prescribed that is enclosed on all sides by walls, with an opening extending for two parts toward each of the four cardinal directions. (41.10)
At the junction of the rafters, the staircase should have a width of two parts at the *karṇa*;
at the base of the main house, the bathing room should occupy two parts.
But for another [type of site], one should apply four lines in the middle of the four [sections] of the ground plot, where the house of Maitra is closely joined and concealed.
There was circumambulation at that gate, and at its end was the outflow of water;
it was adorned with various features such as arches, pillars, and lattices.
One should adorn it like a palace, either as the Vibhadra or the Sabhadraka; the Nikṛṣṭa and Vardhamāna types are suitable for the dwellings of kings.
One should likewise fashion a door on one side with a portion [of that space],
and place the Bhadrāṅga in whichever direction is desired, as well as the dwelling in whichever direction is desired.
That which is joined with doors as desired is called *chanda*; that same [structure], however, when provided with wide doors and joined with a *daṇḍikā* door, is likewise [designated]. (41.16)
Whether it be "good" (sabhadra) or "bad" (vibhadra), it is proclaimed as conceptual construction (vikalpa);
that which is conjoined with the triad beginning with genus (jāti) is proclaimed as appearance (ābhāsa). || 41.17 ||
In the lower measure, one should not arrange a courtyard (aṅkaṇa) in two parts;
rather, there should be a veranda (alinda) on all sides consisting of one part, and the width of the hall (śālā) shall be two parts.
The principal hall (mukhyageha) should be elevated, while the remaining halls (śālās) are considered to be level;
one should decorate them as previously described. When it is low, it is proclaimed as the "Jāti" type.
One should likewise fashion an *alinda* (veranda) on all sides using one part; it is designated by the name *candana*, while the rest of the universe [of the temple] is as previously described.
That very [vessel], with its rim all around or partially so, is a wide-mouthed jar (pṛthuvāraka);
it has the tip of a bamboo tube at the mouth of the water-jar (karkarī) and is provided with a face-cloth (mukhapaṭṭi). || 41.21 ||
With one leg raised to the master’s seat and the other leg extended, this is designated as the *vikalpa* [posture]; therein, the *ābhāsa* is mixed. (41.22)
The middle *vardhamāna* type has two central courtyards (*aṅkaṇa*),
with a path consisting of one part on all sides, and the width of the hall (*śālā*) is two parts.
It should have its covering half-drawn, be endowed with eight eyes,
joined with a staff-like border, and adorned with all ornaments.
The four central halls are respectively six and thirty-four units long;
their width and length increase sequentially according to the proportions of the face, the courtyard, the eyes, and the limbs.
That which is called *jāti* is the *vardhamāna*; it is the *śabda* [pattern] joined with a broad rim (*pṛthuvāra*).
The *vikalpa* is joined with a broad rim and an outer rim. (41.26)
The appearance joined with the *daṇḍikāvāra* is entirely mixed;
however, in the portion of the supreme width (*vyāsa*), the middle courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*) consists of two parts. (41.27)
On all sides, one part [of the width] forms the upper portion in the shape of a pavilion;
the width of the hall is two parts, surrounded on all sides by the area for the porticoes.
Having abandoned the inner enclosure, [one proceeds] to the outer enclosure as desired;
it is joined with the auspicious [deities] as before, and arranged with water-jars as before.
Endowed with a central hall and furnished with all ornaments,
this [temple] called Jātya, known as Vardhamāna, is suitable for Brahmins and kings.
One should determine that very same [meter] as a specific weekday in one part;
it would be the *chanda* (meter) surrounded by the path, designated as "optional" (*vaikalpa*).
But that which arises from the conjunction of genus and so forth is proclaimed as "semblance" (ābhāsa).
Now, that which is distinguished and called *vardhamāna*, being adorned with poetic figures (*sālaṅkāra*), is described. (41.32)
In width there should be sixteen parts, and in length twelve parts;
the Brahma-courtyard (brahmāṅkaṇa) should be two parts in width and four parts in length.
The hall (śālā) and the main house shall each occupy two parts; one should arrange an outer veranda (alinda) outside that, occupying two parts.
Outside of that, leaving one part for the door and two parts for a wide archway,
the construction in the mixed region should be made behind [the main structure].
On the third [section], one should arrange the water-ground in five parts,
following the central line on both sides in the east.
One should arrange the boundary of the field between the southeast and northeast;
in a three-storied temple, there is water within, while in a four-storied temple, there is a hall for the eyes on the ground level.
Provided with six exits, movable, and situated at the edge, it should be on both sides according to the location of the master’s principal hall. (41.38)
There are four [bays] in the eastern direction and two following the porch;
at the four corners of the porch are the four corner-pinnacles (karṇakūṭa). || 41.39 ||
One should construct it at the edge of the fifth story; in its center, starting from the eastern part, it should be provided with a length equal to four parts and a width of two parts.
It is equipped with ear-pinnacles and a continuous front-frieze;
[this is] from the middle of the ear-pinnacles on both sides of the vestibule.
One should construct two penthouses (pañjara) arising from the junction of two peaks;
the side should be joined with water and land, consisting of two parts including the enclosure (vāra).
O best of the twice-born, between the two *karṇakūṭas*, at a distance of two *paraveda* divisions, one should construct the *pṛṣṭhavāra-sabhā* on six stories.
On the two sides, there should be two *netrakūṭas*; the length of the face should be six *tala*s;
and the courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*) should be shaped like a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) or like an assembly hall (*sabhā*).
Situated to the south of the dwelling, adorned with a pinnacle and a palace,
it is provided with a flight of stairs on the left and endowed with two eyes as its door.
The entrance shall be provided with a walkway and joined by secret stairs;
the water and dry land areas shall be distinguished, and this is known as the seven-storied [temple].
This [layout] is called Vardhamāna; it bestows the fruits of all desires upon kings.
Alternatively, it may consist of eight parts and be joined with the Bhadra at the back.
In the southwest or the northwest, a water-vessel or a shallow basin should be provided;
it may be joined with a central hall or even without one. (41.48)
Or one may construct it provided with an eye-chamber according to the prescribed rule;
thus has the Vardhamāna been described here in the Āgama in sixteen ways.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the Vardhamāna hall, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Nandyāvarta Diagram.
(Verse 42.1) I shall now describe the *nandyāvarta* [mandala], which is divided into six, eight, and ten parts; that which is reduced by eight, ten, and twelve parts is known as the "low" (*nīca*).
The middle [portion] is proclaimed to consist of ten or twelve ancestral lineages (manvaṃśa),
while the portion consisting of a single lineage of the Ādityas is remembered as the eldest.
Thus the root [meter] has been specified; the *jātis* increase by two parts, the *chandases* are enriched by a quarter-part of the Veda, and the *vikalpas* increase by six.
When the appearances, beginning with the inferior, are combined by increasing each by one-eighth, they become forty-five in number here. (42.4)
The three long vowels, when extracted and joined with their third [short vowel],
are stated here to total fifty-seven in number when combined.
When the lowest [measurement] is divided sixfold, the courtyard shall consist of two parts;
the middle [measurement] shall likewise have a courtyard of two parts, and the entire hall shall be provided with all ornaments.
The Nandyāvarta design consists of four borders, here devoid of the base;
it may have four doors or even be situated in whichever direction is desired.
One should arrange lattices and door-panels on the outermost exterior; this primary sanctuary is described here as being enclosed by walls on all sides. (42.8)
With the feet spread apart internally, it is proclaimed that there is an outer wall;
one should employ half-peaked structures extending outwards in the four directions. (42.9)

This is considered the *jātirūpa* (archetypal form) associated with the *daṇḍikāvāra* [meter]; that same form, when provided with a covered veranda (*āvṛtālinda*) for four [verses], is desired as a *chandas* (metrical form). || 42/10 ||
That very [structure] may have one opening or be provided with wide openings;
it may consist of many stories according to one's choice, and therein the appearance is intermingled.
The Harmyāṅga and Mālikāṅga [sections] should each consist of multiple stories;
the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should be low, occupying two parts, while the enclosure (vāra) is desired to occupy one part.
The Śālāvyāsa [plan] consists of two parts and is joined with a *daṇḍikāvāra*;
it is endowed with all ornaments and may be constructed as a *bhadraka* according to one's desire. (42.13)
In whichever direction desired, the principal house is constructed with walls both inside and out, adorned with joined latticed windows.
The remaining portion is the wall all around, and that portion is also the base; O Brahmins, this is the "Jātirūpa" style, conceived specifically for kings.
The western gate is omitted here; the *chanda* is prescribed in this manner.
One should arrange the courtyard in two parts in the middle, and the path in one part. || 42.16 ||
The hall (śālā) is two parts wide, and the door is one part on the exterior;
the middle of the four halls is at the top of the center.
The kūṭa should be pure and pure, provided with wing-halls (pakṣaśālā) at the corners;
when joined with four eyes (netra), it is proclaimed as the chanda measurement.
That very [structure] may have a single row of cells or be provided with wide corridors;
it may include a portico, a turret, and a palace, according to one's capacity and as desired. (42.19)
The *savāramukhabhadra* should be constructed with its base adorned by feet,
and its successive tiers of cornices (*aṅkaṇa*) should be placed above the *pakṣaśālā*.

Whether it be an assembly hall, a pavilion, a flower garden, or the construction of a courtyard—these four types of structures are declared to be dwellings, especially those suitable for a king. (42.21)
When those three are combined in a particular way, and joined with a *muṇḍa* and a *prāsāda*, it becomes the *harmyāṅga* type known as *mālika*. || 42.22 ||
The [mandala] called Nandyāvarta is proclaimed for four [deities] in the middle section;
the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should consist of two parts, and one should make the path with one part.
The inner enclosure, however, is one part, while the width of the hall is two parts;
it is joined with the enclosure of the pillars and provided with four faces.
There should be eight halls above, and below,
the four-faced one endowed with twelve faces, from the second [level] upwards and downwards.
Endowed with auspiciousness in the four directions and adorned with latticed windows, this house of the mountain kings is of noble form, like a *nandyāvarta* design. (42.26)
That very [mandala] is desired to have its perimeter enclosed by two lines,
or it may have one line on the outside, or else it may be provided with a broad outer line. (42.27)
Those four halls have their faces turned toward the *nandyāvarta* diagram and possess their own central beams;
above them are situated halls endowed with four peaks.
The Nandyāvarta, however, is an alternative layout for the residence of kings and others; one should construct it as determined for each case, known by the name Muṇḍaprāsāda.
The Mālikāṅga, the Harmyāṅga, and those consisting of one or many stories are proclaimed as the four types of Ābhāsa and Nandikāvarta.
In the middle [type], the courtyard is two parts of the superior [measurement] and has a single path;
the inner enclosure is one part, and the width of the hall is two parts.
The door should be covered with a portion [of cloth] and adorned with all ornaments;
furthermore, the central hall pillars and others should be recessed.
A birth [configuration] endowed with twelve faces is suitable for a king;
however, a birth [configuration] surrounded by two parts and joined with a great week-day is likewise auspicious. (42.33)
This meter is proclaimed to be joined with two *vāra* [syllables];
it consists of a *sālinda*, a *khaṇḍaharmya*, or a *kūṭakoṣṭhaka-bhāraka*.
The four-winged [temple], the Śiras, and that which is joined with the Sabhāmukha-śiras, as well as the Nadyāvarta and the Vikalpa, should be adorned like a palace.
But for each of these, it may be a combination of various elements, provided with the components of a palace (prāsāda),
or the components of a mansion (harmya), or the components of a temple (mālikā), consisting of one or many stories.
Endowed with both primary and secondary arrangements, according to logical principle and according to preference,
the manifestation known as Nandikāvarta is proclaimed for all four [castes].
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the Nandyāvarta has been described in sixteen ways.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the Nandyāvarta-vidhi, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
[Now follows] the Svastika-vidhi.
In that case, the inferior svastika is divided into six, eight, and ten parts;
however, the low svastika consists of eight, ten, and twelve parts.
The middle *svastika* is considered to have ten or twelve *manvaṃśas*; the superior portion is held to consist of one *manvaṃśa* between two *ādityas*.
The base should be square, and its length should be greater by two parts;
the *jāti-rūpa* type of *chanda* should have its length greater by four parts. (43.3)
That which has a length increased by one-sixth is proclaimed as the *vikalpa*;
the *ābhāsa* consists of eight circles and forty-five [units]. (43/4)
Their number is proclaimed in groups of three starting from the lowest;
those that are three times long are the low ones, numbering fifty-seven.
In the six-fold division starting from the inferior [type], the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) is desired to be two parts;
the width of the hall (śālā), endowed with all ornaments, is two parts. || 43.6 ||
On the back, there should be a long cell, and the front cell should likewise be so;
the two outer halls should be joined with the "eye" (netra) and provided with a water-jar (karkarī).

Thus has the nature of the *jāti* for the *bhūmīndra* and *vaiśya* meters been declared; that very same [structure], with its *aṃśa*, *āvṛta*, and *ālinda*, is proclaimed as a *chanda* in the treatise. (43.8)
On the back, it should be devoid of eyes and joined with a back-shrine (pṛṣṭhaśālā), and provided with a daṇḍikāvāra; this is proclaimed as the Bhadrāṅga [temple]. (43.9)
That same [mandala] may have its enclosure covered or joined with a broad enclosure;
it should be known as the Svastika-vikalpa, wherein the Ābhāsa is mixed.

Its parts are adorned with domed pavilions, its upper stories are graced with turrets, and its balconies are decorated with flower garlands; joined with many floors, it is as magnificent as a palace. (43.11)
The *ābhāsa* and *svastika* designs are prescribed for kings as well as merchants.
In the inferior type, the courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*) occupies two parts; in the middling type, the path is one part on all sides.
The hall-width is divided into two parts, with the central beam (*vaṃśaka*) equal to six eyes (*netra*).
In its center are four halls, joined together and extending upwards. (43.13)
The number of eyes is proclaimed to be human (five) everywhere; the assembly hall, joined with a stūpikā and other features, is provided with a beautiful face. 43.14.
One should construct the courtyard in the form of a pavilion, rising higher and higher above;
it should be joined with a series of pillars, featuring a svastika and figures of various species.
That same [structure], with its verandah covered by one part, is desired as the Svastika plan;
or it may have its entrance covered by one part, or it may be provided with a broad entrance.
Alternatively, it may be provided with a pinnacle and a turret; such a variety is considered the Svastika.
However, through the combination of the Jāti and other types, it is proclaimed as the Ābhāsa.
The portion for the *muṇḍaprāsāda* mansions should be described as appearing like a garland;
in the middle courtyard, the path should be one part, as previously stated. (43.18)
Then, one part is for the inner courtyard, and the width of the hall is two parts;
it is joined with a pillar-array and possesses six eyes and an equal beam-structure.
On top of the bamboo frame are four halls provided with eight faces; above these is the structure of the pavilion-shaped palace, and then the courtyard.
The Svastika plan consists of a central hall with auspicious projections on all four sides; that same plan, when provided with doors toward each of its divisions, is designated as the Chanda.
That which consists of two parts and has broad openings is proclaimed as "vikalpa" (conceptual construction);
therein, the manifestation is mixed, adorned with the "muṇḍa-prāsāda" (the severed-head palace).
The Harmyāṅga, the Mālikāṅga, and the Madhyama are thus proclaimed.
In the superior type, however, the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) occupies two parts, while the path on all sides consists of one part.
Then, with one part, there is the inner enclosure; the width of the hall is two parts;
with one part on all sides is the veranda; and the head-piece consists of a covered enclosure.
It is joined with the sun’s eye (arka-netra) and endowed with auspicious features in the four directions;
it is provided with lattices, pillars, walls, courtyards, windows, and archways.
The stone staircase, provided with small steps and other such features,
has its structural members such as the *tula* increased by one unit [of measurement], while the *viṣṭara* is joined to the wall.
This is considered to be the form of the *jāti* style, which should be adorned like a palace;
that very same [form] should be surrounded by a path, with the entrance facing the *vārabhadra-sabhā*.

In a hall with side-wings shaped like an assembly hall, provided with a chamber at the front and at the back, it is called *ekacchanda*; it may have wide openings according to various options. (43.28)
Alternatively, it may be provided with large enclosures, or even a temple with a shaven dome;
there, the appearance may be mixed, adorned with a temple having a shaven dome.
This is declared to be the *harmyāṅga*, the *mālikāṅga*, or the *svastika* type;
it is stated here in the scripture that these are prescribed only for kings and vaiśyas.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the Ritual of the Svastika, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Four-Walled House (Catuḥśālāvidhi)
The one called Sarvatobhadraka, when not joined with the previously mentioned [layout], is known as the Nikṛṣṭa-rucaka; it is suitable for deities and heretics. (44.1)
And those [mandalas] called Sarvatobhadra, which were previously described here,
are to be placed either inside the enclosure and the path, or outside of them.
The outer and the inner [circumference] should be joined according to the desire of the sacrificer in due order;
likewise, the broad rim should be joined by the wise. (44.3)

However, that hall which is deficient in length should be employed for rites for the gods, heretics, and twice-born brahmins, such as acts of giving; it should consist of five parts up to nine parts [of its width]. (44.4)
Having divided [the site] into two parts, one should construct the house with one part;
the width of the hall (śālā) is made with the remainder, which is intended for the courtyard (vāra-aṅkaṇa).
This is declared to be the four-pillared [temple], which is intended for universal use; its measurement may be taken from the middle of the wall, or even from the middle of the pillar. (44.6)

The measurement of dwellings such as villages is intended to be free from devotion [to specific proportions], whereas the measurement for temples, rows of buildings, vehicles, and so forth [is fixed]. (44.7)
The middle portion of the *pāda* (quarter-section) should have a measurement equal to the external width and length;
this four-winged (*catuḥśāla*) structure, devoid of a central hall (*piṇḍa*), is suitable for all social classes (*varṇas*).
A courtyard with a central opening, a common courtyard, and a courtyard at the corner—
such a house is traditionally remembered as undesirable for all social classes.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Four-Hall Temple," in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Five-Hall Temple and Others.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the five-hall temple and others;
I will explain the five-hall temple properly and in due order. (45.1)
Having divided the house into twelve parts on all sides with four halls,
one should likewise provide two courtyards in the middle using two parts.
Likewise, at the front of the *prastara* (pedestal), which possesses the peaks of the neck-divisions,
the middle part has a width of two parts and is joined with a length of six parts.
The Sarvatobhadra, Śālā, and other types are provided with windows on all sides;
the five-hall structure (pañcaśālā) of the gods is likewise joined with a main hall and other chambers.
In the middle six-hall structure, one should arrange a courtyard occupying two parts;
on its two sides, there should be two halls, each two parts wide.
One should design a six-winged structure joined by the extension of the birth-line and so forth;
however, one should divide a seven-winged square structure into nine parts.
With one [bay] there should be a central hall and courtyards on both sides; likewise, with two [bays], there should be halls on both sides and courtyards on the flanks. (45.7)
On one side all around, there should be four halls;
thus, for gods, brahmins, and kings, there should be a seven-halled structure.
The seven-shala structure should likewise be joined with the extension of the birth-measure;
there shall be five parts in width and eleven in length.
One should determine the courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*) and the extent of the house as previously described; however, the courtyard shall be joined with an increased length by one part. (45.10)
In width there should be seven parts, and in length twelve parts;
with two parts on all sides, one should construct the central hall.
The courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should be one-third [of the area] both in width and in length;
however, in width it should consist of eight parts, and in length it should consist of fourteen.
On all sides and in the center, the width of the hall shall be two parts; two courtyards should be made with five and seven steps [respectively]. (45.13)
One may design it with six eyes, eight eyes, or ten faces;
this has been described as the seven-hall temple (saptaśāla), and now the eight-hall temple (aṣṭaśāla) is being discussed.
The Rudra portions (eleven) should be for the width and likewise for the length;
one should arrange a four-winged hall by means of a single portion on all sides.
One should make a courtyard consisting of a single portion, with four halls in the middle,
provided with either eight eyes or sixteen faces.
One should design an eight-hall structure (aṣṭaśālā) with a distinguished half-portion of the stone-slab;
O best of the twice-born, this eight-hall structure is intended for the gods and the Brahmins.
In width there should be eleven parts, and in length thirteen;
one should arrange a four-winged hall (catuḥśālā) with a single part on all sides.
In the middle [section], there should be five halls constructed with one part;
the quadrangle of courtyards, however, is formed by two middle parts.
One should designate the remaining portion made from one part as having two marks;
in the broad [area], there are seventeen, with an excess of two in length.

The four-winged (catuḥśālā) houses are proclaimed to have one part [of the total area] in each direction; likewise, the four-winged houses are proclaimed to have five parts in the middle of the wings. || 45.21 ||
Of these [lines], two parts are declared to be the six-fold division;
furthermore, there shall be nineteen parts in both the width and the length.
There should be twenty-one parts on all sides with a width of two parts;
in the center, there should be five halls constructed with two parts each.
With one part in the middle and six courtyards (aṅkaṇas), this is declared to be the nine-hall (navaśāla) layout; now the ten-hall (daśaśāla) layout is described here.
One should determine the width up to five parts including the defects;
the length should be made double that, or else the length is stated [as follows].
The portions of the eight directions and the intermediate quarters are the constituent parts in sequence;
alternatively, the arrangement of the dimensions for the five [elements] and so forth follows their respective order.
From one part of the solar heart, there are eighteen parts and twenty;
one should arrange the courtyard of the houses there according to the proper rule.
This is declared to be the ten-hall (daśaśāla) temple, suitable for all [deities];
the monastery hall (vihāraśālā) should also be constructed as a single large hall.
One should increase the width of the hall by twenty-one units;
the measurement, joined with twice the first [unit] and so forth, consists of twenty counts.
It should be provided with gabled chambers and so forth, joined in front by an auspicious hall;
it may have a porch in front or at the back, or it may not.
It should be provided with two eyes (niches) and adorned with a prominent nose (central projection);
it may consist of one, two, or three stories, and may or may not be equipped with a pinnacle-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha).
And it is said that the monastery hall (vihāraśālā) is to be provided with all ornaments;
this is declared to be suitable for the Buddhist, Arhat, and other heretical sects.
For all the lords of the earth, it is considered to have eleven stories;
for the twice-born, it should have nine floors, and for kings, it is considered to have seven floors.
The mandalika's [palace] has six floors; that of the crown prince has five; for the vaiśyas it is four stories, as is also that of the commander of the army and the general. (45.34)
For Śūdras, however, it is prescribed up to one story;
for those headed by the Sāmanta lords, five stories are prescribed.
The palace of the Lord of all the worlds may consist of pairs or an even number [of sections];
likewise, for kings, their queens, and goddesses, it may consist of pairs or an even number.
It should be made of clay, covered with grass, and provided with one, two, or three stories; it should have a handle, a roof-ridge, two eyes, and be equipped with a lintel. (45.37)
Seated upon the stūpa, he is praised among all castes.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, concerning the rules for the five-hall structure and so forth, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Elephant Stable.
Now I shall describe in detail the sequence of rules for the elephant stable:
beginning with three cubits, one should increase it by half a cubit [at each stage]. (46.1)
Up to five times the measure of the wall, the elephant stable should be constructed in five types according to the measurement of the wall by the wise man. (46.2)
In width there are six divisions, and in length nine divisions;
or it may be four divisions in breadth, or even with seven walls.

The walls of the hall may be three or five in number, both in width and in length; the front hall (mukhaśāla) shall have a single wall, or it may be one and a half times, or even double [the thickness of the main walls].
Whether in width or length, they should be suitable for coming and going;
on the right side, the place for the bed is arranged according to one's desired devotion.
Rājādana, madhūka, kadara, and again khadira;
tintriṇī and arjuna are declared [to be the trees], as well as stabaka, pihita, and śamī.
The *kṣīriṇī*, *padmaka*, and others are the pillars for the elephant's hall;
they are nine, eight, or seven cubits high, excluding the measurement of the crow's perch.
In width it should be six finger-breadths, increasing by one finger-breadth [at each stage] until it measures twelve finger-breadths; its depth should be according to one's strength.
These are declared to be the pillars of the hall, provided with branches, limbs, and tops;
the post for tying the elephant (ālāna) should be twelve finger-breadths in measurement.
Increasing by one finger-breadth up to twenty-five fingers,
the top of the umbrella-shape should be very broad, consisting of eight parts and joined with a thick [rim].
When the width of the hall has been divided into five parts, having taken one-third from the back and having removed the sixteenth part of the radius on the left and the eighth part; 46.11.
One should establish the peak-pinnacle and the elephant-stable, endowed with the previously mentioned heights; there, one should construct a wall on all sides, protected from the wind.
Half of that, or less by one-quarter, or even less by one-eighth;
above that, one should construct a covering on all sides with structures such as domes (kūṭa).
The breast-like projection (gostana) should be two spans wide and joined to the exterior face;
the surface covering of the planks must be made of very firm wood.
One should not construct a floor using stones or bricks;
rather, one should fashion a thick door provided with a urinary opening.
Starting from the position of the elephant (the second), wise architects should construct the elephant stable by avoiding the eighth and twelfth positions.

In this manner, an elephant stable should be constructed; likewise, a horse stable is prescribed for the city, the royal palace, and so forth, as well as for temples and other such buildings. || 46.17 ||
One should also construct a stable for horses with the same devotion as previously described;
starting from a width of two cubits, one may increase it further.
The measurement of the wall may extend up to nine cubits; this has been declared as the width, and the length shall now be described.
Then, the length is determined as being one-quarter greater than the width, or one-and-a-half times, or three-quarters of two times, or even double the width. (46.20)
One should arrange the position for the horses in a single row, with one wall, two walls, or three walls, or it may be made wide according to the desire of the patron.
Or it may be enclosed on all sides by walls, or walled off in whichever direction is desired;
as for what is not mentioned here, one should follow the general measurements prescribed for a hall.
Beginning with five finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth each time,
the measurement of the pillar here is said to extend up to twelve finger-breadths.
It should be two cubits wide up to the knees, provided with a plank-like surface,
equipped with an opening for the passage of urine, made of solid wood, and firm.
A peg made of hard wood, two times seven (fourteen) finger-breadths in length,
with a width of three finger-breadths, and provided with a needle-like point, is prescribed.
In both the rear-connection (paścādbandha) and the front-connection (agrabandha), one should apply it with a firm blow,
avoiding the eighth and twelfth signs in accordance with the favorable positions.
One should properly prepare the stall even for the lord of horses; one should prepare the stalls for camels and other animals according to this same measurement. (46.27)
The horse-stable is fully described; now the cow-stable is prescribed.
One should construct the cow-stable according to the same proportions and arrangement as those stated for the horse-stable. (46.28)
One should construct it as having one wing, two wings, or three wings;
or even as equal to four wings, or endowed with length.
One should designate a courtyard for Brahmā, either provided with a bull or without one;
one should arrange a place for those [deities] in accordance with the non-conflict of the zodiac sign of Taurus.
One should provide protection for the cows by means of grain and heaps of grass;
one should nourish them with straw, cooked rice, and the like, or even with discarded flower offerings (nirmālya).
The consumption of their *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is not considered a fault;
it is declared to be a place for elephants and other [beings], endowed with prosperity such as long life and so forth.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, concerning the rules for the elephant stable and other structures, in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of a Rosary (Mālikā)

Now, O twice-born ones, I shall describe in detail the characteristics of the *mālikā* (pavilion), which is fourfold: the *śālā*, the *sabhā*, and those arising from the *muṇḍaja* and *saudha* types. (47.1)
In this scripture called the Kāmika, that hall which is adorned by the faces of the hall-ornaments (śālāṅga) emerging [from it] is to be known as the Mālikā hall. 47.2.
That assembly hall which is naturally constructed, adorned externally like a palace, and provided with both opportunities and obstacles, is called Mālikā.

Joined in whatever direction desired and endowed with grounds for enjoyment, a row of palaces (prāsādamālikā) is described as being wide, long, and high according to the dimensions of the palace. 47/4.
Adorned with the aforementioned width, length, height, and ornaments of the pavilion, it is called the Muṇḍamālikā because its form is entirely that of a skull. 47/5.
Each one is said to be threefold: accumulated (sañcita), unaccumulated (asañcita), and semi-accumulated (upasañcita); likewise, there are the Nāgara and the Drāmiḍa styles.
Vesara, as well as Jāticchanda and Vaikalpa;
pure, mixed, and blended; likewise the seed-root and the sprout. (47.7)

That which is provided with a porch (alinda), or even that which is accompanied by the six divisions (ṣaḍvarga), is declared to be "arpita" (dedicated) and "saṃcita" (accumulated); when it has been made into property, it is called masculine (puṃliṅga).
Among the gods and asuras, the siddhas and vidyādharas, the rākṣasas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and among all other praiseworthy living beings; (47.9)
Everywhere it was adorned with verandas that were parts of the grounds for enjoyment; it was endowed with all categories of excellence and filled with mental delight. || 47/10 ||
The feminine gender is desired for the four *anuloma* [compounds]; it is mixed when joined with the five groups and possesses both assigned (*arpita*) and unassigned (*anarpita*) members. (47.11)
This [temple] is prescribed for heretics; it is provided with a neuter [linga], covered by its own expansion according to the directions, and endowed with a length equal to the span of the hands.
The Nāgara style, having been made uniform through the division into even and uneven [bays],
is endowed with internal *prastara* (horizontal layers) and joined with *ūha* and *pratyūha* (architectural projections).
Now, therefore, the Drāviḍa style shall be described, characterized by very firm and auspicious groups of pillars, beams, and supports; likewise, its width and length [will be explained]. (47.14)
Having excluded the rejection of those covered in blood and so forth, according to the distinction between even and uneven [numbers],
one should leave aside that which has become level there, provided it is adorned with auspicious ornaments.
The Drāmiḍa style is said to consist of six groups joined together many times; it should possess the required length and breadth, being neither excessive nor deficient. (47.16)
Or it may be joined with many sections, adorned with rows of pillars,
possessing a great hall above the pavilion, and equipped with turrets and porticos.
That which is endowed with its own [auspicious] field and possesses a middle foot is considered a *veśara*;
it belongs to ascetics, courtesans, those who live by their wits, and those of cruel deeds. (47.18)
Among those, the *vesara* style is praised; for others, the remaining auspicious types [are used].
In the middle of the ears, within the *kūṭakoṣṭha*, it is joined with a *pañjara*.

That which is joined with the sixfold group, whose lineage is indeed unimpeachable, and which is recited into the ear in the midst of the assembly hall—that alone shall be considered the true Veda. (47.20)
In whichever chamber the middle portion has been discarded, that [chamber] is subject to doubt;
it may be constructed with wood, or with bricks, or even with stone and other materials.
A house endowed with this [first type] is called pure;
one possessed of two substances is mixed; and one joined with many is called contaminated. (47.22)
The [measurement] of the gods alone is considered mixed; for others, it is desired to be different.
In its width, it should be four parts, while in its length, it should be six parts.
On all sides, one part shall be for the width of the hall, and from two parts its length;
thus the halls, in particular, shall be square.
It is endowed with an exit leading out from the middle hall;
the exit, however, has a width of two parts according to the measurement of two shares. (47.25)

One should lead the pavilion (maṇḍapa) forward from the front of that [sanctum] joined with the inner chamber (koṣṭha) and the hall (anana); the division of the pavilion, however, is according to its width and its projection. || 47.26 ||
Vyāsa [should provide] the outer enclosure on both sides as well as at the back of the pavilion, and also on its two flanks and in the front area. (47.27)
One part projected outward, joined with a width of two parts,
connected with a continuous row [of pillars], and facing the hall on six sides.
That which is joined with a hall-pinnacle (śālāśikhara) is desired by the name Sindhuka;
this very same [pinnacle], when preceded by a mantra, takes the form of a hall-pinnacle (sabhākāraśikhara).
It was joined with palaces that had abandoned their peaks, necks, and turrets;
it was renowned as "Saṃpūrṇa" (Complete), while everything else remained as before.
It should be provided with the previously mentioned Sindhu, the Vara tree, and the Sthala;
it should be richly adorned on its back like its face, and endowed with all ornaments.
This [type of structure] is named Merukūṭa, and another may exist as previously described; this very form with a peak shaped like a hall is called Kṣema.
And indeed, the previously mentioned *kṣema* [type], devoid of the *pūrvabhadra*, is joined with supreme devotion on the back and the two sides of the hall. (47.33)
One should exclude six parts from the front of both auspicious sides; likewise, one should exclude them from the back of the hall and from both of the two eyes.
The Śālānana (hall-face) should be constructed, fashioned from one or two parts;
it should be made at the front of each [section], to the west of the Bhadra.
On both sides of the square Bhadra [shrine],
one should construct a water-platform (vāḥsthala) at the front, measuring two or three parts in length and width.
On both sides, starting from the ground level, one should construct two corner-pinnacles (karṇakūṭa) made of four parts on the sides of the gateway pavilion (dvāramaṇḍapa).
One should create a single-unit enclosure at the front and on both sides;
in the middle of the four [sides], one should fashion a hall-like structure within the square.
This is declared to be auspicious; everything else is as before.
And this very [mantra], when its syllables are arranged in the form of a water-pot (karkarī) within the ear— || 47.39 ||
In the center is the hall named Sudṛṣṭa; everything else is as before.
This very structure, with a peak in the shape of an assembly hall, is desired as a *harmya* (palatial mansion).
But this Saumya type is said to be preceded by a prastara;
its entire body has the form of a hall (sabhākāra) and is devoid of karṇa and kūṭa.
The hall with its pillars arranged in a square is called "Viśāla.
In the Viśāla, there should be six parts in the width and ten parts in the length. (47.42)
The central hall is prescribed with a length and width of six parts;
outside of that is one part for the enclosure, and outside of that is the bull-pen (vṛṣasthala).
Outside of that, in the four directions, the exit for the water-pipes should occupy two parts;
furthermore, four assembly halls should be constructed, along with the four corner-peaks (koṇakūṭa).

That which is shaped like a ploughshare and extends outward from the *vārsthalā* portion is considered the *sabha* (the hall) for both eyes; it is situated within the *vārsthalā* portion of the two eyes.
Situated outside the hall itself, it consists of two parts joined with the cloth;
at each entrance, there is a *bhadra* (projection) with a width and length of four and six parts respectively.
In the middle of that, one should construct an assembly hall on all sides with four parts;
and on both sides, a space for the entrance with one part.
In the four corners, there should be four kūṭas projecting by one part;
and in the middle of the hall, it should be made with two parts and one part [respectively].
If one should construct a *vārṣṭhala* in the middle, it shall be known by the name Vijaya;
and if this very same [arrangement] is at the rear, provided it is joined with the *bhadra*, it becomes so. (47/49)
It is said that "all is auspicious," while everything else remains as before;
the previously mentioned *vijaya* [mudrā] is for the two *bhadra* positions, both at the front and the back. (47.50)
That which is devoid of the form of a hall (*sabhā*), joined with the form of a pavilion (*maṇṭapa*),
and provided with a head-piece in the shape of a hall is declared to be the principal chamber (*pradhānāgāra*).
The one known by the name Bhadra is another [type], which should be as previously described;
this Bhadra face is endowed with the form of an assembly hall and a head.
This is declared to be the entrance of the stage; everything else is as before.
The previously mentioned *vijaya* [type] is for the two *bhadra* [types] at the front peaks. (47.53)
If there is a *bhadra* in the middle of this very hall, it is called by the name *Alpa*; otherwise, one should proceed as previously described.
In length there should be ten parts, and in width six parts;
in the middle of the cloth, at two-sixths [of the width], one should cause a border to be made on the outside.
Outside of that, one should arrange the courtyard (vārsthala) using exactly one part;
and within the courtyard, which has four corners, one should construct a pinnacle (kūṭa) with one part.

In that very same central portion, however, one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with one or two parts; it should be provided with a front hall (śālāmukha) extending out by a quarter-part from the base.
Outside the courtyard area, the front of the assembly hall should occupy two parts and one part [of the total width];
at the rear, it should likewise be desired to be the same; this is known by the name Koṇa.
This very [structure] is known as the *sabhākāra-śironāha*;
that which extends from the front to the back is known as the *śālāmukhāgata*. || 47/59 ||
If the back of the two eyes is the face, it is declared by the name Geya;
if the ear is the mouth of the hall (śālāmukha), it is celebrated by the name Sāra.
And at both its front and its back, joined with two and four parts respectively,
the hall-like face of the Pārāvṛta is called Puṣkara.
If it possesses both [the aforementioned features] and has ten faces, it is celebrated as "Adbhuta" (The Marvelous);
in its center, it is provided with a hall-like face and endowed with arms, a chest, and a face.
Otherwise, this is recited as being mixed with designations;
and if there is a *śikhara* or a *maṇṭapa*, the two auspicious [elements] are omitted.
Another [measure] is called Puṣkara according to the method previously described;
and this very same [measure] is everywhere termed the "equal staff" (sabhāgadaṇḍa). || 47.64 ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of rosaries, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Garland of Ploughs (Lāṅgalamālikāvidhi)
(Verse 120) I shall now describe specifically the [plan] called Mālikā and Lāṅgalā:
one should make it eight parts in width and twelve parts in length.
On all sides, one part shall be the width of the hall according to two divisions;
the remainder should be made into a terrace for the mansion, provided in the center with an elephant-pavilion.
This [mandala] is said here to be provided with a width equal to four and two parts;
at the corner, it should be joined with a projection shaped like a plowshare.
That which is joined with two eyes is called *gomeca*; if it possesses four eyes, it is designated as *viśva*. (48.4)
Between two *harmya* pavilions, provided with two corner pinnacles (*karṇakūṭa*), it is renowned as the *ādeya*; the *lāṅgala* type shall likewise be of three kinds. (48.5)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the ritual for the Lāṅgalamālikā, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual of the Garland of Root Mantras.
Now I shall describe in detail the [temple type] called Mālikāmaulikā:
it should have ten parts in width and twelve parts in length.
The door on all sides shall occupy one part, while the width of the hall shall be two parts; the remainder, joined with the *vedī* and the *netra*, shall be the area for water and dry land.
The middle pavilion (maṇṭapa) should be divided by two gables (karṇakūṭa);
both the gable and the pavilion should be provided with a projection (niṣkrama). || 49/3 ||
That which is called Yugmanābha is situated in the center of the middle pavilion;
when it is joined with a square, it is designated as Dhana. (49/4)
If that same *kūṭaka* is provided with a hall (*śālā*) at the front, it is called *sukha*;
if it is provided with a hall at the exterior, it is called *raudra*. || 49/5 ||
That which is endowed with six eyes is called "six-eyed" (ṣaṇnetra).
Thus, that Triśālāmaulika is said to be of five kinds.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the Ritual of the Mūlikāmālikā, in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Lotus Garland (Padmamālikāvidhi)
(Verse 50.1) Now I shall describe in detail the garland known as Padmaka,
which is provided with a width of eight parts and a length of ten parts.
One should arrange the enclosure on all sides with a portion;
it should be provided with an inner hall divided into sections and a central courtyard.

With a width of two parts and a length equal to one part of a Veda (four parts), it may take the form of a hall (śālā), an assembly hall (sabhā), or a pavilion (maṇṭapa); such is the courtyard (aṅkaṇa). || 50/3 ||
It should extend out by one part from a width of two parts,
joined with *bhadra*s on both sides, according to the form described for the courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*).
One should perform three circumambulations closely following the principal path;
there are eight eyes, half-peaks, and those joined with the ears.
One should construct the principal sanctum (mukhyadhāma) with a pinnacle resembling a sala tree;
above that should be the pavilion (maṇṭapa), and the side-hall (pakṣaśālā) should be on the ground level.
On the exterior, in the four corners, there should be a hall with an extension of two parts;
in the center there should be either a chamber or a hall, or an elephant-entrance is desired in the middle. (50.7)
Within the peaked hall (kūṭaśālā), one should construct a nose-like projection resembling the back of an elephant;
this should be made with two parts at the front of the hall and one part on its sides.
There should be halls or assembly halls situated at intervals;
one should decorate it with rows of pillars, for this is considered the design that increases prosperity.
This is called the Saubhadra;
it has a truncated summit, while its pinnacle is shaped like an assembly hall and its front face is like a hall.
All else previously mentioned shall apply; it should be named Śrībhadra.
In its width there should be ten parts, and in its length twelve parts.
The Brahmāṅkaṇa should consist of two parts in width and be twice as long;
the inner enclosure (antarvāra) and the outer enclosure (bahirvāra) shall each occupy one part of the hall (śālā).
The hall (śālā) is divided by two parts on both sides;
those four half-halls (ardhasabhās) are attached specifically according to their respective widths.
In the eastern and western portions, with a projection of two parts [of the width] extending outward,
it should be situated in the hall-front (śālāsya), the assembly-hall (sabhāsya), the auspicious (bhadra) type, or within another stable interval.
On both sides, with a width of two parts and a length of four parts,
the central space should be designated for the elephant (vāraṇaka), provided with a door on the exterior of the residence.
The entrance hall should be spacious, and from the entrance area, a pavilion (maṇṭapa) should be constructed;
the remainder should be made into a courtyard (harmyasthala), and the quadrangle (aṅkaṇa) especially so.
This would be auspicious and beautiful; the one most skilled in ritual design should so arrange it that this very structure, having the form of a hall, serves as the principal residence for the head.
This is declared to be the Merukānta, adorned with all ornaments;
it should be twelve parts in width and nine parts in length.
The courtyard, twice as wide as one part of the Veda (four parts), should be on the outside; it consists of one hall divided into two parts.
In this case, the courtyard (aṅkaṇa), the pavilion (maṇṭapa), and the main entrance shall be as previously described;
the front hall (agraśālā) shall likewise be so, while everything else shall be according to the standard (vārsthalam).
The principal dwelling is raised to a height equal to half its own length; that pavilion is further adorned with necklaces and other ornaments. (50.21)
Outside the hall, there should be a portion for the gate; within that, at the front of the assembly hall, there should be eight [pillars] provided with water-jars (karkarī) and joined to the hall.
These are considered to be attached to the hall. 50.22.
In the main hall, at the front, and on both inner sides,
the assembly hall is considered to be according to the extent of the many chambers, facing the front of the hall.
Outside of that, one should arrange a surrounding enclosure with a single part;
and outside of that, in the four directions, by an extension of five parts.
One should construct four *bhadra* projections there, each with a width of ten parts;
and likewise in the four directions on that very same [structure], with a width of four parts.
The central elephant is desired to have two parts [in width] and to extend toward the intermediate directions;
on both its sides, the intermediate spaces are twice as wide as one part.
Eight [pillars] should emerge from a single part; these are the faces of the assembly hall.
Outside the central elephant, however, they should have a width of two parts on both sides.
Two halls should be constructed, one on the south and one on the north, each joined with four bays and provided with single intermediate spaces.
On its two sides, there are two parts and three parts [respectively] for the width;
they are joined with inverted iron [projections] and have an interval of one part between them.
Four halls should be constructed on both sides,
either in front or behind, preceded by a central elephant-hall.
The pinnacle (kūṭa) should consist of four parts with an interval of one part;
or else, the hall (śālā) is described as before, consisting of four parts.
On both its sides there should be two corner-projections (karṇakūṭa),
with a space of two parts between the southern and northern projections.
Thus it is for the Kūṭa and Ardhasabha types; likewise, it is exactly the same for the western [direction].
Everything else is stated to be the same, and this is called Sumaṅgala by name.
For kings, it is proclaimed that [the palace] may extend up to five, six, or seven stories;
that very [structure] is called the primary courtyard, known as the residential hall.
The two *karṇakūṭas* (corner-pinnacles) are located at the front hall-section, starting from the fourth part;
this is prescribed for the day [of the month], while everything else remains as before.
If the assembly hall, the courtyard, or the main chamber is intended to increase beauty, its width and length should be one-twelfth of the total, increased by one-fourteenth. (50.36)
The courtyard (aṅkaṇa) shall be one-fourth [of the total] in both width and length;
the width of the hall (śālā) is proclaimed everywhere to be two parts.
Surrounding the primary sanctum, there should be a hall on one side;
at the front and back of the primary sanctum, there should be two nostrils (side-aisles).
The principal hall named Śālā should be provided with a single wall;
in the corner of the front hall-section, a gable (kūṭa) should be constructed measuring two parts.
The remaining portion of the palace floor inside should be provided with walls;
the exterior should be enclosed by a rampart and joined with flags and walls.
In the outer enclosure, with an extension of two parts and one part in width,
there should be a hall at the entrance of the assembly hall to the east, and a front gable-house for the primary rites to the east.
Outside of that, one should cause a courtyard for the rainy season to be made with two parts;
it should be designed on all sides as being provided with a *khaṇḍaharmya* (a pavilion or upper story).
The projection of the corner-ridge (karṇakūṭa) shall be either its own half-span or half of that;
it emerges from the width of the hall by a fifth part.
On the exterior, however, there should be a *khaṇḍaharmya*; one should employ four *bhadras*, both on the south and on the north. (50.44)
Beside the *khaṇḍaharmya*, however, there is a courtyard (*vārsthala*) occupying one part;
in front of that, in the center of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), it is constructed with a portion of four parts (*vedabhāga*).
And at the two ears, there should be a pair of ear-projections (*karṇakūṭa*);
on the two sides, the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) or the courtyard (*vārsthalam*) should be made with a quarter-part (*vedabhāga*).
The courtyard (vārsthalam) is likewise formed by one part on each of the two sides;
and on both those sides, it is constructed with two parts of the Veda [four parts].
In the case of a *śālā* hall, it should be oriented against the grain; however, in the middle, there should be a courtyard (*vārsthalam*).
On both sides of the courtyard, the hall should be constructed facing half toward the assembly area.
They should be broad by two parts and project out by one part;
one should act in this same manner for the two *bhadra* projections at the back and the front.
Outside the Khaṇḍaharmya, on the eastern side, at one part [of the measurement],
a maṇḍapa is constructed at its front using exactly one-fourth of that portion.
And at the two ears of that [structure], there should be a pair of ear-crests (karṇakūṭa).
The space for the side-pavilions (maṇṭapa) should be one-fourth part of the [main] hall.
In front of that, the courtyard (vārsthala) should be constructed with one part;
in front of that, one should likewise apply a wall (kuḍya) measuring one part.
In front of that, a hall for the entrance (mukhaśālā) should be constructed with a width of two parts and a projection of one part, specifically like a vimāna.
That which is auspicious in the east and west, with a rim and like the eyelashes of a bird, is the *vardhamāna* shape; it is praised for kings. (50.54)
That very same [arrangement], when deprived of the head and joined with a parrot cage,
is known as the *manoramya* (delightful), which is praised by the twice-born. (50.55)
That very primary abode, thus joined with the pinnacle of the assembly hall, should have a courtyard that serves as the site for the assembly; this is declared to be "Śrīkara."
In width there should be twelve parts, and in length eleven parts;
the courtyard should be four parts, and the width of the hall two parts.

In the mukhāgāra (front hall), there should be a promenade (caṅkramaṇa) on one side in the principal chamber (agraśālā). The courtyard (aṅkaṇa) should be provided with an assembly hall (sabhā), while the mukhyāgāra (main house) consists of the inner apartments (koṣṭhaka).

That *bhadra* is joined with the face of the hall (*śālāvaktra*), having an extension and projection equal to two parts and one part respectively attached to it, and is devoid of the [usual] sequence.
To its western part, however, let two arm-halls (bāhuśālā) be constructed in the same manner on both sides of the main hall.
One should construct two pavilions, or even a single pavilion as a residence; surrounding it with one part [of the area], there shall be a hall for both water and land.
One should construct a half-hall at the front of the main hall on both sides;
indeed, wise architects should build halls on both flanks.
The courtyard area is desired to have two external sections and to be provided with a *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion);
one should cause four corner-pinnacles (*karṇakūṭa*) to be constructed there at the corners.
It should have six doors constructed with distinction in the four directions;
its length should be equal to four parts, with doors at the front and on the sides.
One should construct four halls to the north of the two peaks and the central chamber;
an eightfold nesting-place (nīḍa) should be fashioned, which is considered to face the cardinal directions.

This very same [structure], when devoid of the *śiras* (pinnacle) and provided with a *sabhāraka* (upper chamber), has a courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*) shaped like a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); it is called by the name *vipula*. (50.66)
The primary hall (mukhyāgāra) should have the form of an assembly hall (sabhākāra), and there should be a pavilion (śālā) with the construction of a courtyard (aṅkaṇa).
Having excluded two [parts] from the front hall (agraśālā), one should construct a peaked roof (kūṭaka) for the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
In that case, two types [of stone] are to be fashioned; this is considered to be the *sūryakānta* (sun-stone). Its width should consist of ten parts, and its length twelve parts.
In a hall that is twice as long as it is wide, the division for the width shall again be one part;
the front and back portions of the courtyard shall likewise be one part each.
The Śālāvyāsa is proclaimed everywhere as being two parts;
the outer enclosure-ground is one part, and the enclosure-wall is one part.
The projection should be half the length and breadth;
outside the courtyard area, there should be two *bhadras* accompanied by a central *bhadra*.
In a rectangular hall (śālā) measuring two or four [units] in width and [the same or more] in length,
the fire-altar (agni) is desired to be placed within those two [spaces] in the direction of the length (anuloma).
The projection from both sides shall be by one part out of the two external parts;
all the halls are to be arranged with an interval of one part between them.
In the eastern part, at the back, there should be an exit according to the division;
in the middle, the residence of the master is desired to be elevated.
The agrahāra, however, should be similar to that, located at the adjacent *bāhuka* (arm-like extension),
and adorned with lattice windows, arches, and spires.
This has been declared as beautiful and suitable for those who enjoy sovereign power;
that very [structure] is the pinnacle of the main building, shaped like an assembly hall.
The courtyard area of Brahmā, shaped like an assembly hall, is surrounded by elephants;
there should be two *karṇakūṭas* situated at the base of the front end of the eastern wing.
The remainder, however, is considered to be endowed with the *vārṣṭha* style and is dear to Rudra;
the principal hall (*mukhyāgāra*) resembles a cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), while the *koṣṭhāgra* becomes the courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*).
On the side of the front hall (agraśālāṅga), the courtyard grove (koṣṭhakānana) should be constructed;
specifically, on its eastern part, at a distance of two parts from the courtyard.
The six-faced [structure] is said to have one part for its width and its projection;
thus it is "six-eyed" (ṣaṇnetra), and this applies also to the Brahmā-courtyard at the face of the cells.
With its pinnacle entirely abandoned, it is intended to have the form of a pavilion;
this is declared by name to be Jayanta, endowed with all ornaments.
In width, there should be eight parts of a *manu*, and in length, sixteen parts;
the courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*) shall consist of four parts, and the two halls (*śālā*) shall be outside by two parts each.
Outside of that, one part is the *khaṇḍaharmya* on the exterior;
this *khaṇḍaharmya* component is constructed on the outside by means of a quarter-part (*vedabhāga*). (50.83)
A four-peaked [temple] has four corners and is provided with four projections (nāsīs);
between those two [corners], at the fourth and second parts, the four halls (śālās) are proclaimed.
Equipped with a pinnacle shaped like a *karkarī* and provided with nine front eaves, the *hārabandha* is declared to be the *kāmāṅgaṇa* when situated in its proper place. (50.85)
This very courtyard, joined with a length consisting of three parts,
should be made into a corridor in front of the main hall.
The principal hall is proclaimed to have a neck formed by a lofty pinnacle;
its courtyard shall have the appearance of a hall, with its entrance fashioned like a water-jar (karkarī).
The remainder, however, one should make the enclosure of the gate, including the main archway;
when joined with the *bhadra* by means of the *bhadra*, it is considered the *svastika* layout, which bestows happiness. (50.88)
In both width and length, it is joined with divisions as before;
outside of that, there is a courtyard (aṅkaṇa) joined with two or four parts.

The outer enclosure (vāra) should be made with one part, and the width of the hall (śālāvyāsa) with two parts; the vestibule (alinda) and the turret (khaṇḍaharmya) should likewise be made with one part each.
One should cause four peaks to be constructed at the four corners of the hall's section;
and in the middle of all four, one should construct a set of four halls.
One should design a courtyard in the shape of a pavilion, higher than the tall halls, and include a khaṇḍaharmya with internal arrangements.
One should arrange the hall, provided with a central courtyard, in the four directions;
one should construct cages within it, especially in the *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion).
In each secret [mandala], this Viśvabhadra should be endowed with ritual action;
the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) is intended to have a width and length of two and four parts respectively.
One should circumambulate the Nandicchanda enclosure, which is surrounded by the Aṅkaṇa.
One should construct four halls provided with a *nandyāvarta* face;
they should have equal beams and be fashioned as required for the corner of the *khaṇḍaharmya*.
One should construct four halls, each projecting from one side, endowed with the form and appearance of a porch, and extending out by half the width of the hall.
O best of the twice-born, the central elephant is desired to be joined with a length double [that of the others]; one should decorate it like a temple in the form of a Nandyāvarta.
One should construct four halls in the shape of a head (shrine) for an assembly hall;
one should also build a courtyard and a pavilion that is elevated and extensive.
This is declared to be a pleasing arrangement that brings happiness to all;
indeed, everything is described as being in the form of a pavilion for the halls. (50.99)
Joined with a parrot-cage on the outside, beginning with the letter *vā* as before;
this is called the *rucaka*, and everything else is as previously described. (50.100)
The gateway and the courtyard should be equal in their dimensions of width and length;
the width of the hall should likewise be the same, and from that [hall] proceeds the triad beginning with the gateway.

One should construct a pavilion (maṇṭapa) in the four directions and at the corners, provided with a sacrificial altar (vedī); the remaining ground should be made well-established as the site for the enclosure. || 50/102 ||
The main hall, the assembly hall, and the courtyard shall be as they are;
all other places for the rainy season retreat shall be known by the name Jayamaṅgala.
One should construct a courtyard with the form of an assembly hall, and a principal chamber like a palace;
one should arrange a pavilion with a peaked roof on all four sides.
All else, however, is as previously stated; this is considered a marvel.
In its width there should be sixteen parts, and in its length eighteen parts.
In the middle [section], one should fashion a courtyard (*aṅkaṇa*) measuring two or four parts;
outside of that, the door is one part, and the width of the hall (*śālā*) is two parts.
The door on all sides occupies one part, and the outer wall is likewise;
the porch (alinda) is by one part, and the turret (khaṇḍaharmya) is on one side.
One should design the primary hall and the foremost hall as being without windows;
likewise, two arm-halls (bāhuśālā) should be constructed, joined together with them.
In the primary residence and in other locations, it was adorned at its base with excrement,
with middling bells, and with broken palaces.
One should lead the staircase by two parts of the *karṇa* (corner) into the portion of the front hall (*agraśālā*);
or else, there may be a *triśira-maṇḍapa* (three-peaked pavilion) joined with the front hall at the front.
One should determine the place of residence and the enjoyment according to the will of the master;
this is called the *padmaka* [formation], while everything else is as previously described. (50.111)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Lotus Garland, in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Classification of Nāgaras and Others.
I shall now describe specifically the various divisions, such as Nāgara and others,
extending from the Vindhya mountains to the Kṛṣṇā river, and from the Himālayas to the Kanyākumārī.
Therefore, according to the predominance of sattva, rajas, and tamas, the *dhātrī* (the source) is of three kinds:
Nāgara, Drāmiḍa, Vesara, and Sārvadeśika. || 51.2 ||
The Kāliṅga and the Varāṭa are thus proclaimed here as the sixfold [styles].
The Nāgara style occurs in a Sāttvika field, while the Vesara style occurs where Tamas predominates.
One should employ the Drāmiḍa style, which is universal and esteemed everywhere;
likewise, the Kāliṅga and Varāṭa styles are to be adopted when sattva and rajas predominate.
The base is the *masūraka*, the shank is the *kapota*, and the neck is the *śikhara*;
above that, with an *āmalasāra* capital, it is joined by the eightfold group (*aṣṭavarga*) along with the *kumbha* and *śūla*.
Furthermore, the eight classes (varga) mentioned by others as being placed above [the base] consist of the Rathas,
Pratirathas, Koṇas, Anyonya, Adhika, and Bhadrakas.
It should be provided with three, five, nine, or seven compartments,
along with the *caraṇḍaka* (side-chambers) joined to the vicinity of the *nīḍa* (central hall), including the *soṣṭra-bhāva* and other features.

With limbs variegated by all possible forms, performing the act of crossing over with stones, joined with obstacles and counter-obstacles, and endowed with the portions of Ojas and Anojas as well as Muṇḍa.
That which is born from action or non-action, possessing a mandala and a pure core,
is endowed with a śukanāsikā on both sides and at the front opening.
The Nāgara style should indeed be constructed according to proper proportion and for the sake of beauty, joined with a circular pavilion and provided with primary and secondary limbs. 51/10.
It is endowed with functions equivalent to external and internal pillars and walls;
above the *prakṛti* and above the birth [of the deity], it possesses a pedestal (*upapīṭha*) and a *asūraka* [ornament].
That which lies between all the pillars, possessing weight and partaking in the lack of division [between them],
consists of the birth-base, the pedestal, the foundation, the pillar, the stone-slab, and the neck.
One should lead [the measurement] from the two finials of the spire together with the six groups; outside the central axis, one should draw the *sama-sūtra* and the *aṅga-bhadraka* transversely.
Above the interior of the entire pillar, there is the binding of the inner entablature;
this consists of the *nālikā*, *andhārikā*, *dhāra*, *hāra*, and *urasya* ornaments. (51.14)
It should be provided with a pigeon-shaped pinnacle (kapotaśālā), joined with a Brahma-door, adorned with a banner,
and equipped with a parrot-beak (śukanāsikā) at the front pavilion (pramukhamaṇṭapa).
The thirteenth part is considered the most excellent, while the twelfth part is also traditionally taught;
likewise, it possesses six and seven earths, and it takes three, five, and three parts of seven.
Likewise, a dwelling with eight floors is declared to be a nine-storeyed mansion,
having seventeen, sixteen, eight, nine, ten, and eighteen parts respectively.
The arrangement of the sixfold forms, the complete ornamentation of all limbs,
and the inclusion of the proportions of the palace emerging from the middle and the ears.
A celestial mansion (vimāna) with such distinguished features as these is considered Drāmiḍa;
it is joined with the Drāmiḍa arrangement and endowed with Nāgara craftsmanship.
The Nāgara style is adorned with the specific characteristics taught by the Drāmiḍas;
it consists of both types of *khaṇḍaharmya*—namely, those with and without *khaṇḍa* (sections). // 51.20 //
