(Verse 51.21) A *vesara* is a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) whose interior construction is joined with successive tiers of ornamentation, possessing various such diverse components.

From the base upwards, it should be joined in successive tiers; above the *dhārikā* is the ornamentation (*maṇḍana*), and above that, it is provided with a suitable neck (*grīva*), a pinnacle (*śikhara*), and a finial (*stūpikā*).

It possessed pillars adorned with the figures of Bhadra, Upabhadra, and Citrāṅga, with their inner surfaces finished with gold leaf, and it was furnished with stone pillars whose bases were fixed upon a common floor.

The Varāṭa temple is esteemed for its architectural splendor, characterized by rows of forms, functional activity, and the arrangement of shadow-cast stone slabs; such is the variety of its constituent parts.
For this [deity], there is no outer ornamentation with banners, nor the climbing up by the *andhārikā* in the northern half; rather, it is accompanied by the climbing up by the *andhārikā*. (51.25)
Adorned with all its limbs rising and falling, it has the appearance of being square, octagonal, and circular; it possesses a neck like a mountain peak and is fragrant.
The dwelling of Kalinga was esteemed for its limbs and structures of such a kind,
adorned with *nālikā* and *andhārikā* supports, and featuring necklaces and breast-ornaments.
A dwelling provided with a pigeon-shaped pinnacle (kapotaśālā) and a banner at the Brahma-door,
possessing these six types of features, is approved for all regions.
Each [of these] has been declared to be threefold; now, however, the Drāmiḍa style is being described.
It is characterized by the avoidance of cutting off the hands [of the composition], and by the balancing of what is deficient and what is redundant.

Having avoided the cutting off of hands and other such [defects], the architect, who knows the rules for construction, should take away that city-like [structure] which possesses symmetrical limbs and has arisen from his own wealth.

It is proclaimed as being endowed with the Bhadrā ornament and belonging to the Drāmiḍa style; it possesses its own introductory verses (vaktra), is devoid of any missing measures, and contains no excess.

The *vesara* style is considered to be joined with progressively higher projections (*niryūha*), following the sequence of one story (*talaka*) with three, five, seven, two, four, or six bays (*bhakti*). (51.32)
In the case of *nāgara* and other [temple types], the middle [type] is said to be devoid of six variations;
it consists of two, three, four, five, eight, or nine storeys. (51.33)
The smallest is to be known as one-tenth of a tenth part, the middling as one-tenth;
the best is remembered as thirteen parts, while twelve parts is [also] recorded.
Likewise, a building with six or seven storeys may have three, five, or two divisions of its parts;
similarly, a residence is said to have eight floors or nine storeys.
The ten-storied vimāna has seventeen, twice eight (sixteen), nine, eight,
and ten parts, and is joined with thirty-two and seven parts.
The eleven-storey [temple] consists of two parts of three [units] and twenty parts;
likewise, the twelve-storey [temple] consists of four, six, and five parts respectively.
This is declared to be the method for purification, but it is also stated otherwise:
[the calculation] from the portions of seven, three, and two, [yields] a portion consisting of ten, eight, and ten parts.

By increasing the diameter by two parts through the addition of pairs and non-pairs of three earths and so forth, the number reaching up to ten and twelve earths is declared as it occurs in sequence. (51.39)
Among the five types of cities, beginning with the *nāgara*, the smallest is inferior and the middle is superior;
their arrangement and ornamentation, when not in conflict [with local custom], are universal.
In the Nāgara style, the proportions are unequal; in the Drāmiḍa style, they are both equal and unequal.
In the Vesara style, which is universal to all regions, two types of proportions are to be adopted.
In the city of Nāgara, it is diminished by no more than one another;
in Drāmiḍa, it is diminished at the separation of its own limbs; and in Kṣetra, it is appropriately diminished in a moment. (51.42)
In the case of mules and other such animals, the proportions may be slightly less or more; the determination of the ground plan is made by means of three, four, or five measures (kapotas).
Thus is the division of the *bhakti*; now the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) is described:
it may consist of one, three, five, six, nine, or eleven parts of the *bhakti*. (51.44)
For a city temple of a single story, there is one *nālikā*;
for those of superior, middling, and inferior size, the outer wall is formed by the remainder.
In the six, eight, and ten-fold [plans], the *nālī* measures three, four, and five parts respectively;
this is declared to be the width of the *nāgara* style *nālī* in a two-storied temple.
In the case of the Nāgara style, however, one-sixth part is for the sixteen-fold division,
one-seventh for the seventeen-fold division, and one-eighth for the eighteen-fold division of the ground floor.
In the Drāmiḍa style, the width of the *nāli* (the central core) is three, four, or five parts;
the outer portions consist of five, seven, or nine parts, while the remaining sections constitute the walls.
(Verse 51.49) Thus, on a single floor, it is described according to the distinctions of the *uttama* (superior) and other types:
[the divisions] are in parts of seven, three, eleven, four, five, and six.
In a two-storied temple of the Drāmiḍa style, the width of the hall (nālīgṛha) is prescribed;
of the interior (garbha), nine or ten parts are for the central space, while the remaining parts on the outside are for the walls.
In this very manner, the ninth part is considered in the Drāmiḍa style of the three-storey temple;
the shaft (nālī) is divided by three, five, and seven, and then by six, eight, and eighteen.
For a one-storeyed building of mixed materials (vesara), the proportions for the best, middle, and lowest types are respectively nine,
eleven, and twelve parts, with four, five, and six divisions [for the base].
In the *vesara* style, the width of the *nālī* (the central hall) is prescribed for a two-storeyed building;
it is twenty parts when the whole is divided into two, three, or four parts, and nine parts when divided into ten. (51/53)

O best of the twice-born, the inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be on the first floor; however, in a three-storied temple, the inner sanctum is declared to be thus for one, two, or three floors. (51.54)
That which is spoken by the Nāgaras is appropriate for Varāṭa, while that which is fitting for the Drāmiḍas is appropriate for Kāliṅga.
Whatever has been declared by Vesaroka is suitable for the universal [rite];
or that which is external may be applied in due order, or all of it may be used in the universal [rite]. (51.55)
In the *tritala* and other [temple types], there should be an interior consisting of eight, three, thirty, and three parts;
in the *nāgara* and other styles, there is the established arrangement of both general and specific ornaments.
The more excellent is better, not half-as-excellent; this is considered the most excellent.
Thus the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) has been described; now the rule for the Bhadra [temple] is stated.
The smallest crucible (mūṣā) in the center has a width of five, six, seven, or one part out of a total of three, four, or five rows [of bricks], and it extends outward by one part of its own height.
In the smallest [size], it is nine-fifths; in the middle, seven-thirds;
and at the base, it consists of two-fifths, six-sevenths, four-sixths, five-sixths, and six-eighths respectively.
In the middle [section], the middle crucible has an extension equal to half the total width;
its widths [at the respective sections] are six, eighteen, and seven parts of the sixteen-part division.
In the middle [type], the crucible (mūṣā) should be fifteen-sixths;
in the smallest, nine-fifths; and in the medium, seven-thirds.
In the six [styles] beginning with Nāgara, within the one-third and one-sixth portions respectively, let their emergence be conceived in the manner previously described. (51/62)
The fifty types beginning with Śāntika and ending with Kāmada are appropriate for the Drāmiḍa style;
however, in the Nāgara style, those beginning with Kāmada have a height that is double the width.
In the large eightfold divisions, the heights for the rites of pacification and so forth are increased twofold by one, two, three, four, and five parts respectively. (51.64)
In the Varāṭa, Kāliṅga, and Vesara styles, it is as described for the Nāgara;
in the Nāgara style, the hands should be equal, while in the Drāmiḍa and other styles, it is as previously stated.
In the case of the Svāyambhuva and other liṅgas, within the circumference of the portion dedicated to worship,
the height of the *śāntika* [liṅga] shall be five parts out of fifteen.
The Nāgara style is characterized by equal proportions; when its height is divided into seventeen parts, it is called Pauṣṭika-Nāgara, being seven parts high and exceeding the Śiva measurement.
From nineteen parts, the *vardhamānaka* has nine parts;
the *jayada* is *nāgara*, and its height is greater than that by one-tenth. (51.68)
The *adbhuta* [style], the *abhivāra*, half of that, and the *sārvadeśika*;
thus it is in the *nāgara-liṅga*, while the *saudha* is by means of the *ojas* measure.

The Drāmiḍa style is said to arise from the elements of the earth, air, and ether within the portion of the modification concerning the circumference; it brings about peace, nourishment, and victory. (51.70)

When there is an excess of one-quarter [of a degree] or more, or when the difference between the two is less than that, it is called the "wonderful" (adbhuta) and "all-encompassing" (abhivāra) yoga, which grants all desires. || 51/71 ||
When the sun is not in its own portion, but at three, four, or five parts,
the Vesara style is considered to grant prosperity, height, and victory, and bestows victory.
The three triads beginning with the *adbhuta* (wonderful) should be understood according to the previously stated rule,
based on the measurement of equal parts in the Drāmiḍa, Vesara, and Liṅga styles.
O best of the twice-born, a wise man should construct a palace according to the scriptures;
having taken the length obtained for the *mānava* [plan], one should divide it into eight parts. (51.74)
The *nāgara* style, which includes the *bhūta*, *veda*, and *guṇa* proportions as well as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites,
may be increased or decreased by half, a quarter, or two units, and it is characterized by its vastness.
The Adbhuta, Abhivāra, Nāgara, and Sārvakāmika [styles] are for a height of eighteen parts; the Kauśika and Indriya [styles] are for a height of twenty-four parts. (51.76)
In the Drāmiḍa style, rites such as pacification (śāntika) and so forth should be performed as before, beginning with the marvelous (adbhuta).
In the Vesara style, however, when the [image] is divided into twenty parts, there are eight, twelve, and six parts respectively.
In this manner, according to the sequence beginning with pacification (śāntika) and so forth, it is as before;
the width is equal to the height of the liṅga, or else twice the height of the portion for worship.
In that interval, at the eighth part, these nine are the extensions of the pedestals;
one should make the height equal to half the width, or indeed thirty-two parts plus two parts.
In that interval, at one-eighth [of the height], these nine are the elevations of the pedestal (pīṭhikā).
When the length of the liṅga is divided into nine parts, the smallest [pedestal] is seven parts,
while the largest, in the Drāmiḍa style, has a pedestal width of nine parts.
In that interval, at the eighth part, the extensions of the pedestals (pīṭha) are ninefold;
and at its height, at the eighth part, having set aside one [part], there are two or three parts.
The remaining portion, which is the height of the base, is the share for worship above the lower platform;
this is indeed prescribed for the Drāmiḍa style, while the Vesara style is described as follows.

In the case of the *vesara* style, the circumference is the modified portion, while the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is considered to be seven and nine parts for the inferior and superior types respectively. (51.83)
In the interval between those, one should arrange an eighth part as before;
the height of the Viṣṇu-portion is desired, while the remainder is intended to be situated on the ground.

The pedestal (pīṭhikā) may be one-fourth larger than Viṣṇu’s portion; its width is three times the thickness of the supporting pillars (viṣkambha). One should then place the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) at the bottom.
The height of the liṅga should be one-third, one-fourth, or even one-eighth of its diameter (viṣkambha). // 51.86 //
The depth of the pit, however, should be one-ninth or one-eighth [of its width];
this stone, in the case of a *nāgara* liṅga, is called the *brahma-śilā*.
The height of the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is one-fourth of its width; its elevation is one-third of that.
The stone for the Drāmiḍa style of temple has a thickness equal to one-eighth of the width of the *liṅga*.
In the Vesara style, the stone slab is situated with a width reduced by three-and-a-half parts from the garbha, and it is provided with a quarter-part of that [width]. // 89 //
If the stone for the pedestal of the *liṅga* is of the same species [as the *liṅga*], there will be great prosperity;
if it is otherwise, there will be misfortune for both the maker and the one who causes it to be made. (51.90)
This distinction is not accepted regarding the *liṅga* that is universal across all regions;
likewise, O twice-born ones, no such restriction is accepted for the temple or the *liṅga*. (51.91)
In this case, however, no such restrictive rule is applied even to the pedestal stone (pīṭhaśilā);
for, due to its primacy among all lingas, it is accepted as such everywhere.
Likewise, the temple itself and the pedestal should be constructed in that same manner;
it bestows peace, nourishment, victory, wonder, and fulfills all desires. (51.93)
In the Śāntika style, one-eighth of the total height is for the elevation; the height of the base (bhāga) is constructed from that.
The height of the plinth (caraṇa) is two parts, and the entablature (prastara) is reduced by one-eighth.
The neck is said to be three parts, and the height of the spire (śikhara) is half a part;
the pinnacle (sthūpikā) shall be reduced by one-eighth part; this is the Drāmiḍa style with a single storey.

The portion consisting of nine parts and eight desired parts shall be doubled for the *masūra*; the *tāra* and the *ucca-prastara* shall each be one part, and the *gala* shall be constructed from one part.
The height of the pinnacle should be one-third [of the total height], and the rest should be the *sthūpikā* (finial);
this is declared as the Drāmiḍa style for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), with a one-quarter increase in the tenth part.
A quarter-measure twice that of a *masūra* grain is called a *prastara*;
the neck is said to be one-quarter measure, and the head should consist of all the parts combined.
The Drāmiḍa style is proclaimed as having a stūpikā (finial) equal to one part;
in twelve parts, the *masūra* measures one and a quarter parts and occupies three parts.
Two parts are said to be one *pāda*, from which the emergence of the *sapādaprastara* occurs;
one part is said to be the neck (*gala*), and four half-parts shall constitute the head (*śiras*).
The height of the *sthūpī* (finial) shall be one and a quarter parts; this is the Drāmiḍa style.

In the thirteen-part division, the *masūra* is one and a half parts, or it may be one-third of that. The *prastara* (cornice) is said to be one and a quarter parts, while the *gala* (neck) is desired to be one part.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be known as five parts, and the finial (sthūpikā) should be one-quarter of that;
this is proclaimed as the Drāmiḍa style, known by the name Sārvakāmika.
It should be made either as Sabhadra, Vibhadra, or Karṇakūṭayuta;
or it may be Niṣkarṇakūṭa, provided with a niche (sanīḍa), or equipped with an archway (satoraṇa). || 51.103 ||
Thus, that which is endowed with these characteristics and is to be performed must belong to a single stage (*ekabhūmika*).
However, if there should be entry into the throat within the womb, death will occur. (51.104)
One should not provide an entrance for the *nāgara*, *sārvadeśya*, *kāliṅga*, *drāmiḍa*, *varāṭa*, or *vesara* styles [in that location].
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara correspond respectively to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
In the Nāgara, Drāmiḍa, and Vesara styles of architecture, these are considered the presiding deities.
That which is octagonal from the base (upāna) to the pinnacle (sthūpī) is known as Nāgara;
that which is circular from the neck (kaṇṭha) upwards is proclaimed as Vesara.
That which begins from the neck and has eight corners is proclaimed as Drāmiḍa;
this [style] beginning with Nāgara is proclaimed as the abode common to all regions.
That which is square or oblong is proclaimed as *nāgara*;
likewise, that which is octagonal or hexagonal, and those of various lengths, are also [of this type].
The *saudha* style is said to be Drāviḍa, while the *vesara* is proclaimed [as another]. It is celebrated as being circular, oval, polygonal, or circular again in another way. (51.110)
In the vimāna known as Drāmiḍa as well, the lingas and other forms divided into the Nāgara style and so forth were previously described; now their bodily form (vapus) therein is also being described.
In the city-plan, when the portion for worship has been divided into sixteen parts,
one should omit six, five, and four parts from the top and fashion the characteristic marks below.
When the cord is facing the portion of Viṣṇu, one should hang two [lines] at the sides;
then, on the back of those two, where the junctions are absent, there are four, three, and two [units].
In the middle [line], one should omit six, five, four, three, and two [units];
in the superior [line], one should omit at the bottom six, five, four, three, and two parts.

O lords of sages, it is held that one part, three parts, and two parts constitute the intervals between the threads; half of that is declared by the masters of sages to be the width at the tip of the side-thread.

O twice-born ones, the depth and the width of the cord should be one barley-corn; for each lower [grade], it should be eight barley-corns less, while for the highest and best, it should be eight more.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, is the characteristic of the Nāgara style;
in the Drāviḍa style, however, the portion for Śiva is divided into fifteen parts in successive order.
By means of nine parts, a tenth part, and indeed eleven divisions.
The characteristics known as inferior, middling, and superior shall be extracted;
one should suspend [the measurements] sequentially upon the cord according to divisions of seven, eight, and nine.

When reduced by three, four, and two parts respectively, there shall be a conjunction of the two side-threads; and at the center, there shall also be a conjunction by means of five, four, and three *yūkas*. (51.120)

In the *śreṣṭha* (excellent) type, the width of the back is six, five, four, three, two, and one parts; the sum of those two [the front and back] is the width of the thread from its own respective portion, and the wing-thread is as previously stated.
In the sixteen-fold division, the length of the Śivāyāma is ten parts;
above that, it is four parts, and then, having omitted two parts at the back.
Starting from the shape of a bud, it is joined with the two side-lines;
or else, having omitted one-third from above, according to the eleven-fold division (rudrabhāga).
The height of the neck (nāla) is specified; the remainder is exactly as before.
Thus is the Brahma-sūtra (the plumb line) determined for the Drāmiḍa-liṅga.
The height of the neck (nāla) for a hybrid (vesara) temple is prescribed as three-fifths of the height of the sanctum (arcana), or one-tenth of that;
it may extend downward from eight parts of the base.
The junction of the side-line and the cord occurs at the portion of one-sixteenth of the total height;
the section for worship consists of twelve parts, and above that, sixteen double-parts (thirty-two parts).
The length of the stalk (nālāyāma) shall be nine parts; the junction (saṅgama) shall be as before.
When the diameter (vyāsa) is divided into eighteen parts, one part shall be the width of the cord (sūtravistara).
Half of that shall be the wing-line (pakṣasūtra), and the interval shall be as previously described;
thus has the Brahma-line for the Vesaraliṅga been illustrated.

However, this division is not proclaimed in the case of a *liṅga* that is universal to all regions; likewise, for a pedestal (*pīṭha*), the Nāgara and other styles are prescribed according to the region of the pedestal itself. (51.129)
The Drāmiḍa style is inauspicious; the Bhadra and Upabhadra styles are auspicious.
They are suitable for the Nāgara, Vesara, Kāliṅga, and Varāṭaka styles as well. (51.130)
The general pedestal has been described; now the image is also being discussed.
[It is placed] in the womb, in the hearth, on a lentil-shaped mound, at the door, on a pillar, or on its capital.
When the height of the finial (sthūpikā) is ten parts, the excellent image should be seven parts;
when it is four parts, it is inferior. Within the interval of twenty-six [parts], there is a proportional variation.
In the image, the elevations indeed correspond to the number of lunar mansions;
in the Nāgara style they are three times three in number, while in the Drāmiḍa style they are nine in number. (51.133)
Likewise, there are other types of *vesara* in the order of superior, middling, and inferior;
and according to their sequence, they are threefold: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. (51.134)
The *sāttvika* [style] is appropriate for standing postures, the *rājasa* for the form of dance, and the *tāmasa* for other forms; these should be applied by the wise. (51.135)
However, scholars do not accept the application of the universal (sārvadeśika) linga;
rather, for the site of the temple and the deities, the Nāgara and other styles are considered superior. (51.136)
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital,
or in a market-town and so forth, one should [establish] the supreme Lord in a Brahma-sthāna or in the eight directions.
One should begin to construct a palace either outside on the eight directions, or within the walls, or having placed it outside, or in the interval between these [structures]. (51.138)
One should construct the Nāgara style in the north, the Vaiśana style in the northwest;
one should construct the Drāmiḍa style in the south, or in the southeast, or even in the southwest.
One should construct a *vesara* temple on the east or the west;
likewise, on both sides of the moon [the north] and on the side of Yama [the south], according to the injunctions of Yama.
Likewise on both sides of Indra, and similarly on both sides of Varuṇa—
all these abodes are indeed Drāmiḍa.
If it is a temple intended for all regions, one should perform [the rites] everywhere;
however, for these [specific types], one should perform the laying of bricks and so forth in the desired location.
If it is for a Brahmin, the chamber should be located in the southeast corner;
for a merchant, it may be in the southwest, or situated in one part of the assembly hall, provided there is no conflict.
These sanctuaries (dhāman) should be constructed without contradicting the lineage-thread (vaṃśasūtra);
one should lead the temple of Pārvatī in every region according to what was spoken by Śarva.
It should be provided with the Valabhī style or indeed the Drāmiḍa style;
it may be in the center for Vighneśvara, or in the previously mentioned locations as in the case of Śiva.

The head of the structure should be shaped like the back of an elephant or have a common (standard) head; the residence for the commander-in-chief should be constructed according to the tradition approved by Śarva.
In the previously mentioned location, the Nāgara temple of Viṣṇu should be constructed;
in the center and in the four directions, and elsewhere in the southwest, that of Brahmā.
A Vesara temple should be constructed, endowed with the four auspicious features,
either in the western direction, or in the south, or between the southeast and the south, or in the center of the village.
One should construct the Vaiṣṇava Śrīdhāma temple to the south or between the south and southwest; otherwise, it may be built in the center of the village or elsewhere, just like the Brahma-mandira.
Or, in such a case, the Śiva-temple of the Sun is considered to be in the southeast; then, in the eight directions and desired locations, the Drāmiḍa style is for the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa).
O twice-born ones, it is like the abode of Pārvatī, or like the previously mentioned location,
or like the abode of Jyeṣṭhā between Indra and Agni.
The temple of the Teacher (Śāstṛ) should be constructed in the previously mentioned location, or between Vahni and Someśa, just like the temple of Vighneśa.
The house of Soma is in the direction of Soma (the north), or its house is in the southwest;
the Nāgara house is in the northwest, as is the Vaiśravaṇa house.
The temple of Soma should be constructed like that of Viṣṇu, situated between Vahni and Someśa; it may be the abode of Kāma for Viṣṇu, or otherwise located according to the region.
And for all the gods and their wives who have not been mentioned,
as well as for the gods and goddesses previously mentioned, this applies universally to all regions.
Alternatively, one should have a temple constructed, complete with its respective vehicle; now follows the description of the Prāsāda known as the Sārvadeśika.

O Brahmins, the characteristics of the *liṅga*, as well as those of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the characteristics of the Brahma-mountain (*brahmaśaila*), and likewise the characteristics of the image (*bera*) and so forth [have been explained]. (51.157)
The best of teachers should grasp that which is established in each respective chapter.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, concerning the rules for the distinctions of the Nāgara and other styles, in the great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Procedure for Attaining the Grounds.
Now I shall explain in detail the procedure for the descent of the ground;
the arrangement of the four parts and so forth is known as the "descent of the ground. (52.1)
Alternatively, the decrease or increase of the cubits is proclaimed as follows:
seventy cubits are proclaimed for the width, while one hundred are proclaimed for the height. (52.2)
Alternatively, the base known as the *dvādaśa* should be constructed with one less [digit];
it is said there to be sixty-three units wide and ninety units high.
O best of the twice-born, it should have eleven stories, fifty-seven cubits in width,
eighty cubits in height, and consist of ten floors.
But when joined with one [unit], it is fifty cubits high at the pinnacle;
that which is reckoned as seventy-five [cubits] is proclaimed as the nine-storied [temple]. (52.5)
It is proclaimed as having eight stories, measuring five cubits [in width], forty cubits [in length], and sixty cubits in height.
Endowed with thirty-nine cubits and fifty-seven units in height,
this is declared to be the "Sevenfold" [measurement] when joined with twenty-one.
It is declared to have a height of thirty cubits and four stories;
its width is fifteen cubits, and it is twenty-one cubits high.
In this scripture called the Kāmika, it is declared that there is one with three tiers;
or, let it be conceived as having seventy at the end and sixteen (two times eight) at the beginning in its extent.
O best of the twice-born, this should be the maximum measurement for that which is designated as "by birth" (jātya),
being reduced by two or three cubits respectively in both width and height.

The middling and the inferior [mandalas] should be known as having twenty-seven varieties; however, for the desired [superior mandala] on the surface of the earth, no threefold division exists at all.
The one called "Jātya" is proclaimed here as being twenty-eight cubits [in length],
due to the reduction of the intervals between the cubits from one up to eleven.

However, because the six [periods] bounded by two up to twelve [days] are also included within the interval, it is considered that there are thirty-six [periods] within the measure of twenty-seven. (52.13)
Desire, conceptualization, and appearance— each of these is said to consist of two units in measure,
according to the proportions of the abodes ranging from nine up to Rudra.

O twice-born ones, that which is the human celestial palace (vimāna) extending up to sixteen bhūmis—this shall be the measurement of the intermediate [unit]; now the small measurement is being described.
Starting from three or four cubits and increasing by two cubits at each step,
the measurement for a single-story temple is declared to be of four types.
Starting from five or six cubits and increasing by two cubits at each step,
in a double-storied temple, the four measurements range from eleven to twelve cubits.
Beginning from seven or eight cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
the measurement for a three-storied temple ranges from four cubits up to fourteen cubits.
Starting from nine cubits and increasing by two cubits at each step,
up to sixteen cubits, there shall be temples of four or five stories.
A small [temple] is considered to have one or two stories;
its measurement may be in even or odd cubits, combined with quarters, halves, or eighths of a cubit.
Starting from the *vyomahasta* measurement and increasing by increments of *vyomahasta*, a temple chariot (*vimāna*) should be constructed; this is praised for all [temple types]. (52.21)

O best of the twice-born, it is held that in the case of a maṇṭapa, the proportions should be double at the end of the length, and they should be arranged according to the Vedāntas; likewise, O excellent brahmins, they should be executed with devotion according to the length.
For the gods, Brahmins, kings, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, [the measurement] is equal;
in its width, it is increased by three, five, four, three, and two parts respectively.
It bestows peace, nourishment, victory, and wonders, and fulfills all desires;
its width at the top is twice its height, and an increase of one-quarter is also approved.
One should add twice the width plus one-eighth;
this is thus prescribed for the small [temples]. Now, that which pertains to the smallest [temples] is described.
When the width has been divided into seven parts, the height should be seven parts or six parts;
the height being greater than the width—now the intermediate measurement is stated.
Having performed the expansion as before, that which exceeds by four or five [units] is declared to be the middle measurement; for the best [images], it is one-third more. (52.27)

The former may be merely a general indication (uddeśa), while this is a detailed exposition (nirdeśa). It may be joined with one, two, or three measures, or it may be deficient or excessive in measure. (52.28)
The wise man should determine the height for all dwellings;
they know that for gods who are universal monarchs, it extends up to twelve stories.
For Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas, an eleven-storied [temple] is prescribed;
for the twice-born, it should be nine-storied or a ten-storied abode.
The ground of the five elements belongs to the crown prince and the kings;
for the six universal monarchs (cakravartins), it consists of eleven stories beginning with Nanda.
For Vaiśyas and those born as Śūdras, [the palace] should have three or four stories;
for kings, it is considered that it may even have five floors, and that same [measure] applies to those who bear the royal fillet.
Beyond a height of seven cubits and a width of seventy [cubits],
no measurement greater than that is ever accepted by the wise.
For Śiva, all the grounds beginning with the sixteen *kṣmā* (earth) measures are prescribed;
depending on the temple (*prāsāda*), there is either the *liṅga*, or the *prāsāda* itself from the *liṅga*.
A wise person, having examined [the matter], should act according to the scriptures; that is what is taught.
[The lingas are] the self-manifested (svāyaṃbhū), the Bāṇa-liṅga, the divine (daivika), and the one belonging to the sages (ārṣaka). (52.35)
The Gaṇava and the Mānuṣa liṅgas are proclaimed to be of six kinds; however, that which has arisen of its own accord is declared to be the Svāyambhuva.
That which is consecrated by Śiva is remembered as the Bāṇaliṅga;
that established by the gods is divine, while that which is beneficial to the sages is remembered as ārṣa.
The Liṅga established by the Gaṇas is declared to be Gāṇava;
that which is established by cultured men is Mānuṣa, said here to be the sixth.
In the human [scale], however, the measurement of the liṅga shall depend on the temple;
for all others as well, the temple is desired to be proportioned according to the liṅga. (52.39)
The linga, according to its classification as *jyeṣṭha* (largest) and so forth, is measured by the dimensions of the interior of the temple;
it is declared that this is primarily for the sake of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) and incidentally for the sake of liberation (*mukti*).
Those measurements of the hand and other limbs lead to liberation;
through the application of the prescribed rule, they also result in liberation as a secondary consequence. (52.41)
If, out of delusion, one should show the portion below the visible part of the liṅgas of Svāyaṃbhuva and others, it causes all manner of faults for men. (52.42)

One should not [construct] two unstruck [liṅgas]; rather, having grasped them in a broad space, one should fashion them according to the measurement of a man, with the height of the head being the measure for the base.
One should determine the measurement for the lingas of Svāyambhuva and others, including their heads;
by that measurement, one should fashion the portion for worship and thereby construct the pedestal (pīṭha).
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is desired to be two, three, four, or even five times the measurement of the breadth of the liṅga.
For all of these as well, it may be according to the measurement of the ear;
or, having divided [the width] into eight, nine, one, two, or three parts.
One may fashion it as being less or more by one-fourth;
or its measurement may be twice, thrice, or four times that of the pedestal.
The width of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) may also be five or six units;
the thickness of the wall is desired to be one-third of the inner sanctum.

The width of the wall is desired to be half, equal to, double, or even triple the height of the pedestal; or it may be measured by the distance between the corner-posts (karṇa) of these [elements]. 52.49.
In this very manner, it should also be designed for the connection [of the parts];
by means of the width of the pedestal (pīṭha), there should be a pair of nālī-houses situated on the palace (harmya).
If one should perform even a pair [of rites] in that outer portion,
and if it should be a pair, one must not cause them to be mixed together.
Wherever there is a measurement by a specific mark, or a pair, or a pair of cubits—if in that case the hand-measurement should be deficient or excessive—[it is not valid]. (52)
One should make it complete with the measurement of the mind; in that case, no fault is found.
When the measurement of the interior is divided by finger-breadths according to the length of the liṅga... [52/53]
If the *liṅga* is deficient by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), one should bring it to fullness there;
for the sake of the perfection of length and other dimensions, [this is done] by means of one, two, or three finger-breadths.
One who desires prosperity should either reduce or increase [the measurement];
having divided the circle into twenty-one parts, one should take six of those parts. (52.55)
One should remove that one part from the middle of the *liṅga* toward the south;
this is desired for the center of the temple, and likewise for the west as well.
The eastern gate is auspicious, whereas for one facing west there is the opposite;
having first examined [the site] in this manner, one should construct the temple.
The procedure for all of these, beginning with the *āyā* (length), is now stated:
having made the width double [the length], when it is divided by eight (*vasu*), [the remainder indicates the *yoni*].
The remainder is declared here to be the *yoni*; in its absence, however, it is the *śodhaka*.
At the time of rising, the movement of the asterism is said to be by eight and twenty-seven [units].
When the circumference is multiplied by nine, it is said that seven is the number of gates.
Having made the whole threefold, the lunar day (tithi) is divided by thirty. (52/60)
Having divided the *udaya* by eight, the *āya* is determined from the remainder; again, the *udaya* is divided by nine and eight, and this is called the *vyaya*.
Either by the previously mentioned method or by this present rite,
one should construct the temple after having examined the six factors beginning with the site.
Whatever remains, beginning with the feet, all that shall be "sakala" (with parts).
Having multiplied it as before, the quotient and the remainder (tāra) shall be equal to that. || 52/63 ||
Having performed [the calculation] with that very [number], one should divide it by whatever remains as a surplus from the profit;
the "womb" (yonī) is said to be formed by pairs of hands arising from the vowels and the fires (three). 52/64.
Alternatively, the method for determining the *āya* and other factors is stated in another way:

The remainder obtained after dividing [the day count] by eight, nine, and nine (the number of *nāgas*, *sūtras*, and *agnis*), and then further by ten, eight, and four (the *daśas*, *vasus*, and *abdhis*), shall be the *āya*.
When there is no *yoni*, the remainder obtained by dividing [the day count] by eight, eight, and twenty-seven (the *vasus*, *hatas*, and *uḍus*) shall be the *nakṣatra*.
Having multiplied the world-number by thirty-six and divided by the threads, the remainder is the fruit;

the remainder multiplied by eight and divided by thirty becomes the lunar day (tithi). From the conjunction of the house, the day, and the lunar day, the various distinctions of the matrices (yonibheda) arise. || 52/65 ||
Alternatively, one may calculate the *āya* and other factors in another manner: nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one;
these are the *muni*, *nava*, *āgana*, *nanda*, *guṇa*, *nāga*, *nanda*, *dṛk*, *bhānu*, *nāḍi*, *vasu*, and *bha*.
The *āya* is determined by either the birth constellation (*yoni*) or the birth asterism (*ṛkṣa*), according to the sequence of the reduction of the factors of the divisions (*aṃśaka*).
This is considered to apply to the entire linga, as well as to the door, pillars, and so forth.
One should arrange this [image] of Āyā and the others in the half-pavilion, the remaining [images] in the pavilion, and the retinue in the lofty palace or another [structure]. (52.68)
Having thus examined it in many ways, one should design the palace;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should consist of three parts out of nine, or three parts out of five.
In a sevenfold division, it shall be four parts; in a ninefold division, five parts;
in an elevenfold division, six parts; and in a thirteenfold division, seven parts.

The width of the inner sanctum (garbha) is desired to be one-eighth of the width of the temple; however, in the case of the Vasu-proportion, it is one-seventeenth, and in the case of the Nava-proportion, it is one-ninth. || 52.71 ||
The measurement for the inner sanctum (garbhageha) of temples with one, two, or three stories should be one-ninth or one-tenth of the temple's total extent; this is the width of the pinnacle (kūṭa).
The hall (śālā) is considered to be two or three times the length [of the width],
while the cage (pañjara) is half a part, or three-quarters, or one full part.
The *alindas*, *andhārikās*, *andhāras*, and *hārās* are arranged according to their respective proportions;
they may be half a part, two parts, three parts, or even thirty-five parts.
One should arrange the *alinda* (veranda) as the remainder in the layout of the house;
here, the construction of large palatial mansions (*vimāna*) is prescribed.
It may consist of nine or three parts, provided with a central nave and surrounding chambers;
externally, it is extended by a portion for the *āndhārikā*, the *andhāra*, and the *hāra*.
One should arrange the measurement of the necklace (hāra) for the purpose of its design on the exterior;
the measurement situated within the wall should be [calculated] from the outside of the wall.
Having set aside the measurement of the field of composition, one should arrange the measurement [of the letters];
thus is described the internal arrangement as well as the external arrangement. (52.78)
When the width of the temple is divided into twenty-seven parts,
one should determine the placement of the *kūṭa* and other elements by assigning one part to each.
In the first case, it may consist of two parts, or else the pinnacle (kūṭa) may consist of one;
there should be a single base (tala) and a single mouth (grāsa); such is the three-storied *khaṇḍaharmya*.
Alternatively, another method for the internal layout is stated:
this [measurement] of the temple is said to be divided into twenty-seven parts. (52.81)
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be one-third [of the total width], and the wall is desired on all sides;
it should have five porticos (ālindas), six walls, and be surrounded externally by a blind wall (āndhārikā).
This vimāna of the Jāti class consists of three nines (twenty-seven parts) and twelve minute parts;
one should design this for a liṅga made of jewels or for those of Bāṇa and others.
When a temple is desired with a height ranging from ten to fifty cubits,
it should be constructed according to the sequence for the nine types of liṅgas.
When the length and width of that [area] are multiplied by the number of cubits in the heap, the pedestal (pīṭha) is like the linga; otherwise, with one added, there is an interval of three.
The outer wall is increased by two [parts]; the remainder is proclaimed as before.
In the case of the Liṅga and the stones, for the Krodha [deity], they are devoid of five parts of the wall.
One may make the veranda slightly less than the rest, while the remaining parts should be joined to the walls; the base, pillars, and lintels are declared to be common to all.
A structure covered with bamboo frames, other beams, coconut leaves, and so forth, is called a *prapā*; and a roofed pavilion here is called a *maṇḍapa*.
A palace (harmya) endowed with many peaks is well-known by that name; whereas a multi-storied building (mālākārā) consisting of several levels is called a mālikā.
A *śālā* is proclaimed as being provided with a lineage (pediment) and its associated elements, endowed with a pinnacle and a dome (*stūpikā*),
and possessing a primary *nāsikā* (nose-ornament) measuring one-sixth part.

That which is provided with the six divisions (ṣaḍvarga) and endowed with a central sanctum (garbhageha), and distinguished by specific khaṇḍaharmya structures as described for the Andhārya, Andhāri, and Hāra types; 52.91.
That which is provided with peaked halls, equipped with cages, furnished with elephant-backs, and endowed with Indra-halls; || 52.92 ||
The vimāna is endowed with toraṇas described as having the *tilaka* and *kṣudranāsa* motifs,
and is furnished with the limbs such as banners at the Brahma-door.
That which is a pavilion within a pavilion is called the *raṅga*;
it is provided with a root-pinnacle (*mūlakūṭa*) and endowed with a top-pinnacle (*bālakūṭa*). (52.95)
That which is joined with the seizing by the hair is proclaimed as *sabhā*;
the primary object is manifold, while the other is proclaimed as secondary (*gauṇa*). 52.96.
As it has been said: "In this way, it should be primary; however, in its absence, it is secondary.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the procedure for obtaining the ground, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual for the First Brick.
(Verse 53/1) I shall now describe, in due order, the procedure for laying the first brick for mansions and other structures;
[it should be done] in the eastern, northern, or northeastern direction, or at a peak, a pavilion, or a water-shed.
[The ground] extending from the *bhūta* element up to the hand of Viśva, adorned with canopies and other ornaments,
provided with a garland of *darbha* grass, and accompanied by the elephants of the quarters.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar (vedikā) occupying one-third of its area;
it should be one cubit or two cubits in size, or even just the measure of a closed fist.
One should have eight sacrificial pits constructed in the cardinal and intermediate directions, with one principal pit;
or there may be five, or even a single pit, which may be circular or square.
After dismissing the artisan, one should then smear [the image] with cow dung;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should consecrate it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Starting from three finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
the widths of the bricks are considered to extend up to thirty-eight finger-breadths.
There should be three [squares] each for the twelve levels beginning with one;
or else, their extent in the Mahālaya is four times the square [of the side].
The bricks here are said to be one and a quarter, one and a half, or one and three-quarters [of a cubit], or twice that size;
the width of the brick is declared to be half or three-quarters [of its length]. (53.8)
The thickness shall be one-quarter or one-fifth of that [measurement], or it may consist of three or two parts.
The preceptor, being an Ādiśaiva, must be endowed with the Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā). || 53.9 ||
Having bathed well and become pure, with his body consecrated by the ritual application of the kalās, wearing very white garments, a turban, and an upper cloth, and being well-adorned; || 53.10 ||
Adorned with the five ornaments and accompanied by his disciples and attendants, the Guru should wash the bricks with the five products of the cow while reciting the Varma-mantra.
One should bind [the thread] with a golden amulet-string or one made of cotton;
the wise man should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
Half of that [measure] should be combined with rice; half of the rice should be accompanied by sesame seeds;
half of the sesame seeds should be joined with parched grain (lāja), and it should also be provided with *darbha* grass.
This should be considered the supreme ritual procedure; half of that is intended as the middling;
half of that again is to be known as the inferior—thus it is established everywhere.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments,
one should sprinkle the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the five products of the cow while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
And for the purpose of establishing each deity in its own direction, one should have [the syllables] inscribed within the bricks:
the syllable *a* in the eastern part, and likewise the syllable *ā* in the southern part.
One should place the letter *i* in the western direction and the letter *ī* in the north;
one should then worship the letter *u* in the upper portion after covering it with cloths.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, as well as the Śiva-śāstra, are declared here to be the presiding deities (adhidevas) of the directions starting from the east, respectively. (53.18)
The jars, wound with thread, filled with scented water, adorned with white cloths as covers, furnished with golden ornaments, and provided with tufts of grass; || 53.19 ||

In the eight directions, beginning with Indra, one should indeed place the eight lords of the world-protectors (lokapālas), accompanied by auspicious water-pots (śivakumbha) and provided with flowers and mango sprouts.
The wise one should establish [the deity] in the space between Indra and Īśāna and worship it;
thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
The *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *nyagrodha* trees are for the directions starting from the east;
the *vahni* (arka), *apāmārga*, *khadira*, and *vaṭa* trees are for the corners starting from the southeast.

For the primary rite, there should be fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, and an oblation of rice mixed with sesame; this should be combined with the root-mantra and the mantras of the Brahma-aṅgas.
The wise one should offer oblations individually in the center, in the cardinal directions, and also in the intermediate directions;
either a thousand, or half of that, or a hundred, or even half of that.
One should install the image-protectors (mūrtipās) together with the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras).
For them, a fire-oblation (homa) must be performed, and then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
At dawn, having bathed according to the prescribed rite, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images,
shall worship the bricks and the jars and then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) by means of oblations, one should then perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should install those [mantras] in sequence in the locations specified in the method for the arrangement of the womb (*garbhavinyāsa*). (53.27)
Reciting them in their proper sequence— the heart, the crest-lock, the armor, and likewise the head, as well as the root mantra— one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these.
The tip [of the thread] should be placed toward the northeast, and the back toward the southwest;
having understood that the back and the tip are toward the southeast and the northwest respectively, one should perform the ritual action.
In the human [fire-altar], the bricks are long from northeast to southwest; in the divine [fire-altar], they are extended from east to west.
One brick is to be placed first at the beginning, facing east and then north, in due order.
One should establish four bricks in the shape of a *nandyāvarta*;
the fifth, however, is the Śaiva brick, facing east, O Goddess, with its face turned toward the northeast.
Having understood that the faces of men are like those of Kubera, one should thus perform the placement;
then, having first worshipped the preceptor, the wise man should have this performed by him.
The gold of the preceptor, ranging from one niṣka up to nine niṣkas, he should place in the center; furthermore, he should place the gems and other items within the hollows.

The best of teachers should install either a single group, a pair of groups, a triad of groups, or all of them together, according to the method prescribed for the depositing of the embryo (garbhanyāsa).
First, having filled [the vessel] with water from the Śiva-pitcher,
one should place a flower right there, and afterwards deposit the jewels.
A clockwise rotation is auspicious, whereas a counter-clockwise rotation is inauspicious;
if a counter-clockwise rotation occurs, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
In the temple, in the pavilion, in the enclosure wall, at the gate-tower, in the house, in the residence of the attendants, on the pedestal, in the hall, and during the assembly rites. (53.37)
And at a lotus pond, a stream, a well, or the construction of a dam—
one should perform this rite in this very manner.
Whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform all of that as prescribed in the *Garbhanyāsa*.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the "Ritual for the First Brick," in the great tantra named *Kāmika*.
The Ritual for the Upapīṭhas (Secondary Seats)
I shall now describe the procedure for the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), together with its foundational installation;
it should measure one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits, and more on all sides.
One should excavate a space larger on all sides than the width of the vimāna and other structures;
therein, one should fill it with smooth stones, fistfuls of earth, sand, and so forth.
One should complete the foundation by reducing it by six, eight, or five parts; or one may calculate it as reduced by two, three, or four parts. || 54/3 ||
When [the ground] has been made solid with mallets, elephant-trampings, and wooden pestles, and filled with water, if the water remaining therein is not diminished; || 54/4 ||
Having removed that [obstruction] and extracted the pillar from the rock, if only the weight were to fall and there were no depression, [then it would be auspicious]. (54.5)
From that point onward, one should bind [the site] with stones or bricks;
first, there should be the natural ground, which is traditionally known to be of three types.
The natural size is one cubit, which is praised as the best;
it should be eighteen finger-breadths for the medium, and twelve finger-breadths for the inferior.
For the purpose of draining water, one should provide an outlet for each hall;
starting with a reduction of six finger-breadths in the first, it should be half of that in the second.
Three finger-breadths less than the two wings is the *prakṛti*; above that is the *janmabhū*.
That is called the *upāna*, and it is also celebrated as the *bhaumā*.
Above that, the foundation alone is prescribed;
it should be one and a half, two, or three daṇḍas in measurement, according to the width of the base.
But that which has gone out to the exterior region is endowed with many half-measures;
there is either a lotus upon the steps, or the stairs themselves are above that. (54.11)

Just as it has been divided by the portions of beauty, the elements, the Vedas, and the fires—for the sake of elevation, for the sake of beauty, for the sake of protection, and for the sake of strength—so [should it be]. (54.12)
Whether it be Sabhadra or Vibhadra, the Upapīṭha should be constructed in the middle part from the base of the birth [pillar] up to half the height of the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna). // 54.13 //
By one quarter, by three-quarters, equally, or tripled; in a five-part division, by three parts, and in a three-part division, by one part. (54.14)
That projection (nirgama) on the outside of the base should be one-half, three-quarters, or one-quarter of that [base], or reduced by one-eighth; it may be two daṇḍas or three daṇḍas.
Outside the *pāduka* is the *upāna*, which is supported by pillars;
having divided it into nine rows of parts, the *upāna* is prescribed to have a height of three parts.
The lotus above that is desired to be two parts, while the *kampa* (fillet) above it is desired to be one part;
the *karṇa* (ear-moulding) is desired to be six parts, and the remainder is proclaimed to be as previously described.
The *kampa* should be made with one-eighth part, and the pedestal (*upapīṭhaka*) with eight parts;
that same [pedestal] is devoid of a lotus if it is placed above or below.
When divided into twenty-four parts, the *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) shall consist of six parts;
its half is the *karaṇa* (base), and the *uttara* (upper part) is desired according to the same proportion as before.
The pigeon-shaped [pedestal] is here considered to consist of three parts, with one part being the portion of Rudra;
it is separated from the *alinda* by two parts, and its height is equal to that.
The *vājana* should consist of one part, while the *karṇa* is desired to be eight parts;
the *uttara* should be one part, as proclaimed by the portion of Rudra.

The *kapotaka* (dove-cot) is desired to be one-third [of the width], while the *ālinda* (porch) is desired to be one part; the *antarīta* (inner passage) is desired to be one part, and the *prati* (counter-porch) two parts. || 54.22 ||
One part is for the base (prativājana), adorned with all ornaments;
the height is twenty-one parts, and with two parts likewise comes the birth-motif (janma) and the lotus.
With half [of the height] comes the neck, with another half the lotus, and with two parts the molding (vājana);
with half [again] the lotus, and likewise the tremor (kampa), while the fillet (karṇa) is declared to be one-eighth [of the total].
The upper half [of the base] is one part, the lotus is three parts, and the pedestal (upānaka) is three parts;
the upward projection (ūrdhvakampa) should be half a part, while its height is three times seven parts.
The birth [portion] is with two parts; the lotus with three parts; the neck with one part;
the outer wall with one [part]; the eave with eight parts; and the neck [of the dome] with eight parts.
The upper part [of the pillar] is adorned by one, two, or three portions;
it is decorated with lions, elephants, crocodiles, beasts of prey, spirits, and foliage. (54.27)
There should be a *caṣāla* on every face, with its top mounted by a *bāla*;
whether [the *caṣāla*] has been offered or not, one should arrange it everywhere with *matsya* [ornaments].
One should specifically cause an increase or decrease in each individual limb by one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth, or even by one-seventh or one-eighth. (54.29)
Having taken two parts or three parts from the remainder,
one should erase [the rest] and fashion the first limb, namely the *upapīṭha*.
In this very manner, one should indeed cause the foundation to be constructed;
for that is declared here to be of two kinds: the part-by-part [foundation] and the plank-based [foundation]. (54.31)
Having divided the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) into twenty-four parts,
the plinth (jagatī) is said to be one-eighth [of that], and the kumuda is equal to that.

That [pedestal] is specified as having eight parts; the *kampa* (fillet) takes one part, the *karṇa* (ear) takes one-third of a part, the *kampa* should be one part, and the *vājana* (coping) is desired to be three parts.
The *jagatī* is prescribed as before; the *kumuda* should be seven parts, the *padma* should be made one part, and one should perform the remainder as previously described.
The *jagatī* is said to consist of seven parts; the *kumuda* should be six parts;
the lotus (*padma*) should be made with one part, and the *kampa* should be one part.
The neck is said to be three parts, and the upper fillet (ūrdhvakampa) one part;
the lotus is to be known as one part, and the base-ring (vājana) is desired to be two parts.
The upper lotus is one part, and the *upakampa* is likewise;
the *jagatī* is said to be five parts, and the lotus shall be one part.
One part of the lotus and one part of the *kumuda* are each made with a quarter-measure;
the remainder is prescribed as before, resting upon the emergence of the trembling pillars (*kampastambha*).
Birth occurs with one part; the neck is said to be three parts.
Trembling is to be known by one part, and the jagatī meter consists of six parts. (54.39)
One part is prescribed for the lotus, one part for the neck,
three parts for the kumuda, and one part for the lotus.
One part shall be for the base (kampa), two parts for the neck (gala), one part for the base (kampakam), and one part for the petal (dala); the plinth (vājana) is said to be two parts.
One part is declared to be the water-born [lotus]; it is celebrated as trembling by one part;
birth occurs with one portion, and the world-ground (jagati) consists of five parts.
When constructing for others in this manner, one should arrange all of this accordingly:
the height of the fall is twice the height of the afflicted base.
Alternatively, one should fashion that [pedestal] with divisions according to the measurement of the *ārtava* portion:
the water-born [lotus] is said to be one part, and the neck (*gala*) should be half a part.
The upper lotus is likewise half a part; the *kumuda* should consist of four parts;
the lower lotus is half a part, the *kampa* is half a part, and the neck (*gala*) is two and a half parts.
One part for the *kampa*, half for the lotus, two parts for the *vājana*,
half for the lotus, one for the *kampa*, and half for the lotus.
With one part [the base], the birth [pedestal] is formed; with two parts, the lotus; with one part, the *kampaka*;
the ground [plinth] shall consist of six parts, and the *kumuda* (fillet) shall be one-fourth of that.
One part is for the two trembling ears, and the heart-region is fashioned with one part;
the trembling [ornament] is to be made with one part, while the *vājana* is desired to be two parts.
One part is the trembling lotus; with a half and another half, it is trembling.
This is declared to be twenty-six parts, which one should employ throughout the entire temple.
Birth is declared to consist of two parts, while the lotus is desired to be one part;
with one part comes the *kampaka*, and the *jagatī* is formed by five parts. (54.50)
The *kumuda* should consist of four parts, while the *padma* is one part;
the two *kampa-karṇas* are two parts each, and likewise the *kampa* and the lotus (*abja*) are one part each.
The *vājana* should consist of two parts, while the *kampam* is declared to be one part;
thus should the foot-binding be constructed, and it should be trimmed as appropriate.
I shall now declare the obstacles pertaining to the gods and the four classes of the twice-born, divided according to twenty-three parts.
The jagatī is said to consist of eight parts, and the kumuda is equal to that;
the liṅga-base (āliṅga) shall be half a part when [the base] is made in twenty-two parts.
In this manner, when there is a binding of the base (pādabandha), it should be cut as is appropriate;
thus is the *kumuda* described, while the *vājana* would be the *kapotaka*.

The height of the plinth should be one-third [of the total height], and it should be adorned with lotuses extending for five parts; this is prescribed for gods, the twice-born, and kings, but not for other castes.
The lotus is said to have eight parts; in the region of the neck, it measures one part.
The lotus, the lily (kumuda), and the earth-portion are each desired to be one part.
The *āliṅga* should be two parts, and the *antarita* is likewise considered to be so;
the height of each [subsequent element] should be three parts, including the cloth with its lotus-projection.
The one most skilled in ritual design should arrange the third [section] with twenty parts;
the Mahāpadma [lotus] occupies eight parts, and the ambuja [lotus] occupies one part, which is the measure of the eye.
The base (vṛtta) shall consist of five parts, and the upper lotus (ūrdhvāmbuja) shall be one part;
the fillet (kampa) shall be one part, while the ear (karṇa) and the molding (vājana) shall each be three parts.
The pigeon [niche] is fashioned with one part of the *nidrā* and two and a half parts;
it is situated between the two embraces by means of two parts each.
The upward tremor occurs with half a portion when the [total] is thirty parts;
however, it is proclaimed that the birth-portion occurs with twenty-one parts.

With one and a half parts there should be a lotus, with half a part a tremor (kampa), and from a division into seven parts, the base-moulding (jagatī) and the water-lily (kumuda) are made with six parts each, while the neck-ring (aliṅgagama) and the cloth-band (aṃśuka) are made with one part each.
It is stated that the space between [the two] is divided by two parts; the *vājana* (pedestal) for each lotus, however, should be made with one part, adorned with creepers, leaves, and so forth.
When the height is divided by thirty-two, birth occurs at two [units] or on one side;
the *vājana* (pedestal) is said to be a great lotus (*mahāpadma*) consisting of seven parts.
The *karṇa* should be one part, the *padma* one [part], and the circle (*vṛttaka*) four parts; the lotus (*abja*) should be one part, the *kampa* three parts, and the neck (*gala*) three parts.
The *Kampa* [type] occurs with one [unit], and likewise the *Padma* with four;
the *Kapota* with two, and the *Āliṅga* with two parts between [the two]. (54.67)
One part, together with its lotus-base, is adorned with all ornaments;
one part consists of the six birth-portions, and the jagatī is one-eighth of a share.
The *kumuda* should be one part and the *bhāga* a *vetra*; the *kaṇṭha* is proclaimed to consist of three parts.
The *kampama* is one part, the *gala* is three parts, and the *kapotaka* is [three parts]. (54.69)
When the twenty-second degree has been traversed, there shall be one high tremor;
that very same [tremor] shall occur again further on, separated by a single degree.
The *pratiratha* is made with two parts, the *kapotaka* with three parts from the neck,
the *kampa* with one and a half or half a part, and the *mahāpadma* with five parts.
The neck-circle should consist of three parts, with one part for the neck;
the lotus should be one part, and the *kampa* is proclaimed to be one part.
The *pratira* is separated by one part, or the *vājana* by two parts;
the *padma* is said to be from two parts of the *janman*, and the *kampa* by one part.
The *jagatī* should be divided into five parts; the *kumuda* shall consist of four parts (*vedāṃśa*), the *padma* one part, another *padma* one part, and the *kaṇṭha* two parts.
The lotus is formed by one part of the *kampam* section, the *kapotaka* by two parts,
the three-sided [projection] by one part of the *kampam* section, and the *pratī* by two parts.
When the height is divided into twenty-six parts, the base (vājana) is one part;
having set aside three parts for the fillet (prati) and one for the tremor (kampa), other elements are desired by others.
With one part, the lotus; with two parts, the base (kampakam); with four parts, the plinth (jagatī); and the base (kampakam) and the lotus each consist of two parts.
The lotus should be circular with three parts, including one part for the filaments;
likewise, there should be one part for the embrace and one part for the interval.
In the twenty-five-fold [fist], the weight is determined by two parts for each [unit] of the prati;
beginning from one barley grain (*yava*), it increases by one barley grain at a time.
One should calculate an increase or excess of five mātrās for the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna), the base (vastu), the support (ādhāra), and the ground-level (dharātala). || 54.80 ||
"Floor," "paved ground," and "first part"—these are indeed synonyms;
and from the moment of departure on the earth, it remains exactly the same until the lotus [is reached]."
For all types of lotuses, the emergence is considered to be according to their respective [proportions];
for all types of vetra reeds as well, the emergence is one-fourth.
The exit for the great door should be equal to itself, or one-third [of it];
thus it should be completed, or according to the requirements of beauty and strength.
The entry and exit of all the limbs should be made within the *masūraka*;
the *praticchanda* should not be employed anywhere by the wise. (54.84)

The demarcation for the purpose of the door, as well as the absence of the "door of prosperity" (sampaddvāra), is sufficient; in the *liṅgas* of Svāyambhuva and others, the specific architectural style (*praticchanda*) does not constitute a fault. (54.85)
The binding of the feet and the foundation are to be severed as appropriate,
within the five groups beginning with birth, at their respective concluding degrees.
In the case of the beam-component (paṭṭikāṅga), however, it should be inferred in the same way through other foundations;
and now, O best of sages, let the measurement of that foundation be heard.
For the gods it should be four cubits; for the twice-born, it should be equal to that.
For kings it should be three and a half cubits, and for a crown prince, two cubits.
Two cubits are prescribed for merchants and one cubit for a Śūdra;
this is stated here according to caste and according to the nature of the ground.
From the *daṇḍa* [measure], for the killing of six [beings] and for the twelvefold [rite] and so forth,
the desired [height] for the excellent three-tiered [stūpa] is two cubits less one-quarter.
In this case, one should bring the measurement for both the large and the small [units]:
the *masūraka* is five cubits high and thirty-two finger-breadths wide.
Alternatively, it may have a base of thirty finger-breadths, increasing by two finger-breadths at each stage,
reaching thirty-eight finger-breadths at the end, with a width of thirteen finger-breadths.
For the five [mandalas] beginning with Ṣaḍāra, starting from thirty-one finger-breadths,
that [measurement] for the fourteen-hand [mandala] shall be thirty-nine finger-breadths.
In the case of temples measuring three or four cubits, the determination is made according to that same rule;
or else, the measurement for the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is prescribed as one part of the height of the sanctum (ārtotsedha).
The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) may be half of the respective foot's rise diminished by one-sixth or one-eighth, or it may simply be less than the height of the foot. (54.95)
Having set aside the portion from one-third up to the solar portion, the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) should be constructed by means of a part,
or by means of finger-breadths (aṅgula), or even by barley-corns (yava).
One may make it either less or more according to the desire of the builder;
one should act in this very same manner regarding the sixfold group beginning with the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna).
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the procedure for the consecration of the secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), in the great tantra called the *Kāmika*.
The Chapter on the Rules for Measuring the Foot.
Henceforth, O wise ones, I shall explain the measurement of the foot (pāda).
The foot is of two kinds: the sacrificial fire-pit (homa) and the pillar that serves as its support.
A pillar that is concealed by a base (adhiṣṭhāna) is considered a "pillar with a foundation" (nirghātastambha).
Above the height of the foundation, the extension up to the top of the capital (uttarānta) is prescribed.
The height of the foundation pillar (pratistambha) is considered to be eight cubits plus one span (savitasti).
This [calculation] would apply to each level of the twelve stages, one level after another.
One should reduce [the measurement] by one *vitasti* on each level; a height of three *karas* is desired for the first floor.
Following this very sequence, it should be brought down to sixteen stories at the ground level.
For the *dbyantarā* species, a reduction of six *vedāṅgula* is prescribed;
for other species, the reduction is by two or three *aṅgula*. (55.5)
The expansion of the solar day on Tuesday is exactly twenty-eight [nāḍīs];
there is a decrease of two aṅgulas on the earth, and on the earth itself, it is six aṅgulas.
The width of a single pillar-base is considered to be on the surface of the floor;
for all those with two intervening spaces, it is by two or three finger-breadths [more].
When making adjustments for deficiency or excess, one should likewise calculate for the others;
the height of the pedestal (pāda) is double the height of the afflicted base (ārtādhiṣṭhāna).
Alternatively, let the height of the pillar be determined by the measurement of the *ārta* portion;
however, the measurement for the height of the *ārta* [base] should be six, seven, eight, or nine parts. (55/9)
One should determine the height of the pillar as either less or more [than the base];
or else, it may be set at one-eighth, one-ninth, or one-tenth of the pillar's total height.
In all wooden-legged [structures], the width of the pedestal should be one part;
one should then determine the height of the leg as half of that width, or as three or two parts.
The width of a stone pillar should be considered two or three times that of a wall or a [wooden] pillar;
or one may determine the width of a stone pillar as desired.
Starting from one-sixth and extending up to one-twelfth as the limit,
having divided [the height] into parts, the height of the pillar increases by one part for each successive level.
Just as it has been described from the base to the top, so too is the wall considered;
the width of the wall is desired to be two, three, four, or five cubits (daṇḍas). // 55.14 //
The decoration of the pillar is desired to be five or six times [the base], and it is declared to be either square or circular; thus it is proclaimed.
One should know that which is entirely square, provided with a *kumbha* and *maṇḍī*, and pleasing to Brahmā, according to a measurement three times its width.
One should fashion an eight-sided [structure] in the middle, ending with a small vessel;
it should be joined with an eight-sided shape everywhere and provided with a water-pot, a mandala, and so forth.
That which is stepped upon by Viṣṇu is called by its own name; that which is six-cornered is Kaumāra; that which is at its tip is Bhānukānta; and that which has sixteen corners is Candrakāntaka.
At the base, it is square with a measurement equal to the ear; above that, the eastern corners are said to be endowed with the previously mentioned shapes.
That which is circular in every part and pleasing to the Lord is known as the *īśakānta*;
it consists of four or eight sides with a circular perimeter, measured by equal divisions.
That which is accompanied by the *kumbha*, *maṇḍī*, and so forth, is proclaimed as the beloved of Rudra (*rudrakānta*);
that which is joined with the *śuklabheda* is proclaimed as the beloved of Īśa (*īśakānta*). || 55.21 ||
It is called *piṇḍapāda* because of its broad base; it is square at the bottom, but above that it is joined with sixteen sides and so forth. (55.22)
It may be square at its base, with a height equal to twice the width of the pillar;
its upper portion should be wider, and at the base there should be a lotus pedestal (padmāsana).
However, if the remainder of the shape is as desired, it may be a root-lotus seat (mūlapadmāsana);
if the mortar is wide and tall with two or three staffs from its base, [it is likewise].
Above that, there should be a tree with eight sides (an octagon) joined to it, which is the base of the mortar;
its height, however, consists of four parts, marked by lions, serpents, elephants, and spirits.
At the root, it is joined by a man and a woman, endowed with whatever form is desired;
and above that, many feet are considered to be present, each bearing its respective name.
The emergence from the wall for pillars with eight facets is prescribed as half the thickness of the pillar;
for circular ones, it is one-third; and for those with four facets, it is one-fourth.

The *kumbha* is said to be of four kinds: with a quarter [of its height] added, with half added, one and three-quarters [of its height], and double [its height], according to the sequence of their elevations.
Śrīkānta, Brahmakānta, and others are proclaimed as the Moon-beams (candrakānta);
Bhanukānta is said [to be the beam] when it is in its own exaltation Navāṃśaka.
The eye is one part, the neck is four parts on one side, and the mouth is one part;
then the lotus is one part, and its circular base is half a part.
The two [pillars] should be made half as high as the base, measured at double the height of the pillar;
the width of the *kumbha* is prescribed, and its mouth is said to be one and a half times that.
The base and the feet should be broad, while the knees and the feet should be narrower;
the eyes and the neck should be fashioned according to the measurement of the width of the feet.
Endowed with that same width, but twice as great at its base, and slightly diminished at the tip— that shall be the lotus situated below it.
The diameter of the base should be increased by one-eighth, while the height is one-quarter [of that];
this shall be the location of the base at the bottom. Now, the measurement of the shaft (daṇḍa) is stated.
That [altar] is increased by one and a half times three [units], square and equal in length;
having divided it into five parts, the seat for the wooden plank is made with one and a half [parts].
That is said to be equal to the cane (vetra); the remainder should be fashioned as the base (maṇḍī).
The staff-portion (daṇḍākrāra), ending at the cane, should be equal to the foot-portion (pādākāra). || 55/36 ||
The *pālikā* is like a lotus bud, and likewise shaped like a serpent’s hood;
the *maṇḍī* is declared to be of three kinds, and above the base there should be a *potikā*.
It is of three types: the *nāgavṛttā*, the *patracitrā*, and the *samudrormi*;
it measures three times the thickness of the pillar and is joined with the height of the shaft (*daṇḍa*).
The *nāgavṛtta* is proclaimed as being characterized by the projection of shadows;
it has a length equal to four *daṇḍas* and is joined with a rise of three-quarters [of a *daṇḍa*]. (55.39)
It is equipped with leaves for casting shadows, adorned with various leaf-patterns,
five staffs in length, and as high as the measure of a single staff.
Joined with pairs of waves measuring one-fourth [of the total height], and with waves of desired dimensions on both sides, it is known as the *samudrormi* (ocean-wave) [band]. 55.41.
The width of all the *potikās* is equal from base to top;
its height is one-third of that [width], and at its summit there is a fillet (*paṭṭikā*).
O twice-born ones, the *kṣepaṇa* (the base) should be made with half of that [height] again;
one should then determine the length of the shadow to be half of that height, or alternatively, two or three parts.
The tip-decoration is desired to be one-third of its own diameter; it should be provided with a stalk-base, have a level surface, and be adorned with lions, serpents, and other such figures. 55/44.
That which is placed above the clenched-fist shape, or adorned with serpents and the like, is proclaimed as the *nāgavṛttā* among the eastern triangles and squares. (55.45)
In all types of *atihāra* movements, the *patracitrā* is proclaimed;
likewise, for other [movements], the *samudrormi* is considered the foot and the *phalaka*.
The *śikhā* (spire) shall be one part out of three or four parts of the width;
from one cubit up to five cubits, it increases by six finger-breadths at each stage.
The space between pillars should be employed as either odd or even;
in a temple intended for all regions, all the intervals between pillars should be equal.
If the section of the pillar is uneven, the building will quickly perish;
therefore, one should have all of that constructed in the proper manner in the evening as well.
The pillars for the gods are made of stone, while those for others are not so prescribed; all pillars should be constructed by the wise using bricks or wood.
For the gods, even numbers are preferred, while for humans, odd numbers are considered appropriate.
Internal pillars, external pillars, and straight pillars are all regarded as equal [in their application].
Furthermore, the base (adhiṣṭhāna), the plinth (pāda), the wall (bhitti), and that which is known as the lintel (uttara) [are likewise to be arranged accordingly].
