The *tulā-jayantī* is proclaimed, and that which is known as the "shadow" (*chāyā*) is celebrated.
Whatever object is superior to these is remembered as the "subtle body" (*tanukāya*).
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the "Ritual for the Measurement of the Foot," in the great tantra named *Kāmika*.
The Chapter on the Ritual for Spreading the Grass Mat.
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of rules for the sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara),
including the upper reed (uttara), the lower reed (vājana), the fist-binding (muṣṭibandha), and the lotus-stalk (mṛṇālika).
The staff, the circle, the small coverings for concealment,
the embrace, and the intervening space— these are the ornaments for each limb in successive order.

One should join [the parts] one above the other by means of three parts, one and a half parts, one part, five parts, one part, two parts, three parts, and one part; and by means of three parts and one part. || 56/3 ||
These are the components of the *prastāra*, and the subsequent [analysis] is of three kinds: the *khaṇḍottara*, the *patrabandha*, and the *rūpottara*, O twice-born ones.
It should be known as the Khaṇḍottara, which is twice the width of the base, endowed with an equal elevation,
and possesses a height of one-quarter [of its width].
That which is released from the width of the foot and bound with leaf-patterns is known as *patrabandha*.
Here, *rūpottara* is said to have a height of half [the width] and a width of one foot. (56.6)
The projection of the corner (karṇanirgama) should be three-quarters, or half minus one-third, or half the measurement;
its form is like a svastika or a nandyāvarta.
Alternatively, the placement of the response may follow the *sarvatobhadra* layout;
it should be joined with the previously mentioned height, and its width should be measured from its base.
Alternatively, one may conceive of it as joined with the tips of the feet of the *chandas* [verse], combined with an emergence and ascent of three or four parts of that height. (56.9)
The pedestal (vājana) may be square or lotus-shaped, positioned above the upper part;
it may be elongated by three, four, five, or six daṇḍas, or half, or three-quarters [of that length]. || 56/10 ||
Its width and height should be equal, and it should be fashioned with the decoration of a small boat;
above that, there should be a lotus-stalk motif complete with its stalk and bud.
Between the *tulā* and the *avalīkā*, the pillar should be like the earth or like a person; its width should be one-third of its height, and its breadth should be half of that, less a quarter.
A great balance (tulā) should be constructed specifically above the rafters;
the Jayantī [beam] should be situated atop the balance, equal in width, length, and height to the balance.

The *sthānamārga* (stationary path) is provided with half a *daṇḍa* and a *ghana* [in thickness], with a height of one and a half [units] and an equal belly; it is located above the *jayantī*. The *uttara* (northern gate), however, should extend sideways. || 56.14 ||
The *vājana* beams are declared to follow the path of the scales everywhere;
the *jayantī* and *vaṃśaka* rafters should be known to follow the path like the face of the scales. (56.15)
The *prastara* (beam), the *pādaviṣkambha* (supporting pillar), and the *tridaṇḍa* (triple staff) should be half a *daṇḍa* in length;
or alternatively, between the *tulā* and the *avalīkā*, it may be two *daṇḍas*.
Alternatively, one may construct the Jayantī and the Uttara [shelters] with a single staff's interval;
however, by increasing the measurement by one foot at a time, one should arrange them up to three staffs.
In the same way, an interval is prescribed between the paths;
one may cause it to be made either joined with a path or even devoid of one.
Then, having covered it above according to one's strength and for the sake of beauty, it should be made solid with wood or bricks according to one's capacity. (56.19)
Alternatively, Bali may take the form of a swan, or sleep with his body bent like a staff,
or he may be placed upon a mirror with three-quarters of him visible.
One should fashion the *kapota* (dove-cot) externally above the *vājana*;
its projection and elevation should be one and a half, two, or three *daṇḍas*.
It may have a staff measuring half or three-quarters [of the height], or it may be supported by pigeons (kapota);
having placed it above the northern part, it should be positioned above that base (vājana).
Or, with an interval separated by a balance-beam,
it is said that starting from half a *daṇḍa* and increasing by a quarter *daṇḍa* at each step, it extends up to three *daṇḍas*.
The thickness of the steps is desired to be one-half, one-quarter, one-third, or one-eighth [of the height];
one should cover the perimeter with planks having widths of one-fourth, one-eighth, one-sixth, or one-eighth [of the step's width].
O best of the twice-born, one should place pillars upon that [foundation], with their shapes and dimensions as desired, and cover it with iron clods or earthen clods.
The projection of the *daṇḍikā* should extend from the same point as the projection of the steps;
the *daṇḍikā* should be half the width of a foot, and its thickness should be half of that.
It is endowed with a staff, broad, and half of that [measure] joined with a neck;
the decorated limb possesses a stalk and is joined with the emergence of the staff.
The wise man should fashion a separate "fist-clench" (muṣṭibandha) upon the base of the pillar,
or he may fashion it with a "scale-cut" (tulāccheda) joined to the broad upper part of the pillar.
The wise one should lead the body-quarter, which is half of that [measurement] and provided with an exit, along with its own front fillet, into the space between the staff and the threshold.
The space between the body and the feet should be covered with planks made of solid wood,
provided with handles and grips at the ends, and joined together with iron.
It extends for three-quarters of the staff's length and possesses a density of half of that half;
it has the shape of an elephant's head and is provided with a frontal globe (*kumbha*) and a neck-base (*maṇḍī*). (56.31)
Adornments should be fashioned between the staff and the fist-binding, provided with heads at the top and bottom and endowed with various types of movement. (56.32)
One should visualize a lion with a mane of tigers and other beasts in the center,
having the form of a clenched fist and a square shape.
It should be as wide and high as desired, with its entrance measuring half its height; above the *daṇḍika* there should be a *valaya*, and above that, the *gopana*.
Having abandoned the remaining conceit, the wise man should offer his protection above the sacrificial ground,
whether it be Vasantaka, Ālinda, or Vidheya.
The height of the three-footed [pedestal] should be above that, and the height of the *kapota* (dove-niche) should be as before;
thus it shall be firm, whether constructed of stone, brick, or wood.
The wise should apply the stability of the practice accordingly:
either one-third of the height of a pigeon, or a quarter, or a small *nidraka*.
The *kapotanāsikā* (dove-nose) is situated above the small *nīvra*;
it possesses a *karṇikā* and is provided with a width of one and a half *daṇḍas*, or two *daṇḍas* including the base.
For one whose ears, crest, and liṅga are adorned with lion-patterns, a band should be fashioned in the shape of a svastika above the nose. 56.39.
The measurement for the *kukṣikā* and other parts, or whatever is aesthetically pleasing, should be made;
the construction of the *karṇikā* is like a beautiful, swaying creeper shaken by the wind.
Above the *prativājana* (the counter-stone), the elevation of the *nāsikā* (nose-moulding) is not desired;
it should be provided with a thickness of one-quarter of a *pāda*, and its projection should be one *pāda*.
The *āliṅga* should be situated above that; it is considered to be separated from that by an interval.
Its width should be half a *pāda*, and the front fillet (*agrapaṭṭikā*) is formed by the removal of half [of that].
When one foot has entered within another foot, it is called *pādabāhyaka*;
it takes the form of a foot and is joined with an elevation equal to half of three feet.

One should fix the *prati* (pedestal) for it using one-third or one-fourth [of the height]; immediately after that, the *vājana* (top-ornament) should be made with one-quarter [of the height]. Thus it is stated.
If all that [universe] were subject to rising and falling, it would lead to the destruction of the lineage of the gods;
indeed, there would be a transformation of the gods, as well as of the twice-born and the kings. (56.45)
O best of the twice-born, for the other two [deities], a reflection resembling a half-moon should be fashioned;
one should extend the projection of the staff by one-quarter or one-and-a-half [of its length].
O best of the twice-born, one should determine the deficiency or excess of the limbs of the *prastara* by means of one, two, three, or four *yava*s in measure. (Page 144)
One should likewise apply it to the toes and to the *masūraka* on the neck.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Prastara [Diagram], in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for Adorning the Temple.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the ornamentation of the temple:
there should be a stone-paved floor at the base, and at the root of the neck (grīvā) section, there should be a pedestal (vedikā).
The first [type of wall] is one and a half [parts], extending up to three *daṇḍas* in width;
its height may be six, seven, eight, or ten [parts], and the moat should be equal in size to that. || 57.2 ||
The altar-platform (vedikā), topped with a stone slab, should have a height double that of each successive elevation;
and below the neck (grīvā), it should be stable, extending for one-third of the height of the neck.
In the division of five and seven parts, two or three parts constitute the height of the pinnacle and its binding;
the remainder shall be the section of the lower pillar, and the wall shall possess a width equal to one-fourth [of the total].
Its foot is the quarter-measure (pādanirveśa), or indeed six, seven, or eight parts;
having made the binding fourfold, one should cause the shaking with one part. || 57/5 ||
Above that, however, the *nidrā* (sleep) should be two parts, while the *vājana* (fillet) should be one part;
or, in a five-part division, the *nidrā* should be one quarter and the *vājana* should consist of three or two parts.
One should fashion the *nidrā* with half a *kaṃpa*, the *kaja* with one and a half [units] from the half,
and the *vājana* with half a portion of a *kaṃpa*.
When the height is twenty-two parts, the *karṇa* (ear) is twelve parts;
likewise, the *nidrā* (sleep) is one part, and the *kapota* (dove-cornice) is four parts. (57.8)
Above that, there should be one *vājana*, and likewise the *karṇa* should consist of two parts;
above that, the *nidrā* should be fashioned, provided with six *paṭṭas*.
When the height is twenty-two parts, the *karṇa* (diagonal) shall be twelve;
the *vājana* (projection) shall be one part, the *nidrā* (resting part) one, and the *vājana* three.
The lotuses of the neck should be like those [of the face], and the ears should be two parts;
in that height of sixteen parts, the neck is desired to be nine parts.
The *vājana* is one part, and likewise sleep (*nidrā*) is three parts;
the *paṭṭapadma* is one part, and the *padma* is said to be one part. (57.12)
O best of the twice-born, one must not cut [trees] for the sake of a railing or a lattice;
however, they may be cut as is appropriate for the purpose of a door or a temple.
The rule regarding the altar (vedī) is not intended for a temple that serves all regions;
thus has the altar been described. Now, O twice-born ones, let the door be heard.
In the region of the pillar, [the height] is divided into nine, eight, or seven parts, and the door occupies one part;
its height should be half of that, and this is the width in the temple.
The *nālī* chamber shall be one-third, one-half, or one-ninth or one-fifth [of the width];
its height shall be thirty-five units; this indeed is the specific rule.
The width has been indicated as before; alternatively, it is described thus:
the breadth should be three spans (vitasti) and the length seven spans.
From that [measurement], by increasing the width and length by increments of six and twelve finger-breadths respectively,
[the altars] range from three and five units up to six spans (vitasti).
The twenty-five measures are indeed the heights of the door-arches; of these, twelve are for the bedchamber and twelve for the main house. (57.19)
The wise have declared those same [measures] for threshing floors that are enclosed;
for cities, villages, and forts, as well as for other dwellings, the remaining [measures] have been prescribed.
The width should be twice the height, or it may be six units more, or even nine units more; this is declared for all [temples]. (57.21)
One should employ a measure of six mātrās with two tālas, two tālas with three mātrās,
a small measure of two tālas, and one and a half tālas.

A house for Brahmins and the other castes is considered auspicious when its height is twice its own width, or six *mātrās*, or three *mātrās*; however, even less than that is deemed favorable. (57.23)
In the eighth part of the pillar's height, the length of the door is six and a half [parts];
in its half, at the ninth part, the elevation is eight and a half parts.
A door that is twice the height of its threefold width is not desired for a human dwelling;
on the ground, it should be constructed according to the height of one's own feet, and this rule applies specifically to the ground level.
It may be increased by one, three, or five *aṅgulas* beyond the stated height;
likewise, even in a large [shrine], it should be so, or by six, seven, or eight parts.
On both sides of the door, however, there should be a pair of decorated pillars;
this ornamentation should be made for all dwellings as well.
Having specifically divided the measure by its own parts, one should calculate the *māna* that has attained its rise, excluding the cutting off of fingers and so forth. (57.28)

And with eight, nine, and three; with eight, nine, four, and four; with three, two, five, ten, ten, and the directions (ten); with the forms (eleven), the constellations (twenty-seven), and seven, nine, and three degrees.
Having subtracted the *māya* and the *vyaya*, the remainder that is the *vāraka*;
the remaining *aṃśakas* are to be calculated by the teachers (*deśikas*).
One should properly place a pillar between the two sides of the site, having left a space on both its sides for the purpose of extending it toward the wall. (57.31)
The main gate is on its left, while the shaking gate is on the other;
and the shaking gate is in the middle, provided with many [features] for the sake of yoga.
One should construct the *kampa* (moulding) at equal intervals, or otherwise as it appears beautiful;
the door of the *kampa* should be appropriately placed on the three sides of the root-base (*mūlavāstu*).
If one does not vacate a gateway that is shaking, situated at the edge of a wall and supported by pillars, its owner will meet his death.
The width of the pedestal is considered to be one and a half times the width of the pillar, or equal to the width of the pillar, or even half of that; this is generally accepted.
Alternatively, one-third [of the height] below the top is the *pratīka*; that is its own base (*svavājana*).
For the rising of the door, the remainder is divided into either three or five parts.
One part or two parts shall be the ornamentation from below upwards;
with the remainder, one should fashion the ornamentation for the middle, which is the pure doorway.
Above the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalaka), creepers and other ornaments are considered appropriate all around;
[the width of] the pillars is determined by a division of three, four, five, or six parts.
It is said that there should be many door-panels, or their thickness may be half a *daṇḍa*;
odd-numbered planks are to be used, avoiding a joint in the middle. (57.39)
It is prescribed that [the ornament] should be placed either above the bed's decoration or on its exterior;
having left out the middle, it should be applied according to one's strength.
The staffs of this [palace] with a floor-thickness of one unit have widths that are half, double,
or three times that thickness, numbering three, five, seven, nine, and eleven [units] respectively.
Or having the luster of a horse’s shoulder or hoof, or resembling an *aśvattha* leaf, [these are found] on a large double bed and on a door-panel situated on the right side. (57.42)
When the width and the length have been divided into three parts and five parts respectively,
one should discard the upper third and the lower part on both sides.
Among those, the gate which is here called the Maṇidvāra is strengthened with iron bands according to its strength and its beauty.
With glorious primary [arrows], left-handed staffs, slings, and jointed arrows; likewise with crescent-shaped arrows, horn-tipped arrows, and various kinds of flower-arrows.
It is adorned with the bolts that secure the yogic bonds and with deities and other ornaments;
its base and summit are joined by peaks extending from top to bottom.
One should bind [the head] with bands made of gold or other materials at the ankles, the forehead joint, or indeed all over the body, according to one's beauty and strength. (57.47)
Its shoulder-band was as thick and dense as a mattress, twice as wide [as the staff],
its surface variegated with lotus petals, and fashioned from fine cloth.
The charming Manoharā should be placed on the couch to the right of the entrance;
the bolt is on the right side, while the couch itself is on the left side.
The door-panel, however, should be made from a single tree; the distinction between the outer and inner parts has been specified—having understood this, one should perform the ritual work. (57/50)
A pair of door-panels is prescribed for the temples of the gods, the twice-born, and kings; for the other two [classes], one is indicated, while at the great gate there are four panels.
A pair of door-panels should be fashioned, equipped with many chains, adorned with numerous earrings, and fitted with a *kokila* bolt.
Whether on a stone slab or a wall, one should construct a doorframe that has either entered or emerged [from the surface],
using various kinds of mechanical contrivances.
A door that creaks should not be desired; even if it is superior, it should be treated in that same way.
A door is perfected by its doorway, which is said to be like the form of a street and so forth.
O Śiva and the twice-born, if the temple is already established, the desired door [should be placed] such that,
having constructed the wall, there are fifty [units] inside and thirty-two outside.
Having reduced it by seven parts, or by four or three parts, it is called the inner yoga;
or else, the expansion of the yoga may be by means of exactly three finger-breadths.
By increasing the measurement by one finger-width (aṅgula) at each joint, the distance between the tips of the fingers is thirty-two finger-widths;
this is declared to be the "full" measure as before, or it is said to be one-quarter [of the next size].
Having established the height of the door from five parts up to eleven parts,
that measurement reduced by one part is declared here as the pure (śuddha) door.
In that regard, the measurement exceeding [the previous] by two units is suitable for the deity;
thus the door has been fully described. Now, O twice-born ones, hear concerning the archway (toraṇa).

The width of the archway (toraṇa) is considered to be three, four, or five times the thickness of its pillar; or else, it may be one-quarter, one-and-a-half, or two-thirds of that [pillar's thickness]. (57/60)
Alternatively, the width of the archway pillar may be half a pāda;
its height, measured from the northern edge, should be divided into nine, eight, or ten parts.
One-third of the height of the main pillar (maulikotsedha) shall be above and below the vīrakāṇḍa;
the capital (uttara) should be three daṇḍas, and the base-ring (vājana) should be half of that.
The fillet (paṭṭikā) here is said to be equal to the northern [part];
the molding (vājana) above should be half of that; all of this is eternal.
The archway (toraṇa) is of three kinds: the leaf-archway (patratoraṇa), which is adorned with sea-monsters (makara), and the variegated archway (citratoraṇa); now their ornamentation is described.
The leaf-arch is adorned with leaves resembling the young moon;
it is joined by the mouths of two makaras, with the space between them filled.
This makara-archway is adorned with various kinds of creepers;
it fills both sides as well as the middle between them.
And with the tusks, beaks, and trunks emerging from the mouths of those two,
as well as with Vidyādharas, Bhūtas, lions, elephants, serpents, and swans.
With *vāla*, *sragdaṇḍaka*, and other various *maṇibandha* ornaments,
this should be a variegated archway (*citratoraṇa*) for the gods, O best of kings.

In the caves, there should be images and the like; the pedestals should be adorned with all their limbs, square, octagonal, or circular in shape, and provided with pot-shaped bases (kumbha), ornaments, and so forth.
They are proclaimed to be either accompanied by a *potikā* or separated from it;
one should make the support extend down to the *utsandhi*, shaped like the back of a crocodile.
Beginning with a single *daṇḍa* and increasing by half a *daṇḍa* at each step,
the measurement up to four *daṇḍas* is prescribed for entering the cave.
The deities are to be installed in the caves on all sides of the temple;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is in the south, and that which arises from the Liṅga is to its west.
The best of preceptors should place Brahmā in the northern region,
and Vighneśa in the form of a dancer in the half-maṇḍapa at the third part.
To the north of Durgā, one should place Rudra, or according to the universal rule,
one may install him in various forms or even as a single form everywhere.

One should perform [the rite] precisely according to the method described for the characteristics of the image; one should likewise perform it for the deities on each tier and also on the neck. (57.75)
In some cases, there is this distinction: one should first place Subrahmaṇya, or else one should install Indra joined with his vehicle, or in the form of Rudra.
One should place the two door-keepers on both sides of the door;
two caves should be fashioned on both sides of the door.
The northern end should be high like a cave, or it may be prescribed as level in the middle;
and having left the exterior of the cave, one should station the door-keepers there.
Alternatively, the deities may be installed on an altar constructed with an external wall;
Nandin should be placed on the right, and Mahākāla on the left.
Or there may be a reversal of those two: either at the eastern gate with a western face, or joined with a southern face, or likewise with a northern face.
One should place eight gatekeepers in the four-gated enclosure;
whichever direction the door faces, one should designate that as the east.
Alternatively, one should designate the east as the direction of the sun's rising;
in all cases, the tube in the north should face toward the moon.
The water-channel (praṇāla) is prescribed to be either in the northeast or in the east;
thus the water-channel is described, especially in the middle of the lotus.
A door-architrave (dvāratoraṇa) is desired either at the neck or at the location of the doorway;
it should be equal in height to the door, with the distance between the two pillars being one-third of that height.
With nine auspicious objects arranged in ascending order,
there is a five-faced board above which is joined with a trident.
The painted banner of Citraketu, the Śrī-bherī drum, the pitcher, the lamp, and the Nandyāvarta— these are the eight auspicious emblems (aṣṭamaṅgala) of all the gods.
The drum, the bull, the elephant, the two chowries, the lion, the fish, the banner, and the lamp— these are the eight auspicious symbols of the gods.
The mirror, the full water-jar, the bull,
the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp constitute the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala).
Banners, svastikas, conchs, a full water-pot together with a lotus,
an umbrella, the goddess Lakṣmī, and lamps— these are the eight auspicious signs for the twice-born.
A banner, a full water-pot, a conch, a discus, a lotus, a goad,
an umbrella, and a lamp— these are the eight auspicious signs of kings.
A full water-pot, a lamp, sandals, a parasol,
a pair of drums, two auspicious Nandikas, and a great conch shell— these are the eight auspicious signs for Vaiśyas.
A mirror, a full water-pot, a plow, a pair of fish,
a lamp, an umbrella, and a drum— these are the eight auspicious objects for Śūdras.
The archway known as Makara is prescribed for gods, the twice-born, and kings;
however, the archway named Citra is ordained for Vaiśyas.

For a Śūdra, the archway known as Padma is prescribed; it may be made entirely of this material everywhere, or it is desired that the lattice-work, the beam, the stone, the brickwork, and the wall be composed of it. (57.94)
A wall is considered to be provided with many lattice-windows;
it is so called when lattices are placed within the intervals between pillars.
It may be covered with planks made of heartwood,
consisting entirely of such planks, or it may have a wall-structure with lotus-shaped projections above and below.
A wall made of stone or brick, endowed with appropriate proportions, rising to its full height or reaching only halfway, and completed either to the top or including the base; 57/97.
Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, a wall made even of clay is desired;
upon that wall, at the base of the pillar, one should fashion a creeper above the support of the vessel.
Above and below the vedikā, the [arrangement] of the kūṭas, koṣṭhas, and so forth is remembered as threefold:
the first is the citrakumbha-latā, and the other is the stambhakumbha-latā.
And another type is the *kumbhakumbhalatā*; their characteristic is now described:
at the base of the *kumbhakumbhalatā*, the width is twice that of the stalk (*daṇḍa*).
The height shall be one and a quarter, or one and a half, or one and three-quarters, or even one and a half times the base; or it may be half of that [base]. || 57.101 ||

The lotus at the feet should be positioned above the base, with its stalk extending horizontally; it should be supported by a *nandyāvarta* motif, and the emergence of the feet should be from the *kumbha*.
(Verse 103) At that time, the emergence of the petals from the mouth-portion shall be one-third of a third part;
and for the lotuses and other [flowers], the measurement of the *kampātī* follows the strength of the beauty.
The winding of the creeper is desired to extend from the pitcher (kalaśa) to half the height of the pillar.
Above the pitcher, the work consists of the star-patterns (tārā), the crocodile-leaf garland (nakrapatrāvalī), and the pillar.
Desirous of the two sides of the foot, she is adorned with every limb of the feet;
like a pearl situated between shells, she is spread across the expanse of another beauty.
The hall of pillars should be spacious, and its width should be equal to that of the pillars;
its decoration should be adorned with the ornamentation of creepers as appropriate.
Emerging from the wall, she takes the foremost place in the garland of forms;
her manner of exit and entrance should be performed according to what is beautiful.
In the center, bounded by the foremost petals, is liberation with its stalk and bondage;
it is variegated with lotus-patterns extending from foot to foot.
In the middle, on both sides of the *gratī*, [the measurement] extends up to the limit of its equal rising;
above the fist-bind (*muṣṭibandha*), it reaches as far as the serpent (*vyāla*) and up to the pinnacle (*kalaśa*).
The legs are like those of a striped beast, elevated and adorned with leaf-patterns;
at the heart is a lotus joined with a lotus, and above that is the binding of men.
All of that is recited up to the edge of the *phalaka*;
the earth [is described] up to the *vīrakāṇḍa*, and above that is the *nakrapaṭṭikā*.
The *lasanmakarakāṇḍa* (the shimmering crocodile-shaft) should have a band of emerging serpents;
above the crocodile-mouth, it is filled out like a head-binding (*maulibandha*).
Above his crest-jewel, one should depict Vāyu;
or alternatively, one should have Bhūta, who is like a heated conch, fashioned below the north.
Just as a beautiful creeper with all its parts intact is called a "kumbhalatā," so too would it be a "citrakumbhalatā"; otherwise, it would be a "stambhakumbhalatā. (57.114)
Above the pillar, there is a lotus-seat with a width double that of the pillar;
there is a fillet supporting the lotus, and above the lotus, another fillet.
The Kumbhakumbhalatā [mudrā] is considered to have fifteen branches (three, five, and seven), to be seated upon a noble lotus,
and to be marked by an overflowing pitcher placed above.
Then, standing in the lotus posture (padmāsana), there is a pillar for throwing [the body] upwards;
its limbs extend as far as the sword and other implements, and above that is like a full water-jar (pūrṇakumbha).
The pitcher (kumbha) should have oblique petals and be joined with petal-ornaments;
the pillar, pitcher, and creeper (latā) should be of this nature, and other elements should be inferred in the same way.
Thus the Kumbhalatā meter is described; the Vṛttasphaṭika is said to consist of six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, and sixteen mātrās respectively.
Emerging by one and a half Vyāsas or two-thirds [of the width], it should be circular and equal; or, like the leg of a torana, it may be elongated, consisting of two parts.
Above that, however, is the neck (sakandhara), adorned with a śukanāsa;
it is said here to be circular and made of crystal, adorned with celestial dwellings.
The pedestal and the two necks (galas) shall occupy seven parts of the upper base;
the spire (śikhara) shall be three parts, and the emergence of the finial (sthūpyudaya) shall be one part. || 57/122 ||
The measurement for the gables, inner chambers, and niches is proclaimed here;
all parts of the gables, inner chambers, and so forth should be projected outward from the central axis-line (mānasūtra). 57/123.
However, entering [the site] from inside the measurement-line bestows all defects;
[the shapes are] square, octagonal, sixteen-sided, and circular.
This is considered the Karṇakūṭa [type], which is provided with a stūpa-like pinnacle at its summit;
it is joined with a nose in the middle and endowed with half a koṭi [of cubits]. (57.125)
Equipped with a face-band and provided with two shafts, the central chamber should be endowed with numerous finials. 57/126.
O twice-born ones, the cage is fashioned with a shape resembling a swan’s beak at the back, and like a needle-point at the front; there is an interval between the two peak-chambers.
That same [shape] with a side-facing mouth is desired as the elephant trunk (hastituṇḍa), which is circular;
this is declared to be the sequence of types, provided with the ear-cavity (karṇakoṣṭha).
In the center is a peak (kūṭa), and between those two, it is adorned with small cells (kṣudrakoṣṭha) and so forth;
this is declared to be the *chanda* meter, whether it be a peak or a cell.
That which is accompanied by an internal layer, or is either depressed or elevated, is designated as "conceptualization" (vikalpa); it is an appearance mixed with that [object]. (57.130)
A celestial mansion endowed with the distinctions of caste and so forth is the abode of prosperity;
it is certain that in the opposite case, it leads to destruction. (57.131)
The nose is to be known as eightfold; at its beginning is that which is named "Lion" (siṃha), another is the "Half-Pañjara," and the third is considered the "Pañjara. (57.132)
The fifth is the penthouse with a hanging nose;
the sixth should be the lion-ear, followed by the broken penthouse.
There may be another type called the Jhaṣapañjara; its characteristics are now described:
it has closely joined porticoes and towers, is spacious, and possesses symmetrical projections. (57.134)
The lion-cage is provided with a panel at the front joined by a banner and a trident, adorned with a pedestal, lattices, and pillars. (57.135)
O twice-born ones, it should be provided with three to fourteen prongs, be broad, possess a suitable length, and have two needle-like feet. (57.136)
One should employ the middle of all the enclosures for the temple,
which is closely joined to the palace, very lofty, and half-extending outward.

It is endowed with the five components beginning with the base (adhiṣṭhāna), possessing the banner of power (śaktidhvaja), provided with a face-band (mukhapaṭṭikā), and equipped with a pedestal and lattice-work (vedikājālakā). || 57/138 ||
The half-pañjara is prescribed as being provided with ears and feet;
it is joined with the *vipula* as before and endowed with the protrusion of the feet.
Or else, the cage may extend out by one-third [of its height] and resemble a round crystal; the remainder here is declared to be as previously described.

This penthouse-lattice (niryūhapañjara) is joined at its top with a crest (śikhā) corresponding to itself, has its corners firmly attached to the limbs, and is connected with the pigeon-hole (kapota) and other architectural members. 57.141.
The head has its ears and feet closely joined, forming the surface of a serpent; it is devoid of a frontal protrusion (niryūha), possesses all its limbs, and has a long nose. || 57.142 ||
That very [hair] which has a crest resembling the mane of a lion,
being unobstructed at the face and resting upon the ear-base, is called "lion-ear" (siṃhaśrotra).
In its width, it should be one-fifth [of the total], provided with a projection of two parts;
below the *nīvrā*, its form is adorned with *kapota* (dove-cots) and other such elements.
Having correctly understood the "Khaṇḍaniryūha" by name, one should employ it:
[with] staffs, the ends of staffs, exits, and those that are dense below and above. (57.145)
O twice-born ones, when it is provided with limbs such as pigeons and the like, and the neck is adorned with arches, this is known by name as the eighth type, the *jhaṣapañjara*.

On the high [pedestal] situated between the other bases, which is divided into five parts, the plinth (pāda) shall consist of two parts including the base-moulding (sāṅghri), and the emergence of the entablature (prastara) shall be half [of that]. || 57.147 ||
That is said to be equal to the neck; the remaining portion is the middle peak.
Having placed the section above, one should fashion the head with that.

One should construct the base (adhiṣṭhāna) beneath the pillar with a measurement equal to half the height of the pillar, or increased by one-eighth of that; the remainder shall be the pedestal (upapīṭhaka).
Thus has the measurement for all the enclosures (pañjara) been declared;
between the two upper platforms (pādukā), there is a pedestal (upapīṭhaka) consisting of one-ninth [of the total height].
The *masūraka* should be two parts, and the height of the pillar twice that;
the height of the entablature (*prastara*) should be one and a half parts, and the elevation of the pedestal (*vedikā*) one part.
That which begins from the north and ends at the pigeon (kapota) is called the "arising of the stalk" (nālodaya);
it is joined with the form of a cage and extends out from the pigeon.
In accordance with what is beautiful and what is appropriate, this pigeon-cot (kapotapañjara), endowed with a spear and a banner, should indeed be placed on a temple that faces all directions.
In the center, it should have an extension of two, three, or four walls with equal projections;
it may be shaped like a hall or an assembly hall, and be surrounded by a temple and a pinnacle.

Alternatively, that which is surrounded by great arches (mahāvāra) and features a pinnacle situated upon a necklace (hāra) is called the "Brahma-door" (brahmadvāra), the eternal form for temples (vimāna).
The archway (toraṇa) should be as wide as a single wall; its supporting beams (bhārakas), adorned with banners, should extend outward and be provided with rafters (lupas) equal to their width.
It is joined with the great enclosure (mahāvāraka) and provided with a hall (śālā), a courtyard (udyataka), and a well (kūpa);
it has a width of two or three cubits for the womb-chamber (garbha), and at each opening there is a parrot-nose (śukanāsā).
A nose should not be made on the upper part of the vimāna, nor should there be a [separate] nose;
the first window should follow the sequence of straight lattices, such as the gavākṣa and the kuñjarākṣaka.
Cow’s urine, the leaf of the *gaṇikā*, and the *nandyāvarta*— these seven,
when arranged straight and accompanied by a tremor, are called the "straight lattice" (*ṛjujālaka*). (57.159)
When the ear is described as a "window" (gavākṣa) because it reaches to the ears, that same [ear] arising from the four [directions] is known as "elephant-eye" (kuñjarākṣa). // 57.160 //
The gaze directed toward the intermediate directions is celebrated as "cow's urine" (gomūtra).
The root [of the gaze] is also at the tip of the ball, resting within the interior of a soft wall.
A lattice-work of reeds (*gaṇikājālaka*) consists of various interconnected holes; a lattice-work of leaves (*patrajālaka*) is desired when the holes are decorated with leaf-patterns. (57.162)
The opening situated within the five threads, following a clockwise sequence, is called the *nandyāvarta*; one should lead the lattice-work above the altar.
In the case of the *svāyambhuva* and other types of liṅgas, however, one should apply the measurement according to one's desire,
excluding the middle portion between the wall and the base, and extending up to the end of the seven staffs (*daṇḍa*).
Beginning with a single staff and increasing by twice the width,
the height of the *kampocca* (the upper part) should be one and a half times that, or perhaps increased by one-eighth.
Having abandoned the middle foot-space, it is joined with the movement of the even and odd feet;
from the center of the wall, it extends outward, provided with pillars, junctions, and door-panels.

Either a single pair of door-panels or those capable of being both closed and opened should be placed in the section for the feet; the placement of the window should be in the section for the neck. (57.167)
One should fashion the stairway for the purpose of ascending;
the base is declared to be of three kinds: square, circular, and rectangular.
The conch-shaped mandala (śaṅkhamaṇḍala) should be made fourfold and divided into three sections;
above it, the creeper-shaped mandala (vallīmaṇḍala) is provided with cow's urine.
It may have three sections, or it may be two-sectioned with half at the base;
that which tapers gradually from the base to the tip is desired as a conch-staircase (śaṅkhasopāna).
There may be a circular enclosure of creepers, functioning like a creeper that climbs a tree;
its width shall be twice or four times the width of a horse's hoof.
Therefore, by increasing the measurement by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) up to thirty-two years of age,
the width of the sleeping plank is declared to be six finger-breadths.
Starting from double [the width] and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time, the length should extend up to fifteen times [the width], or it may be according to one's desire.
The *śayitavya*, *āsapādārdha*, and *tripādasadṛśodaya* [types of staircases], as well as the *hastisopānaka*, *lājasopāna*, and that known as *vṛddhi*, [are described]. (57.174)
An equal division is declared to be "sama"; the combination of such divisions is "samāgama.
One should employ a width of one cubit, ranging from a single staff (daṇḍa) up to three staffs.
That foot and that mass are said to be according to one's strength, or otherwise; the stairs, being odd in number, should be led in a clockwise sequence.
One should apply the staircase at the front of both sides of its base;
that base shall be the *adhiṣṭhāna* (pedestal), provided with the proportions of the plinth and the floor-slab.
Standing upon the hoof of a horse and ascending with the right foot—
such a staircase, endowed with these characteristics, is the very seat of prosperity.
The wise man should fashion the water-channel either to the north or to the east;
however, he should not apply the channel outside the fivefold group beginning with birth.
The stalk may be at the edge of the band, or there may be a hole;
beginning from five finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
One should determine the length of the tube to be thirty-six finger-breadths, beginning from three finger-breadths and increasing by half a finger-breadth [at each stage]. (57.181)
One should fashion each tube from the tube [preceding it] up to a length of twenty-four finger-breadths;
they should be equal, or their middle portion may be three-quarters [of that length], with a thick opening in the center.
In two or three parts, one should arrange one part; or in four or five parts, two parts;
or in six or seven parts, three parts; or one may likewise arrange four parts.
Its depth should likewise be such that it becomes slightly curved at the top;
one should determine its depth from the base to be one-fifth, one-third, or one-half [of the height].
Alternatively, one should determine the tip by means of a portion within the section for the binding;
it may be fashioned as falling from the mouths of lions and other such creatures, or it may be fashioned as purely simple.
The height of the *bhāga* should be two or three parts, endowed with all its members;
it is devoid of a *potikā* and is joined above the *vīrakāṇḍa*.
The upper vessel has a lotus-protrusion and a recessed base; above that should be a fish-stalk, adorned with various diverse patterns. (57.187)
That which is joined with the form of an archway, possesses a neck adorned with lotus stalks, and is furnished with all ornaments is declared to be a pillar-archway (stambhatōraṇa). // 57.188 //

One should construct [the gateway] either at the end of the foot, or within the foot, or in the middle of the *karṇaprāsāda*, or in the interval between the middle of the hall, in all types of temples.
Having made the height of the base (mūlapāda) one-eighth [of the total],
it should be provided with the six sections beginning with the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna), just like the main sanctuary (mūladhāma).
One should construct a small vimāna within the space between the pillars;
it may take whatever form Śiva possesses—whether with parts (sakala), without parts (niṣkala), or a mixture of both.
The form of others, such as deities and so forth, conforms to that of the Ṛṣis; whereas the form of my devotees is human, or like that of an elephant, and so on.
Or else, their [ritual] may end with the removal of ants;
everything must be performed within the sacred space (dhāman), or specifically within the sixfold group of the sacred space.
Whether it be a vehicle, or a bed, or even the shape of a city gate; or the shape of a seat, or even the shape of mountains such as Meru and others. || 57/194 ||

Or, in a temple having the form of the *nandī* and so forth, it should be established in the desired location—whether in a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), a gateway (*gopura*), a rampart (*vapra*), or in the abodes of the retinue and other such places. (57.195)
In this very manner it should be performed, for thus it is distinguished on earth;
however, here the synonymous terms such as "cage" (pañjara) and so forth are being explained.
The *pramāṇabhavana*, the eightfold *karṇaprāsāda*, the *sabhā*, the *kūṭa*, the *chāyā*, and the *valabhī*—these indeed are the names of the [various] types. (57.197)
Then, in the center, the Brahmadvāra is considered to be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) within a square cell;
the Dvijāvāsa has straight faces, while the Krīḍa has a lion’s face.
The designation for *pañjara* would be *hastipṛṣṭha*; furthermore, it is called *gajapṛṣṭha*, as well as *tuṇḍa*, *gajavaktra*, and *gajāpara*. (57.199)
The structure on the back of an elephant is called *hastipṛṣṭha*; at the entrance, there is the wall (*kuḍya*) and the paved floor (*kuṭṭima*).
What has been described as the wall (*bhitti*) is now followed by the description of the house-pedestal (*gṛhapiṇḍī*).
In the middle is Vāsāvṛta, Vāsā, Piṇḍī, and Andhārikā; by these names the house-piṇḍas are known, and Andhāra is the first house.
The circular porch is called *sālinda* or *avalinda*;
the seat is the *masūraka*; the base is the *adhiṣṭhāna*; and the supporting surface is the *vastu* or *dharātala*.
The floor (*tala*) is declared to be the first member of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
[the other members are] the pillar (*sthāṇu*), the post (*sthūṇa*), the foot (*pāda*), the shank (*jaṅghā*), and the toe (*caraṇāṅghrika*).
The pillar (stambha), the base (talipa), the shaking (kampa)—these are the designations for the feet;
as well as the beam (prastara), the eaves (gopāna), the pigeon-hole (kapota), and the couch (mañca).
O best of the twice-born, the term *nīvra* is thus declared as a synonym for *prastara*; likewise, *kandhara*, *gala*, *kaṇṭha*, *grīvā*, and *śirodhara* are synonyms for the neck. (57.205)
Thus, "kaṇṭha" may be its name; furthermore, it is called "śikhara. Also, "śikhara," "śiras," "mūrdhan," "śikhā," "mauli," and "mastaka" [are synonyms]. (57.206)
The wise should know that *śīrṣa* refers to the head;
furthermore, it is also called *sthūpikā*, *ghaṭa*, *kīla*, *culuka*, and *sthūpi*. (57.207)
O best of the twice-born, *śikhā* is known as *sthūpī* and *cūlikā*;
furthermore, *vimāna*, *bhavana*, *harmya*, *saudha*, *dhāma*, and *niketana* are synonyms for a palace or mansion.
Prāsāda, sadana, sadma, geha, āvasaka,
gṛha, ālaya, nilaya, vāsa, āspada, vāstu, and vāstuka are synonyms for a dwelling or house.
Kṣetra, āyatana, veśma, mandira, dhiṣṇyaka, pada, laya, kṣaya, agāra, and likewise upavasita; || 57/210 ||
Thus have the synonymous terms for "abode" (sthāna) been correctly explained; in this same manner, other such terms should be understood.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the ornamentation of the temple, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Rules for the Characteristics of the Neck.
(Verse 58.1) O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the characteristics of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) in brief:
at its base, a pedestal (*vedikā*) should be constructed measuring one-third of the height of the neck.

One-third of the wall of the sanctum (garbha) constitutes the base of the pedestal (vedi), and its entry [into the wall] is at one-quarter of the pillar-base; the upper pedestal (adhivedikā) is placed at the fourth, fifth, or sixth part [of the height]. 58.2.
Then the neck-projection (grīvāveśa) should likewise be seven or eight parts; it may be equal, or one and a half times, or even double or triple [the base measurement]. 58.3.
One should determine the height of the neck according to the measurement of the altar's elevation;
likewise, the upper rim, the binding-fist, and the lotus-stalk ornament.
The *daṇḍikā* and the *valaya* are intended as ornaments for the neck; the region up to the end of the *daṇḍikā* is called the neck, and above that should be the *śikhara*. 58.5.
A bull should be installed above the sacrificial grass (prastara), especially in the abode of Śiva;
those [other images] should be installed facing upwards, all around the base of the temple.
In the region of the inner circle, however, [the deities] should be installed together with their pedestals;
one should also place the vehicles of the other gods within their respective abodes.
In the same manner, the goddesses have been described; one should then install the throat-deities (galadevas), either accompanied by Ekapāda or joined with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
One should likewise install Maheśa endowed with such a form,
or else one should place him within the group of feet according to the previously stated procedure.
One should place the nose and the feet in the four directions around the neck;
right there, one should fashion a circle that is clearly defined on all sides.
Thus the throat has been fully described; above that, there should be the peak.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the throat, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Spire (Śikhara)
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the *śikhara* (spire),
according to the measurement of the height of the *śikhara* in its own parts or by means of the measurement of the portions [of the temple].
Up to the *daṇḍikā*, it should be one-fifth or two-fifths of the *tāra*;
likewise, among the divisions of seven, nine, and eleven, it is the thirteenth and the fifteenth.
The seventeenth part is for binding; five, six, and seven parts, as well as seven and eight parts, and half of a star—these are the eight types of *śikhara* (spire) elevations. 59/3.
Also the Pāñcāla, the Vaideha, the Māgadha, and the Kaurava;
as well as the Kosala, the Śaurasena, the Gāndhāra, and the Patrika.
The wise should understand these names according to their sequence; all these parts are said to be situated above the hips. (59.5)
All [the measurements] for the Taitila [style] should be half a unit less than that;
starting from the eleventh part of seventeen, they increase by one part [at each stage]. (59.6)
After Avantikā and the others, there arise Ardhāviṣṭa, Lupodaya, Vyāmiśra, Kaliṅga, and likewise Kauśika. (59.7)
Varāṭa, Drāmiḍa, Barbara, Kollaka,
and likewise Śauṇḍika— thus arise the mixed castes and others.
For these are renowned among the gods and also among the ascetics dwelling in hermitages;
they are quadrangular, circular, hexagonal, and octagonal. (59.9)
And the twelfth [lotus] has sixteen petals, resembling a lotus bud;
likewise, it has the luster of an *āmalaka* leaf, being long, round, and delicate.
The peaks of the palaces and other structures have eight, eight, and eight tiers respectively; the shape of the spire is considered to extend from six to sixty corners. (59.11)
In the abode of the Goddess, the number of *lupas* is of four kinds: from five to eleven, and from four to ten. (59.12)
The two intermediate high points previously mentioned are the lotus named Vyāmiśra;
the lotuses situated above and those situated below are half the size [of the preceding ones]. (59.13)
Beginning from the half-measure and increasing it, one should subsequently chant the ascending and descending sequences when the half-measure is reached; this is declared to be the secret.
Up to the limit of the staff-mark, one should take the half-tāra that has been made square and equal,
and lead the appropriate thick thread known as the boundary of the black uṣṇīṣa.
There should be an abundance of staffs and upper arms; below the seat of the Sūtra, one should place the ten points beginning with the four parts upon the seat.
One should measure from the junction of the crown-protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) up to the height of the hair-parting (sīmanta);
then, measuring downward from that height, one should place the seat (āsana) at the root of the head.
For those very [lines] become the boundaries for Daṇḍika and the others; from the junction with the turban (uṣṇīṣa) down to the final dot at the edge is the *lupāyana*. 59.18.
One should again lay out the respective extent up to the limit along with the measuring cord;
or one may lay it out on the seat, and its measurement should extend as far as the threshold (lupā).
By meditating upon this in the middle, one increases according to the number of castes;
having thus repeated it, one subsequently ascends or descends.
That which arises in each respective square shall be joined with its corresponding *malla*;
the placement of the *lupā* is considered to be of two kinds: either with a central point or without a central point. (59.21)
The middle, the middle-ear, the across-ear, and the following-corner—
these are called "corner" (koṭi) respectively, with the five colors elided in sequence.
From each of those respective lines, one should draw lines downward along the spinal column;
then, at the top of that peak, one should fix a peg at the end of the line marking the reclining position.
Having placed them like a half-moon, one should draw all the *cūlikās* (top-knots) evenly;
that form of the *cūlikā* is situated within the middle and ends of the *lupāvilupa*.
Thus it should be for the straight body; in the same way, other [measurements] should also be inferred.
The width of the Bālakūṭa [portion], according to the line of its position, is the distance between the breasts. (59.25)
But the *lupātāra* [measure] is either a *daṇḍa* plus one-quarter, or indeed one-and-a-half, or of a size according to one's preference, even from a great extent. (59.26)
The width is three, four, or five parts, and its thickness is one part; the width of the knee-mold (jānu) is half of the upper portion, or even just a quarter.
The *daṇḍikāvipula* [measure] is three-quarters [of that], while its thickness is half of that;
the *valaya*, *jānu*, and *nīvra* are [measured] from half the width of the *daṇḍikāvipula*.
Then, from the middle of the *malla* (the base), the thickness should measure one *tāla*;
it should extend from the edge down to the knees, or even just to the portion of the *cūlikā* (the head).
From the bed, there should first be a cloth for the head-covering; the axe-shaped mark, the forehead, and the hips are likewise prescribed.
Or, at the neck of the *pādaviṣkambha*, it is likewise twice the width of the *viṣkambha*;
the width of the *kūṭa* is the middle of the *lupā*, and its two corners are twice that [width]. (59.31)
Half of that is the suspension of the *nālikā*; above it is the junction of the tips of the *mallās*.
The opening should be the size of its neck, or it may serve as the entrance for the *mallās*. (59.32)
The backbone should extend from above to below, reaching to the knees at the center of the *lupā* beams;
it should be level with the height of the *nīvrata* stars, or the *cūlī* portion may be one part of the *lupā*.
Whether it be a *lupā*, a *sughana*, or a *valaya* with an extension of bamboo, the *nīvra* is prescribed for the *valaya* at half its width.
After placing the fruits above the *lupa* and securing them with a foot-binding at half the height,
one should smear the bamboo beam (*dhanurvaṃśa*) and place it upon that.
One should cover it with iron and clods of earth and bind it with the eightfold binding;
then, a hole is made in the middle of the frame for the ring.
Five lines for the ritual action (kriyā) should be drawn, numbering sixteen;
one-eighth of the width of the belly is known as the measure of their extent.
By that measure, through an increase of half-parts starting from seven and a half,
sixteen [divisions] numbered up to fifteen are to be drawn.
Then, having placed the *lupā*, the upper limit, the end, the bindu, and so forth, in that manner,
those skilled in drawing forms should subsequently delineate the bonds and other such features. (59.39)

These [proportions] have been declared for palaces; however, for houses and the like, there are sixteen. A wise man, using that measurement which is double the length of the *lupā* and other parts, [should proceed]. (59.40)
Below the crown of the head and the boundary of the seat, one should draw a row of fish;
above that, the wise man should have the wrestler's figure drawn.
Having divided the half-measure of the *mallāyata* sequentially into eighty-three parts,
one should draw each respective [line] at the end of its corresponding portion, precisely in the middle of it.
This sequence has been proclaimed for all the *parilekhas*; now, O twice-born ones, it is described individually for the *pāñcālī* and other *lupās*. (59.43)
The Malla and other lines, joined with a straight body at the tips of the Rekhāsana, form a line of action (kriyā-rekhā) made in the middle; that is known as the Parilekhā.
One should fashion a square water-clock (ghaṭikā) according to the measurement of a *lupāghana*, four fingers in length, straight, with a cord tied at its center.
Having placed the middle ghaṭikā of the horizontal thread from the interior of the cūlikā,
one should afterwards cut it off like the sleeping-thread (śayanasūtra).
One should place that [thread] upon each individual letter;
when the remaining portion of the cast thread is cut, it is within the belly of the *varṇalupa*.
One should draw it equal to the stable thread of Daṇḍika’s upper circle;
when drawn in the middle of the width of the belly, it becomes a *karaka*.
Just as the water-clock (ghaṭikā) situated between the forehead and the middle [of the face] is equal to the hand,
so too is the vessel for the treasure (nidhāna-ghaṭikā), which is elongated due to its narrow belly.
One should cut out the form of the forehead, including the circular ornaments and the like, which arise from the *lupa*;
one should cast the shadow onto the desired side and into the opening of the circle.
By means of each respective ghaṭikā, according to the midday conjunction of each,
the shadow falling upon the forehead of each of those [deities] shall be determined.
The holes for the middle ghaṭikā should be at the staff, the ring, the gap, the breast, the knee, and so forth; however, the gaps for the *valaya* (bracelet) are in the middle of the *ghaṭikā*.
One should place a skull upon the balance at the center of the head and the center of the lower part;
its middle bands are golden and resemble the leaves of the date palm.
A *lupā* adorned with various animals should be fashioned within the space between the pinnacles;
the height of the lotus should be four or five parts of the height of the pinnacle.
The base of the spire (nīvraka) should be equal in width to the altar;
the width of the nose (nāsikā) should be one-third of the spire. || 59/55 ||
The great *nāsīvi* (nose-ornament) should extend out by one-third or half [of its width];
likewise, the height of the shoulder-part (*skandhāṅga*) should be reduced by three or four parts [of that same measure]. // 59/56 //
The height of the banner-staff (śaktidhvaja) should be half or three-quarters of that [measurement];
its width should be one and a half staffs or two staffs, and the breadth of the small nose [ornament] should be [proportionate].
The width of the face-cloth and its staff should be one and a half [parts], or with a quarter part, or three-quarters; its thickness may be according to one's preference.
At the base of the Śakti-banner, the staff should be broad and bent; its measurement, including the face-cloth, as well as its neck and other parts, should be of that same proportion.
The leaf at the top of the neck should be measured as half the width of the pillar;
above the neck, the cheek-moulding should be twice that size, or indeed one and a half times.
Or it should be made with three prongs, or the neck may consist of half [the height];
it should extend that far up to the end of the spear and banner, or it may have leaves or a trident.
The *netrasaṃśliṣṭamalla* [posture] is adorned with a crest and breasts, and is embellished by the *śayita*, *sthitapaṭṭa*, fingers, and so forth. 59/62.
With the ears joined and the upper bands raised, and with the uppermost band further elevated, there is a fist-binding;
from above that, it should emerge beautifully as a three-faced form.
Wherever one may design various [ornaments] upon the temple;
thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Spire," in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Stūpikā (Finial)

I shall describe the eternal characteristics of the *sthūpikā* (finial) for temples and other structures: its height should be one-eighth or one-half of the height of the lotus-base; above that is the length of the *sthūpikā*. (60.1)
In a [shrine] consisting of three parts, the pinnacle-staff (sthūpikā) is desired to be either one-third as high as the head-part or even slightly less;
it may be made of metal or wood, and is provided with a pin (kīla). // 60.2 //
The height of the upper portion should be one-quarter [of the total], and its width equal to one-quarter;
the width at the top should be one finger-breadth, tapering gradually from there.
One should make it square and even; then, one-third from the bottom, one should make the upper part circular and place the "feet of the fire" (śikhipāda) at the bottom.
The wise one should make the width three times the length, and the height equal to the width starting from the base; however, the length should be made according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Alternatively, the length of the wedge at its tip should be twice the [thickness of the] pillar;
its width should be half the diameter of the pillar, or else one-third or one-fourth.
The width at the top should be half a finger-breadth, while the foot of the fire-altar (śikhipāda) may be as desired;
the peg (kīla) should be shaped like a peak or according to the form of the liṅga.
The lotus is said to be one and a half parts in height when the total length is divided into twenty-two parts;
its width is seven parts, and above that is the fillet (vājana).

The width [of the neck] is said to be two or three parts, while the height of the *vetra* (the neck) is half [that]. The width at the top is three parts, and the *vājana* (the fillet) is said to be above that.
The lotus above, fashioned from a portion [of the base], has a width of three parts;
the pillar has a width of five parts, and the capital (kumbha) is fashioned from five parts.
The width [of the base] should be nine parts; above that, a lotus [pedestal] should be made from one part. Its width should be five parts, and the *vetra* (staff) should be fashioned as half of that.
Its width shall be three parts, and its fillet (karṇa) shall be fashioned from one part;
the upper molding (vājana) shall be two parts in width, extending halfway [upward].
In width, it should be three parts, fashioned from the *vetra* (cane) portion;
its width should be four parts, and the *kampa-karṇa* should be equal to the *kampa*.
As before, the lotus should be half [the height], with a width of five parts;
the fillet (vājana) should be one part, and its width should be six parts.
Just as there is an upper lotus below, so too above it there should be a cane-work (vetra) for one part;
its width should be one-third [of the total], and above that is the bud of the lotus.
One should fashion the base from the bottom with a width of three parts according to the Veda-portion;
it may be square, sixteen-sided, provided with a pedestal, or circular.
Alternatively, one may fashion the ornament for the spire (sthūpikā) in another manner:
it should have five corners, be shaped like a lotus, and its height should be five units.
One should fashion the lotus-vessel according to the same measurements previously stated;
the corner (karṇa) is said to be one-fourth [of the base], and above that, one should proceed as before.
Therein, twenty-two parts are arranged as before;
a celestial chariot endowed with such characteristics is the abode of all prosperity.
If it were otherwise, there would be misfortune for both the doer and the one who causes it to be done;
therefore, having reflected upon the meaning of the scriptures regarding such matters as oaths and the like, a wise person should write [the agreement].
Once the site has been properly established, one should have the common [foundation] prepared by him;
having reflected upon it at the time of commencement, one should carry out all the necessary materials.
In this world, the reversal of what has been done leads to misfortune;
likewise, it may be accompanied by valid means of knowledge, or else it may be beginningless.
It should be constructed in the aforementioned locations with the proper measurements;
one should perform it according to the measurements prescribed in the Kāmika and other Āgamas.

In that regard, if what ought to be performed by one [text] is not stated there, it should be taken from another scripture; however, if it is not mentioned even in the Siddhānta, then one should resort to the Gāruḍa and other such texts.
If even in that case [the site] has not been specified, one should rely upon the science of architecture (vāstuśāstra).
A single face is declared to be the best; a single tantra would be middling.
The lowest is the unity of streams, while the mixed stream is inferior;
that which lacks even this would be debased. Having understood this, one should act accordingly.
The Śiva-knowledge known as Kāmika is declared to be common to all;
because of its preeminence among all scriptures, it is celebrated everywhere. (60.27)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Stūpikā," in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Nāla and Other Elements.

(Verse 61.1) O twice-born ones, listen as I describe the installation of the feet of the Lord who possesses no foundation, the installation of the upward-flowing stone, and the installation of the *stūpikā* (the pinnacle). (pṛ0 156) sthāpanaṃ nālayogāṅghreḥ sravadūrdhvopalasya ca | stūpikāsthāpanaṃ caiva vakṣye tacchṛṇuta dvijāḥ || 61/1 ||
Whether during the northern or southern solstice, once the proper location has been reached,
the rite must be performed without delay on an auspicious day at a favorable moment.
One should construct a pavilion to the north of the front of the palace,
measuring between nine cubits and five cubits.
One should construct a central altar (vedikā) using one part out of nine parts;
then, one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around it, numbering five and four [respectively].
One should prepare every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as either circular or square;
furthermore, one should first perform the rite for the auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
Alternatively, one should perform this installation even if it is devoid of those [previously mentioned elements];
having thoroughly decorated the pavilion, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Then, having sprinkled the stalk and other parts with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
one should install it together with the five earths, the five products of the cow, and pure water.
Having smeared [the image] with sandalwood paste and other substances, covered it with flower garlands,
and performed the binding of the *kautuka* (protective thread), the preceptor should encircle it with *vañja* fibers.
One should prepare the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) either upon the altar-platform or on the ground;
it should consist of eight droṇas of śāli rice, or half, or half again.
Half of that [quantity] should be combined with rice, and half of that with sesame and parched grain;
having covered these with cloths and darbha grass, one should do so with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should worship all [the deities] on every side and again cover them with cloth;
one should place eight jars, provided with cloths and other offerings, around [the central vessel].

The wise practitioner, desiring to speak, should perform worship with perfumes and other offerings to those who are complete with their respective sūtras and attendants, and joined by their presiding lords such as Indra, while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
If the installation of the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) is performed at Pūrvaśailaka,
one should place the syllable *i* in the south and the syllable *u* in the west.
The wise man should wrap the letter *E* in a separate cloth in an auspicious place and worship Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, and Pūrṇā in their proper order.
Thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the path prescribed for the rites of the sacred fire;
the wise practitioner should offer sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), and sesame seeds into the fire.
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa are located in the directions starting from the east;
the Palāśa should be for the principal [fire], or else one [tree] may suffice for all the sacrificial pits.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) one hundred times, or half that number, with the Śiva-mantra;
having concentrated the mind, one should satisfy the ancillary mantras (aṅga) with a tenth part of the oblations offered to Śiva.
Having placed the principles beginning with the Self (ātmatattva), one should place the presiding deities beginning with Brahmā;
having placed the embodied forms and their lords, one should place the principles and their respective lords.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
one should subsequently place the stalk and other parts, either together with the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
At the base, however, one should place either the nine gems or the five gems; or, if those are unavailable, gold, and then establish it with the heart-mantra.
Having performed the ritual for the crown-brick according to the procedure for the initial stone-slab,
one should then place the pinnacle-pile upon it.
One should perform the same procedure for those with many finials and for plastered structures; likewise, if it is a temple made of wood, or one constructed of bamboo, or with a foundation-pile.
The wise one should place the pinnacle-pin (sthūpikīla) without laying bricks;
however, if it is the installation of a pillar, he should instead place it in the womb-chamber (garbhasthāna).
If the installation of the pillars (nāla) is to be performed, one should place some [portion] depending on the northeast;
if the erection of the beams (lupā) is to be performed, it should be done to the south of the primary sanctuary.
One should place the feet in the west, and afterwards place everything else;
at the entrance of the inner sanctum, one should first establish what is appropriate.
One should worship the preceptor, the image-keepers, the astrologer, and the architect with garments, gold, and other offerings, and one should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus has been prescribed the abode that brings about all prosperity and happiness.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Nāla and Other Elements," in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Single Ground and So Forth.

The characteristics of the single floor and so forth are now specifically declared: one-third of the height of the mansion, or one part out of eight, or one part out of nine, constitutes the [first] storey. (62.1)
In the case of a division by eight, there is a share of two; in a ninefold division, a share of five; in an elevenfold division, a share of six;
and in a thirteenfold division, a share of seven. (62.2)
One-eighth of the lunar day, or seventeen and nine-ninths of a unit,
as well as half the width— all of this is known as the *nālīgṛha*.
One, two, three, four, five, or six parts [of the total height] constitute the single level;
however, the width of the base (pādaviṣkambha) is desired to be three, four, or five parts.
One part shall be the base, the length of the feet two parts,
the entablature one part, and the neck is proclaimed to be one part.
The *sthūpika* is declared to be one part out of two parts of the *śikhara*; when it is joined with a circular neck and a head, it is known by the name *Vijaya*. (62/6)
If it is provided with *karṇakūṭas*, it is celebrated as *Śrībhoga*; if it is provided with a *bhadra* in the middle, it is proclaimed as *Śrīviśāla*. (62.7)
O best of the twice-born, a neck with eight-sided peaks is desired as the "Svastibandhana" (the auspicious bond); a neck with four-sided peaks brings about prosperity.
That which has two slopes, a rounded head, and a neck like the back of an elephant is known as *hastipṛṣṭha*.
That which has a six-cornered peak and neck, and is beautiful at the shoulders, is known as *skandakānta*.
Furthermore, that which is endowed with the *bhadra* in the middle and possesses *karṇakūṭas* at the top is [known as *madhyabhadra*]. (62.9)
The *koṣṭhaka* type has a beautiful nose and limbs, while its neck and head are circular;
it is called by the name *kesara*, or it may have a neck and head that are quadrangular.
When divided by seven and five, with three and two parts respectively, this is declared to be the Madhyabhadraka;
it is said to have one ground floor, though it may also be constructed with two stories.
The width of the *sauṣṭhika* (the central projection) is prescribed as seven parts out of three;
the length of the *koṣṭhaka* (the cell) is two parts, and the remainder is for the *hāra* (moulding) together with the *pañjara* (lattice).
One should divide the height of the vimāna into twenty-eight parts;
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of three parts, and the pedestal (pāda) is said to be six parts.
The *prastara* (the base section) shall consist of three parts, and the upper section shall consist of five parts;
the *prastara* shall consist of two parts, and the *karṇa* (the corner section) is proclaimed to consist of three parts.
The crown-protrusion (śikhara) is constructed with three and a half vedīs,
and the square base (adhiṣṭhāna), as well as the neck and the head, are likewise [constructed with one and a half vedīs].
Endowed with four peaks and provided with four compartments, with eight small niches above—it is known by the name Svastika. (62.16)
If that very same *sauṣṭhika* type has its central courtyard (*koṣṭhaka*) sloped and elevated, and is provided with an internal terrace (*antaraprastara*), it is called the *vipulasundara*. (62.17)
The neck and head [of the image] should have a prastara (projection) of one part, three parts, three and a quarter parts,
and four parts respectively, with a height of three parts and a width of one vitasti.
When one-tenth of the height is added to the base, it is described as a two-storey vimāna and so forth, provided with an intermediate *prastara* up to the pinnacle chamber (*kūṭaśālā*). (62.19)
If that very same *koṣṭhaka* is low and high, well-proportioned,
and provided with an inner floor, it is called *kailāsa*.
That very [structure] is circular, with a neck like an altar, a pinnacle, and a dome;
it possesses eight peaks, is endowed with four halls, and is adorned with a cage-like lattice.
The central chamber should have an exit with two or three pillars for structural stability;
it should be provided with a neck and head, and joined with a peaked roof-chamber.
Endowed with various foundations, this mountain is designated by that name;
its very summit is joined with half-cells in all directions. (62.23)
Endowed with a square-shaped top and possessed of four peaks, joined with various pedestals— by this name it shall be known as the Svastika.
That very same *sauṣṭhika* hall, when provided with an inner gallery (*antaraprastara*) and joined with a *hārapañjara*, is desired by the name *kalyāṇa*.
If that very same *śikhara* is devoid of the half-cell (*ardhakoṣṭhaka*) and is joined with four *nāsīs*, this is desired as the *Pāñcāla*. || 62/26 ||
That same [structure], having eight corners, with a pedestal, neck, pinnacle, and dome,
and joined with eight great nostrils at the pinnacle, is the Viṣṇukāntaka.
That very same [structure], excluding the inner roof of the peaked halls (kūṭaśālā), should be four-cornered and extended in length by a measure of one-fourth of that [width]. || 62.28 ||
The neck and the pinnacle (śikhara) should likewise be elongated and provided with three finials (stūpika); by that name, it is known as the Sumaṅgala. || 62.29 ||
If that same [head] is elongated and rounded, with a neck like a sacrificial altar and all its limbs fully formed, it is considered Gāndhāra. || 62.30 ||
It is joined with a square measuring one and a half *tāras*,
provided with two ears and a circular top, and endowed with windows and a front hall.
This elephant-back [style] may be either two-sided (rectangular) or circular; the base platform (adhiṣṭhāna) may be square, and the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be circular. || 62/32 ||
Adorned with all ornaments, this [stūpa] shall be called "Manohara" (Charming);
it is the same [structure], but if the [recesses] from the base up to the dome (kumbha) are progressively wider outwardly. (62.33)
The remainder is indicated as before; it is called the Īśvarakāntaka.
Thus has the two-storied [temple] been described; now the three-storied is being discussed.
When the width of the palace is divided into seven or eight parts,
the width of the *kūṭa* (pinnacle) shall be one part, and its length shall be two or three times that of the *koṣṭha* (cell).
The *lambapañjara* occupies one-half part, while the *hāra* section is equal to that;
in the upper region of six parts, the width of the *kūṭa* is one part.
One should arrange the courtyard (koṣṭhaka) with a double length and the entrance (hāra) with one part;
the central auspicious section (madhyabhadra) is prescribed with two parts of the upper floor.
The projection of the eaves is desired to be one *daṇḍa* or one and a half *daṇḍas*.
Furthermore, one should divide the height of the pavilion (*vimāna*) by twenty-four.
The base (dharātala) is said to consist of two parts, and the foot (pāda) of four;
the entablature (prastara) is two parts, and the foot consists of three and a half parts.
The *prastara* should be one and a half parts; the [second] part should be three-quarters of a part;
the bed (*mañca*) should be one and a quarter parts; and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) is said to be one and a half parts.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should have one and a half sections; the finial (sthūpikā) should consist of one section.
The turret (kūṭa), the chamber (koṣṭha), and the nest (nīḍa) are declared to be eight in number.
That which begins with birth and ends with the pinnacle (sthūpikā) is remembered as having four corners;
in the second and third [sections], there are sixteen wheel-nests (cakranīḍas).
The great nose is proclaimed to be on the summit; however, it is not prescribed everywhere according to what is aesthetically pleasing. Rather, four [smaller] noses are proclaimed for all parts.
The inner chamber is elevated, the peak is low, and the interior is fivefold;
it is shaped like a celestial palace (vimāna) by name and endowed with all ornaments.
One should determine the length to be four parts more than the width;
there should be eight parts in the width and twelve parts in the length.
According to the measurement of its width and height, it should be made circular;
one should cause the portion from the base (masūraka) to the top of the head to be a circle of two parts.
Alternatively, O twice-born ones, one should bring the peak to a two-sided circle and a section;
below that, from the base up to the two-sided circle, it should be square.
One should make two circular portions at the front, on both sides, and at the back;
the width of the peak-cells and the nesting-cells is prescribed as one part.
The inner chamber (koṣṭhaka) is twice as long [as it is wide], and the necklaces (hārā) are said to be one part;
