on the pinnacle (śikhara), however, four great noses (mahānāsya) are proclaimed.
A pinnacle that is elevated at its core and depressed in the middle is called an *añcaka*;
that same type with three stories is known as a *svastika*, which brings pleasure to Śiva.
In the *tāra* (the central width), the expansion of the *sauṣṭhika* (the decorative molding) should be nine-sevenths;
likewise, two parts for the length of the hall, and one part should be fashioned as the *hāra* (the neck-molding).
That compartment is prescribed as having eight peaks and twelve [divisions];
there should be eight nests, and the channels (nāḍīs) arise by virtue of the beauty of the nest.
It has eight heads, shoulders like a sacrificial altar, and eight noses;
it is of pure form by name and endowed with all ornaments.
One should determine the length to be one-fourth greater than the width;
in the width there should be eight parts, and in the length twelve parts.
One should cause it to be made circular with a measurement half that of its width;
from the base of the *masūraka* up to the top of the head, one should make it both triangular and circular.
Alternatively, O twice-born ones, one should lead the neck (kaṇṭha) and the summit (śikhara) as an oval with two sides;
below that it should be square, from the base up to the two-sided oval.
From the front, from both sides, and at the back, one should leave a space of two solar parts (two-twelfths);
the width of the nest-like chamber for the peak-cells is desired to be one part.
The enclosure (koṣṭhaka) is twice as long [as it is wide], and the necklace (hāra) is proclaimed to be one part;
there shall be six parts above that, on its back and on both sides.
Having made the height of the *kūṭa* (the pinnacle) two parts of the sun (twelve), the *koṣṭha* (the base chamber), and so forth, as before;
one should determine the upper floor (*ūrdhvabhauma*) as four parts according to the requirements of the proper application.
On the front of the head is an eye, provided with a śālā-face,
joined with a central chamber (garbha) and a pinnacle (kūṭa), and adorned with a small nose.
One should lead [the structure] either provided with a gabled chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) or even devoid of it;
on the pinnacle, there should be three small-faced [ornaments] accompanied by pedestals.
That compartment shall indeed have eight peaks, while the nest has twelve;
in the *harā* line, there shall be a small nest with a number double that of the sun (twelve).
Or rather, it may consist of one [unit] up to twelve units, joined with the *vartanā* technique;
this is known by the name *Hastipṛṣṭha*, endowed with all ornaments.
Its width shall be eight parts, and its length ten parts. (62–63)
One should arrange for the *kūṭa*, the *koṣṭha*, and the *nīḍa* by means of a single part;
likewise, the *hāra* should occupy one part, and the upper floor six parts.
Above that, however, the length shall be four parts, with an additional eighth part;
the neck of the pedestal (vedikā) should be oval and elongated, possessing two ears.
One should construct all its parts, such as the towers and inner chambers, as previously described.
This palace, beginning with the elephant-shaped structure, is the ancient Gajapṛṣṭha.
When the *tāra* is divided into nine parts, the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) shall consist of three parts;
the wall-mass (*gṛhapiṇḍī*) shall be one part, and the neck (*kandhara*) shall be two parts.
The *andhārikā* should be known as one part, and the *sauṣṭhika* likewise becomes one part.
The length of the *koṣṭhaka* is three parts, and the width of the *nīḍa* is one and a half parts.
In the middle of the *koṣṭha*, provided with the exit of the channels by means of three staffs (*tridaṇḍa*),
even in the upper ground, the peak (*kūṭa*) shall be one-sixth [of the width] and twice as long as that.
The necklace situated within the compartment should be adorned with lattices;
on the upper floor, it extends outward from the center by one-third of its width, supported by a staff.
At first, there is the base (tala) with four corners; at the top of the four corners is the peak (kūṭa);
on the upper floor it is eight-sided, and this is the summit of the sauṣṭhikas.
The foundation should be square, with the neck and the head shaped like a vase;
likewise, there should be eight peaks, as well as a chamber and a nesting-place (nīḍaka).
Likewise, there are eight small niches and eight [cells] with necks and noses;
this is known by the name Bhadrakoṣṭha, endowed with all ornaments.
That very [structure] is circular at the base of the ear-projections (*karṇakūṭa*) on each successive floor;
its head should be circular and endowed with four faces.
This structure, complete with all its constituent parts, is known by the name Vṛttakūṭa;
it is square in shape and elongated by one-eighth of its own length.
The pinnacle (karṇakūṭa) should be four-cornered, elongated, or circular at its summit;
it may be devoid of the *koṣṭha* and *bhadra* projections, while the remainder should be executed as previously described.
This [stūpa], endowed with three domes (stūpikās), shall be known by this name as "Sumaṅgala.
Its width should be fifteen cubits, and one should add a tenth part [of that] for its height.

The inner sanctum (garbhageha) is declared to be four parts; the Gāndhārī portion is one part; and the *alīndra* (veranda) is one part; the *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion) is one part, measured from the exterior.
One should create the intervals in the middle of the *karṇa*, as well as the *kūṭas*, *koṣṭhakas*, and *pañjaras*.
The wise consider the length of the *koṣṭhaka* to be one part, while its width is considered to be double that.
In the upper level, however, within the portion consisting of the *rasa* units, there is a section for the expansion of the *sauṣṭhika*;
one should join the *koṣṭhaka*, which is twice as long, with the *hāra* by means of a unit.
And above that, in the fourth part, the projection should emerge through the middle;
it may be one daṇḍa, one and a half daṇḍas, or two daṇḍas.
The foundation is square, and likewise the neck and the head;
the nest is eight-peaked, and the chamber is exactly the same.
Above, there should be eight hanging nests, provided with water and land,
joined with the nose and other limbs, and endowed with all the constituent parts.
If the two peak-chambers (kūṭakoṣṭha) are elevated and provided with internal flooring, it is thus called Gāndhāra; its neck and head may also be octagonal.
If that same circular structure has a neck-like altar and a pinnacle,
and the rest is as previously described, it is intended by the name Śrībhoga.
Circular, oval, triangular, circular, octagonal, hexagonal; circular, oval, triangular, circular, octagonal, hexagonal. || 62/86 ||
The upper story (harmyakhaṇḍaka) is adorned with niches and gabled chambers; it may be broad on its straight sides, or have two corners, or be circular.
The portion may be somewhat less, or it may be exactly equal;
[one should calculate] the rising degrees from the upper portion by means of an eighth or a tenth part.
The wise man should employ the pervasion of power according to what is most beautiful;
now, O best of sages, I shall describe the four-storeyed mansion.
Starting from three, four, or five cubits and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step, it ends at twenty-one cubits; its width and height are as previously described.
Then, one should divide the thirteen-cubit width into eight parts;
one part is the width of the *kūṭa*, and the length of the hall (*śālā*) is two parts.
The width of the cage (pañjara) shall be one part, and its height eightfold;
the arrangement of the assembly hall and the cages is to be done exactly as previously described.
The width of the pinnacle (kūṭa) above is said to be six parts;
the length of the box (koṣṭhaka) is two parts, and the nest (nīḍa) is desired to be one part above that.

In the upper portion, by means of a share consisting of a fraction of the qualities, the auspicious [portion] is formed; in the middle, it is formed by the staff. One should divide the height of the temple into thirty-nine parts.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) measures two and a half parts; its length is five parts.
The height of the architrave (prastara) above it is three and a quarter parts.
The height of the pedestal (utsedha) for the upper storey is one and a quarter parts;
the shank (jaṅghā) is twice that, and the emergence of the entablature (prastarodaya) is two parts.
The height above [the base] shall be four and one-quarter parts;
the *prastara* (moulding) shall be three-quarters of a part, and the *vedikā* (pedestal) shall be one part.

The portion for the neck is one Aśvinī (two degrees), and the head shall be four and a half [Aśvinīs]; the measurement of the crest is by the remaining degrees, and the area up to the top of the temple is square.
The *sauṣṭhika* compartment shall be twelve [units] in number, and likewise the *sapajjara*;
on the pinnacle there should be four *vedanās*, and the *alpanāsya* should be exactly the same.
O best of the twice-born, this most auspicious hall, adorned with every ornament, likewise contained various storehouses and chambers situated here and there within it.
The *mastaka* (the upper part) should have the appearance of a mandala, and likewise the head (*śiras*) should be circular;
it should be provided with a sanctum (*garbhageha*) measuring half its width.
The remaining portion is covered by two parts; the *piṇḍī* is likewise, as are the *andhāra* and *hāraka*.
With various *masūraka* and other members, this is known by the name Śrīviśālaka.
When the width of fifteen cubits is divided into nine parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhageha) occupies three parts, and the structural mass of the house (gṛhapiṇḍa) is derived from those same portions.
The *alinda* (veranda) extends around with one part, and the *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion) likewise with one part; the width of the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭhaka*, and *nīḍa* is by one part.

Its length is three times its width, and its projection is equal to its own breadth; the great throne (mahānāsī) is in the middle of the hall, with its projection extending to the center of the [central] part.
The height of the *bhāraka* is half the distance between the *bhadrakoṣṭhaka* and the *nīḍa*;
above that, the width of the *maṭṭa* is one-eighth [of the total height].
The width of the chamber is proclaimed to be exactly the same [as its height], while its length is two parts; in the middle of that, a nesting-place (nīḍa) is made by a portion.

Above that, in the portion for the *rasa* (six), there should be a peak (*kūṭa*) with one part, and a chamber (*koṣṭhaka*) twice as long as its width; in the middle of that, there is a cage (*pañjara*) half [the size] of that.
The upper portion consists of four parts, emerging from the middle shaft;
the corner-pinnacle should be octagonal, and the cell should be fashioned like a water-jar (karkarī).
The great peak is adorned with eight hermitages and eight faces;
the number of its summits, chambers, and nests is declared as before.
One should determine its height in the same manner as before;
this is known by the name Bhadrakoṣṭha, and it is the ground of the fourfold Vedas for the inhabitants of heaven.
One should divide a width of seventeen cubits into ten parts;
one should apply the *nālibheda* as four parts and the *andhārikā* as one part.
One should arrange the *alinda* on all sides with one part, the *khaṇḍaharmya* on all sides [with one part],
and the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭhaka*, and *nīḍa* with one part.
The length of the hall (śālā) shall consist of two parts; the remainder is declared to be the width (dhāra). Above that, excluding the water-course (jala), it is divided into eight parts.
The *sauṣṭhi* is one part, the hall (*śālā*) is two parts, and the cage (*pañjara*) is one part;
above that, in the sixth part, the width of the *sauṣṭhi* is one part.
The length of the enclosure (koṣṭhaka) is double [the width]; in the neck (hārā), there is a small lattice-work.
Above that, at one-third [of the height], there is an outward projection from the middle by means of a staff (daṇḍa).
The base is square, the head and neck are octagonal,
and likewise the eight pavilions and cages consist of twelve compartments each.
Indeed, there are eight long lattices and sixteen small niches;
it is joined with eight [parts] for the throat and nose, and the chamber is somewhat elevated.

Adorned with various *masūraka* (mouldings), pillars, altars (*vedī*), lattices (*jāla*), and so forth, it may have a pedestal (*upapīṭha*) and a base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), or consist of the *masūraka* alone. || 62.119 ||
Joined with the shape of a svastika and provided with nostrils, its elevated portion should be as before; this is known by the name Jalāvaha.
When the width of the nine-row [mandala] is divided into ten parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhavāsa) occupies four parts, and the pedestal of the house (gṛhapiṇḍikā) occupies one part.
The neck [of the structure] is surrounded by the shoulder, and the small pavilion (khaṇḍaharmya) is surrounded by it;
indeed, the width of the peaks, storehouses, and niches is exactly one part.
The length of the cell is two parts, while the necklace-moulding is considered to be one part;
this includes the peaked cell and the niche, provided with an intermediate floor.
Leaving aside the water and land [sections], the uppermost eighth part shall be the *sauṣṭhika*;
likewise, there should be a hall of double that size, and between those two, a *pañjara*.
Above that, in the portion for the flavor (rasa), the kūṭakoṣṭha and so forth are as before;
likewise, what was declared for Vijaya should be joined above the remainder.
They know all the parts, such as the peak-chamber (kūṭakoṣṭha) and so forth, by the same number as before;
this Mahānīḍa consists of sixteen [parts] and is known by the name Bhadrakūṭaka.
That same [structure], when another ornament is placed in the middle of the *koṣṭha* and it is auspicious (*bhadra*),
joined with a neck and head, is called the *manohara*. That same [structure],
when another ornament is added such that the neck and head are four-cornered (*vedāśra*), [is likewise known].
The supreme abode of Śambhu is called by the name Avantika.
In a temple measuring twenty-one cubits in width, divided into ten parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall occupy four parts, and the pedestal for the image (gṛhapiṇḍikā) one part.
One should fashion the body of Maṅgala with a portion consisting of dark lines;
and one should arrange the peak-cells and the nesting-chambers as before.
It is adorned with altars, halls, archways, and other such features;
having set aside the areas for water and land, it is divided above into eight parts.
One should arrange the hall, the *sauṣṭhika*, the *nīḍa*, and so forth as before;
the upper floor should consist of six parts, and one part shall be the width of the *sauṣṭhika*.
The length of the hall is divided into two parts; from the upper portion above the height of the nest (nīḍa), the middle-bhadra is prescribed by means of two parts of the upper floor.
Its exit is one *daṇḍa*, while the neck-channel (*grīvānāḍī*) is two and a half *daṇḍas* wide; it is provided with a circular altar (*vṛttavedi*).
It had four great nostrils, with necks and peaks resembling rounded mounds.
O twice-born ones, at its base there is a small area measuring eight nālikās.
It has equal and lofty peaks, with gables, chambers, and turrets;
it possesses high halls and two stories, while at its base there are additional gables.
The corner-pinnacles (karṇakūṭas) at the base appear square, octagonal, and circular;
they possess various *masūraka* ornaments, pillars, pedestals, lattices, and arches.
It is declared to bring various kinds of happiness and is considered the abode of the gods;
O best of sages, listen as I describe the five-storeyed [temple]. 62.138.
When the height is sixty-eight units, the height of the *masūraka* (the base platform) is declared to be two parts plus one-third;
its plinth (*pāda*) shall be four and a half units.
The image (bimba) should be two and a half parts, the pedestal (pādaka) one and a quarter parts,
and the plinth (prastara) is proclaimed to be two and a half parts.
A quarter [of the height] should be one-fifth; the leg of the bed takes two quarters.
The frame (talipa) should take three-quarters or four quarters, and the mattress (prastara) should take two quarters.
Furthermore, the emergence of the prastara (the base course) is desired with three and a half parts and a quarter part;
and the vitardi (the cornice) is one part.
The neck is said to be two parts; the head should be four parts along with the feet;
the pitcher (kumbha) is said to be one part; thus the divisions are proclaimed.
One should fashion the five levels starting from the *rasa* (sixth) portion up to the *rudra* (eleventh) portion;
I shall now describe them in order, beginning with the six-fold base, together with the divisions of the five grounds.
The pedestal (prastara) and its foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) are proclaimed to be above the root-base (mūladhāman) of the five-tiered temple, according to the measurement itself. 62.145.
A quarter [of the height] should be derived from one-third of the base;
thus is the six-storey [temple] described, generally endowed with proportional divisions of width.
Below that, one should fashion the pillar (stambha) and the masūraka with seven and a half parts and three and a quarter parts respectively, when the width (tāra) is divided by eleven and twelve.
This celestial palace (vimāna) is renowned as having seven stories and is accessible from all regions;
beneath it, the two floors of the pedestal are adorned with jewels and portions of the [nine] qualities, together with the sages.
O lords of sages, this eight-story [temple] is said by the wise to consist of thirteen divisions, divided according to the parts of Dharma, Rudra, and Arka.
Below that, with seven and a half parts, one should construct the pillar and the base (talipa) in a space measuring three and a third parts; the proportions for the width have been stated previously.
Thus the nine-storied [temple] has been described; now the ten-storied one is being discussed here.
Below that, a quarter consisting of eight parts of a yuga is intended for the base (adhiṣṭhāna).
In the *tāra* [scale], the previously mentioned divisions should be used, or alternatively, the division of the *manu* is considered;
below that, with portions of five and a half and two and a quarter [respectively]. (62/152)
One should fashion the *masūraka* as one quarter, ending with eighteen parts;
one should arrange it as previously described, and this is considered the eleven-storied [temple].
Below that, the *talaka* (flooring) shall consist of one-quarter of the *nandā* parts;
from sixteen parts at the top down to twelve parts. (62.154)
Having made that determination, the best of teachers should arrange the kūṭas and so forth there;
[he should do so] by dividing the two, three, or four vedīs into six parts, or according to the proportions previously mentioned, for the house.
One should extend the chambers, the porticos, and the star-shaped projections outward from the central core;
having divided the width of the temple into sixteen parts, [one should arrange them accordingly]. (62.156)
The house is said to be constructed with one *vedabhāga* [for the central space] and fashioned with one *piṇḍībhāga*;
the *pañcālindra* and the six walls are each made from half a *bhāga*.
Alternatively, when the length and width are divided into twenty-four parts,
the inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall consist of two parts, while the body of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍa) shall consist of one part.
One should likewise join the *pañcālindra* and the wall from the outside according to the proportions;
all parts, such as the *kūṭa*, the *koṣṭha*, and so forth, should be arranged as before. (62.159)
Having divided the width of the temple into twenty-seven parts, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of five parts; the remainder is declared to be as previously described.
One should likewise arrange it by grouping [the parts] even in other sections;
thus there shall be twelve stages. Now, that which follows this is being described.

The teacher should first apply the measurement of the base, then half that for the foot-measurement; as for the measurement of the pillar, he should apply an increase according to the specific requirements.
Beginning correctly from sixteen squares, [the width] should be twelve units;
then, starting from a twenty-first part of a square, it should extend up to a thirty-first part.
One should especially determine this according to the specific desire of the sacrificer;
alternatively, one may make the *alinda* half of the [main] portion, and apply the remainder to the walls.
Or one may likewise have it constructed with even or uneven hands;
or, in the case of a division into even parts, the width of the kūṭa shall be twice as long.
The hall (śālā), however, may consist of four parts, or likewise of even or odd parts;
there may be one floor (tala) as a single unit (grāsa), or a multi-storied structure (khaṇḍaharmya) with four floors.
O twice-born ones, on a building of two, four, five, six, or seven stories, there should be one *grāsa*;
on an eight-story building, three *talas*; and likewise on a nine-rowed structure.
The width at the level of the Rudras and Ādityas shall be fifty-four [yojanas];
likewise, it is sixty at the level of the Vasus and Earth, and fourteen at the level of the Caturdaśa.
It is declared to have seven levels, or sixteen, eight, or one;
from the foundation, one should properly construct the peak, the chambers, and so forth upon the surface of the earth.
In such a house, one should employ towers and other features according to the proper method;
the distinctions regarding towers, halls, and so forth have been previously described as stated.
The exposition, joined with the differentiating [principles] residing in the abodes, has been declared as before.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Single Ground and the Others," in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Topmost Brick (Mūrdheṣṭakā).
Now I shall describe the supreme installation of the upper floor for celestial mansions (vimānas); whatever material constitutes the final layer, that, in my view, is considered to be made of brick.
The dimensions of the first bricks should be as previously stated, or they may be considered reduced by one-eighth;
the installation should be performed precisely according to the method that will be described hereafter.
One should first perform the rite of planting the sprouts according to the prescribed rule,
to the north or to the east of the pavilion or the temple.
Alternatively, it may be provided with five or one sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or accompanied by that same number of leveled altars (sthaṇḍila);
the central one should be provided with a raised altar (vedikā) and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and other ornaments.
Afterward, having dismissed the artisan, one should smear [the area] with cow dung;
then there should be a meal for the Brahmins, as well as the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Having first performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice,
one should then prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) using eight droṇas of śāli rice, or half that amount, or half of that again.

Then the preceptor, having prepared the bed with rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, [should purify it] with the five earths and the five products of the cow.
Having washed the brick of the *sthūpī*, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should then inscribe the syllables of the Vedas, preceded by the vowels, in order starting from the east.

On the bricks, the mantra-practitioner, having placed them upon the bed smeared with white sandalwood paste while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra, should then set the *sthūpikā* (the pinnacle) to its left. (63.9)
Having tied the *kautuka* (sacred thread) and covered it with a cloth, the preceptor,
having placed eight jars all around in the directions of the world-protectors, [should do so] over them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install the forms and the presiding deities of those forms upon the bricks— namely Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā.
One should place [the deity] together with its site upon the stūpa and perform the rite of fire-offering (homa),
having carried out the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual.
One should shake [the vessel] in sequence with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, parched rice, fried grains, sesame seeds, and so forth;
and the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are located in the directions starting from the east.
The *palāśa* wood may also be used for the principal [oblation], or it may be considered appropriate everywhere;
one should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) a hundred times with the mantras of the limbs of Śiva-Brahman.
At dawn, however, the preceptor, having bathed and performed the ritual worship of the mantras and other rites,
shall worship the pinnacle with bricks, as well as the water-jars, the sacrificial pit, and the guardians.
Having performed the complete expiation and worship with a satisfied mind,
[he should do so] with image-bearers who have received a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of five niṣkas or more.

Accompanied by the three beginning with the astrologer and the artisan, the supreme preceptor, having taken the brick for the pinnacle (sthūpī) and performed circumambulation of the temple (dhāma), [proceeded].
Having ascended to the summit, one should place bricks in sequence upon the top;
in the center, one should deposit gems and other materials according to the same procedure prescribed for the first brick.
Above that, the preceptor should place the *stūpī* with the root mantra;
its base he should sprinkle with water from the pitcher using the respective mantras for each.
Leaving aside the portion of the pinnacle (sthūpikā), one should bind the lower part with bricks and other materials;
the mortal who causes this to be done shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Topmost Brick," in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Characteristics of the Liṅga.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the characteristics of the *liṅga*:
it may be made of clay, wood, stone, or metal, and may originate from gems, arrows, and so forth. (64.1)
The earthen linga is of two kinds: baked and unbaked.
The baked one, when it stands more than two cubits high, is for malevolent rites (ābhicāra).
Having taken white clay and other such earths mixed with milk, oil, and so forth, as well as flour of barley and wheat combined with the bark of milky trees; 64.3.
Having thoroughly kneaded the clay with a smooth, fragrant powder,
[one should add] śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, as well as guggulu and sugar.
Then, according to worldly convention, the preceptor should take earth mixed with five types of resin, equal in number to these [five].
On a mountain or near a mountain, in forests or groves,
on a riverbank, at a tree, or on a rock, one should collect materials for the sake of the Liṅga.
Those golden, dense, and lustrous [trees] that were submerged at the junctions of the mountains, their inner waters rendered pure by being washed by the currents of rivers; (64.7)
Sheltered by the shade of trees and situated at sacred fords and hermitages, they are rich in length,
breadth, and height, and are red, yellow, white, or black.

Charming stones, considered auspicious for one's welfare, should be taken when they are in their prime; those licked by wind, sun, and fire, and resting upon the saline waters of the Mṛdvīkṣā river. (64.9)

Those waters which are taken up by other ritual acts, those which are utterly defiled, those belonging to outcastes, those not to be used, and those situated on the banks of rivers or mountains; || 64.10 ||
Rough stones and trees that are too old or too young should be avoided; [the preferred trees are] the Khadira, Candana, Sāla, Madhūka, Sarala, and Asana. (64.11)
The bilva, kadamba, khadira, devadāru, and śiṃśupā; the panasa, arjuna, and aśoka; the milky trees (kṣīriṇaḥ) and the red sandalwood (raktacandana). || 64.12 ||

Those that have a glossy color, large bodies, bestow auspiciousness, and originate from auspicious regions—one should especially employ them for the collection of materials as will be described hereafter. (64.13)
That stone [liṅga] is considered to be up to nine cubits in size, and the earthen one is likewise regarded as such;
the wooden one is considered to be one-third [of that size], and the metallic one half of that, which is deemed the best.
The middle measurement is said to end with a reduction of six times six finger-breadths;
if that is not available, however, it may be made by reducing one finger-breadth at a time within that range.
A linga measuring one hundred and ninety cubits in height,
according to the measurement of the interior of the temple, is called the lowest (adhama) size.
Half of the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is to be known as the middle [measurement], while the other [the upper part] shall be five-thirds of that;
and in the middle [section], by means of an eightfold division, there are nine *liṅga-udayas*.
O best of the twice-born, beginning from the largest in the month of Jyeṣṭha and decreasing by one quarter [of the size] for each subsequent month,
thirty-three measurements for the liṅgas have been proclaimed.
Alternatively, the measurement of the womb is prescribed in another manner:
the lowest [measurement] shall be one quarter of the womb, while the highest measurement shall be three quarters.
Having made the middle [section] as before, measuring thirty-three [units], one should divide it by means of the *mānāṅgula* for the sake of achieving purity in length and so forth.
Or, for the sake of their purification, one should divide them into portions; that is stated here as beginning with a sixteenth part and increasing up to twenty-four.
In that case, the preceptor should divide [the total] into a hundred parts and add one part;
or, as previously mentioned by me, he may add six parts, provided it is conjoined with auspicious factors such as the *āya*.
Regarding the measurement of the earth-element, it has been taught in brief by one fearing prolixity;
[it is determined] by the portions of the modifications of the four elemental tastes in their respective order. (64.23)
O twice-born ones, when the three parts are increased by one-third each, it is called Āḍhyaka;
the Āḍhya liṅga is equal in all dimensions and is proclaimed as the most distinguished.
Among those, one should divide each of the eight parts in the middle into nine parts;
however, in the case of the length of the liṅga, it should be divided into seven, eight, or nine parts.
The heights of the portions belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa have been fully proclaimed;
this is declared to be the common characteristic for all of them.
One should arrange the proportions for the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, in sequence: equal parts, increasing by one part, exceeding by one part, and three parts respectively.
In the opinion of those who hold that [the measurement] should increase according to Śiva’s superiority and be appropriate for all castes,
one should divide the length of the liṅga into three parts, and the portion of Brahmā shall consist of one part.
In that same way, it may be a portion of Viṣṇu or indeed a portion of Rudra;
such a *tāra* (vowel) which resembles a single part is described here as having equal segments.
The fourth, fifth, and sixth parts; the fifth, sixth, and seventh parts;
the sixth, seventh, and eighth parts; and the seventh, eighth, and ninth parts. (64.30)
This is declared to be the "Vardhamāna" [mandala] for the Brahmins and the other castes in their respective order:
seven-sevenths, eight-sevenths, five-sevenths, five-sevenths, and six-sevenths.
The portion consisting of four Vedas, five Vedas, and five arrows (55), and the portion consisting of three qualities, three fires, and two ages (236);
thus has the measure exceeding that of Śiva been declared for the twice-born in their respective order.
Having divided the height of the liṅga into nine parts, one should take portions consisting of the qualities of the bonds (three) for the base;
then, for the circular, octagonal, and quadrangular [forms], the circumference should be six, seven, and eight [parts] respectively.

This [calculation] is the rule of three (trairāśika) in the treatise; now, however, the svastika [measurement] is described. According to the measurement of the linga, it is ninefold: two parts in the middle and three parts [above].
In the Vṛtta [meter], the length is one-eighth of a yuga; this is also recommended for the Śūdra.
However, the Trairāśika [meter] is considered to bestow all desires upon everyone.
The thousandfold Dhārā-liṅga, worshiped by both the wealthy and the poor as well as by the lords of the gods,
is declared to be common to all, including the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
The *dhārāliṅga* is praised when it increases from a single stream up to a hundred streams;
now, the [liṅga with] a thousand streams is described.
In a square plot measuring nine cubits, divided into eleven parts,
it is situated in the ninety-first part, placed in an odd-numbered division.

(Verse 64.39) Or else, for one thousand liṅgas, the face-liṅga should be exactly one-ninth [of the total height]; I shall now describe the face-liṅga which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

That [mandala] may have four faces, three faces, or be endowed with a single face. That which is the high Tārā, when divided by two, becomes the downward-facing head through the abandonment of the qualities (guṇas).
One should fashion the forehead, the nose, the face, the chin, and the lips;
now, O wise ones, the emergence of the neck and arms is being described.
On the length of the liṅga, at the portion of the modification,
one should fashion four faces on the four sides outside the liṅga-base for the purpose of their emergence.
The remainder should be fashioned into the form of the *liṅga* according to the proportions of Viṣṇu’s portion;
the neck should enter the knees at a measurement of four *aṅgulas*.
In the same way, that which is joined with the long [measure] and the remainder is like the Pratimoka;
having divided [the height] starting from Nanda-mātra and so forth, there are four types of six tālas.
For the purpose of exit, one should arrange an enclosure on the four sides;
it should be fashioned with a width of six and a quarter *mātrās*.
Or, one may divide that upper portion into three faces equally, like the seasons;
the arms and shoulders should extend out by half a part, measuring six finger-breadths.
The neck should be one-third [of the height], and the crown should be two parts;
the remainder should be divided into four parts according to their respective measurements.
One should fashion the head, forehead, nose, face, and chin,
as well as the crown, resembling the twelve parts of Viṣṇu.
The portions for the exits from the faces shall each be eight units;
in the case of one face, the height of the face is three units less than half the length of the face. (64.49)
The crown should constitute one part; when the remainder is divided into two, the best of teachers should increase the neck and shoulders in that same sequence.
One should fashion the opening of the mouth with a measurement of nine units;
when the length of the liṅga is one hundred and eight [units], this [nine-unit] portion is desired for the length.
I shall describe their head-ornaments (*śirovartana*), which are considered to be of many kinds:
the one called Puṇḍarīkaviśāla, Śrīvatsa, and Śatrumardana. (64.52)

When the degrees of the *kāṣṭhā* are divided by four and increased by one part for each subsequent division, the various types beginning with *puṇḍarīka* arise, leading to the attainment of distinct results. (64.53)
From Puṇḍarīka one attains fame; from Viśāla, vast prosperity;
from Śrīvatsa, one gains everything; and from Śatrumardana, victory.

By increasing the head of the cock's egg by one-fourth of the size of the image, there is an increase in progeny; for the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is the source of the attainment of offspring. || 64.55 ||
Because it increases by one-third and is like the crescent moon,
it attains supreme longevity, the highest world, and excellent good fortune.
Because they increased their prosperity by one-sixth, they have the form of a cucumber;
for it was from them that the Sādhyas and Siddhas attained supreme prosperity, O Maruts. (64.57)
Alternatively, another method for the head-ornament (*śirovartana*) is described:
one should divide the *tāra* into eight parts by turning it with an additional half-part. (64.58)
What is called the *chatraśīrṣa* (umbrella-top) is described as resembling a gourd;
it may consist of six parts, or the curvature may be two and a half parts.
The *kukkuṭāṇḍaśiras* is said to be fashioned with a width equal to half [the height];
it is described as resembling a crescent moon, fashioned with a width equal to one-third [of the height].
The head, resembling a bubble, is one and a half parts when [the height] is divided into eight;
these indeed are the eternal heads for all liṅgas.
A linga endowed with auspiciousness in its dimensions and other qualities accomplishes all goals;
however, one should know that in the case of an inauspicious one, it brings inauspicious results, and for that purpose, one should place [the consecrated image] above it.
In a one-cubit [image], there should be one finger-breadth; in two or three cubits, three mātrās;
in four or five cubits, five; and in six or seven cubits, seven.
In the Vasunandaka style, it is considered to be one part greater than the measure of Nanda;
however, in the Śirovartana portion, it is either one-fourth or one-sixth [of the total].
One, two, or three [parts] should be given from the portion of Brahmā in sequence;
one-third of the portion for the head-ornament (śirovartana) is placed above the portion for worship.
Alternatively, having placed [the measurement] upon the length of the liṅga, the wise one should apply one part in six parts of its height;
specifically, one part for the base of the liṅga and two parts for the middle.
O best of the twice-born, one should apply one-third [of the measurement] to the upper part of the *liṅga*,
or alternatively, having fixed the measurement of the head alone, one should fashion it.
Having mixed the portion with the head and supported it on both sides,
one should draw two circles on both sides according to that measurement.
One should place the third mandala in the upper region, in the middle of the head;
by means of these three mandalas, two fish-diagrams (matsya) arise here.
Standing at the point where the two threads located at the mouth and the tail of that fish intersect, one should fashion the auspicious head by means of three [threads].
The head is considered to be of two types according to the distinction of caste and gender:
that of Brahmins is shaped like an umbrella, while that of Kṣatriyas resembles a hen's egg.
For Vaiśyas it has the appearance of a half-moon, and for Śūdras it should be made of tin;
furthermore, another [type] is described according to the distinction of other liṅgas.

In the case of a broad-liṅga (liṅgavyāsa), there are four types according to the proportion of the modified part (vikārāṃśa) being one, two, three, or four times the height, respectively; among these, the first type is like an umbrella when the liṅga is symmetrical.
If there is a predominance of Śiva, it shall be the third; if it is Vardhamānaka, it shall be the fourth.
However, a mutual intermixture of these is ordained to lead to inauspiciousness.
O twice-born ones, the specific characteristics of the liṅgas of Svāyaṃbhuva and the others are not required;
rather, one should perform their classification according to well-known conventions. (64.75)
The *liṅga* endowed with all auspicious marks is the accomplisher of all goals.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the *Liṅga*," in the great *tantra* known as the *Kāmika*.
The Ritual Procedure for the Planting of Sprouts.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa);
at the beginning of all auspicious rites, the auspicious sprout-offering must be performed.
It is proclaimed to be of three kinds— superior, middling, and inferior—
whether it lasts for nine days, seven days, five days, or even three days.
Alternatively, having worshipped Śiva, one may perform the immediate offering of sprouts;
the offering of sprouts for the deities begins from the evening of that day.
On that day, however, which is esteemed by both humans and gods, Soma is the lord of seeds; therefore, one should offer them at night.
It should not be performed during the daytime; if it is performed then, it brings destruction to the performer.
It should be done in a place in front of the house, or to the left, or to the right-front.
Beginning from three cubits, one should construct the pavilion up to eleven cubits;
it should be built there, or in a location previously determined.
Or one should perform the rite of offering the *tīrtha* and the *aṅkura* in the sacrificial hall of the Īśāna direction,
which is provided with a canopy, banners, and door-arches.
On a site joined with a garland of *darbha* grass and provided with strings of pearls,
one should perform the sprinkling for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*), or otherwise purify it with the *astra-mantra*.
The *śarāva*, the *pālikā*, and the *ghaṭikā* are remembered as being of three kinds.
That which is made with the two superior classes [of materials] is the *śarāva*; that which is made with the two middle classes would be the *madhyama*. (65.9)
The characteristic of those [vessels] is said to be that they consist of a single group ending with the little finger;
they are known to be fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or clay.
The width of the mouth of the *pālikā* is declared to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
it should be reduced by one finger-breadth each for the medium and the smallest sizes respectively. (65.11)
The height is equal to the width, and the thickness of the base is half of that;
the remainder all around is said to be one-eighth of the width. (65.12)
The pit is said to be one-third of the width;
the width of the staff is desired to be one-fourth of the width. (65.13)
The *ghaṭikā* is shaped like a water-pot (*kalaśa*), while its staff and base are as before;
the width of the jar is one *vidyeśvara-aṅgula* and it is provided with five faces.
The tripod or the Śarāva vessel should be made with a measurement equal to half that of the Pālikā;
or the Pālikā and the others may be proclaimed according to whatever measurement is available.
One should avoid for the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) that which is cracked, black, hollow, foul-smelling, old, or joined with broken liṅgas and the like. 65.16.
The shallow bowl has Brahmā as its deity, and the *pālikā* has Viṣṇu as its deity;
the *ghaṭikā* is associated with Īśāna; the Guru should worship those [deities] within them.
The supreme [number] is proclaimed as sixteen individually;
the middling is reckoned as twelve, and the inferior would be ten.
Thus, the supreme method consists of sixteen [deities]; the intermediate method is indicated by three, two, or one; and the inferior method would likewise consist of three, two, or one. (65.19)
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the installation of all [the deities]:
having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should decorate it with various powders of flour.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then perform the laying of the lines;
the extent of the lines is ten [units] toward the east and likewise ten toward the north.
Having gathered nine in the center, one should discard sixteen on all sides;
in the four directions, there are four doors, each measuring two squares.
In the corners, there should be twelve [squares], and within them shall be the *pālikā* and other vessels;
in the center, on the nine squares, is the lotus, and the *pālikā* is placed in the corner region.
Water-clocks (ghaṭikās) should be placed to the left of the door, and shallow bowls (śarāvas) to the right of the door;
in this manner, the best of preceptors should arrange them at all other doors as well.
Having laid out the eastward line reckoned as eight squares and likewise the northward line,
one should leave a space of one square in the center and discard eight squares on all sides.
In the center there should be a jar for Soma; furthermore, in the two rows to the east, there are Pālikās numbering according to the Manus (fourteen), while in the west, Ghaṭikās are prescribed.

And in the six intermediate spaces between them, O twice-born ones, there are two water-cups (śarāvaka) on the right and left; two are said to be at the sides of the jar, one in the east and one in the west.
Thus, there would be superior, middling, and likewise inferior;
the eastern thread is reckoned by the number of sages, and the northern thread is exactly the same.
Having left the space for the Vedic verse in the center, one should place the water-pot (kumbha) there;
starting from the northeast corner, the small bowls (pālikās) are arranged in the outer row.
In the southern direction (the direction of the Rākṣasas), the bowls are prescribed up to the corner;
in the intermediate directions, two each are recommended, while in the northwest and northeast, more are considered appropriate.
The superior and inferior [measures] have been declared; now the medium-superior is being described.
Having divided [the ground] into five sections of five steps each, one should place the water-pot in the middle section.
One should place the *pālikās* outside in the four cardinal directions and the corners;
and it is taught that there are eight *ghaṭikās* outside the *kumbhas*, within their own interior.
One should place the shallow bowl (śarāva) outside, and then inside the *pālikās*;
the middle one is declared to be the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), and now the "middle-middle" (*madhyamadhyama*) is described.
Six lines should be drawn first with their tips pointing east, and likewise six going north;
having thus formed a nine-square grid in the center, excluding the northeast and southwest corners.
The five *pālikās* are situated in the east, and the *śarāvakas* in the west;
three are established in the south, and six *ghaṭikās* are positioned in the north.
In the intermediate space toward the northeast, however, a single earthen bowl is situated;
likewise, in the region toward the southwest, a shallow cup is well-placed.
Then, having divided [the area] into sixteen parts, the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva* are established in the center according to the Vedas, in their proper sequence.
Beginning from the northeast corner and ending with the southeast, these have been declared;
in this very same sequence, one should install them starting from the southeast and proceeding to the southwest.
Having formed a grid of nine squares, a jar for Soma is placed in the center;
then, as before, one should arrange the *pālikās* and other vessels, beginning with Śarva.
The remaining portion outside the *soma* [mandala] is proclaimed as the *kanyasādya*.
Having fashioned nine squares as before, [one should place them] at the eastern and western gates.
Beginning from the northeast corner, one should place the *pālikā* and the others;
this shall be the medium-small, and thereafter the small-small. (65.41)
Having also laid out nine squares, one should omit the four corners;
then one should place a water-pot in the center and the ritual vessels (pālikās) and so forth starting from the east.
Thus the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) has been declared; now its performance is described.
A wise man should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared with eight droṇas of rice.
Half of that is declared the middling [measure], and half of that would be the lowest.
As prescribed for the Śiva-kumbha, one may use a kumbha, a prastha, or a pratipālika.
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp;
half of that [area] should be filled with rice, along with sesame seeds and parched grain.
Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should place a water-pot in its center,
filled with either a *droṇa* or half a *droṇa*, and accompanied by the prescribed number of jars.
The golden disc of the moon should be provided with its sūtra, its lid, and its beard, joined with water, and endowed with a face covered by a fine cloth.
O twice-born Śivas, one should place the moon in the center of that with its own mantra;
the wise man should then cause milk-rice (pāyasa) to be offered, and thereafter cause betel-leaf to be given.
One should place the *pālikās* and other vessels with the Īśāna mantra;
using *darbha*, *kuśa*, or *palāśa* grasses, one should ensure they are without holes and well-perforated.
One should fill the *pālikā* vessels and others with earth produced from a pure location;
thereafter, one should sow the substances that have indeed been saturated with milk.
One should sow sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, peas, and aduki; these are the seven seeds for the highest quality field.
Mudga, māṣa, kulattha, sesame, and likewise mustard—this is declared to be the middling [measure]; the smallest consists of sesame and mustard.
The lowest [type of gift] is described thus; alternatively, another is mentioned here:
sesame, mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, peas, and horse gram. (65.53)
Rice, priyaṅgu, apāmārga, barley, and śyāma are mentioned here;
or else, the characteristics of substances are stated in another manner.
Then sesame, mustard, mung beans, as well as black gram, horse gram, flat beans, rice, apāmārga, peas, paddy, and adhakas are prescribed. (65.55)
Green wheat, rice, and bamboo are proclaimed [as the materials];
one should offer these, having soaked them in milk, with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
O twice-born ones, the sprouts should be nurtured so that they become beautiful;
one should sow the seed facing either eastward or northward with the most excellent [seed].
One should place the *pālikā* vessels and the others using only the water contained in that jar;
before the water in the jar has dried up, one should fill them with fragrant water.
Having worshipped daily with sacrificial oblations, he should cause them to be given until the end of that day;
when the designated day arrives, the wise man should dismiss the Moon-god.
At the conclusion of the extinguishing rite, one should cause it to be placed down, covered and protected by mindfulness.
White sprouts are auspicious; they should be tender and growing upwards. (65.60)
One should avoid wood that is black, smoke-colored, tawny, or dark-green,
as well as that which is horizontal or crooked, in rites of purification.
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the very purpose of averting those [obstacles];
furthermore, a circumambulation of the village and so forth must be performed for the sake of the sacred site's sprout (tīrthāṅkura).
Provided with the clay that has been taken up, accompanied by the *pālikā* and other vessels,
endowed with the trident, and provided with the *kundālī*.
One should avoid circumambulating [the image] together with Caṇḍeśvara and adorned with all ornaments;
or rather, one should avoid the circumambulation of all others as well.
Regarding the collection of clay and so forth, one may either perform the act of wandering or not;
[this applies] by a riverbank, a pond, in a forest, or even in a flower garden.

In the case of constructing long ponds, embankments, and the like, one should collect earth according to the prescribed rite; the wise practitioner should thoroughly sprinkle the ground with the water of Śiva.

Then, having invoked the Earth, one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings using the *hṛdaya-mantra*; having praised the world-protectors all around, one should worship them with the weapon-mantra.
Having dug the ground three times with a weapon while facing north,
he should take up earth with his left hand and fill the interior of the small mound.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, or by means of his attendants, and having caused the clay to be carried [around], he should afterwards cause it to enter the temple and so forth. (65/69)

The rite of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed with three groups, beginning with the *pālikā*, for the best; with two groups, it is called middling; and with a single group, it is the lowest. // 65.70 //

If the aforementioned [time] is not obtained, then at a time close to it, the immediate offering of sprouts—consisting of a coconut flower accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*)—should be performed. 65/71.
One should cast [the seeds] into the middle of the small pots while recollecting the seed-mantra;
the planting of the sprouts may be done in either three hour-glasses or three shallow bowls.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Offering of Sprouts," in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Liṅga.
Now, O twice-born ones, listen to the consecration of the *liṅga*;
one should determine the time for the installation and other rites according to the previously mentioned rule.
One should avoid Yama, Āśleṣā, Agni, Śūrpa, Śraviṣṭhā, Vāruṇa, Jyeṣṭhā, and the three Pūrvās for rites such as the installation of an image.
The fourth, eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lunar days are considered inauspicious. Mars and Saturn should be known as undesirable, yet when conjoined with benefics, they bestow auspicious results.
The zodiac signs should be excluded from the movable [category]; the remainder is declared as before.
However, the rite of offering seedlings (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed beforehand according to the prescribed rule.
One should construct a pavilion for the purpose of sacrifice upon a palace or similar structure, on the front and sides,
and also in the north, with dimensions of three cubits and so forth, or eight, six, and ten [cubits] respectively.
For the others, it should increase by a barley-corn [at each step] from that [central point], or likewise starting from the Arka [digit] and so forth;
in the same manner, the bathing pavilion should be situated to the north.
It should be equal in measure to the altar, or as large as may be suitable for bathing;
likewise, it should be provided with a girdle and adorned with a moat.
The altar in the central part should be eight finger-breadths high and four cubits wide; for those [altars] larger than one cubit, one should calculate by increasing the size by one cubit.
Alternatively, a platform (vedikā) two cubits wide may be constructed by hand;
or, according to the measurement of that platform, there should be a pavilion (kūṭa) or a water-shed (prapā) on its exterior.
Alternatively, in every region, there should be a water-shed of great extent;
or else, there should be a pavilion on all sides, according to the strength of its beauty in smaller areas.
For the three smallest types of liṅgas, the altar (vedī) should be one cubit (hastamitā) in size;
for the three middle types of liṅgas, it should be provided with twelve pillars.
The altar should be provided with twenty limbs in the three highest categories;
one should arrange the outer rows according to the measure of devotion for each respective case.
Thus, in the first [arrangement], there is a row; thereafter, there shall be eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
In the middle [arrangement], it should be known that there is a division by two, resulting in twenty-four sacrificial pits.
Or, even when combined with three divisions, there may be forty-eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
or there may be the triad of Jyeṣṭha-liṅgas, accompanied by thirty-two sacrificial pits.
One should arrange the external [circumference] so that it rotates according to its beautiful proportions;
the other [inner part] would be primary, and it is considered to be within the circle.
In all cases, nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) are prescribed for a stationary liṅga of the smallest or even smaller size;
alternatively, five or even one pit is said to be appropriate even for a mobile liṅga.
In the five [directions], one should place squares, half-moons, semi-circles, and circles;
in the other directions, one should arrange hexagons, octagons, lotuses, and corners.
The primary enclosure should be circular in this way, or it may be square;
likewise for the inner enclosure, but the outer one is square.
One should also perform the *vṛtta* (the square enclosure), either as a single one throughout or otherwise;
everything not mentioned here should be carried out according to the previously stated rule. (66.19)
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
endowed with the eight auspicious symbols, and beautified by sprouts of auspiciousness.
Equipped with nine banners and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and other ornaments—this is the pavilion for the *liṅga*, and especially for the image. (66.21)
It is recommended for all rites, especially for festivals and the like;
in the previously mentioned location, one should construct a pavilion marked with the prescribed characteristics.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] there, one should mark it, or else it may be done in a pure location;
one should protect the liṅga and its pedestal from stones, sand, water, and the like.
In that manner, the preceptor should perform the purification of the linga with earths,
the group of astringents (kaṣāya), cow’s urine, and likewise with water.
Then, with cow dung and fragrant, very purifying waters,
[he should sprinkle] while employing the *praṇava*, the *astra-mantra* "huṃ phaṭ," and the gesture of salutation (*praṇati*).
Then, one should worship with either a general mantra or with the Sthāṇu mantra,
having encircled the liṅga and the pedestal (piṇḍī) with kuśa grass, cloth, garlands, and so forth.
In the pavilion, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice,
and cover it with sesame seeds, rice grains, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers.
One should place the liṅga together with its pedestal upon the sacrificial ground with the head facing east;
having covered it with a red cloth, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should divide the length and width, which are equal to the portion of Rudra, into sixty-four parts; the width of a single part of the thread is likewise desired as its depth.
Half of that is known as the lowest; when that [measurement] is divided into eight parts, the width of the cord is proclaimed to be ninefold for all liṅgas.
Having divided [the area] into nine parts with a thread smeared with saffron,
the six marks should be delineated so that they appear on the lower portion.
A fracture of the face, nose, or forehead may occur above the neck; however, that which occurs below it is not desired, so one should examine the marks there.
In the length of the *liṅga*, one part is for the day-portion (*dināṃśa*), while the width of the *lakṣma* is one part;
the earth is depressed, and its line is one-ninth of that width.
The descent of the wing-lines should be measured at half the length of the mark-line;
its width should be made equal to that excavation so that it is beautiful.
When the area of the wings is reduced by eight parts through a rotation of one-sixth,
having given nine parts to the sages, two parts indeed remain below.
The increase is by two and a half parts of the division by fire;
or, having subtracted two parts from below the division by the vikāra [element], it is likewise.
Or, having divided the fortnight by nine suns (days) according to the sequence of fire (three),
or else another characteristic of it is equal when divided into nine parts.
Having multiplied the sixth part by the [number of] qualities, this [measurement] is divided threefold for the abandonment of the parts;
one should then fashion a beautiful mark measuring half a barleycorn at the two divisions.
From below the tip of the ear, one should gradually draw a single Brahma-line until it reaches the Vaiṣṇava portion at the base of the thread, which is like the eye of an elephant.
Alternatively, the lower second portion is characterized by the shape of half a barley grain;
both of these, excluding the wing-lines, are proclaimed here.
Three lines should be drawn along the entire surface;
having set aside four parts out of sixteen at the top, [one should leave] twelve parts.
Excluding the two lower portions of the stalk along with the lotus and its bud,
one should divide the height— measured from the portion of Rudra— into three parts and discard the uppermost part in sequence.
Having divided the portion of the wing into ten parts, the portion of space shall be the bud;
its width should be known as equal to that, while the stalk is one-eighth part.
Starting from the bud (mukula), one should draw the lines of the wings;
these two are to be known as the jeweled lines (maṇirekhā), and their junction occurs at the back.
Upon the portion of Rudra, which is the share of Rudra, one should place the portion of the qualities (guṇa) above;
with one [unit] as the bud and the stalk, it is celebrated as the sevenfold part (saptāṃśa).
Having divided the portion of Rudra into nine parts, one should discard three parts at the top; the bud shall be made with one part, and the stalk shall consist of five parts.
Furthermore, within that [measure], one should discard four parts from the top at the sixteenth division;
the bud is made with one part, and the stalk is desired to be ten parts.
In the twelve-fold division, having set aside the portion for worship, there are two parts above that;
one part is to be known as the bud, and eight parts are desired for the stalk.
O twice-born ones, having placed the length of the stalk horizontally below from the base of the bud, one should draw a thread along both sides so that it becomes straight.
Then, having likewise produced two squares—one below and one above the two sides—and having placed a cubit at the corner situated above the exterior; 66/50.
Starting from the lotus bud and extending to the end of the stalk, one should rotate it outward;
having divided the length of the stalk into nine parts, one should increase it by one part at each stage.
Therefore, there should be a ninefold increase by means of the ninth measure;
within the interval of the stalk, when divided eightfold, it is increased by half a part at each step.
O twice-born ones, there shall be a mark of four mānas within the interval of the wing-lines;
and the wing-line must be drawn from the base of the bud-line.
The tip of the *liṅga* may be like a bud, or like an elephant’s eye, resembling a lotus,
shaped like a plantain bud, or like the tip of a trident or an *aśvattha* leaf.
It may possess the foremost weapons and missiles of the world-protectors, or indeed the supreme weapon of Śiva;
thus, O twice-born ones, has the characteristic of the universal Liṅga been proclaimed.
This [redness] is not found in a linga made of gems, nor even in one of metal;
it is not present in a Bāṇaliṅga, nor in one of iron, nor in those originating from rivers or springs.
In the case of radiant gems of fire that transcend their own formal characteristics,
whether they are produced from jewels or from metal, a mark may or may not be applied.
In the middle of the opening, the wise preceptor should draw the seat of the *lakṣma* in the shape of a vulva with its apex pointing upward,
using a golden stylus.
Recalling the mantra of the weapon, one should draw the mark with eyes and metal,
or else have it drawn by those two according to the various treatises on the arts.
Therefore, one should rotate it exactly according to the scripture;
for a line that is deficient or excessive destroys both the patron and the artisan. (66/60)
Therefore, one should turn back the king together with his kingdom;
the preceptor, being fit for the mantra, shall cause the master-craftsman to perform the work.
Then, having dismissed the artisan, one should lead [the image] to another sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila),
where there is either a copper vessel or a bronze bowl filled with honey and clarified butter.
The wise man, while recollecting the Netra-mantra, should touch this [image],
and then [touch] a heap of grain, a cow with its calf, and likewise the Brahmins.

Following the very procedure for the giving away of a maiden, the Guru should cause the disciple to behold Śiva through the Brahma-mantras; having brought forward the concealed cloth, he should lead him from place to place.
On a wooden seat or upon *kuśa* grass, the installation should take place as before;
to the north of that, however, is the installation of Bhavānī, or alternatively, right there.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having especially adorned them,
one should carefully place the God and the Goddess upon a chariot or similar vehicle.
O highly fortunate ones, one should perform the circumambulation of the site or the temple with various kinds of ornaments; some specific distinction is now being stated.
Within seven days prior to the day of installation, having fashioned both the liṅga and the pedestal (piṇḍikā),
one should join the liṅga together with the stone slab.
Having joined the pedestal and performed the eight-fold binding (aṣṭabandha), one should then perform all the rites;
first, however, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snāpana) with substances such as the thousandfold [offerings].
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having performed a circumambulation of the village,
one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the purpose of the preliminary consecration in water.
Then, having examined the liṅga and the pedestal, one should worship them with garments and other articles.
Having tied the protective thread (kautuka), one should [worship] upon the pedestal of the liṅga in due order.
Having covered one who possesses a long beard on all sides with garments,
and having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) within the mandala, one should arrange a bed there.
In the center of that, one should place the pitcher named Śiva along with the Vardhanī vessel;
all else shall be the same, and a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is prescribed in front of the womb-chamber.
Therefore, setting aside this digression, I shall now speak of the subject at hand:
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the deity, together with the pedestal, in water for two or three nights.
For one night, or for a day and night, or even for just a single watch,
having prepared a water-distribution hall adorned with pavilions in water reaching up to the navel. (66.75)
Having thus prepared two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) in sequence on the bank of the water,
one should then install the God and the Goddess upon the auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*) in their proper order.
Having covered [the image] with a new cloth and provided it with a hanging fringe,
one who is composed should place eight jars around Śambhu and the Goddess.

Then, one should place within the water those jars, which are richly adorned with primary *kūrca* grass and cloth, joined with gold, and containing the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), as well as the God, the Goddess, and the jars themselves.
One should cause it to lie upon a wooden plank or similar surface with the head toward the east and the face turned upward;
thereafter, having dismissed the artisan, [one should place it] in the consecrated sacrificial pavilion.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should smear the ground with cow dung;
then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.
One should perform the decoration of the Paṇṭapa with the previously mentioned procedure; the Śivācārya, having bathed and wearing clean garments and an upper cloth, [should proceed]. (66.81)
The image-protectors (mūrtipās), likewise adorned and wearing the five-fold ornaments, are distinguished only by being devoid of turbans.
Having reached the sacrificial ground, the Guru, holding the general *arghya* water,
should worship the doors together with the gatekeepers stationed at the eastern and other directions.
Nandi and Mahākāla are in the east; Bhṛṅgi and Vināyaka are in the south; Vṛṣabha and Skanda are in the west; and Devī and Caṇḍa are in the north.
Bhadra, Vijaya, Vijṛmbha, and Lohita follow in sequence;
at the archway, beginning from the east, are the kalās of Śānti and the others at the door.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the Guru— whose body is purified, whose essence is mantra, and who has performed the internal sacrifice— should enter through the southern gate.
Having performed the purification of the materials for the *arghya* offering, having worshipped his own hands and himself,
and having adorned his five limbs, he should be fully engaged in the worship of the *vāstu*.

Endowed with the consecration of the pitcher (kumbha-saṃskāra), accompanied by the rites of scattering and strewing flowers, it includes the worship of the Śiva-pitcher and the weapon (astra), as well as the adoration of the world-protectors (lokapāla).

Endowed with his own command, accompanied by the whirling of the water-pot weapon (kumbhāstra), having performed the full worship of the water-pot weapon, and joined with the formal request for its employment; || 66.89 ||
Endowed with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa-saṃskāra) and accompanied by the generation of the Śiva-fire,
one should bring the Supreme Lord from the place where he has been consecrated in the water.

In the pavilion known as the *snānamaṇḍapa*, one should begin the ritual bathing as before, using earths, the group of astringents (*kaṣāyavarga*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and water infused with fruits. (66.91)
One should bathe the Bull-bannered Lord with offerings of flowers, water from leaves, scented water, water containing minerals, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), or water from *kuśa* grass.
In this very same way, one should perform the supreme bathing ceremony for Bhavānī as well;
having clothed her with a pair of garments, one should worship her in due order with perfumes and other offerings.
Having prepared the auspicious thread for Śambhu and the Goddess in due order,
the wise man should then prepare a bed with rice grains and other such materials.
One should spread out eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, half as many of husked rice,
half as many again of sesame seeds, along with parched grain, *darbha* grass, and flowers.
One should prepare the pillows in this sequence: made of leather, made of hair, made of wool, made of feathers, and likewise made of cotton.
If these are unavailable, one should prepare the bed using a mixture of five types of cloth;
having worshipped it with the seat-mantras, one should install Śakti as the presiding deity of the bed.
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should lead it followed by Bhavānī;
when the gateway is reached, one should offer the *arghya* in due order.
Having placed the Lord upon the bed with His head toward the east,
one should place the Goddess named Kriyā, whose form is the pedestal, to the north of the Liṅga.
One should install the Goddess at the base of the *liṅga* together with the nine cavities (*navagarta*),
along with the installation of the forms (*mūrti*) and the lords of the forms (*mūrtīśvara*), and accompanied by the principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are indeed the lords of the three principles (tattvas) within the Liṅga;
these are declared to be the three principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
The eight forms— Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Space— should be installed in each section.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra,
Bhava, Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the guardians of the eight forms.
In the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the five forms, the elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
these are considered the forms in the liṅga, and Brahmā and the others are regarded as the guardians of those forms.
The pervasion of the stones upon the pedestal of the *liṅga* proceeds from the beginning in sequence;
furthermore, there is the conceptualization of three sections ending with Śiva, Śakti, and Manīṣā.

The sequence [of the principles] ending with Vidyā, Śakti, and Śiva, as well as those belonging to Māyā, Sadāśiva, and Śakti, and ending with Śabda, Citta, and Manīṣā, [are located] respectively in the Liṅga, the Pīṭha, and the Stone.
Action, knowledge, and likewise will are considered the presiding deities of the three principles;
they are the Sustainer, the Radiant, the Fierce, the Moonlight, the Consciousness, and the Exalted Power.
Dhātrī and the goddesses are proclaimed as the Mūrtipās;
in the Nyāsa consisting of the five forms (pañcamūrti), Vāmā and the others are considered the Mūrtipās.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānī, and Icchā are thus proclaimed;
having worshipped these deities, the lords of the paths, in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (66.109)
Then, having worshipped Brahmā of unmanifest form, Śiva whose body is knowledge,
and the limbs of Śiva, in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having covered [the vessels] with new cloth, one should worship each portion;
then, one should place the jars, which have Viśveśvara as their essence, all around upon the altar.
One should place the "sleep-jar" (nidrākumbha) at the region of the head and the "augmenting jar" (vardhanī) to the north;
having wrapped the jars with cloths, they should be provided with golden lotuses.
Having offered abundant food offerings along with betel leaves accompanied by mantras, [the vessels] should be provided with covers and strainers, and adorned with sprouts.

One should commence the rite of fire-offering (homa) together with those who bear the forms of the Guru. The image-bearers (mūrtipās) should be knowers of the Śiva-scriptures and born of the five spheres (pañcagocara). || 66.114 ||

The disciples, sons, grandsons, and others of the Guru should be experts in the sequence of rituals taught in the tantras commenced by the Teacher, and knowledgeable in the mantras and tantras for consecration.

The Brahmins, established in the four directions, were endowed with the power of their own forms, beauty, and capability, as well as the application of focused concentration; they were the givers of the mountain-like four Vedas.
Reciting mantras containing the signs of the deity for the sake of its presence,
they become known as *mūrtipās*, consecrated by means of the *śivaśambaras*.
And in the intermediate directions, those of immeasurable splendor scatter rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, and drops of honey, effecting the destruction of any obstacles to the sacrifice.
Urged by the Guru, the image-bearers, consecrated by Śiva,
having brought their own portions from the principal fire, should install them within their respective [images].
He should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, and likewise honey-drops;
and [he should place] Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa branches in the directions starting from the east.
The *śamī*, *khadira*, *pālāśa*, and *śrīvṛkṣa* trees [should be placed] in the southeast corner;
however, for the principal [fire], it should be the *pālāśa*, or indeed everything may be made of *pālāśa*.
The sacrificial fuel and clarified butter for the fire-pits should be placed in their respective directions in due order,
in quantities of one thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again.
Then, one should perform oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
for the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*), the number should be a tenth part of the root mantra, or equal to it, or half of that.
The oblation to the Mūrtipās is prescribed with the limbs of Brahmā in the eight directions, in due order in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
Having gratified Īśāna in the principal [fire] or the eye-weapon in the central pit, they should then accomplish the supreme [rite] by offering libations to the mantras at the end of the pitcher.
O best of beings, the garlanded water from the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha) causes the presence of peace;
with that [water], one should indeed perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) below each respective portion.
Having purified everything and gathered it together, they should recite their own *śambara* mantras;
then, by the touch of the *darbha* grass, the pure portion becomes the Lord (*Īśvara*).
Having established the supreme reality (paratattva), they should thereafter purify it;
[they should perform] the recitation and other rites of the preceptor with the root-mantras, the atomic mantras (aṇu), and the combined mantras (saṃhitā).
One hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five, or even ten;
[one should perform] the oblation for the forms and the lords of the forms, together with the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles.
Then, by means of pure ghee, or all substances, or sesame seeds,
for one who is engaged in the yoga of pervasive concentration through the power of the form of his own deity.
The image-keepers, who are the supreme teachers performing the yoga of all the junctions,
having thus purified the portion of Brahmā, [proceed] for the sake of purifying the portions of Viṣṇu and the others. (66.131)

Having performed everything as before— the number of oblations, recitations, and so forth— one should, in due order, [offer] the portions for Brahmā and the others using the roots, middle sections, and tips of *kuśa* grass.
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), stationed in their respective directions, should touch [the site] with their own *śambaras*.
In this manner, one should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) and other rites upon the pedestal and the stone slab.
One should sequentially contemplate Kriyā, Ādhāra, Śakti, Mūrti, Mūrtyadhipa, and so forth, as well as Manonmanī and Ananta.
One should fashion the pedestal, the stated root-form, and the Lord upon the stone;
having performed the expiation with the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having performed protection with earth, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds using the Astra-mantra,
and having cast the outer and inner offerings (*bali*), one should cast the offering for the Kṣetrapāla.
If the officiant is uninitiated, he should be initiated here in the interim;
