then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, [should proceed].
Having completed the daily rites such as bathing, the Guru, holding the general *arghya* vessel, worships the gatekeepers and others, and then causes Maheśvara to arise.
Having raised the Goddess, the knower of mantras should worship her with perfumes and other offerings;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should enter the abode of the Lord.
Having sprinkled the stone with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should place it in the center;
in the twenty-first part, specifically in the middle of the door's width.
When the portion has been divided sixfold, the central thread from the middle of the Brahma-thread to half of one part to the left of the Brahma-thread is known as the Śiva-thread.
In the middle of Śiva and Brahmā, and between Hari and Indra,
one should place the Śivasūtra as a measure to the east of the Saumyasūtra.
Having placed that [foundation] in the middle of the joint, the Guru should install the Kaśilā stone,
having uttered the Praṇava, the word of salutation (praṇati), and the words "Vyāpinī" and "Sthirā."
Having uttered the words "Acalety" and "Dhruva" loudly, followed by the syllable "Dhara" from the *Māyāgarbha* mantra,
and ending with the word "Svāhā," one should contemplate all-pervading stability.
Then, having ascended the lotus seat and restrained it with firm support,
one should deposit gems, medicinal herbs, metals, minerals, and seeds as before.
There, one should place either a tortoise or a bull made of gold;
having drawn [the design] with iron, one should then make a pit and cover it with a cloth.
Having protected [the site] with the armor-weapon mantra, one should offer oblations to the lords of the directions;
then, having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should offer a hundred oblations with the sword-mantra.
Having worshipped the God and the Goddess, and having mounted them onto the chariot or other vehicle,
one should offer the *arghya* at the entrance and then touch the upper branch.
One should place [the image] upon an auspicious throne situated within the door-opening;
once it has been made stable, one should clear away any remaining cavities with the weapon-mantra.
Once it has been properly held by the mechanical device and straightened by the plumb line,
one should then lower it into the cavity containing the heavy image.
One should meditate on the power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimant), for there is no difference between the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmī).
Having recited the mantra up to its dissolution, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) by way of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
Then, having joined four *nandyāvarta* stones from the southeast corner with the mantras beginning with *Dharma*, one should perform the rite of raising the Goddess.

First, having uttered the syllable *praṇava*, the syllable *hrīṃ* follows immediately after; then comes the word for the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) in the dative case, ending with the word *manonmanī*. (66.153)
Having joined the pedestal, one should bind it with the eight-fold binding using equal parts of lac,
beeswax, and guggulu resin.
Of all these as well, equal parts of resin (sarjarasa) should be taken;
or else, [resin] should be added in a portion equal to the previously mentioned share of brick powder.
Oil should be poured from the base of all [the vessels], and the cooking should become glossy;
then, the space between the liṅga and its pedestal should be completely filled with sand.
Above that, one should apply the binding material ending with the portion of Viṣṇu;
having made equal parts of sugar and resin, one should grind them into powder.
The supreme guide should knead buffalo butter;
this is praised as the "vajra-bind" (diamond-firm bond), which he should apply within the cavity.
Then, having performed the eightfold binding with lac, guggulu, and sarja resin,
as well as crystal, sugar, and *guruvindaka* [66.159].
Or oil mixed with [the eight substances], or thick curd— the wise one,
having thus applied it upon the pedestal, should commence the ritual placement (nyāsa) therein.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should purify the pedestal of the *liṅga*;
then, one should consecrate the Lord of Gods with the waters contained within the *śānti* pitcher.
O best of the twice-born, this [rite] is for the purpose of pacifying the touch of artisans and others;
the Guru should then install the principles (tattvas) ending with Īśvara upon the fourth finger.
The categories ending with Śakti are within the portion of Viṣṇu, while the Śiva-tattva is within the essence of Śiva;
there is an arrangement of sixty-three words, with nine in each of the two [portions].
The letters from *kṣa* to *ka* are placed in the lower portion; those beginning with the creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with the end (*anta*) are in the middle;
and the form of *sadā* (the eternal) is in the circular portion—such is the arrangement of the phonemes.
The Guru should install the worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Īśvara;
then, he should install the [worlds] beginning with Sūkṣma in the center, numbering eight.
In this manner, the arrangement of the worlds within the *vṛtti* consists of Nivṛtti and the others;
and from Śakti up to Puruṣa, these correspond respectively to the heart (*hṛd*) and the other limbs ending with the armor (*kavaca*).

One should place the mantras in the Brahma-space; Śiva in the space of Hara; the guardians of the world (lokeśas), the weapons, and Gaṇeśa in the space of Īśa; and the Vidyeśvaras in the Brahma-space and Hara.
One should place the mantras in sequence upon the elevated portions of the womb;
one should place the mantra ending in Śānti in the portion of Brahmā, and Śāntyatīta in the center.
One should place the supreme, partless *bindu* within the circular portion;
one should place the mantras of the seats upon the pedestal, and those pertaining to the *liṅga* and the *mūrti* [should be placed] there.
One should install the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) in the liṅga and the power called action (kriyā) in the form of the pedestal;
these mantras, however, should be installed during the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the preceding day.
Having thus performed the placement of the mantras, one should carry out the ritual placement of the jars (kumbha-nyāsa).
Having brought all the jars and placed them upon the altar...
Having performed a circumambulation of the village accompanied by all auspicious rites, he should install [the deity] as before upon a sacrificial mound prepared in front.
Having taken the seed from the water-pot, one should place it upon the top of the *liṅga*;
then, with devotion, one should recite the mantra beginning with the "bulb" (*kanda*) as instructed by the Guru.
Consisting of the power of sound (nāda), subtle, and spreading like the resonance of a bell,
it has emerged from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) through the yoga of abandoning the causal body.
It shone with the brilliance of a thousand suns and possessed a luster like a mass of lightning;
it illuminated the quarters of space with a canopy of shimmering jewels.
Distinguished by mantra and mind, it brings about the arising of the essence of bliss;
it extends to the end of the engagement in the path of emanation and resembles a continuous stream of moons.
One should bring the orb of light situated on the forehead to the door of the uvula,
meditating upon it as it emerges through the *suṣumnā*, shimmering like a flickering star.
One should place the two pervasive [deities] as they enter through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
in this manner, one should effect their presence everywhere by means of the placement of the living soul (jīvanyāsa).
In this very manner, one should install the Śakti upon the pedestal;
then, with water, one should bathe the liṅga and its base (piṇḍikā) using the water-jar and the vardhanī vessel.
One should place the Vidyeśvaras and Ghaṭasthāṇus on the pedestal starting from the east;
one should then bathe the Supreme Lord with the water contained within their respective pitchers.
"As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains,
so long, O Lord, must you remain here in this presence."
Having thus fulfilled his request, he should perform the ritual for the Goddess right here,
or else the installation of the Brahma-stone on the day of consecration.
Having first established that [image] in the temple and prepared the ground, one should perform everything as prescribed for the site of the liṅga according to the ritual manual (kalpa). || 66.183 ||
Prior to the formal establishment of the temple, one should perform the installation of the *liṅga*;
this procedure is general for all [deities], such as Bāṇa and others, when they are made of stone.
The preceptor, having emerged from the Lord’s abode together with the guardians of the images,
shall accept the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) prepared by the patron.
In the scripture, there may be four kinds: the excellent, the middling, the inferior, and another;
beginning with sixty niṣkas, they decrease in sequence by five niṣkas each.
For a preceptor of gold, the sacrificial fee is considered to be five *niṣkas*; [the fee may also consist of] cows, land, gold, fine houses, vehicles, clothing, and so forth. (66.187)
One should offer all things, including male and female servants and so forth, to the Guru; for others, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be according to the method prescribed in the Lambasthāna.
Having accepted the sacrificial fee and being satisfied, he should bestow upon the requesting patron the merit of the consecration ceremony, accompanied by water and flowers.

The Guru, having meditated upon [the disciple] as resembling a mass of light, places in the right hand of the practitioner— joined with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice grains and accompanied by kuśa grass— a [flower] in the right hand of the disciple.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipatis), should perform the fire-oblation once, twice, thrice, or for three days, or for two days, or even for one day.
Or the Guru alone may perform [the rite] with the Śiva, Brahmā, Aṅga, and Śambara mantras;
likewise, it may be done a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of times with the Śakti mantra.
Having completed the ritual, he should bathe [the deity] again on the fourth day;
having bathed both the God and the Goddess according to the procedure prescribed for bathing, [he should proceed].
Having offered abundant oblations accompanied by various soups and other side dishes,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) as before, using sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, and cooked food.
This is declared to be the general form of the installation of a Śiva-liṅga; however, another installation, which is of a modified form, has also been described.
Thus, whichever mortal causes this to be made, or whoever, being the best of men, performs it himself,
shall enjoy vast pleasures and, at the end of the body, attain liberation.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Liṅga," in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Characteristics of Images.
I shall describe the characteristics of the image; listen, O best of sages! [The height] may be equal to the height of the linga, or twice or three times that.

Or else, the measurement may be by three kinds of finger-breadths (aṅgula) arising from the body's own proportions; or it may be determined by the sanctum (garbha) and the door of the temple (prāsāda), according to the measurement of the base (adhiṣṭhāna).
The measurement of a cubit (*hasta*) is prescribed as being three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), excluding the measure of a barley-corn (*yava*). (67.3)
The remainder may be equal to the *mānasa* or the *samāna*, or when the sixteenth part has been made;
and in the midst of that, in the portion of modification (*vikārāṃśa*), there is an increase by one-third.
One should determine the measurement as either exceeding or falling short of the previous measurement up to the limit of Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, the portion for worship is designated by the term "liṅga."
Starting from three finger-breadths and increasing by two units (mātrās) at a time,
it is said to extend up to one hundred and twenty-five mātrās.
Beginning from seven barley grains and increasing by two barley grains at each step,
the measurement of a *yava* is proclaimed to extend up to one thousand barley grains.
The widths of the houses should be measured in finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula), while the minor [dimensions] are prescribed in barley-corns (yava).
Above the sixty-eighth, the sun, the row, and so forth, there are four types: the Vedas (4), the pair (2), and the six (6).
Having divided [the result] into parts and joined it with one part, it is endowed with the limbs of the birth;
when that is multiplied by eight and divided by twenty-seven, [the remainder indicates the lunar mansion]. || 67/9 ||
The day beginning with the Brāhmaṇa (Sunday) and so forth has been declared; for them, this [day] brings auspiciousness.
One should not plant a tree of noble species at a depth of three finger-breadths.
If auspiciousness is not desired for dwellings such as royal palaces or villages, one should divide the height by five or six parts for rows of buildings and the like. (67.11)
The sky-portion (vyomabhāga) should always be added according to whatever auspicious rise it may have;
likewise, the life-portion (āyāṃśa) is not desired in the three types of finger-breadths (aṅgula).

Even when the measure is a barley-corn (*yava*), one should not plant it with a portion of the *jāti* or a portion of *māyā*. Alternatively, one should determine this by multiplying by eight and dividing by twelve. (67/13)
The number of days is stated as eight and five; when divided by twenty-five, multiplied by nine, and divided by seven, one should indicate the day of the week.
Multiply by nine and divide by ten; one should indicate the expenditure (vyaya).
When multiplied by three and divided by eight, it is called the "birth" (yoni). 67/15.
When multiplied by four and divided by nine, the quotient is desired as the degrees;
the result for two asterisms is declared, and the sign is derived from the asterism. (67/16)
When thirty [degrees] have elapsed, a lunar day (tithi) is said to be complete; the yoga and the weekday (vāra) shall be diminished.
If it is joined with the portions of the birth [ascendant] and conjoined with these [other factors], let that be accepted. || 67/17 ||
If it is not joined with the Āyāṃśa, one should begin with that which is auspicious;
or it may be determined simply by the height of the image that has been taken. || 67.18 ||
The image may be made of stone, wood, metal, clay, or precious gems; likewise, it may be made of minerals or ivory—thus there are seven types. (67.19)
When the auspicious moment has arrived, the wise man, having taken the measurements, should have an image fashioned by a craftsman and mutter the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Thereafter, one should worship the image with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the heart-mantra;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.

In that same manner, one should thereafter worship the expert artisan, the best among craftsmen; and the image of Sadāśiva and the others should be fashioned according to the supreme ten-tāla measurement.
At the beginning, Sadāśiva is proclaimed; thereafter, he who delights in the form of dance, the moon-crested Lord, should be situated together with Umā, Oṃ, and Skanda.
Then Tripuraghna is proclaimed, followed immediately by Liṅgodbhūta;
after that comes Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and beyond that, Geyamūrti.
Then Caṇḍeśādhipati, then Kālakāmādināśaka; thereafter Sukhāsana is proclaimed, and then Kalyāṇasundara.
He is the half-form of Umā and Viṣṇu, accompanied by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
he is then described as mounted upon a bull, and likewise as being joined with two Gaṅgās.
Thereafter, Kaṅkālamūrti shall be the bearer of the oblation;
and immediately following him is Nandīśvaraprasāda, endowed with feet pointing upwards.
One should perform these and other such [deities] according to the previously mentioned tāla:
Manonmanī, Gaurī, Vighneśa, Skanda, and Nandin. (67.28)
Likewise, one should have Caṇḍeśvara made with ten intermediate *tāla*s,
as well as Brahmā, Hari, Lakṣmī, Moṭī, and Vāgīśvarī.
One should [represent] Durgā, Arka, and the Seven Mothers with a height of ten tālas at minimum;
likewise Jyeṣṭhā, Savitṛ, the Ṛkṣas, Indra, the Aśvins, Mahī, and the Sages.
One should fashion Kṣetreśvara with the largest [measurement] of ninety tālas;
one should have the eight Lokapālas and the Vasus fashioned as images with the medium [measurement].
One should have the yakṣas, apsarases, the intermediate classes, the hosts of Maruts with weapons as their forms, and the vidyādharas made at nine tālas by the shortest [measure]. (67.32)
One should likewise treat the Rākṣasas, Yātudhānas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Asuras, and Pitṛs in the same manner.
One should fashion human beings with a height of eight tālas, piśācas with seven tālas,
kubjakas with six tālas, and the most excellent [deities] with nine tālas.
One should have Vighneśa made with either the middle or the lowest [proportion];
the other spirits should be made four *tāla*s in height, including their halos.
One should perform [the dance] for Kinnaras and other men with three *tālas* or two *tālas*, for headless trunks (*kabandha*) with one *tāla*, and for the two parts likewise. 67.36.

Or one may make all of these with a measurement of four or eight *tālas*; that which was previously described regarding the proportions and so forth, beginning with the vertical height (*lamba*), applies to this alone.
And because they differ in their internal scope and in having two, one, or various objects, those measures are distinct; their definition is now stated.

Of those [measures], one part shall be the *mātra*; then, when divided as before, there shall be what is called the portion of a *kalā*, a *kola*, and a *bhāga*, measuring two, three, and four *aṅgulas* respectively.

If one's honor is deficient, there will be a great disease; if it is excessive, there will be an increase in enemies. If one's dignity is deficient, there will be destruction; and if it is excessive, it leads to ruin.

If it lacks the correct proportions, there will be poverty; if it is too large, there will be the loss of one's wife. If it is deficient in its hanging [pendant], it causes the destruction of the king and the kingdom. (67.41)
But if it lacks the proportions, it destroys the artisan and the preceptor;
however, when endowed with all the characteristics, it bestows everything.
The uṣṇīṣa should be known as one aṅgula; the hairline (keśānta) should be three aṅgulas.
The measurement of the face is prescribed as thirteen and a half mātras.
The portion from the hairline to the end of the eye-line is known as the *vedayabādhika*;
and the distance from the eye-line to the edge of the eyelid is declared to be equal to that. (67.44)
The outer portion from half of that cup, however, exceeds the measure of the *veda*;
the neck should be known as half a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and the ear has a height of one unit (*bhāga*).
The distance from the *hikkā* (the cardiac notch) to the heart is considered to be one and a half *viśva*-aṅgulas;
the distance from the heart to the navel is likewise proclaimed to be the same.
From the navel down to the genitals is known as Viśvāmitra;
from the base of the genitals to the knees is twenty-seven finger-breadths (mātrās) long.
The knee should be one *vedā* (four) units, and the shanks are considered equal to the thighs;
the height of the *tāla* should be one *bhāga*, which is recorded as the measurement of the body.
This is indeed the best of the ten-tāla proportions; its middle [measure] is now described.
From the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) to the end of the hair, it is traditionally held to be four mātras.
From the hairline to the end of the chest is known as Viśvāmitra;
the neck is said to be four finger-breadths [in height], and from the neck to the breasts is likewise measured.
That which extends up to the navel should be known as Viśvāmitra; it is equal to that [region].
That which extends from the navel to the penis is remembered as Viśvāmitra. (67.51)
Those two [the thighs] should be as long as the thighs, reaching down to the knees;
the knee should be one part in measure, and the shanks are considered to be equal in measure to the thighs.
In the middle *daśatālaka* [image], the height of the palm tree (*tāla*) shall be one part;
the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) is said to be one *aṅgula*, and the hairline (*keśānta*) shall be three *aṅgulas*.
From the hairline to the end of the bow [the forehead], the measurement is considered to be twelve and a half [finger-breadths].
The neck should be known as half a finger-breadth; this is the height of one part at the throat. (67.54)
From the *Hikkāsūtra*, it is proclaimed that from the heart to the end of the breasts is twelve and a half *mātrās*;
and from the end of the breasts to the navel, it is said to be equal to that.
From the navel to the root of the genitals it is eleven and a half finger-breadths;
from there, up to the tip of the front part, it is twenty-five finger-breadths.
The shank is considered to be one part, equal in measure to the thigh;
the length of the sole is one part—thus is the measurement proclaimed.
The lowest [image] is said to be ten *tālas*, while the ten-*tāla* [measure] is declared to be of three kinds;
for the eldest [type], which is nine *tālas*, the *tāla* consists of twelve *mātrās*.
The division should be four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula); everything else is the same.
It is said that one should construct the characteristic marks using eight tālas for the four-fold division (vedabhāga). || 67/59 ||
One should employ the entire measurement (sarvatāla) for the eight faces, which constitute four parts;
one should divide the measurement of the image (bera) into twenty-eight parts.
One part is called one share; three such shares are said to constitute a *tāla*.
[The height] from the crown of the head to the ears, knees, feet, and the extent of the face [is measured in these units]. (67.61)
Having divided it into twelve parts, one should construct [the image] according to that measurement;
this is remembered as the eternal rule for all deities.
O twice-born ones, the measurement of the *tālas* beginning with the *daśatāla* is now being stated:
the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) shall be three finger-breadths, and likewise the hairline (*keśānta*) shall be three finger-breadths.
The portion up to the end of the eye-line should be three and a quarter parts;
half of that is proclaimed as the jaw, consisting of three and four parts.
The neck is said to be one and a half parts, and the ear is declared to be three mātrās;
from the heart to the navel and down to the genitals, it is stated to be twelve finger-breadths.
The portion from the mouth to the end of the knees, as well as the measurement of the knee itself, each receives one share;
the two shanks, being double that length, shall be one *tāla* in height, consisting of one share.
The width of the face shall be one-tenth of the width of the head;
likewise, the forehead shall be one-eighth, and the neck shall be one-eighth.
The two eyebrows should be fashioned with four parts [of the face], having the luster of smooth, glossy collyrium;
they should be shaped like a bow, and the space between them is considered to be two parts from the middle of the brows.
The measurement ending at the tip of the ear-lobes is for the ear; it should be eight units at the opening.
Furthermore, the middle portion should be one unit, and the tip of the ear-lobes should consist of half a unit. (67/69)
At the openings of the stalks, the width and thickness are half a quarter-part;
they are provided with four parts and increased by one part, and are adorned with earrings.
The two ears, extending for one and a half parts of a *cūli* and emerging with a slight slant,
reach to the edge of the ears, being depressed internally and elevated externally.
The two ears are two parts in width; the *āvartī* is shaped like a pearl-oyster shell (*śukti*), and the *puṭa* is likewise.
The eye is two parts in length and one part in width, with its center being the pupil.
The western portion consists of three parts, with one part in the center being a black circle;
in the middle of that, its fifth part is the vision of light, extending from half of that [circle].
When a figure equal to that is to be constructed upon the two white circles (śuklamaṇḍala),
the two pupils (kanīnike) should have a length equal to half of eight parts (four parts) of the diameter.
The red and white circles of the eyes are shaped like fish;
the upward extension of the eyelashes is indeed only half the length of a big toe.
The eyelashes number in the hundreds, resembling black collyrium; with such beautiful, sleepless eyes, he is fit for the task of all embodied beings.
For one with eyes that are peaceful and soft, [the measurement] should be reduced by four parts from Vyāsa's;
for those with rough eyes, it is considered that they should be made with an increase of half of eight parts.
From the outer corner of the eye to the end of the ear-binding, it is proclaimed as five parts;
the distance between the two eyes shall be two parts, or perhaps slightly less.

O best of the twice-born, the eyebrows should be raised by one-eighth part [of the face]; their width at the middle is considered to be one-quarter [of the face], and they should be joined at the ends with a quarter-part.
The nose at its base, middle, and tip should be twenty-one and a half [finger-breadths] wide;
it should be that high and shaped like a sesame flower.
The width of the bamboo should be one part and its length two parts;
its thickness should be like that of the leaf-sheaths, provided with an additional height of half a quarter-part.
The two ear-lobes (puṭau) should be equal to a *niṣpāva* bean; indeed, they should extend exactly half of a *śrotra* [or ear-length].
They should be straight, horizontal, and three-quarters of a unit less, joined with a width according to the desired proportion.

The *puṣkara* (nostril opening) should be three times the width of the upper part of the nose, or even one-eighth; the tip should be curved toward the end of the nose, and the nostrils (*puṭa*) should likewise be broad.
The *gojirā* (neck-ornament) is half a quarter [of the width] in breadth and height;
it is depressed and elevated from the *gojirā*, four quarters in length, and the *nīvra* (pedestal) is one part with equal lines.

The upper lip should be three parts higher [than the lower], and the two lips should be separated by one-eighth of a quarter [of the total height]. The width of the lower lip should be twice its own length.

The jaw-circle (hanucakra) should be two parts wide, being one-fourth of the width of the broad forehead; it is depressed at the center and elevated at the edges, with its tip slightly raised like the end of a bow.
One should join [the parts] by looking at that which is low and below the lower lip;
the width of the ears is eight parts, and it is joined with a nose of five and five parts.
The throat, the jaw, and the portion of the neck occupy two parts each, while the head extends from the back of the hair to its limit; thus, the face shall be four aṅgulas in length.
The neck is two parts long, and the curvature of the ear is likewise increased;
the head has a width of eight parts at the back, between the curvatures of the ears.
From the starting point of the hairline to the end of the forehead, and from there to the tip of the ear-lobes, the measurement is one *nāha*.
The distance from the hairline to the crown is six or five parts of a *nāha*, and the circumference of the head is eight parts of a *nāha*.

The wise consider it appropriate that the area from the cheek to the temple should have a slight upward curve; the shoulder should be level with the throat, and the base of the arm should be proportionate to the base of the neck. (67.91)
The root-line (mūladosta) is eight parts; from there, the flank (pakṣa) and the armpit-interval (kakṣāntara) follow.
The position up to the sides of the breasts consists of twenty parts diminished by one-third. (67/92)
The middle part is less than that by one division; from that, the hips and the waist are each greater by two parts. Each of these [sections] consists of four parts. (67.93)
The navel is half a part in width, deep at the base and elevated;
from the tip of the feet to the mouth, each successive opening is completely filled with the shape of a cow’s face.
The neck is one-fourth [of the height] from that; then the elevation from the boundary up to the hairline [is equal].
The hiccups (the space between the chin and the hairline) are small, being less than the distance from the tip of the nose to the end of the forehead, and it is divided into equal parts.
The space between the breasts should be two parts; the nipple occupies one-quarter part.
The horizontal ear-attachment at the back consists of twelve times two parts (twenty-four parts).
The sūtra from the front of the chest should be equal [to the height];
that diminished by nine would be twenty at the junction of the hips; and the shoulder-blade [measurement] is three times eight.
The neck is twelve parts, while the back is four parts;
the hips, the waist, and the middle [are likewise], both for the front-facing and the sideways-facing [postures]. (67.98)
The length and width of the penis and scrotum together should be five and two-fifths [parts];
their breadth should be four parts; and the penis itself should be circular, straight, and firm. (67.99)
The buttock-mass at the base of the thighs is one-eighth [of the total height] and circular, being three parts wide;
the base of the thigh is elevated, with its width at the base, middle, and tip [decreasing progressively].
The width at the top of the knee should be twelve parts or eight parts;
its length should be four or six tāras, and the knee should be both long and circular.
The lower leg (jaṅghā) shall consist of six parts, and the shank-bone (nalakā) shall possess a width of four parts;
the heel (pārṣṇi), situated at the middle of the sole, shall measure four, five, or six parts.
The height of the middle surface is one *tithi* (fifteen units); the elevation of the heel (*pārṣṇi*) is five parts;
the ankle-bone (*akṣa*) and the ankle joint (*gulpha*) are four parts each; and the two circles (*maṇḍala*) are two and a half parts respectively.
The middle of the side of the ankle bone should be the midpoint between the knee and the ankle;
the back of the heel should be well-rounded, and the area from the heel to the tip of the big toe should be long. (67.104)
Its sixteenth part is known as two-sevenths;
from the outer edge of the heel to the end of the little toe, the width is four parts.
The height of the heel-guard (pārṣṇirakṣa) should be four parts;
its width should be four parts, and if the thumb is four parts long, its breadth should be two parts.
The length [of the second tier] is four parts plus one quarter, while its circumference is three parts;
for the third [tier], it should be one-third [of the first], joined with a circumference reduced by two quarters.
The ring finger may be three-quarters of a unit in length;
it should have a height and width of one-eighth of a unit, with its length being three units.
The smallest [type] is three-fourths of the length of the divine part and possesses a width of three-fourths of its height;
the nail of these fingers, however, occupies three-fourths of its own tip.
The fingers are slightly reddish, smooth, and elevated, and they are well-rounded;
the second finger, the index finger, has a length exceeding [that of the thumb] by one-eighth part.
The length of the arm is two cubits; half the face is desired for the mouth.
The length of the palm from the wrist to the tip of the fingers is one-sixth [of the forearm].
The section from the middle fingers to the elbow should be as long as that [forearm], with a width of six, five, or three parts; from there, it extends down to the end of the wrist.
The thickness at the base of the pedestal (talamūla) is two parts, and one part at the top;
its length and width are thirty-four [parts], and it is described as being sloped toward the end.
The root of the thumb and its finger is called Śukrodara by that name;
it consists of five parts, has a width equal to the palm, and its middle portion is depressed according to the measure of the palm.
The outer floor should thus be made level with the top of the plinth;
its width is four parts plus one-quarter, while its length is equal to the thickness of the thumb.
The length of the joint at the tip is reduced by one-tenth, while it possesses two parts [of the total length];
its width is reduced by one-eighth part of the index finger, and its tip is reduced by one-eighth part.

The middle finger is considered to have a length of five parts and a half, with each subsequent finger being shorter by one part; it is joined by three mountain-like [joints], and its length and breadth are respectively one-sixth and one part [of the total].
The index finger and the ring finger are equal; the little finger is one unit shorter than that;
its width is reduced by one-tenth of that [length], and it is provided with three joints.
The width at the tip is one-tenth less than the width at the base of the fingers;
it is divided into three, two-and-a-half, two, and four parts respectively.
The width and length of the fingernails have been proclaimed;
the length of the nails should be twice that of the tip-joint of the fingers.
The interior surface is elevated while the exterior is depressed;
however, when the finger is directed inward, it is considered elongated due to the greater number of divisions.
The palms of his hands are red, marked with distinct and unbroken reddish lines,
and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, trident, lotus, and vajra.
His two arms, well-rounded with smooth hair on their surfaces, extend down to his knees;
the space between his palms and thighs is covered by the shadow of his hanging arms.
The outer part should consist of twelve, ten, and eight parts; from the middle of the side, it extends to the crown, the forehead, the neck, the thighs, and the middle of the navel.
The *brahmasūtra* line extends forward from the middle of the genitals to the soles of the feet;
it passes through the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), the eyebrows, the nose, the chin, the navel, the penis, the anus, and between the heels. (67.125)
One should indicate the Brahma-sūtra as straight, firm, and turned back;
it extends from the top of the head to the edge of the ear-lobes, passing through the middle of the ankles, neck, and shoulders.
O twice-born ones, the line from the flank to the hip-joint (sphik) passes through the interior of the body;
the hump (kakud) is greater than the flank-to-hip-joint line by four or five parts.
The thread for the three parts [of the body] should be fifty [units], and the arm should extend outward by ten [units];
the hip-thread should be one-tenth [the length], while at the mouth it should have six units on the back.
From the sūtra at the root of the thigh to the end of the ten [finger-breadths], two parts are outside;
the side-sūtra at the knee is three or four parts, and so on at each face.
From the sūtra line, the distance from the ankle to the heel is equal on both sides;
thus, the side-measure is proclaimed to be five parts from the sūtra line.
The face should be one, two, or four parts between the base of the pillar, the thighs, the knees, and the shanks;
and the distance from the exterior of the *nalaka* should be four parts.

Thus, that which is depicted straight on and visible from all sides is known as *citra* (full painting); that which is attached to a wall [and seen from one side] is indeed *ardhacitra* (half-painting), and is known as *dṛṣṭacitra*. || 67.132 ||
The appearance [of the deity] on a wall-painting is said to be this general [proportion].
Now I shall describe the measurement for women; that is ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the crown of the head to the hairline, the *kolaka* measures four barleycorns;
the measurement for the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance) is three finger-breadths and eight barleycorns in both width and height.
Therefore, the eyes, the nostrils, and the jaw should each be three, two, and one and a half mātrās respectively;
the neck should be three mātrās, and the chest five and a half mātrās.
The middle part [of the body] is ten and a half finger-breadths; the navel is ten finger-breadths from the yoni.
The thighs, knees, shanks, and the soles of the feet should be progressively higher in sequence.
The state [of the breath] is said to be established by twenty-two or twenty-three mātrās;
from the crown of the head to the hairline at each opening of the face, it measures nine or ten finger-breadths.
The forehead, ending at the hairline, is twenty-nine [finger-breadths] in measure; it is known to be arrow-length (five finger-breadths) in width at its center, extending forward.
From the line of the eyes, the height of the ears should be two finger-widths above the middle of the eyebrows;
the middle of the eyebrows should be one barley-corn in width and height, and its length should be three finger-widths.
The space between the eyebrows is gradually tapered at the ends;
it is one finger-breadth wide, and the bow of fine, smooth hair is even.
In the middle of the space measuring eight barley-corns in height and sixteen in width, the two eyes have an extent of five barley-corns; in their center is the black pupil.
In two white mandalas, each with a diameter of four and a half barleycorns,
there are two pupils situated within them, each as long as a barleycorn and marked by a star.
The vision of light is one barley-corn in size, situated in the middle of the black portion [of the eye];
its width is that of the upper and lower eyelashes, and its height is two barley-corns and a half.
The ear is equal in width to the eye, with an additional five *yavas*;
from the attachment of the earlobe, the tip of the ear is recorded as being seven *yavas* from that point.

The ear-ornament (śrotrabandha) should be three barley-corns wide; its two tubes should be one and a half finger-breadths long, provided with earrings, and they should be further reinforced with pins.
The two ears are said to be neither too short nor too long, measuring two or four barley-corns in width;
they are traditionally described as being either half a mātrā longer or eight mātrās in length.
The *piñcasī* [vowel] should be known as having one and a half *mātrās*, like the whirlpool of the letter *la*; its interior is deep within the ear, while its exterior is curved and rounded. (67.147)
The width of the ear-lobes is one barleycorn; they extend downward and are slightly bent.
The back of the ear is likewise equal to the ear, and above it is five [barleycorns].
From the edge of the forehead to the corner of the eye is two mātrās and six yavas;
from that, the outer corner of the eye (apāṅga) is seven yavas; and from that, the mouth is three and a half aṅgulas.
In painting and drawing, however, the ear is one finger minus half a barleycorn;
the distance between the eyes, up to the nostrils, is the measure of the pupil.

The remainder, however, should be the width of the mouth; the distance between the eyes and the ears is considered [the same]. The elevation at the base of the nose should be half a mātrā in the middle of the eyes.
The base, middle, and tip of its [the nose's] width are proclaimed in sequence as two and a half yavas, seven yavas, and half a kalā respectively. // 67.152 //
The two flaps [of the lid] have a width and length of seven barley-corns; the expansion of the bamboo [frame] is one *mātrā*.
On the head, however, the length is five and a half finger-breadths.
The *puṣkara* is six barley-corns in height; its middle is one barley-corn in width. The two *puṭas* are said to be like *niṣpāva* beans, not endowed with excessive height.
The skin-fold (puṭatvac) of the nostril should be one and a half finger-breadths in height;
from the base of the gojī to the edge of the fold, the elevation should be equal to its width.
The tip of the nose should resemble a sesame flower, suspended from the nostril like a barley grain;
or the eye, arising from the lotus of the day, should be slightly reddish with a white orb.
The [vowel] *ū* is high, measuring two, four, or as many [mātrās], situated above or in the middle of the mouth;
however, when it is low, it measures one and a half mātrās, being wide and long at the upper lip.
The upper lip may be three barley-corns in height, while the lower lip, situated below it,
should be elevated, long, and wide by six barley-corns, or even more than six barley-corns.
The measurement of the lower lip of the mother extends as far as its middle and its elevation;
it resembles a slice of *tuṇḍīra* fruit and has the luster of a *kiṃśuka* blossom.
Then the jaw-circle is joined [to the neck], protruding three finger-breadths from the neck;
the neck has a width of five finger-breadths, and its length is three times its width.
The shoulders, five fingers in width and one and a half fingers in height, are located below the jaw;
the mandibular circle is one and a half mātrās, while the form of the mouth is as previously described.
The upper teeth are two and a half barley-corns [in height], while the lower teeth are two barley-corns wide and high;
from the root of the teeth, the lower teeth are half as long as they are wide.
The fangs should be half a barley-corn longer than the teeth; the teeth should be smooth, even, and well-set;
and one should join the eyelashes, which possess the luster of very smooth collyrium.
The hairs of the head are reckoned by number to be eighty or ninety; they are straight, pure, fine, glossy, and evenly situated. (67.164)
One should fashion the face of women so that it is well-proportioned and captivating, complete with curls, a parting line, and hair-ornaments upon the forehead.
The width of the base of the arm is considered equal to the breadth of the neck;
the space between the armpits (the *pakṣa*) is seventeen finger-breadths in breadth.
The nipple of the breast should be made ten *mātrās* in length;
the space between that and the belly, as well as across the chest, should be two *bhāgas*.
The breasts are five finger-breadths in height, rounded, with two types of nipples;
at their base they are seven finger-breadths in width and face each other like the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
Indeed, within the well-rounded [body], the chest is high with its limit established internally;
it extends fourteen finger-breadths from the end of the breasts to the heart.
From the base to the end of the two arms, it should be twenty-nine finger-breadths;
from the heart to the bottom of the arms, the length of the arms should be twenty-two finger-breadths.
The elbow should be four mātrās long, and the forearm twelve aṅgulas;
the width of the wrist is one kalā plus three yavas.
The palm-base (pāṇimūla) is considered to be one *kalā* thick with two *yavas*;
the width of the palm (*talavyāsa*) is five *aṅgulas*, and the length of the palm (*talāyāma*) is two *kolakas*.
The length of the middle finger is considered equal to the length of the palm;
the width at the base of the fingers is equal to the thickness at the tip of the palm.
The big toe has four and five barley-corns at its tip and nail, and possesses two joints;
its root and tip are six and five barley-corns respectively, and it is four and a half finger-breadths in length.
Its roots, middle, and tip are joined together as one solid mass, and its joints have an extent of three or four barleycorns; it is endowed with dark and reddish nails.
The index finger is slightly longer than a barleycorn;
its circumference at the base is nineteen barleycorns and at the tip it is fifteen.
The middle finger is considered to have its tip at the third joint, as before;
the ring finger is equal in length to the index finger according to the characteristics of measurement.
It is three *yava*s and two *yava*-widths at the base, then five *yava*s;
at the tip, it is four *yava*s, then three and a half *yava*s, and finally one and a half *nakhas*.
As before, that little finger (kaniṣṭhikā) should be well-rounded and joined at its three joints;
the fingers, from the base to the tips, should be well-rounded and perfectly aligned.
For this [surface] within the palm has a level surface similar to the depression;
however, the base of the outer surface is greater than that at the wrist.
A line that is deep red, very smooth, possessing the luster of marks such as the Śrīvatsa,
and shaped like a cow’s mouth is prescribed for young women. (67/181)
From below the *hikkā-sūtra* down to the end of the *āyāma*, [the length] is six and eight [units];
its width at the base, middle, and top is one and a half, two, and two and a half *kalās* respectively.
This is recorded as the rule for the hands of women, reaching up to the middle finger.
The neck should be three mātrās in length, measured from the lower lip, and the nape of the neck should be likewise.
The increase of one measure (mātrā) for that [line] is half a barley-corn (yava) across the armpit;
from the back to the limit of the armpit, the line measures ten kola-units.
The neck possesses a length of twenty-one finger-breadths up to the waist-cord;
from the waist to the mouth is one *tāla*, and the back is six *yava*-kolakas.
The width at the end of the waist on the back is twenty-one units;
when the navel-cavity is level with the back, the hips are seventeen finger-breadths wide.
The buttock-muscle (sphikpiṇḍa) should be three mātras higher than the base of the thighs and eight mātras [in width];
a line equal in length to the distance from the buttock to the hip-joint (tārāṅga) should be drawn at each opening.

It should be eleven finger-breadths in diameter at the middle, provided with a circumference three times that, endowed with three folds, auspicious, and resembling the slender waist of a beautiful woman.
O lords of sages, the navel should be made half an aṅgula in width and equally deep, with its whorls turning in a clockwise direction.

The hip should have a width of seventeen [units]; the waistband should be three times seven measures; and the space from the end of the buttocks to the navel should be made slightly depressed, with three pins at the edge of the buttocks.
The vulva of the female elephant is eight finger-breadths in measure and equal in size to her head;
its external form should be grasped as being like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, captivating to the mind.
The line of hair reaching to her belly is a source of intoxication;
it is smooth, free from the pair of deer-marks, and devoid of hairy pores.
A wise man should duly draw two lines on the buttocks and sides of women, starting from the edge of the vulva, according to the prescribed method.
The hip is situated within the black finger-measure (kālāṅgula); it rests above the root-thigh.
The broad palm (tāla) is at the middle of the root-thigh, while the five-kola measure is at the [upper] thigh.
The *trikala* at the end of the knee is three finger-breadths;
the kneecap (*jānumaṇḍala*) is five finger-breadths in width, and the portion of the shank (*jaṅghābhāga*) is six barley-corns [in height].
The shanks are three finger-breadths in width and three times that in circumference;
the thighs resemble the trunks of elephants, and the kneecaps are hairless.

The shanks, from the limit of the ankles to the knees, are like the tips of bubbles; the length of the soles of the feet should be equal to the distance from the tip of the big toe to the tip of the little toe.

The big toe is one finger-breadth in length and slightly more than half a finger-breadth in width; the other toes, starting from the big toe, are six barley-corns in length, with each subsequent one being one barley-corn longer.
The ring finger (pradeśinī) is half a barley-corn less [than the middle finger], and there is a decrease of one barley-corn for each of the other two;
the thumb (aṅguṣṭha) should be broad by half a barley-corn, and its nail is six barley-corns long.
O best of the twice-born, the nail of the other fingers is said to be two or three parts at the tip; this is declared to be the general characteristic of images.
O twice-born ones, in the construction of an image, the measurement should begin with one barleycorn and increase up to eight barleycorns;
it may be applied to all the limbs by either increasing or decreasing [the proportions].

Beginning with the measure of a lunar day (tithi) and increasing by the measure of the void (vyoma) until it reaches three finger-breadths, the head-wheel (śiraścakra) is perfectly circular and adorned with a crocodile (makara).
The projection should be half of that, and the height of the crown should be three *tāla*s;
one should design it by decreasing by one *aṅgula* starting from that, down to the end of a single *tāla*.
Beginning with five finger-breadths and increasing by the measure of a finger-breadth at a time,
up to thirty finger-breadths, one should proceed according to the rules for the bow, arrow, and other implements.
One should fashion the weapon according to the proper method and likewise provide it with a radiant luster.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the general characteristics of images, in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Trident (Triśūla)
(I shall now describe) the installation of the trident; its characteristics are manifold.
[The wood for it may be] sandalwood, madhūka, khadira, and likewise sarala. (68.1)
Śamī, tiniśa, tāpiñcha, tilaka, devadāruka, kramuka, saptaparṇa, vakula, kunda, and candana. || 68/2 ||
Piṇḍika, stimiśa, red sandalwood, and likewise panasa;
śrīparṇī, khadira, sāla, tintṛṇī, sālabilvaka—these [trees]. || 68.3 ||
The Kadamba, the one called Śiṃśupā, Dhanvin, Śūlin, Kujā, Panasa, Devadāru, Padma, and the one known as Tinduka. (68.4)
The *tilaka*, the *saptaparṇa*, and the *vakula* are said to serve as the trident for Viṣṇu; furthermore, the *kuṭaja*, the *piṇḍita*, and the *tiniśa*. (68.5)
The Dhanvana, Arjuna, and Aśvattha trees are considered the trees of Brahmā;
for whichever deity belongs to whichever goddess, her tree is indeed that very same tree.
The Vaikaṅkata, Khadira, Śamī, Durgā, and Kuja are prescribed for Jyeṣṭhā; the Pāṭalī is declared for her, and the one called Śiva is among the seven Mothers.
The *vakula* is the *caṇḍavṛkṣa*, and the *rājavṛkṣaka* is for the guardian of the direction;
the *khādira* is for all the gods, as is the milky *khādira*.
The Śrīvṛkṣa tree is proclaimed for all deities;
for Gaṇeśa, Skanda, the Teachers, and the Mothers, there are the trees sacred to Śiva.
All [the images] should be made everywhere according to the requirements of the ritual, whether they are fashioned from copper, brass, silver, or gold. // 68.10 //
For a single [deity], there may be a single tree, but many trees are not desired;
one should perform the collection of substances according to that specific procedure.
For the purpose of measuring the hair, fingers, and so forth, one should bring the half-measure like wood;
the width of the Brahmadaṇḍa is traditionally recorded as five fingers.
From the penis up to the navel, the shape should be square; from the navel down to the heart, it is described as having eight corners (an octagon).
Above that, one should fashion a *vakula* (blossom);
its width is known to be seven *aṅgulas*, and its thickness should be one *kalā*.
The extension of its crest is two mātrās at both tips;
the width of the crest is desired to be the measure of one *vyoma*-mātrā.
Those [lines] numbering one, two, three, or four are proclaimed to end at the crest-lock (śikhā);
the aperture in the middle of the chest-staff (vakṣodaṇḍa) is formed by a star consisting of a portion of Viṣṇu.
Below the *hikkāsūtra*, however, is the location of the breast-rod (*vakṣodaṇḍa*);
the width of the hip-rod (*kaṭidaṇḍa*) is declared to be seven finger-breadths.
One kalā should be known for its density on both sides;
by the measure of one fire-finger (agni-aṅgula), the flame becomes horizontal-faced.
One should lead a hollow through the center of the Brahma-portion by means of the *tāra*;
for the square portion, one should set aside half the measurement, which is two *aṅgulas*, by means of the *tāra*.
Having left two finger-breadths below the navel, one should join the pelvic staff (kaṭidaṇḍaka) here to the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa), leading it in a very smooth and very firm manner.
The width at the top of the staff-section is considered to be that of a *kola* fruit;
at its base, one should fashion a cavity according to the measurement of the *śikhā*.
In front of that, one should fashion a crest (śikhā) measuring approximately one cubit;
one should then join the thigh-staff (ūrudaṇḍa) to both the waist-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa) and the crest.
It should be grasped with the length of the shank and provided with four mātras;
the width at the base of the shank is declared to be three aṅgulas.
Its width at the front is recorded as one and a half units;
at its base, however, one should fashion a hollow according to the measurement of the crest.
The wise one should join the staff of the arms to the staff of the chest at the topknot;
he should then join the staff of the thighs to the circle of the knees.
The width of the kneecap is declared to be one yuga (four fingers);
its length should be known to be the same, and the shank there is half of that.
The width of the base of the staff is declared to be four mātras;
the width of the base of the arm is declared to be three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula). || 68.27 ||
The width of its tip is considered to be one and a half finger-breadths;
at its base, one should fashion a hollow with a measurement of seven [finger-breadths].
One should join the base of the arm at the crest of the chest-pillar;
the width of the base of the forearm is declared to be three *mātras*.
The width of its tip is declared to be one and a half finger-breadths;
then, one should make a hollow with a base of two mātrās.
And with the tips grasped by the arms, one should join them with the forearms;
starting from the chest-staff (vakṣadaṇḍa) and proceeding in sequence to the end of the hip-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa).
The side-staff (pārśvadaṇḍa) should be known as long;
its width (tāra) should be equal to that [of the central staff], and its thickness (ghana) should be known as equal to that, positioned above the side-staff.
And below, a hollow should be made measuring one finger-breadth;
one should join the side-staffs to the chest-staff and the waist-staff.
One should avoid the side-stroke between the two staffs and at the front for a distance of one *ṛṣi*;
this is especially forbidden for women in the case of the side-stroke.
When measuring these [limbs], a wise person should omit the measurement of the flesh, beginning from one-quarter of an *aṅgula* and increasing by one-quarter of an *aṅgula*. (68.35)
The rule should be applied ending with two mātrās, with decrease and increase according to reason;
O twice-born ones, let thirty-two be taken for the Brahmadaṇḍa and the final daṇḍas.
The head, palms, ears, garments, feet, and so forth should be made half the measure of one's own height, or even less, according to what is appropriate.

Thus has the specific distinction regarding the seat been declared for the *sthānaka* posture; however, at the base of the *brahmadaṇḍa*, one should join it with a space of four finger-breadths (*yugāṅgula*).
The region at the base of the shank, however, should be joined as being one-and-a-half finger-breadths less;
thus the characteristics of the trident (śūla) have been declared, and its installation is now described here.
The time, as well as the offering of the sprouts, should be understood as before;
the pavilion and the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are to be nine, five, or one in number.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be square, or likewise shaped according to their respective directions;
then, having dismissed the artisan, one should thereafter cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having performed the Vāstuhoma at the end, O twice-born ones, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having prepared the bed there, one should recognize the Brahmā-daṇḍakas and the others.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and then having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth,
and having clothed it in pure water and covered it with a cloth, one should worship it.
Having prepared a seat upon the couch with the subtle seats (āsana-aṇus),
one should, by means of the heart-mantra, cause that trident to enter as an embodied form.
Having tied the protective amulet (kautuka), one should place water-pots all around it—
equipped with tufts of grass, adorned with gold, covered with cloth, and filled with water.

One should worship the lords of the worlds (lokeśas) in the center and around the mantra of each respective form; one should then install the forms and the lords of the forms, accompanied by the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras).
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with the Brahma-mantras, one should install the form there,
worshipping it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while recollecting the mūrti-mantra.
Having first offered milk-rice (pāyasa), one should then commence the rite of oblation (homa).
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other preliminaries, one should invoke the deity’s form and offer libations.
With fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and parched grain mixed with sesame and mustard seeds,
[he should offer oblations] from the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees in the directions starting from the east.
Śamī, Apāmārga, Mādhūka, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees are for the southeast corner;
the Palāśa tree is for the principal [deity], and there should be one hundred [offerings] for the principal deity.
In the tenth part, an oblation with the Brahma-mantras is likewise approved, as well as with the Netra-mantra;
and with the Tattvas, the Lords of the Tattvas, and so forth, three [oblations] are performed for each in sequence.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, at dawn the preceptor, together with the *mūrtipas*,
having bathed and worshipped the deity and the jar, should worship the fire nearby.
Having remained there and eliminated any defects, one should then cause the full [offering] to be presented through the *mūrti*.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction (*sulagna*), the most excellent Guru, having received worship,
should take up the [liṅga] from the primary abode and follow it while circumambulating.

Having entered the inner sanctum and identified the portions belonging to Brahmā and the others, one should establish the site according to the divisions of the locations and so forth, having prepared the ground for the ritual pot. (Page 187) 68.54
There, one should install the foundation, known as the *ādhāra*, using bricks and other materials. 55.
Whether standing, sitting, or sleeping, or traveling by vehicle and intent on departure;
And those eager for drama are of six kinds, according to the designations of the *sthānaka* (postures) and *ādhāra* (supports). 56.
In that very same way, she was indeed devoted to dancing and delighted in walking about.
If she is positioned on a place such as a cowhide or similar seat, she is "seated" (āsana-sthā); if she is on a throne, she is "seated on a pedestal" (pīṭha-gā).
If she is intent upon a bed, she is "asleep" (suptā), and that is generally not desired for him.
That shall be the manifestation of Viṣṇu and the others; now the support (ādhāra) is described.
The measurement of the support is one and a half times the width at the base of the trident.
By increasing the measurement by one finger-breadth from that base-finger measurement, it shall reach a size of four finger-breadths; it should be equal and square.
That [state of] density is said to be threefold, arising from the successive increase of each one. 60.
The measurement should end at four mātrās, according to the requirements of the ritual action.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, and so forth, or with materials such as wood;
having placed nine squares in its center, they may be joined by diagonal lines (kūṭa).
The eloquent preceptor should place the jewels and other items there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
he should install them there while recollecting the [divine] form.
One should apply other staffs (daṇḍas) along with the Brahmadaṇḍa according to the stated method;
or else, the height of the pedestal (pīṭhikā) should be [measured] from the base of the Brahmadaṇḍa.
Having made it possessed of the length of a trident, or else possessed of the desired measurement,
one should place that object, known as the "support" (ādhāra), in its designated location.
One should secure the cavity with the "stable and other" [techniques] by means of the "binding of the pedestal" and so forth,
using well-stabilized spikes made of solid wood that have emerged from the image.
Having joined [the mantras] from the Brahmadaṇḍa down to the Daṇḍa with those endowed with the desired number and possessed of the desired syllables, the most excellent Guru [should proceed].
One should achieve stability here according to the method of construction,
using straight iron plates and various kinds of iron nails.
Having bound [the body] according to its karma, or with a moist wrapping of cloth, one should fill the entire body with medicinal pastes, ointments, and the like, so that it is not visible.

One should have it painted with various colors, as in the case of the Pratimokṣa, by artisans who are most skilled in painting and who belong to the four castes, the anuloma classes, and so forth. (68/70)
One should perform the opening of the eyes at the conclusion of the work of painting;
prior to the opening of the eyes, it remains merely a material object.
In that case, O twice-born ones, cutting and other such acts are desired; beyond that, they are not permitted.
There, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) must be performed according to the procedure prescribed for installation (sthāpana).
Having established the bases known as the *ādhāra* (supports), measuring the width of the soles, and the pillars of the image consisting of the shanks and thighs, one should place them above that.
Having joined the waist-staff (kaṭidaṇḍa) to the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa),
and having equipped the image and so forth with all the staffs and other components.
Having bound it with silk cloths and the like, and having placed it upon a bed,
one should either install it after performing the ritual placement of the principles (tattvas), the forms (mūrtis), and so forth, or simply set it down there.
If the image is made of stone, one should make the base out of stone;
everything else remains the same, though the footstones and so forth may differ.
Having fashioned a *kūrca* that is gradually tapered and endowed with strength, one should insert it into the hollow in the center of the pedestal according to its smoothness.
Having prepared the seat with those mantras and performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa) with his arms,
he should place the form-mantras residing in the water of the pitcher into the heart of the image.
Having bathed the guardians of the world with that water, one should place them around [the mountain];
having smeared that mountain with white plaster and wrapped it with cloth, one should decorate it.
At the time of installing the trident, one should consecrate it with the Mūrti-mantra.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for Installing the Trident, in the Great Tantra named Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of Deities.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the locations for the installation of deities:
whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital. (Verse 69.1)
First, on the auspicious banks of a river, in temples of the deities, on the shore of the ocean, at a bridge, and on the banks of a lotus pond. (69.2)
Either near a great body of water, or in the vicinity of a large crowd, or in a garden, or in a sacred place—whether it be the formless or the formed [deity]. (69.3)
Whether it be made of stone, metal, wood, gems, or clay; whether it be made of plaster, half-painted, or even a mere representation on a pedestal.
The wise preceptor, who knows the portions belonging to Brahmā, the gods,
and others, should establish [the layout] starting from five-fifths (one) and increasing by one square at each step.
Having made the sanctum sanctorum up to thirty-two padas,
there may be one, two, or three [shrines] in the Brahma-mandira.
Having likewise performed that intermediate [measurement] for the divine and the annual [portions],
one should designate the Paiśācika portion within the Brahma-bhāga.
One should separate this [mantra], beginning with Brahmā and the others, in a village or similar location;
however, the partless (niṣkala) form belongs to the portion of Brahman, while the formed (sakala) belongs to the divine portion.

But when establishing a village and so forth, one should establish the human [deity] in the portion of Brahmā, which is the long rectangular section; some maintain that this may also pertain to the Mother.
That image, however, should be joined with Citrā even in the outer Paiśācika [direction];
the Rakṣasas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others, as well as the Piśācas and others, are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās). || 69/10 ||
Whether in a human or a piśāca settlement, the residence of the twice-born is desired;
there, one should construct the assembly hall and other structures in the four corners beginning with the northeast (īśāna).
Having divided the Brahma-portion into four parts, one should lead the assembly hall toward the northeast;
furthermore, a step-well should be placed in the southeast region, along with a cow-pen and a well.
In the southwest (nairṛta) should be the site for the marketplace, or it may be provided with a temple;
one should construct a temple in the northwest (vāyu), for if these are reversed, misfortune will occur.
In a small dwelling, however, all of that is not desired in the portion belonging to Brahmā;
rather, all of that is prescribed for Śarva in a residence for the twice-born.
O best of the twice-born, Viṣṇuvāsa should be in Varuṇa, as well as Keśava and Śarva; [these should be placed] from five-fifths less [of the total] and above that.
The sky is the foot extending for a thousand [yojanas], belonging to the Piśācas in due order.
The Sun is the lord of the group of Kandas; Durgā and others are the deities of the site (vāstu).
In the Vāstupaiśācika [system], Moṭī, Madana, and the Seven Mothers are recognized;
or else, they are considered to be the seven deities excluding Moṭīśāstṛ. (69.17)
If there are more than a thousand Brahmins, the assembly hall and the area for the Brahmins and others should be prepared;
however, if there are fewer Brahmins, one should omit the specific compartment or the courtyard.
Above that, at the end of a thousand [yojanas], Gaurī or Kamalālayā resides;
Brahmā, Vaiśravaṇa, Saumya, and Kandarpa are situated within.
Externally, Jyeṣṭhā is the presiding deity of the field; the aforementioned deities are remembered [as such], and above them, all the gods are praised as bestowers of fruit.
Among these, however, Śiva, Gaurī, Vināyaka,
or Skanda should be assigned to one of those portions, such as the portion belonging to Brahmā and so forth.
The Teacher is to be placed both inside and outside; those who are fierce are proclaimed to be on the outside.
As for the deities satisfied by the layout of the site, they are the gods established here in the east.

Is it in the aforementioned location or elsewhere? Those [deities] partake of the site (vāstu). Without the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the deities, how could the ritual placement on the site (vāstunyāsa) take place? (69.23)
Therefore, with every effort, one should arrange for the deities;
the Guru should install the Rudra-deities and thus accomplish the Śaiva rite.

Having observed the ancient sites, such as those abandoned by sages or like temples here on earth, one should perform the ritual placement of the site (vāstunyāsa) after considering the purpose of the old [structure]. 69.25.
Everything beginning with the ritual placement of the site (vāstunyāsa) has already been explained;
nevertheless, the specific details regarding that are stated once again here.
The measurement of a village is prescribed as ending with the *pada* [unit] up to the *paiśāca* [unit];
there may be an increase or decrease in the rows of houses, whether on the exterior or the interior. (69.27)
Whether in length or in width, there may be a discrepancy in their measurements;
or a small path may be desired for either a small or a large site. (69.28)
In the case of both external and internal rites, or when there is mutual inequality between them,
an imbalance caused by the Vāstu-piśāca is recognized during the construction of the dwelling.

In the same way, one should conduct oneself among those who are proud as one does in temples, so that there may be no injury to their positions and the like, and should lead everything accordingly. (69.30)

Affliction situated in the portions belonging to Brahmā or the gods does not cause harm; therefore, having selected the vital points (*marman*) and so forth in the aforementioned locations, [one should proceed]. (69.31)

Then, one should install Śiva and the other deities in the constructed temples, according to the specific distinctions of the nagaras and so forth, and particularly according to the divisions of the directions.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, the Ritual for the Installation of Deities, in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Consecration of an Image.
I shall now explain, in brief, the consecration of images:
first, the collection of materials, and then the actual fashioning of the image. (70.1)

Afterwards, the construction of the pavilion; following that, the placement of the jewels (ratnanyāsa); then the opening of the eyes (nayanonmīlana); and immediately thereafter, the purification of the image (beraśuddhi). (70.2)
Afterwards, there should be the circumambulation of the village, and the entry into the water shall be the eighth;
then follows the decoration of the pavilion, and after that, the Vāstu-homa.
Then the preparation of the bed is proclaimed, followed by the installation of the image;
thereafter the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) should take place, and then again the mounting upon the bed.

Afterwards comes the installation of the water-pot (kumbha), and immediately following that, the worship (arcana). Then follows the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the deities and so forth, and after that, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa).
At the conclusion, there should be the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and beyond that, the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Beyond this, there shall be bathing and worship;
beyond this, twenty-two rites have been proclaimed, and their characteristics are now described.
Stone, clay, metal, wood, gems, minerals, lime, cloth, and ivory—these are said to be the materials for the construction of an image (bera). // 70.7 //
At an auspicious moment, during a favorable conjunction of stars and lunar mansions,
the Lord, having reached the site for the stone and other materials, was worshipped upon a consecrated sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having offered oblations into the fire, honored the guardians of the directions, and given bali-offerings to the spirits, the pure practitioner should sprinkle the stone and other materials with water, enclose them with a cloth while reciting the Varma-mantra, and worship them.

Having wrapped the chisel and other tools in a cloth at the heart [of the image] and soaked them with honey and clarified butter, the artisan, with the permission of the Guru, should strike it three times and split it open with the Astra-mantra. In that same manner, he should split it open again.
Having honored the preceptor as well as the chief architect with garments, gold, and other offerings.
Therefore, having collected that substance, one should lead it again to the ritual hut;
first, it has been sprinkled, liquefied, and then poured out with water while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the pavilion, one should pour the sprinkled [water] right there;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should envelop it with a cloth while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having given that material to the artisan, one should have it fashioned so as to possess the proper characteristics;
at the time of its creation, the preceptor should face the north.
One should recite the root mantra of the image one hundred and eight times;
then, in the northern direction of that [image], one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma).
One should honor both the guide and the artisan with gold and other offerings.
When selecting a tree, the preceptor, having worshipped the tree, should speak as follows: [70.16]
O abode of glory, salutations to you, O tree cherished by the gods! May this place of transition be excellent, virtuous, and beautiful. (70.17)
Having cast it away with this mantra, one is declared to have transcended the self;
remembering Mṛtyuñjaya, one should cut [the bonds] with an axe smeared with clarified butter.
Falling upon the auspicious quarters of the lords of the Yakṣas, it grants all desires;
through fire, it effects the eradication of affliction, death, great obstacles, and thorny shrubs.
The collection of materials and the preliminary construction have been described; the characteristics of the image have been proclaimed, and now the pavilion is being discussed.
One should construct pavilions on the four sides of the palace, as well as at the front and the two flanks,
beginning with a size of three cubits and increasing by one cubit at each step.
One should fashion [the image] up to fifteen cubits in length, endowed with the proper characteristics; whatever is not mentioned here, all that should be conducted according to the previous rules.
One should arrange nine, five, or one sacrificial pits as before;
they may be square, circular, or have corners according to the cardinal directions.
One should fashion the forms of the wombs for all the Śaktis;
having well-decorated the pavilion, one should place the pedestal there.
One should worship [the image] with sandalwood and other offerings, whether it is adorned with nine silk ribbons, five silk ribbons, or even a single silk ribbon.
The Guru should place that which is called the Foundation (Ādhāra) and Ananta in the center,
as well as the four world-protectors (Lokapālas) and various kinds of jewels.
Māṇikya, indranīla, vaiḍūrya, and coral; pearl, diamond, as well as topaz, and likewise gomedaka. || 70/27 ||
Emerald, gems, and the five beginning with the nine gems—
these are declared to be the "five jewels," or alternatively, even just the single ruby (māṇikka).
Or else, the vajra is said to be in the center; it is known as the "Great Entrance.
One should install [the deities] with their respective world-protecting mantras, following the sequence starting from the center.
Having placed the deity upon the jewels, one should cause it to be made very smooth and firm;
if it is made of stone, one should deposit the jewels and other materials according to the rule at the time of installation.
At the time of installing the sacrificial post (śūla), however, one should place gems within the earthen [image];
for other [types of images], one should especially avoid the placement of gems.
One should perform the consecration of the eyes (netramokṣaṇa) under a lunar mansion associated with the two eyes (the asterisms Aśvinī and Bharaṇī),
in a beautiful, well-concealed pavilion smeared with cow dung.
In a place covered with a concealed cloth and adorned with all ornaments,
a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared there using eight droṇas or more of grain.
The best of preceptors should place the image facing east in the center of that [altar], which is joined with sesame seeds and rice, and provided with parched grain and flowers.
While recollecting the mantra of the eye, one should strike with the golden needle twice:
first the right eye, and second the left eye.
The Guru should first draw the line of the eyelashes, and then the circle of the eye; thereafter, he should mark and worship the third [line] situated on the forehead.
Having drawn the circle of light, the artisan— marked by a vajra and golden thread— should perform the opening of the eyes and likewise the unveiling.
O Three-eyed One, as if with a chisel fashioned from a flower,
one should release [the vital energy] through the nose, the ears, the mouth, the penis, and the anus.
One should perform the opening of the eyes for those who have become limbs of the respective deities;
for the deities such as Citrābhāsa and others, one should perform it with their respective colors.
Then the preceptor should perform the opening of the eyes with a golden needle;
after dismissing the artisan, he should then lead [the image] before a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having placed the image upon it with the heart mantra,
one should likewise place the water jars, complete with threads and lids, in the eight directions.
Having placed them all around with their respective mantras— provided with cloths, water, brushes, and sprouts— one should worship the Lokapālas there.
In the case of a minor [rite], having omitted the eight jars, one should perform everything else;
one should cover the eyes with golden *dūrvā* grass and satisfy them with honey and clarified butter.
The most excellent guru, having consecrated with either the heart-mantra or the eye-mantra,
should perform this rite for [the image] made of metal, stone, wood, or even precious gems.
One should also perform the rite of satiation for all other [deities].
With the middle of the index finger, ring finger, and middle finger, one should visualize the eyes of the Sun, Moon, and Fire. (70.45)
One should place it in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal, or even in a shallow bowl, together with its seed-syllable and pierced by golden nails.
Each should be filled with ghee and honey, one *prastha* each;
or alternatively, they may be filled separately with half of that, or even a quarter of that.
The mantra-practitioner, recollecting the eye-mantra, should display the clarified butter;
he should then display the vessel of honey while uttering the Mṛtyujit-mantra.
The knower of mantras should then show that cow with the heart-mantra;
