he should show a heap of grain with the principal seed-mantra.
The measurement of those [weights] is proclaimed to range from one *śiva* up to ten *bhāras*.
Afterwards, while recollecting Pavamāna, he should show them to the Brahmins.
With that very [mantra], one should show the maiden adorned with all ornaments;
having drawn away the concealing cloth, one should display her to the assembly of people.

One should effect the purification of an image, or apply it to a painting and so forth, using earth, ashes, kuśa grass, cow urine, and cow dung— these five products of the cow— as well as the inner bark of trees, or by means of a mirror.
One should prepare it with substances such as ground turmeric and others that ensure purity;
then one should adorn it with garments, perfumes, garlands, and worthy ornaments.
One should perform the circumambulation of the village while adorned with all ornaments;
however, one should avoid performing the circumambulation of the village when it is depicted in paintings and the like.
Or, if it is even larger, that [shrine] should be abandoned, and one should then bring water there;
having constructed a water-shed (prapā) in the middle of the water, provided with four pillars.
Furthermore, having established a leveled sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the bank adorned with garlands of darbha grass and other ornaments,
the preceptor should worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of it, the preceptor should place eight jars there and worship the lords of the world-protectors (lokapālas), enriched with gold.
Having removed his ornaments and covered him with a garment and armor,
he was endowed with a long beard measuring thirty-two [units].

One should have [the image] lie upon a pedestal or a wooden plank in the midst of water; having invoked the holy waters of the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites, one should place ritual jars all around it.
One should perform the ritual immersion in water for one to nine nights, lasting for four, three, two, or one watch of the night; this may be done on a painting and so forth, or not on a mirror.
Thereafter, one should decorate the pavilion, which is covered with a great cloth;
there, one should feed the Brahmins, numbering from ten up to a thousand.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should perform the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice;
having performed the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), one should sprinkle [the site] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*).
Thereafter, one should cause the Puṇyāha recitation to be performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on top of an altar (vedikā),
which is considered to be made of eight droṇas, or half of that, or half of that again, of śāli rice.
One should properly prepare [the altar] with sesame seeds, parched grain, *darbha* grass, and flowers;
one should arrange the bed above, using materials such as skins and so forth, in their proper sequence.
One should arrange the bed upon the painting and other such supports according to the respective positions of the feet;
one should sprinkle it with the *puruṣa* mantra and worship it with perfumes and other offerings using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having emerged from the water, one should place the image in the bathing pit;
having removed the cloth and the *kūrca*, one should perform the ceremonial bath as previously described.
Having wrapped [the image] with a cloth, one should worship it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Afterwards, one should tie the *kautuka* (protective thread) on the right hand with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
for all the *śaktis*, it may be tied either on the left or on the right.
Thereafter, one should place jars endowed with all auspicious characteristics, provided with threads, containing gold, accompanied by *kūrca* grass, and wrapped in cloth.
Having placed all [the vessels] filled with scented water and adorned with fruits and sprouts around [the central image], one should worship them all with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Then one should perform the ritual placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) according to the method for the installation of the liṅga; [placing] Ātman, Vidyā, and the one called Śiva up to the knees, ears, and head respectively.
At the conclusion of that, the fire-offering ritual (homakarma) should take place according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are to be used in order, starting from the east.
With *śamī*, *apāmārga*, *śrīvṛkṣa*, and *pippala* wood in the southeast corner,
and with *palāśa* for the principal [fire], the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) are thus prescribed. (70/72)
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, and mustard seeds; bamboo, barley, millet, and rice; and mung beans, black gram, and horse-gram. (70.73)
In honey, milk, molasses, parched grain flour, fruits, and so forth, water is prescribed with three,
five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, and fifteen oblations respectively.
Or one should perform the oblation with all seventeen substances together;
those [mantras] known as Brahmā and the others are assigned to the cardinal directions, while the Heart-mantra and the others are assigned to the intermediate directions.

The root mantra (mūlamantra) should be used for the primary deity when accompanied by the limb-mantras (aṅga) and the Brahma-mantras; however, if the five-fire ritual (pañcāgnisādhana) is being performed, one should omit the heart-mantra and the others.
If there is only one fire-sanctuary, one should perform the oblation in a single place with substances [numbering] a thousand, half of that, half of that again, a hundred, or eight hundred.
In this manner, one should perform half [of the total] with the ten [auxiliary mantras] and the root mantra;
from the tenth part of the root [mantra], one should perform the oblation for all the limbs, beginning with Brahmā.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before with the Tattvas, the Lords of the Tattvas, and so forth;
at the end of each substance, one should recite the Vyāhṛtis, and at the conclusion of the oblation, it should be accompanied by the Pūrṇāhuti.

One should perform the touching as before, followed by the sprinkling with water for pacification; whatever has not been mentioned here, all that should be conducted according to the procedure for the installation of a *liṅga*.

One should perform the study of the Āgamas in the cardinal directions and the recitation of mantras in the intermediate corners; however, one who has been initiated here should perform the study of the Āgamas in the northeast.
Accompanied by dance and song, and with hymns of praise uttered by those reciting auspicious words, he should pass the remainder of the night; then, at the clear dawn, [he should proceed].
The preceptor, together with the image-keepers, should perform the ritual bath as before;
then, his body armored by mantras, he shall enter the sacrificial pavilion.

Having first lifted the image, one who resembles the presiding deity of the form should remove the cloth, the broom, and other such items, and worship with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Thereafter, one should worship the jars and then perform worship at the fire-pits;
or, for the sake of expiation, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora mantra.
One should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with the syllable *vauṣaṭ* at the end, using the *hara* mantra itself.
There, one should honor the preceptor (*ācārya*) with garments, gold, and rings,
beginning with five *niṣkas* and increasing by increments of five *niṣkas*.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the installation of the images is said to be ninefold;
or, if one is poor, it may consist of five niṣkas, beginning with a single niṣka.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Guru has been prescribed; one should avoid what is less than that.
For all others as well, the sacrificial fee shall be as previously stated.
One should perform the installation during the period preceding the muhūrta-nāḍikā;
the preceptor, having lifted the Śiva-kumbha together with the Vardhanī,
accompanied by the surrounding vessels and adorned with all ornaments.
Having performed a circumambulation of the palace, one should bring the water-pots before the image.
Having taken the seed-syllable from the pitcher, one should place it upon the heart of the image.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the very water contained in that jar.
Having taken the seed-syllable with the Vardhanī vessel, the Guru should place it upon that pedestal.
If the goddess is together with the god, one should place her upon his heart.
If the Goddess has separate seats, one should begin the installation individually.
But on one made of clay, or on one that is half-painted, or likewise on a mere image or a cloth painting;
Is there some special quality in the mansion, or rather, it is due to their very presence?
Having placed a mirror there, one should then perform the ritual bathing.
The bathing of the ritual image (karmārcā) should take place either on its pedestal (pīṭha), or on a grass mat (kūrca), or on the bare ground.
Having worshipped it thoroughly with garments, ornaments, and flowers as prescribed for the ritual of worship.
One should offer abundant sacrificial oblations accompanied by betel leaves and other items;
or one may arrange for an ablution ceremony, perhaps even joined with a festival.
Whatever else has not been mentioned here should be understood as being like the installation of the *liṅga*;
thus has the installation been described both for that which is primary and for that which is subordinate to another.
That which is endowed with a retinue is known as "self-principal" (svapradhāna);
the other is devoid of that [retinue], and it is said to be of two kinds.
The internal limb and the external limb reside within the first abode;
whether moving or unmoving, they are located in the inner sanctum of the abode and so forth. (Page 193)
A mountain that is falsely embraced [by clouds], variegated with paintings, or situated within a village. || 70/100 ||
That which is situated within the surrounding enclosure is known as the "inner" (antaraṅga);
it is located in the temple, the pavilion, the hall, the gate-tower, and the sacrificial altar.
O twice-born followers of Śiva, listen to the specific distinction regarding that which is known as the "external" when it is well-established in the archways and other such structures. (70.102)

One should perform everything as before— whether including the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana), the placement of gems (ratnanyāsa), the circumambulation of the temple (dhāmapradakṣiṇa), and the preparation of the bed (śayyākḷpta)— or even without them.
For all of these as well, the first brick is the drawing [of the site],
as well as the arrangement of the abode, the daily sacrifice, the festival, and likewise the ceremonial bath.
The procedure for the monthly worship, the sequence of rites for expiation,
the restoration of dilapidated temples, the construction of new houses for children, and likewise the re-consecration [of deities] therein.
In the case of a portentous event, one should perform the rite for pacification and whatever else is prescribed according to the nature of the occurrence.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, the ritual procedure for the consecration of images, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Celestial Vehicle (Vimāna).
I shall now describe the installation of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), which bestows the fruits of one's desired aims.
At the conclusion of the previously mentioned lunar mansion (*dhiṣṇya*) and at the prescribed time, the ritual offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) should be performed.
In front of the temple, one should construct a pavilion provided with an altar,
and equipped with either nine sacrificial pits or five sacrificial pits.
Having adorned the pavilion, one should perform the dismissal of the artisans;
one should feed the Brahmins there during the three days preceding that day.
Then, O twice-born ones, there was the sight of palaces, bodies, and elephants, as well as the sight of honey, clarified butter, grain, cows, and brahmin maidens.
Having sprinkled it with the products of the cow while reciting the respective heart-mantras,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then sprinkle the temple.
One should install the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras) from the pair of shanks up to the top of the head;
having installed the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras), one should perform the same procedure for the images as well.
Having covered everything with cloths, one should spread flowers and darbha grass;
then, having entered the pavilion, one should thereafter cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
On the sacrificial mound and the altar, one should arrange rice grains in the measure of a *droṇa* for each of the eight directions (*vasu*),
with half that amount of pure *taṇḍula* rice, and half again of sesame seeds and parched grain (*lāja*).
One should place the Śiva-pitcher together with the Vardhanī in the center;
outside of that, one should place pitchers all around in the cardinal directions according to the number of the directional deities (eight).
[One should offer] vessels together with their threads, together with their lids, together with cloths, and joined with gold;
filled with sandalwood water, provided with kūrca-grass and accompanied by sprouts.
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings up to the food offering (naivedya),
one should likewise perform the consecration of the fire according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).

In the principal sacrificial pit of the palace, one should place [the offerings] with the mantras of Śiva’s limbs and Brahma-śambara; on the east, with the mantras of the deities of the eastern direction, and on the right, one should install them.

One should offer oblations a hundred times with the [mantras] of Varuṇa situated in the west, with those of Soma situated in the northern direction, and with the Heart-mantra and others in the intermediate directions.
One should perform the homa with mantras that lack even five of their constituent parts.
The sacrificial materials are: fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), sesame (tila), grains (sasya), indra-vaiṇava, and bamboo (vaiṇava).

The *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, and *nyagrodha* trees are situated in the cardinal directions; the *śamī*, *apāmārga*, *khadira*, and *bilva* trees are situated in the intermediate corners. (71.15)
The *palāśa* wood should be used for the principal oblation; having understood this, one should perform the rite.
Having offered oblations with the *tattvas*, the *tattveśvaras*, and so forth, one should then perform the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

At dawn, the preceptor, having bathed and become pure along with the image-keepers, wearing new garments, garlands, and a turban, together with an upper robe and well-anointed with unguents; || 71.17 ||

Adorned with the five-fold ornaments and offering ten *niṣkas* and other gifts as a sacrificial fee, he is accompanied by the presiding priests (*mūrtipas*) who are provided with new garments and other requisites. || 71.18 ||
Having worshipped the deities stationed within the temple and the fire-pitchers, and having performed the expiatory rite and the full oblation together with the image-bearers; || 71.19 ||
Having taken up the jars, he should then perform a circumambulation of the palace;
he should place the jars upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the area to the south of the palace.
Having worshipped the temple, one should establish the seat of Śiva (śivāsana) upon the foundation;
then, within the body, one should install the form of the Vidyā-tanu, endowed with the thirty-eight kalās.

Having performed the ritual placement with full attention, one should take the *śambara* from the *kumbha* and place it upon the body of the temple, specifically on the *vastvādhāra*, which is *manonmanī*.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the respective waters, one should then place [the deities] within the forms of the directions;
then one should worship them individually, from scents and other offerings up to the food offering (naivedya).
In this way, the mortal who acts thus shall enjoy worldly pleasures and then go to Śiva.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the celestial chariot (vimāna), in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Mandapa.
O best of Brahmins, the characteristics of the pavilions shall now be described;
among all the aforementioned sanctuaries, the foremost pavilion stands at the front.
However, that which is equal in measure to the mind (tanmānasamamāna) is declared to be the most excellent;
provided that the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is of equal measure, including the intermediate space and the entrance chamber.
It should be provided with twin pillars, beautifully adorned in all its parts according to the proper method,
measuring one and a half cubits or two cubits, or even half the size of the temple.
The interval between [the two] should be long; that which is situated at the junction is called "medium. When it is threefold [that length], it becomes "superior."
His dwelling may consist of one staff, two staffs, or three staffs; if there is space for an intermediate area, it should be two or three times that size. || 72.5 ||
It may be provided with side-staircases and a wall for the main staircase,
or it may have a wall measuring half of that, or a wall measuring one-eighth of that.
Having divided the temple into eight parts, one should reduce it by one-eighth part until the measurement reaches twelve units.
If there is a pavilion on both sides of the root-shrine,
it is proclaimed as being "provided with an entrance" (veśayukta), as described for the intermediate space.
Such should be the front pavilion (agramaṇḍapa), equal in height to the temple;
however, in the case of a self-manifested (svāyaṃbhuva) or other types of liṅgas, it may be either less or more [in height].
Similarly, its floor may be considered as being without walls,
provided it is joined with open pillars, unless there is a door at its front.
According to the path characterized by the door, two door-keepers are considered to be on its sides;
if they are joined with open pillars, they lead to the entrance of the primary sanctuary.
Having left that pavilion there, a *śukāgra* (a pointed pinnacle) is prescribed; this [structure] extends out by half the measurement of the interior of a pure *nāgara* temple.
Its height should be half that of the spire, adorned with a *śukanāsa* (gargoyle);
at its front should be the *antarāla* (vestibule), measuring according to the dimensions of the side regions.
Either a space for the exit or a pavilion is prescribed;
it should be provided with side doors, or alternatively, it may be without any doors at all.
In front of that, one should construct a pavilion for the purpose of installing the image;
in front of that, there should be a pavilion for the ritual bathing, and in front of that, a pavilion for dancing.

For all of these as well, the measurement of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) and so forth is equal to that of the primary abode (mūladhāma), being the most excellent, or perhaps slightly less or slightly more by one-eighth.
It is proclaimed as being either less by one-sixteenth or greater; for this measure in the Mānava tradition is declared to be the general standard.
Whether it be a pavilion (maṇḍapa), an assembly hall (sabhā), or a peaked structure (kūṭa), their forms are similar;
now the measurement for all of these is being stated.
Beginning with three cubits and increasing by one cubit for each hand,
the width of the pavilion should extend up to ten cubits.
It is joined with a palace-like structure made of iron, provided with desired side-walls,
endowed with various lattices, and furnished with various doors.
Provided with separate bricks for the first [section] and joined with auspicious elements such as *māyā* and others,
one should multiply the width by eight, three, and seven, and divide the result by twelve.
O twice-born ones, whatever remains as wealth or debt after being multiplied by eight times Manu (148),
and when the final result has been divided by thirty-seven, it becomes the birth star and the lunar mansion.
The pavilion and other structures are prescribed according to the sequence of lunar days (tithi) and weekdays (vāra);
however, this [specific rule] is not enjoined for the village pavilion or the intermediate space.
In this case, even the primary bricks and so forth are not to be prescribed separately;
rather, one should perform everything mentioned in the root text for all others as well. (72.24)
Starting from one and a half cubits and increasing by three finger-breadths at each step,
the measurement of the wall in the pavilion should extend up to five cubits.
In the same way, there should be a pillar, but it should end with the row of hands;
beginning from five finger-breadths, it increases by the measure of a void (aṅgula).
The thickness of the pillar is proclaimed to extend up to thirty finger-breadths,
beginning from the row of space (vyomapaṅkti) and increasing by the row of space.
Up to fifty rows, the rows are considered to be within the pavilion;
it is joined with the Bhadra and Upabhadraka [sections], with the central pillar shining forth.
Abounding with walls shaped like ploughs and adorned with various ornaments.
It should be provided with a Brahma-courtyard or else arranged as its counterpart,
equipped with door-sills and lintels, and adorned with gables, inner chambers, and so forth.
O lords of the twice-born, this very measurement is declared to be for the assembly hall;
one should construct the pavilion for the court in the cardinal and intermediate directions of the temple.
According to the previously mentioned measurement, a pavilion (maṇḍapa), a gabled hall (kūṭa),
or an assembly hall (sabhā) should be constructed there, provided with openings facing the eight directions.
It may have four equal sides or be elongated, and it should be provided with auspicious features at its entrance; it may consist of one or many stories and be equipped with side staircases.
Having thus completed that, the assembly hall and other structures are described as being built;
starting from five cubits, they increase by one cubit up to ten cubits.
Its width is considered to extend up to thirty-one cubits;
by increasing the width by one-quarter [of its own measure], it may reach up to four times that amount.
One should determine its length; regarding its width, the wall is said to begin from the fire-wall (*vahnibhitti*) and extend up to the space-wall (*vyomabhitti*). (72.36)
The walls are considered to extend up to the end of the universal enclosure;
having established the earth as the wall of the expansion, one proceeds by increasing [the measurement] by half and half again.
The width of the innermost [enclosure] shall be one and a half times [the width of the outermost], with equal doors and walls;
in the case of double walls, the width of the pillars situated in the middle shall be odd-numbered.
One should increase that measurement in the middle and decrease it on the side walls;
or, in the case of odd-numbered walls, one may [increase] two rows of central squares.

One should leave a space all around it and construct a door according to the prescribed rule; its size should be equal to the measurement of the foundation wall, or one-quarter, or half, or three-quarters of it.
The measurement of the door has been fully described; one should determine its sub-divisions (pādas) through logical application.
Furthermore, regarding those sub-divisions situated at the door which are established here from the primary base (mūlapāda): || 72/41 ||
The wise should arrange them either by placing them inside and outside with a wide space between each pair of feet, or by positioning them in their respective individual places.
Whether it be the assembly hall, the central stage, or the seat of the deity—
now the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of all these is being described.
Having first performed the offering of the sprouts and likewise the sprinkling for an auspicious day,
one should feed the Brahmins at the outset and avoid their leftovers.
Having again performed the *puṇyāha* rite, one should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then, having performed the *vāstuhoma*, one should carry out the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having adorned the pavilion with perfumes and other offerings, the preceptor should worship it,
having placed the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti upon the four central pillars.
Then one should tie the auspicious thread (kautuka) in the south-eastern corner;
having encircled it with cloths while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should thereafter adorn it with garlands and other ornaments.
Having worshipped them again with perfumes and other offerings, together with the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras),
one should then install the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras) in the center of the pavilion.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice measured by one droṇa or more,
one should cover it with rice grains, sesame seeds, parched grain, darbha grass, and flowers.
In the center, however, is the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha), endowed with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti; to its left is the Vardhanī vessel, into which one should invoke the Goddess with devotion.
Having established four jars provided with gold, cloth, and other offerings, one should [place] Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya within them, starting from the southeast.
One should worship [the deities] individually with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, ending with food offerings;
then, having established the Śiva-fire, [one should offer oblations] with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one hundred or half that number [of oblations] using Śiva and the other deities;
these are prescribed for the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated in the eastern direction, consisting of the principal deity Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas).
Or, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed from the southeast corner with the heart-mantras of Dharma and the others;
then, having offered oblations with the mantras of the Tattvas and so forth, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then at dawn, the preceptor, having bathed and being accompanied by the image-keepers, put on new garments,
a turban, and an upper cloth, and applied auspicious marks.

Having received the sacrificial fee, one should commence the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, assisted by architects, astrologers, and craftsmen.
One should prepare the pavilion, the body of the altar, the jars, and the fire;
having performed the expiation with the Aghora mantra, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having placed the Manonmanī [power] upon the body of the Śiva-maṇḍapa, which serves as the substratum for the ritual objects, and having sprinkled it with those waters, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
At the conclusion of the food offering, the preceptor-mantrin should perform the sprinkling with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
O wise ones, the sprinkling of the assembly hall and other such places should be performed in this very same manner.
Thus, the mortal who acts in this manner is separated from all that is undesirable.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the pavilion, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Enclosure Wall.
Now I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the enclosures (prākāra).
Half the width of the temple (prāsāda) is designated as the "staff" (daṇḍa).
The construction of a single enclosure wall, starting from the center and extending outward with one, two, three, four, or five walls on all sides, is proclaimed to be of five kinds. (73.2)
When the extensive root-abode is divided into three parts, one part shall be the pedestal;
outside of that, it should be either double or triple that portion.
The construction of two ramparts is desired as having three or four qualities, or four or five qualities, or five or six qualities.
Thus, the fourfold [measurement] has been declared; now the three-fold enclosure is described.
That which is called the *daṇḍa* here is one-fourth of the temple (*prāsāda*). (73.5)
Of that [length], there are [sections] consisting of two, three, and four parts; likewise, three, four, and five parts;
as well as four, five, and six parts; and likewise, five, six, and seven parts. (73.6)
It is declared to have six, seven, or eight [divisions] and the dimensions of three enclosures;
listen, O twice-born ones, to the fivefold description of the enclosure consisting of the Vedas.
Outside the triple enclosure, one should increase [the dimensions] by one finger-breadth at a time on all sides until reaching nine parts.
Thus, the measurement for the four enclosures has been declared in five ways;
likewise, even in the case of the four enclosures, there is a spacious layout for the temple.
The wise one should join together the entire measure, the half-measure, and the measure of three or four parts; this is stated according to the measurement of a cubit (*hasta*).
Starting from two cubits and increasing by one up to nine cubits—
among these, the measurement of the enclosure wall for small temples is considered to be eightfold.
Two cubits and three cubits, and likewise three or four cubits;
four or five cubits, and likewise five or six cubits. || 73/12 ||
It measures six, seven, and eight cubits, as well as eight *nandas*;
it consists of eight long *nandas* and has the dimensions of two enclosures.
From this, by means of a single supernatural power (ṛddhi), [the space] up to the hand of Rudra is indeed measured in three ways, as well as the enclosure wall of the Vedas.
By increasing the measurement by one cubit at a time, ending at twelve cubits, the dimensions for the four enclosures of the small [temples] and others are proclaimed. (73.15)

However, for those [images] that appear as conceptual constructions of desire for birth and so forth, no such restriction exists, just as there is none for a temple that is accessible everywhere. (73.16)

For the birth-chambers of those who cause rebirth, as well as for other residences, they should be constructed in sequence with proportions of one-and-a-half, three-quarters, and two parts [of the total width]. || 73.17 ||
One should employ the *nāgara* and other styles according to the straight and curved paths;
the temple should be spacious, symmetrical, and provided with a base platform. (73.18)
Or, one may construct a structure suitable for a great highway with a width of three-quarters of a cubit, following the previously mentioned procedure.
This distinction does not exist at all in a palace that is universal; it likewise applies to one with five, six, or seven pillars, as well as to one surrounded by eight or nine [enclosures].
One should first increase it on all sides by means of hands and feet according to the previous measurement;
having first made that equal and square, one should proceed thereafter.
One should fashion the length of the opening facing toward the deity; or one may fashion it at the back or on the side, as in an ancient temple structure.
Or, in a case where space is cramped, it should be constructed anew;
beginning with one cubit, increasing by one cubit at a time.
One should increase or decrease [the measurement] from the previously mentioned Viśālaka up to eleven cubits,
until the desired requirement is fulfilled.
One should fashion it on the back, or on the face, or on both sides, or even on one side; thus one should determine its length along the face.
Then, it may be one-quarter greater, or one-and-a-half times, or three-quarters less than double;
or it may be double, or one-and-a-half times double, triple, or quadruple.
Starting from two cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
one should determine the height of the opening up to five times that [width].
One should determine the measurement of the enclosures (prākāra) as being either the space between the walls, outside the walls, or within the walls.
For the sake of establishing the six dimensions beginning with length, one should calculate increase and decrease by means of cubits through the path of the base when designing the enclosure wall.
In a temple where the hand-projection (hastaprāsāda) has been severed, the missing portion of the severed hand must be restored,
or it should be filled in, even if it remains within the measurement of a single cubit.
This which has been described for the gods is indeed the *khalūrikā* for men;
having grasped only what was stated there, one should apply it according to the measure of what was spoken. (73.31)
Having multiplied the income by seven and added the qualities (guṇas), one should divide by twenty-seven;
the remainder shall be determined as the asterism (ṛkṣa) from the width or from the total.
One should divide that which was stated by either one or eight times the number of suns (twelve).
Then, having multiplied the income by three, one should divide it by ten times the number of mantras (twenty-eight). || 73/33 ||
The expenditure, however, is declared by the scriptures to be double; one should divide [the total] by eight.
The origins, beginning with the banner (dhvaja), are said to extend up to thirty.
The lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāra) should be calculated by the sages through division;
one should then examine it either by the cubits of the original temple or by other means.
Starting from one cubit and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
the width of the halls is prescribed up to the limit of two cubits.
Starting from three times that measure, it should extend up to thirty times the width,
whether for a small or a large temple.
The height of the wall is specified as being less at the top than at its base;
starting from a reduction of one-sixth, it continues until it is reduced by a sixteenth part.
Having performed that many times, [one should construct] one part with its root and the tip of that [other] part;
it should be enriched with the groups beginning with the base (adhiṣṭhāna) and adorned with the khaṇḍaharmya and other features.
Alternatively, one should construct a wall endowed with straight devotion (or straightness),
equipped with a pinnacle such as a parasol, and topped by a bull standing above.
Its height should be equal to the length of the staff, or half of it, or three-quarters, or one and a quarter, or one and a half, or one and three-quarters.
The projection of the base and the wall should be twice [the thickness];
the plinth (upāna) is said to be above that, according to those measurements.
The pedestal (pādaka) indeed increases from half [the height] by increments of one-quarter up to double;
above that, the base-moulding (kampa) should be made according to a measure of one-fourth of that.
One should fashion [the other parts] as half of that, or three-quarters, or one and a quarter,
or one and a half, or even up to double, ending at twice the size.
There may be one or even two steps, or there may be an upper landing (ūrdhvopāna).
The inner courtyard (sālāṅkaṇa) should be lower, while the outer courtyard should be higher.
The width between the walls (sālānām antare vyāsam) should be such that the outer courtyard is elevated.
Starting from two finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
One should fashion the recessed area for each pillar up to its end, measuring nine units,
with dimensions of six, five, four, eleven, ten, and two finger-breadths respectively.
Indeed, this rule is not intended for those who appear with conceptualizations of desire for birth, nor for the lowly,
even within a temple that is accessible to all.
The wise should construct the courtyard (aṅkaṇa) of the halls surrounding the liṅgas of Svāyaṃbhuva and others, such that it is either internally sloped, level, or externally sloped.
Between the pillars, there may be a structure in the form of a flower-garlanded pavilion or in the shape of an assembly hall; it should be constructed with one, two, or three walls.
It may also be provided with four walls and consist of one or more stories;
starting from the base (upāna) up to the height of the main temple (mūlaprāsāda).
Then, having divided the northern end into seven parts,
one should fashion the *masūraka* as two parts in length and determine the remainder as the width.
One should divide a quarter of the primary abode by the number nine;
one should fashion a quarter with the first two parts and the remainder with the rest.
Beginning from two cubits and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
the height of pillars is proclaimed to extend up to seven cubits.
The measurement of the wall in a small temple and a small vimāna should be the same;
beginning from one and a half finger-breadths (pakṣāṅgula) and increasing by half a finger-breadth [at each stage].
The width of the base (stambha) is desired to extend up to twenty-four units;
the height of the pedestal (pāda) is half of that, while the plinth (adhiṣṭhāna) is one-seventh, one-eighth, or one-ninth of it.
Whether it be less or more, the same applies to the height of the pedestal (pādocca);
or else, the plinth (masūraka) may be three or four parts of that height.
One should apply the foot-binding (pādabandha) and the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) of the same kind;
and the measurement of the plinth (prastara) and so forth should be performed as prescribed for the temple (prāsāda).
One should construct the central core (garbha) and the first brick in the southeast, southwest, northwest, or northeast corner, or even at the center of the four corners.
The walls are described as having inward-facing openings; they should be situated either on the southern portion of one's own [site] or within the corner of the gate. (73.60)
In Gṛhakṣata, Mahendra, Bhallāṭa, or Puṣpadantaka, the location of the *garbha* is indicated; there, the first brick is placed. (73.61)
One should construct that [structure] from the base, enriched with bricks at the summit and stakes above;
one should place a brick in one of the four corners situated above the wall.
The first should be the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala); the second is the inner necklace (antarhārā);
the third should be the middle necklace (madhyahārā); and the fourth is called the boundary (maryādā).
And the fifth is proclaimed as the one called Mahāmaryādikā;
there, the preceptor should establish all the attendant deities.
And that [arrangement] for the provision of the retinue is stated briefly:
the measurement of the retinue's celestial chariots (vimānas) is indeed half that of the central sanctum (garbha). || 73/65 ||
One-third, one-half, or one-quarter of the root area should extend outward as the base;
this begins from a single cubit and extends up to eleven cubits.
The width and height of the temple (prāsāda) are indeed as previously stated;
the dwellings for the retinue are considered to be shaped like the limbs or the phallus (liṅga) of the temple.
The ancillary shrines (parivāra-ālayas) are considered to be either supported by walls or distinct [structures];
they are provided with a base area, a frontage, and an entrance, while the portion of the footprint-form is omitted.

Those situated in the east should face west; those situated in the west should face east. Those situated on the right (south) should face north; those situated in the northern direction should face south.
Kṣetreśa and Dakṣavaktra, as well as Caṇḍeśa,
should be in the region of Nāgarāḍīśa, and Agastya likewise.
Dhanada is likewise mentioned, and Caṇḍeśvara is similarly regarded; as are the Vasus, the sages, the Ādityas, and indeed the eleven Rudras.
The Aśvins and the deities of the dwelling (vāstu-devas) are situated both outside and inside;
this [procedure] is proclaimed as common to all retinues. || 73/72 ||
One should place the bull in front of the deity, or facing toward the deity;
one should likewise cause a pavilion with four doors to be constructed for the bull.
From the beginning, this first retinue is concentrated with the trident;
the second retinue shall consist of Caṇḍeśa, and the third likewise.
The fourth is proclaimed as being joined with Vighneśvara;
thereafter, the fifth is now declared to be joined with Saptārcis (the Seven-Flamed One).
The two heroes, conjoined with Skandajyeṣṭhā, are in the sixth and seventh [houses];
the eighth house shall be the retinue, conjoined with the seven Mothers.

One should station the gods outside the *sakala* and other positions according to the proper method; one should then conceive of them within the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) as being devoid of their eightfold retinues.
Vṛṣa, Agnimatara, Vighna, Skanda, Jyeṣṭhā, Caṇḍikā, and Āditya should be placed in sequence; or alternatively, the Gaṇas and the Vidyeśvaras.
O lords of sages, one should install Caṇḍikā to the north or south of the Mothers;
one may also install Brahmā or Viṣṇu, or even omit them.
Then, having left Durgā, one should place Viṣṇu, or Kubera, or Soma,
as well as Caṇḍeśa in the direction of the Lord (the North), and Kṣetrapāla in that very place.
One should install Śrī either between Vighneśa and the root (Kanda) or in the western direction;
or one may install her as the third deity, separately, together with Vighna and Sarasvatī.
Alternatively, there may be the world-protectors (lokapālas), including Yama accompanied by the Mothers;
they should be large in the eight directions, either together with their pedestals or alone.
Vighneśa is situated in all regions, as are Gaurī and Skanda;
they may be twelve, or sixteen, or twenty-four in number.
The inner and middle great rays should each have thirty-two attendants;
among these, this one with sixteen attendants is called the gentle (saumya).
Having established the site for the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), one should install [the deities] from the solar region:
Āditya, Supraja, Vahni, Kinnara, and likewise Mātṛ.
Cibuḍha, Vighnarāja, Śrī, and likewise Varuṇa;
Skanda, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Caṇḍeśvara. || 73.86 ||
O best of sages, let those born of the field and those born of song be established hereafter; or rather, let the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) or the gatekeepers be stationed within this very place.
There should be two times eight surrounding retinues; now, thirty-two [divisions] are described.
Having established them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in their respective places, they are divided into thirty-two parts by the sun.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Gaṅgā, Vahni, Nāga, Agastya, Yama, Suśānta, Bhūteśa, Vighneśa, and also Bhāratī. (73.89)
Śrī, Varuṇa (the Lord of Waters), Skanda, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, Manonmanī,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and finally Kāśyapa and Nandin.
At the end, one should place Kṣetrajña and Vimala, and outside, one should station Gajendra; or else, one should install the Īśvaras within, or the Ṛṣis, or the Vasus.
Then the supreme instructor should arrange eight attendants;
he should apply them with appropriate logic everywhere, even in temples consisting of a single hall or more.
The attendant deities are considered to be either seated upon pedestals or situated within images;
[they are] Vṛṣa, Śūla, Caṇḍeśa, Mahāpīṭha, and Gaṇādhipa.
One should thus imagine these [deities] as Nāga kings everywhere;
or else, one may install from among them whichever are desired in a temple with five or more shrines.
In the four directions, there may be four seats, or two at the front and the back;
or, omitting the back, there may be three, or else one at the front.

The pedestal (pīṭha) may be located at the corner door, situated in the corner, or facing the cardinal directions; or there may be a pedestal for each hall, while the Paiśāca [pedestal] should be outside.
Beginning from five finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
the width of the front pedestal (agrapīṭhaka) ends at twenty-five mātrās.
It should be half, or three-quarters, equal or greater in height than its width;
having divided the height into two, three, four, six, or seven parts,
there should be one, two, three, or four tiers of girdles (mekhalā) above that.
The lotus should have a pericarp, or it may be a pericarp alone;
the lotus should be twice, three times, or four times the size of the girdle (mekhalā).
The *padmocca* is proclaimed [as the height]; the *veśa* should be similar to a girdle (*mekhalā*).
One may conceive of it as having three feet or two feet. || 73/100 ||
The pericarp should be made higher than the girdle by half a lotus, or by one-quarter,
or by three-quarters, or according to the strength of its beauty.
A small pedestal is said to be either circular or square;
now listen, O excellent ones, to the characteristics of large pedestals.
It may be equal to the interior of the temple, or half of that, or even a quarter;
within that interval, at the eighth part, the width shall be ninefold.
Starting from the measure of Rudra (one cubit) and increasing by two or three finger-breadths,
the width of the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) extends up to nine cubits.

The height should be equal to the width, or one and a quarter times, or even one and a half times; or it may be three-quarters, or even two-thirds, or whatever proportion is appropriate for that particular case.
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be either one-sixteenth [of the total height], or one part;
it may also be equal to the width of the pedestal, or elevated by one, two, or three finger-breadths.
The *jagatī* should consist of four parts; the *kumuda* should be three-quarters [of that];
the *kampa* is one-quarter, while the *karṇa* is proclaimed to be three-quarters.
Above that, there should be a projection (kampa) consisting of one part, and a fillet (vājana) of two parts;
above that, there should be another fillet of one part, and a lotus (padma) is desired above that.
It may be equal in shape to a pedestal (pīṭha), or it is desired that the width of the leaf be one, two, or three finger-breadths high,
or reduced by a sixteenth or an eighth part.
Its height shall be desired as either half or three-quarters of its own width;
O twice-born ones, the measurement of the interval between those two shall be nine times the height.
The pericarp is considered to be one-third of the lotus petal, or half of that;
its width is declared to be one-eighth of the space between the petals, which is nine units in measure.
The width of the pericarp (karṇikā) is said to be equal to one-third [of the lotus], or even equal [to the whole];
the height of the pericarp is desired to be endowed with an interval of half that measure.
The width of the front part of the thick portion [of the pillar] should be reduced by one-eighth of a foot;
or, one may fashion the upper part according to the measurements prescribed for the base (adhiṣṭhāna) or the pedestal (upapīṭha).
Or it should be made in the form of a temple, with the highest gurus ending at the *pastara*;
or it may be joined with the central *bhadra* and adorned with various chowries.
It is joined with various elements, endowed with the asterisms situated in the corners,
possessing a manifold network of nostrils, and provided solely with its own pedestal.
Whether circular, square, triangular,
or octagonal, it should be taken from the center of the temple or ship, excluding the middle of the foot.
Starting from the root abode and having removed the staff of fire,
one should establish the pedestal there; then, beginning from that point, one should expand it.
The best of teachers [should fashion] the pedestal with a width of fifty *daṇḍas*, using half a *daṇḍa* as the increment;
this may indeed be on the back of a bull.
One should construct it either in the middle of a grove of *sāla* trees, or on the path between villages, or in the center of a village, or in the northeast of the house. (73.119)
One should examine the first *āya* and other characteristics by the very path described for the types of *dhāmas*;
the preceptor should perform the laying of the first brick in the center according to the previously stated rule.
One should fashion a staircase for it on the south or the west;
that staircase is said to be either joined or detached.
One should arrange the bull and the trident joined with the western gate,
as well as the great seat (mahāpīṭha), the banner, and so forth, in the west.
One should perform the same procedure at the southern gate and likewise at the northern gate;
or, in a temple with four gates, one may face the actual gate which is marked by a trident.

Then one should place the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) together with the banner and other items in a single location; the gateway (pratolī) should be in the eastern direction, or in the west, or in all four directions.
In the southeast (Āgneyī) is the place for wealth; in the southwest (Nairṛtī), the armory;
in the northwest (Vāyavī), the sleeping quarters; and in the northeast (Aiśānī), a well is desired.
Sadāśiva and the others should be installed everywhere on all sides;
or, the place for wealth may be situated between Indra and Agni.
In the southeast is the place for cooking and the sacrificial hall;
and there, in the middle between the directions of Yama and Agni, there should be the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa).
There should be a flower-bathing hall and a water reservoir;
the location for the Śiva-knowledge of the Kāmika and other scriptures is situated in the southern direction.
The location for perfumes and other offerings is desired in the midst of Yama and Rākṣasa; one should arrange the placement of flowers in the direction of Nirṛti, or alternatively, on its left.
One should arrange the proclamation of the Dharma here, or in the western direction;
or else, one should arrange the treasury of knowledge in the northwestern or the southern direction.
There, the place for the bed may be situated between the Moon and the Wind,
or at the location of Kubera, or to the east of that, in the region of Vaiśa.
The sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) should be desirable; musical instruments are desired to its right, or one may arrange the place for the bed in the northeast.
One should designate that site either to its south or in the north-west;
and one should prepare a well at the place of the bed and a pavilion for flowers and bathing.
The location for my devotees, the place for books, garments, and gold, and the place for the implements of the deity have not been described by me, as I am wary of prolixity. (73.134)
One should arrange all of that according to the wishes of the patron;
likewise, one should arrange a place for those who subsist upon the deity. Furthermore, the residence of the preceptor should be near the temple.
There is the residence of the worshippers and the stationing of the attendants. || 73/136 ||
One should arrange for the location of flower gardens and the like everywhere;
one should also establish various assembly pavilions in every region.
"O wise ones, let another location be determined according to the method described for villages.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, the "Ritual for the Characteristics of the Enclosure Wall," in the Great Tantra known as the Kāmika;
followed by the "Ritual for the Installation of the Retinue."
O twice-born ones, listen briefly to the installation of the retinue: beginning with three cubits and increasing by one cubit at a time. (74.1)
Indeed, the width of this pavilion should be exactly nine cubits;
in its center, it should be provided with an altar and joined by sixteen pillars.
Or it may be provided with twelve pillars, or even with four pillars;
and there should be either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) numbering fifty-five [in measure].
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is either circular or square, with its sides oriented toward the cardinal directions;
or there may be nine pits for the Mothers, or even a single pit.
For those who are worthy, there is the arrangement of jewels, the opening of the eyes,
purification with the five products of the cow and other substances, and the preliminary consecration in water.
Then follows the consecration of the pavilion, then the purification of the image and so forth, the tying of the protective thread, the mounting upon the bed, and the placement of the ritual jars.
O twice-born ones, having performed everything as before, one should worship properly with the first syllable of one's own name in the respective positions of the letters, [conceiving them] as Śiva.
Having performed the arrangement of their forms and other attributes, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with Palāśa,
Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa wood in the directions starting from the east.
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and sesame seeds in sequence;
then, at dawn, one should worship the image and other objects, as well as the water-pots and the fires.
Thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the preceptor and others according to the prescribed rule;
it should range from one niṣka up to ten niṣkas for the guru, and for others as previously stated.
One should begin the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) one muhūrta or nāḍikā prior [to the main rite].
Taking the seed-syllable from the water-pot (kumbha), one should place it in its respective location.

The plinth (jagati) and the base (pādukā) on the exterior should be equal to the height of the temple's upper portion, or half of it, or three-quarters; or they may be one-quarter more, or one-half more.
Having placed them down, one should establish the pedestals, or else having first prepared them,
one should perform the consecration, excluding the ritual placement of gems (ratnanyāsa), while circumambulating clockwise.
One should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) and then commence the other rites;
now the procedure for the consecration of the great seat (mahāpīṭha) is being described.
One should construct the pavilion as before in the eastern, western, and northern directions;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four-cornered according to the number four, or it may be a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila).
Having performed the purification of the pedestal with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, as well as the tying of the protective thread (kautuka),
one should then perform the ritual placement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍanyāsa) upon the altar on the sacrificial mound.
Then, in the jars situated in the center, the east, the north, the west, and at Śaṅkara (the northeast),
one should likewise place Avighna, Amoda, Pramoda, and Pramukha.
Having placed Durmukha, the creator of obstacles, one should meditate upon the [other] colors:
Avighna, who resembles coral, and Āmoda, who is dark green in color.
Having thus meditated upon Pramoda as being black in color, Pramukha as having the luster of crystal,
and Durmukha as resembling saffron, the Guru should perform the worship.
On the pedestal (pīṭha), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Tattveśa, Mūrti, and the others, as well as the fire-oblation (homa).
One should place the principles beginning with Ātmatattva up to the shanks, the throat, and the lotus.

The wise one should offer oblations in sequence: fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds, using wood from the Palāśa, Udumbara, and Vaṭa trees.
Beginning from the eastern direction at the *aśvattha* tree, one should perform the fire-oblation as before;
having worshipped the pedestal, the jars, and likewise the fire at dawn.
Having given the sacrificial fee as before, one should begin the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa);
one should place [the mantra] without obstacle in the center of the pericarp, situated within the pitcher.
The wise one should place the incense (āmoda) and other offerings in the four directions and the northeast corner;
he should then reverently bathe the pedestal with the water from each respective pitcher.
Thus it should be for the Bhūtapīṭha; one should act in this same manner even for the Paiśāca [pīṭha].
However, for the central jar, one should place Nīlalohita in the center.
One should place the constellations in the eastern quarter, the zodiac signs in the south,
the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) in the west, and the hosts of Viśvedevas in the north.
One should place the Rudras in the pitcher of the eastern direction, the groups of Mothers in the southern,
the Gaṇas in the western part, and the Yakṣas in the northern direction. (74.27)
One should place the planets in the north-eastern direction, the Asuras in the southeast,
the Rākṣasas in the region of the ancestors (south), and the hosts of Nāgas in the northwest.
Outside of that, the preceptor should place the water-pots (kalaśas) presided over by the world-protectors (lokapālas),
and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, ending with the food offering (naivedya).
This alone shall be the distinction; everything else is the same.
One should place the five groups in the pericarp and the eight [groups] upon the petals.
The wise one should place the World-Protectors outside the door, each situated in their respective direction;
this is the specific mantra-installation for the sacrificial altar of the Piśācas.
Whatever has not been stated here, one should apply it all as described in the procedure for the installation of the image.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, the "Rite for the Installation of the Retinue," in the great tantra named Kāmika.
The Ritual Procedure for the Worship of the Retinue.
I shall now describe the worship of the retinue; listen, O best of sages!
First, there is the eight-syllable mantra joined with the Praṇava and accompanied by Viṣṇu.
The mantra for the worship of the retinue consists of one's own name in the dative case, joined with *bindu* and *nāda*, and preceded by the word of salutation (*namaḥ*). (75.2)
One should worship them in the forenoon, or at midday, or at night; or else, one may worship them at a single time, while performing all other rites as usual.
One should cause the bali offering to be given three, two, or once a day in due order;
for them, the worship is performed with a mantra ending in "namaḥ," while the bali is offered with a mantra ending in "svāhā."
One should especially offer the bali-oblation, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, food, incense, lamps, musical instruments, and so forth, extending from the entrance to the sacrificial pedestal.
Facing either the east or the north, wearing a lower garment and an upper cloth,
[one should draw] with the size of a hen's egg, or half of that, or half again.
One should first offer [oblations] to Nandin, and to Mahākāla in the east,
as well as to Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka near the four gates.
In the southern and western regions, one should place the bali offering for Vṛṣaskanda;
then, for the Goddess, Caṇḍa, and Soma, one should subsequently present the bull bali.
Then one should offer the bali-offering for the eight attendants and others in sequence; having offered water, one should again offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
One should offer sacrificial food (haviṣya) along with water during the bali-rite;
standing in the south-eastern direction facing the deity, one should then proceed in a clockwise circumambulation.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), one should indeed offer the oblation (bali) there;
[specifically] to Avighna on the pericarp (karṇikā) and to Āmoda on the eastern petal.
One should offer the bali-oblation with their respective names to Pramoda, Pramukha, Durmukha, Vighnakartṛ, Dakṣiṇāpi, and Uttareśa.
If there is a Paiśācika seat, one should also perform the offering (bali) there;
or else, one may offer the bali in either the Paiśāca or the Bhautika [seat].
An offering is prescribed for Nīlarudra in the center of the pericarp; one should cast offerings to the constellations and other deities in the east, south, west, and north.
One should offer to the Rudras in the east, likewise to the Mothers in the south;
to the Gaṇas in the western part, to the Yakṣas in the northern quarter; to the Gṛhas in the northeast, and to the Asuras in the southeast.
On the petal in the direction of Vāyu, one should offer an oblation to the *pālāśī* nāgas who feed on leaves;
outside the petals, one should offer oblations to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) by their respective names.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the procedure for the worship of the retinue, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of the Bull (Vṛṣabha).
(Verse 204) I shall describe the installation of the bull (*vṛṣa*), preceded by its defining characteristics.
One should first fashion the bull to the east of the inner door.
The second [image] is in front of the pavilion, and the third is to the east of the pedestal;
on each pedestal there is a special feature, and the bull is stationed in the west.
Having left aside half the pedestal, or an equal portion, or twice or thrice that amount, or even four times, one should place the bull in front of it.
The best [measure] is equal to the portion of the worship; the middling should be half of that;
the lowest is known to be half of that, or else it may be four, three, or two times [the standard].
Alternatively, for one made of iron, the bull is considered to have the measurement of those respective intervals;
for one made of stone, it is considered that the interior cavity (garbha) should be made with nine parts, divided into nine sections.
Having divided the height of the door into eight parts, by increasing each part successively up to four times that measure, the dimensions for an earthen bull are prescribed.
One should place an iron [image] at the door and a stone one in the surrounding area;
it is taught that an earthen or a stone [image] is approved for the front of the pedestal.
An image made of metal should be fashioned whether standing or reclining;
one made of stone or plaster should be made, especially in a reclining posture.
O best of teachers, the bull (Ṛṣabha) should also be fashioned even when [the image] is stationary;
furthermore, the bull is considered to be in front of the common liṅga.
Known as Svayaṃbhū, Bāṇa, and Lauha, it is worshipped in the world of Rudra;
marked by the guardians of the quarters, perfected, and consisting of a hundred thousand liṅgas.
The face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga) and the image (bera) are declared to be the distinguished liṅga;
elsewhere, the bull (vṛṣa) is said to be [the symbol], or it is also stated to be that very same thing.
The flagstaff is likewise described; its characteristics are stated here:
it should be joined at one-third of the height of the *liṅga*, and its alignment should be verified by means of a plumb line and visual inspection. (76.12)
Equipped with a high backrest and a seat, with the tip of its beard-like fringe reaching the top, it is measured by breaking down [the dimensions] up to eighty-four [units]. || 76.13 ||
The width of the region of the prong is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas); its length should be the same, while the diameter of the mouth is six units (kalās).
Between the corners of the mouth and the nostrils, it is fashioned with ten finger-breadths;
the eye is equal to the eye in length, and half that in width.
The pupil (tāra) should be one-third of that [eye], and the light-circle (jyotis) should be one-fifth of it;
the thickness of the eyebrows should extend to half an eye-measure, and their length should be two mātrās.
The nose is said to be two finger-breadths [in height], and its middle part should be four finger-breadths;
the width at the tip of the nose should be such that the face measures twelve finger-breadths.
Above that, it should be ten *mātrās*, and above that, eighteen *aṅgulas*.
The distance between the eyes is four *mātrās*, while the two cheeks are triangular.
Both sides [of the face] have four eyes each, while the two ears are at the junctions of the mouth;
from the base of the ear to the end of the mouth, it is proclaimed as having five eyes.
From the root of the ear to the tip of the ear, it is said that the distance should be twelve finger-breadths (manvaṅgula).
The two roots of the ears, however, should each be two mātrās in width and likewise endowed with height.
In that very same circular area to be constructed, measuring ten finger-breadths in circumference,
the two ears should have a length of five finger-breadths and arise from the circle of the *kalā*.
The middle parts are five finger-breadths wide, becoming gradually thinner toward the ends;
they are six finger-breadths in circumference at the base and adorned with straight lines.
The base of the prong is four mātrās long and six aṅgulas in height;
its width at the tip is half an aṅgula, and it is slightly curved.
Leaving aside the mass situated at the base of the horns,
it is held that the mass between the divisions should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in measure, elevated at the two bases of the horns.
The distance from the tip of the horn to the hollow (avaṭa) is considered to be six eyes (dvādaśāṅgulas);
the neck is eight eyes in length, and the height of the hump is three eyes.
The measurement for the three eyes is stated as one ucchraya; the face and the head [are measured] likewise.
The hump is below the lower lip and the eye, while the shank is five dṛg long.
The joint is said to be one finger-breadth, with four eyes for the calf;
then half an eye for the ankle, and two eyes for the hooves.
Below the ankle, the two stirrups are made of bell-metal; the foot of the netra is equal [in width].
The covering for the base of the shank is proclaimed to be seventeen mātrās.
At the top of the shank, it should be fifteen digits (tithi) in measure, increasing by one digit (aṅgula) for each finger-breadth;
the circumference at the base and the tip of the lower leg is thus proclaimed.
The height of the two hooves, excluding the circumference, should be eight mātrās;
the measurement of the back from the hump is said to be thirty-six mātrās.
In that context, three *trikaṭas* are traditionally known as six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
while the measure of three *trikaṭas* bent is said to be twelve finger-breadths.
And beyond that, the tail-continuation is proclaimed;
the base of the tail is four mātras, while its tip is fashioned with one finger-breadth (aṅgula). || 76/32 ||
The length of the tail is proclaimed to be thirty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure;
from that [length], the mass of hair should be six finger-breadths in measure.
On the back and at the region of the sacrum, the *tāra* is twenty *mātrās* long;
however, in the middle of the body's width, it is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
At the region of the hollow of the neck, the width is one *mātrā*;
below the neck, it is four *mātrās*, which is proclaimed as the extent of the hanging dewlap.
That [measurement] from the end of the shank should be eighteen mātrās;
the belly, extending from the navel, is proclaimed to have a width of eighty finger-breadths.
The middle, the back, and the front parts are traditionally held to be sixty finger-breadths [in length];
the navel is formed by two eyes, and the two testicles are considered to be two eyes.
The lower leg (parajaṅghā) is ten finger-breadths in length and width;
the joint (sandhi) is two mātrās, and the upper leg (upajaṅghā) is proclaimed to be twelve [finger-breadths].
The two ankles are to be known as having two eyes (two units), and the two hooves are considered to be five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula).
At the base of the hoof, two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula) should be made, while [the total length] is twenty-two finger-breadths.
The circumference of the middle of the calf should be three [units], while at the joint it is three again;
the circumference of the lower part of the calf is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The length of the back should be two finger-breadths, while the lower part is considered to be eight finger-breadths;
this is the procedure for the bull, endowed with the pervasion up to the limit of the Śakti.
Alternatively, the characteristics of a bull are stated in another way:
having divided the height into five parts, the hoof is said to be three *mātras*.
The width at the base should be four mātras, and the tip of the horn two mātras;
the forehead should be nine mātras, and the width of the face seven fingers (aṅgulas).
The total height [of the face] is two mātrās; the length of the eye is two mātrās, and its height should be one and a half aṅgulas. The middle of the eye should have the shape of a mouth.
The back is four finger-breadths [in width], while the neck is six finger-breadths; the height is one-fifth of the wings; by this, the measurement is proclaimed. (76.45)
O best of sages, it is taught that its length is five or six finger-breadths;
starting from the top of the head down to below the throat, it is recorded as being ten finger-breadths.
The height of the neck should be six mātras, and the length of those two [the neck and the head] should be six aṅgulas;
the height of the navel should be six mātras, and the knee should be two mātras in height.
The two shanks are two or three finger-breadths in length; the hoof is said to be three mātras.
The distance between the two horns should be two mātras, and their length is six finger-breadths.
O lords of sages, the width at the base is four mātrās, as is the height of the forehead;
the distance between the eyes and the ears is likewise, and the length of the ear is five aṅgulas.
The upper lip is three mātras high and the lower lip is two mātras;
the height and width of the base [of the face] are two, one, and three mātras respectively.
The width of the ear is five netras and one angula, as stated at the base;
the width of the neck is fifty [units], and its width is the same as that of the base.
O best of the twice-born, it is said that [the base] is six *vasu* (eight) *aṅgulas* in sequence;
the width of the *kakut* is six *aṅgulas*, and its height is two or three *mātras*.
One should skillfully place the tip of the ear, which is two mātrās wide;
the height of the body from the hump is said to be eighteen aṅgulas.

The width at the back should be exactly twice seven [fourteen] finger-breadths, while the width at the front is twelve finger-breadths; the mutual expansion from the base to the middle and from the middle to the tip is by four finger-breadths.
O twice-born ones, by means of eight finger-breadths for each direction, it should be formed in due order;
likewise, the length [of the knee] is five finger-breadths, and the region of the knee is two finger-breadths. (76.55)
The shank should be five finger-breadths in height and three finger-breadths in width; the height of the hoof should be two mātras, and the same should apply to the base of the tail.
The tip of its tail hangs down to the end of the shank, measuring one and a half finger-breadths; while the length and width of the scrotum are each two measures, respectively.
The length of the shank should be three mātras; the abdomen should be one aṅgula in width;
the remaining length should be three mātras; and the anus should be one māyā-aṅgula.
The width at the base and the top of the thigh is traditionally recorded as four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula);
the top of the shank should be three measures (trimātra), and the remainder should be determined according to the requirements of proportion and structural logic.
One should fashion [the image] either from solid metal or non-solid metal; one should construct the residence from bamboo, cloth, and the like, or from cane. || 76/60 ||
Alternatively, whatever the measurement of the entire [temple] may be, that same measurement applies when the bull has arisen;
thus, eight and a half barleycorns and so forth are stated as the measurement for the height in barleycorn-fingers.
Whether the work is inferior or superior depends on the desire of the artisan;
it should be adorned with various ornaments and provided with a network of bells.
The portion for the Pratimokṣa is of pure gold and likewise beautiful with its base;
thus has the characteristic been described—now hear, O twice-born ones, about the installation. (76.63)
The time should also be understood as before, and the planting of the sprouts should be performed in the same manner.
One should construct the pavilion according to the path described for the retinue.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in a single kuṇḍa or likewise on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
furthermore, the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) should be carried out in an image made of stone or even one made of metal.
For the sake of the jewels, one should avoid using a golden lotus made of clay or similar materials;
thereafter follows the opening of the eyes, purification, and the circumambulation of the village and other sites.
Having performed the preliminary consecration of the water (toyādhivāsana), one should then perform the purification of the pavilion (maṇḍapa-saṃskṛti),
the feeding of the twice-born (dvija-sambhojana), or the sprinkling of sacred water (puṇya-toyasecana).
The preceptor should likewise perform the Vāstuhoma, the bed-rite, the ceremonial bath, and the tying of the protective amulet;
he should bind the amulet upon the right horn of the bull.
One should perform the mounting of the bed and the placement of the water-pot as previously described;
[the mantra] ending with the fourth letter of the seventh group, adorned with the seven vowels.
At the beginning, it is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, combined with the *praṇava*;
at the end, "namo vṛṣabhāya" is added—within that, one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs of Brahmā.

In the central pitcher, Taurus is proclaimed; around it, in the eight [directions], one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas), or alternatively, the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras) surrounding the bull.
Ukṣā and Gopati, as well as Śaṅkukarṇa; likewise Tīkṣṇaśṛṅga, Nandin, Viṣāṇin, and Paśubhṛt. || 76.72 ||
One should place Mahodara as the eighth among these [deities] using their respective seed-syllables;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present an offering of mung-bean rice.
Likewise, in the Caru-kalpa, one should likewise install the [deities] such as Tattvamūrti;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) according to the previously mentioned procedure.

In the morning, the pure preceptor should shake out the sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mung beans, and black gram in their proper order, and then perform the worship and the fire sacrifice.
At the conclusion, there should be worship of the preceptor and also sacrificial fees for the officiating priests;
then, at an auspicious hour and a favorable moment, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
If the position of the bull (Vṛṣabha) is mobile and is perceived within its own region,
one should establish it with the root mantra and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, having brought the jars, one should place them upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the bull.
Taking the seed-syllable from the jar, one should place it upon the heart of the bull.
Having taken seeds from others, one should place them all around that pedestal;
then, one should respectfully bathe the bull with the water from the ritual jar.

The same procedure applies to the raising of the banner as well; however, at the base of its staff, the ritual consecration with the water-pot (kumbha-abhiṣeka) and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) must be performed.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the bull, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The Ritual for the Installation of the Gopura (Temple Gateway)

(I shall now describe) the installation of the gate-towers (gopura) according to their defining characteristics. When the width of the main temple (mūlaprāsāda) is divided into seven, eight, or nine parts— (77/1)
In the tenth and eleventh parts, however, the measurement for the door-ornaments and so forth, up to the gopura, shall be according to those respective ninth parts in terms of width.
That which was prescribed for small and minor [temples] is ordained as the medium measurement;
in the case of a great temple, it is divided into four, five, or six parts.
When those [measures] are divided into seven or eight parts, the division ending at the gate-tower (gopura) is established;
the width of the door-ornament (dvāraśobhā) and so forth is proclaimed as fivefold.
One-third, one-fourth, and one-half [of the width] at the third part; two parts at the fourth part; three parts at the fifth part; and four parts at the fifth part. (77.5)
For those of the Jyeṣṭha class, the width up to the gopura should gradually increase from two cubits to sixteen cubits, by increments of one aratni.
Each [section] should be three cubits wide up to the end of the gopura;
however, from three cubits, it should increase by two cubits each time until reaching twenty-one cubits.
As before, the details regarding measurement, beauty, and so forth are determined by the number of lunar days; beginning with seven cubits (nandahasta), they increase by two cubits at each step.
The width at the gateway (gopura) extends up to thirty-seven cubits,
increasing by one cubit from three, fifteen, and seven [cubits].
The fifth measurement is considered to be two [units] for the eight [deities] and one for the five;
otherwise, the width is prescribed according to the measure of a cubit.
From five hands up to a thousand hands, increasing by one hand at a time,
the width of the door-ornaments is prescribed for the first enclosure.
In the Dvāraśālaka [temple type], the dimensions range from twenty-three cubits starting from twenty-one cubits;
however, from twenty-five cubits, they extend up to thirty-three cubits.
The width of the gateway-palace (dvāraprāsāda) is proclaimed as the fifth [measurement], beginning from twenty-five and ending at forty-three [tala-s]. (77.13)
The width of the gateway-pavilion (dvāraharmya) should begin at nine or five cubits and extend up to fifty-three cubits; such is the width of the gopura.
In the case of cities, villages, settlements, and the like, the measurement for the width of the gate-tower (gopura) may be less or more by one, two, three, four, or five cubits.

One should design the door-ornament (*dvāraśobhā*) and other features with a length of two and a half parts, three parts, one-third of three parts, one part, and two parts; [and] it should consist of seven parts and ten parts. (77/16)
