One should calculate four parts in the case of six parts, four parts in the case of seven parts,
five parts in the case of nine parts, and twice that [five] in the case of eleven parts.
For the purpose of making the gateway-pillars lofty, the measurement of the *khalūrī*, the *gopura*, and so forth should be taken,
and the projection should also be equal to that.
O best of teachers, having made the width of the gopura twenty parts,
the proportions of the gopuras range from one part up to eighteen parts.
One should perform the exit either from outside the *sāla* wall or within it,
at distances of one and a half cubits, one and three-quarter cubits, and two cubits respectively.
The best of instructors should increase [the measurement] by six, nine, or ten units;
the width of the door should be five, seven, or nine units respectively.

The number of lunar days (tithis) should be used for the inferior [type], while the middling is considered excellent when [the width] is divided by seven and the fifty-second part is taken; this applies when the width of the door is fifty [units].
The height [of the spire] is fivefold, being twice the tenth part and greater than a quarter;
in the main sanctum, it begins from one-fourth of the height of the lentil-shaped plinth (masūra).
Having made the conclusion at the solar portion and leaving aside one part,
and having made a quarter of a lentil (masūra), the pedestal is formed by that very remainder.
One should construct the gateway (gopura) with a height that is either half [the total height] or increased by increments;
furthermore, it may be increased according to the previously mentioned proportions or made equal [to them].
The entire measurement stated for the body of the temple (dhāma) may optionally be applied to the parts of the gateway (gopura);
one should then cut away that [measurement] from the base (adhiṣṭhāna), but only in the case of a temple with a pedestal (sopapīṭha).

One who is learned in the science of architecture should cause the height of the northern end to be half [the total] and its width to be equal to that; or he may make it as high as the gateway of the city gate.
One should construct [the temple] with one, two, or three stories, increasing by one for the sake of beauty;
thereafter, one may also construct it with five, six, or seven floors, beginning from the first story.

A gopura (gate-tower) should likewise be constructed; this same principle should be inferred for the middle [section] as well, including the door-decorations, the door-hall, and the palace-terraces at the gateway.
By means of the gateway itself, they are established within the mandalas and so forth up to the five-fold end;
the measurement of the pillar has already been explained previously.
The measurement from the top of that *prastāra* up to the pinnacle (*stūpī*) is stated as follows:
having divided that height into six parts, it is [constructed] with *prastaras* consisting of one and a quarter parts each. (77.31)
Similarly, the portion for the *stūpikā* (the pinnacle) consists of one and a half parts of the neck and head;
thus is the single-storeyed [temple] described, and now the two-storeyed is prescribed.
Dividing that height into nine parts, the emergence of the plinth (prastara) together with the base (aṅghri) shall consist of one part;
the neck (gala) is said to be one part, and the head (śiras) shall be two and a half parts.
The remainder is said to be the head-protrusion (śiroddhṛta); this is declared to have two storeys (dvitala).
The height of the three floors is twelve parts, while the cornice (kapota) occupies one part including its plinth (aṅghri).
The height of the base (pāda) shall be two and a half parts, while the plinth (prastara) is indeed one part;
the length of the base shall be two parts, measured according to the eightfold division.
The height of the neck (grīvā) shall be one part; the head (śiras) shall be two and a half parts.
The elevation of the pinnacle (sthūpikā) shall be the remainder; thus is the three-storeyed [temple] described.
The measurement from the northern edge to the tip of the crest, which consists of eighteen parts,
is increased by one-third of a part to determine the height of the *antocca*.
The height of the base (pāda) shall be two and a half parts; the elevation of the single moulding (prastara) together with the plinth (aṅghri) shall be one part.
The measurement of the neck (gala) shall be one part, and the elevation of the spire (śikhara) shall be three parts.
By the remainder, the pinnacle (sthūpikā) is declared; beyond that is the five-tiered [structure], extending from the northern direction to the crest (śikhā), consisting of twenty-nine parts.
One should make the *prastara* half a share; the height of the base (*pāda*) is four parts;
the platform (*mañca*) is one and three-quarter parts; and the pillar (*pādapa*) is two and a half parts.
The bedstead (mañca) shall be one-third of the [total] height; the projection of the legs shall be one-third [of that];
the height of the cornice (kapota) shall be one and a quarter parts; and from the upper portion, the [upper] part shall be two parts.
The height of the pedestal (prastara) shall be equal to the height of the neck (kandhara) by means of two parts;
the height of the head (śiras) shall be two and a half parts, and the remaining portion shall be the projection of the head (śirodaya).
Thus the six-tiered [structure] has been described; now the seven-storied one is explained.
That platform which extends from the northern direction to the top pinnacle consists of thirty-six parts.
The *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be two parts including the *saṅghri*, and it may be greater than four and a half parts;
the height of the *prastara* (frieze) is two parts, and the height of the *pāda* (base) is four parts.
The couch is three-quarter parts, while the leg is two and a half parts;
the couch is made with two parts less a quarter, and the leg is three-quarters of a part.
The height of the stone slab (prastara) shall be one and a half parts; the length of the lower floor (antatalā) shall be two parts;
the height of the couch (mañca) shall be one and a quarter parts; and [the height of the upper part] shall be two and a half parts.
The neck should be one part, equal in height to the pigeon-peak;
the head should be two and a half parts, and the remaining portions are considered to be the crest.
This excellent [temple] consists of seven stories; above that, it possesses the proportions of the former [lower part].
On the ground floor, it is fashioned with two parts consisting of the pillar and the entablature (prastara).
In this scripture, the desired number of gate-towers (gopuras) is said to range from twelve to two;
one should divide the components of the gate-tower into four parts.
Beginning from one-eighteenth part, among those, one part shall be nine parts;
it may also be two, three, four, five, or six finger-breadths.
One may increase or decrease [the dimensions] according to the logic previously stated;
when the width is divided into five parts, the extent of the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be three parts.
O lords of sages, the remaining portion is said here to be the wall on the ground of the sky;
Vyāsa is seven parts and four parts, while the inner sanctum (garbha) and the pinnacle (kūṭa) each possess one part.
The length of the interior of the chamber is desired to be five parts of its own width;
in the space between the corner chambers, it should be adorned with lattice windows and the like.
Thus the two-storey [structure] has been described; now the three-storey [structure] is being explained.
In the ninth part of the *tāra*, the inner sanctum (*garbha*) should be one-third; outside of that, [the proportions] follow in sequence.
One should sequentially fashion the house, the courtyard, the veranda, and the doorways;
all parts such as the towers, storehouses, and so forth, should be fashioned as before. (77/55)
In the broad section of the layout, within the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) divided into three parts,
the thickness of the wall is one and a half parts, and the portico (alindaka) is one part.
The *khaṇḍaharmya* (fragmented palace) is formed by one part; the gables, chambers, and so forth are as described previously.
At the front and back, there is a great hall (*mahāśālā*) measuring five parts or six parts.
This [temple] is renowned as having four stories and is beautiful in all its limbs;
in its width, it consists of eleven parts, while the nālī-house occupies three parts.
The thickness of the wall shall be two parts, the portico (alindaka) shall be one part of the void, and the turret (khaṇḍaharmya) shall be one part; all the rest shall be equal.
The five-level [temple] has been fully described; now the six-level is being discussed.
When the width is divided by twelve, the house for the tube (nālī) occupies four parts.
The width of the wall is proclaimed to be two parts, while the door is one part;
the *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion) shall be one part, and everything else is the same as before.
This sixth stage has been declared; now the seventh is being described.
With a width of thirteen parts, the central chamber (garbha) shall occupy one part.
The wall should be two and a half parts; the porch (ālinda) is desired to be one part;
the khaṇḍaharmya here is one part, and the kūṭaśālā and so forth are as before.
The *mahāśālā* is proclaimed to have six parts on its back and front;
the *hastipṛṣṭha* has five parts and is joined with wing-halls (*pakṣaśālā*) and other such features.
This seven-storied gateway (gopura), adorned with various lion-figures, pillars, altars, lattices, and arches, is declared to be suitable for all regions.
The width of the upper door should be one-fifth of the width of the base door; alternatively, it may be four-fifths of that width. (77/66)
The door should be positioned higher and higher, corresponding to the middle, lower, and upper [sections],
and one should apply this principle for each floor in a house with an internal staircase.
On the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha), which has four necks, a flight of stairs is provided;
O masters of the learned, the doorway should resemble a pavilion for the sake of beauty.
The gate-hall (dvāraśālā) is proclaimed to have a form similar to a staff-hall (daṇḍaśālā);
the gate-palace (dvāraprāsāda) is taught to be like the shape of a palace (prāsāda). || 77/69 ||
O best of sages, the gateway-pavilion (dvāra-harmya) should be shaped like a garland;
one should make the final gate-tower (gopura) similar in form to a hall (śālā).
One should construct a gatehouse (gopura) everywhere according to one's capacity, especially [in the center]; it may consist of five parts or other divisions, up to a maximum of thirty-one parts.
Having divided the broad base of the gateway (gopura) into two parts,
one should arrange the divisions by increasing them by half a measure up to the fifteenth part.
O lords of sages, the interior of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be spacious for the sake of beauty and other qualities;
by that same proportional measure, it may extend up to twice the portion of the sky (vyomāṃśa).
One should fashion the inner sanctum (garbhageha) as either square or rectangular; its length above that [width] should be greater by the measure of the door's width.

O best of sages, one should construct the gopura in such a manner that it extends from all sides of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) by increments of one-quarter, starting from half the size of the sanctum.
The best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion the wall extending up to three parts, along with the sky and other elements in great number, as well as the vestibule and the gateway.
The gate-tower (dvāratāra) or the city-gate (gopura) may be constructed according to the measurement of parts (aṃśa);
beginning from three parts, it may extend up to fifteen parts by increments of half a part.
One should apply the proportions here for the purpose of making the door wide,
as well as for the ornamentation of the temple or the ornamentation of the hall.
Or one may construct the entire [temple] at the city gate, according to the various divisions such as the *sañcita* and others,
provided with various *masūraka* ornaments and endowed with various pillars.
It is joined with various types of stone, connected to the necks of the four corners of the altar,
provided with a crest such as a *valabhī*, and endowed with many *stūpis*.

One should construct [the temple] with gabled halls (kūṭa), single-chambered halls (śālā), single-peaked pavilions (ekatuṇḍa), cages (pañjara), and wing-halls (pakṣaśālā), either with dimensions exceeding the proportional parts or with equal proportions.
It was provided with various gates, endowed with a pedestal for the bull,
and further adorned with all the ornaments of the sacred abodes and other decorations.

One should perform this according to the procedure prescribed for the construction of a *khalūrikā* (practice ground), whether it be on the fundamental site, in the sky, on level ground, or on elevated ground. (77/83)

In the cardinal and intermediate directions, that which is desired should be done as before; one should perform the rite for the first brick and the rule for the head-brick according to the procedure prescribed for the temple.
Either something may be in the middle of two, or there may be one among the *stūpikās*;
having fashioned the upper mountain for each individually, one should arrange them in a number of four.
Then, having placed the finial (sthūpikā) above that according to the procedure prescribed for the finial,
one should also [worship] its presiding deities along with the ritual known as Jñāna.
If there are three [principles], they are the three *tattvas*; if four, they are known as the *kalās*. They are devoid of Brahman and lack manifestation, yet they are indeed the cause.
Alternatively, the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta, or those beginning with Nivṛtti, are assigned to the five [faces];
the placement of the six kalās within the cosmic egg is thus proclaimed.
The seven [deities] beginning with Kalā are to be known as the Vidyeśas in the system of eight;
those beginning with Vāmā are in the system of nine; and the Lokapālas are in that which is called the tenfold.
In the Rudra-number [eleven], there are the Rudras; in the Arka-number [twelve], the Ādityas;
and in that which is endowed with four and fifteen [nineteen], the Viśvedevas and the Aśvins are said to reside.
The lunar days (tithis) are said to be the worlds, beginning from Dakṣa and ending in the west;
one should install them in their respective constructed abodes with their own individual name-mantras.
One should perform the installation of the gopura once a pavilion has been constructed in front of it,
either in a fire-pit prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Or, on an altar consisting of nine or a single pit, accompanied by the sprinkling of the auspicious day,
one should place eight jars upon the raised platform of the sacrificial mound.
And in the center and the great directions, one should worship Śānti and the others there with those mantras,
using a hundred or half that number of sacrificial fuels and other offerings.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation and being satisfied, the Guru, having first performed the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and so forth upon the water of five jars, should consecrate [the disciple] while reciting the mantras associated with those [deities].
O best of teachers, this primary ritual action should be performed extensively;
however, in other cases there may be a secondary alternative, or it is proclaimed that [the action] should be extensive.
The Nandī and other [deities] should be positioned facing the gopura on both sides;
in the Niṣkala form, the western door is recommended, while in the Sakala form, the southern door is beneficial.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the gate-towers (gopura), in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
The *Pūrvakāmika* is completed.
